en: Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll One, with Preface, composed by Shi Sengzhao of the Later Qin.
Preface to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*: This work is, in essence, the ultimate exhaustion of the subtle and the perfection of transformation; it is the most exquisite [teaching].

This is its designation. Its purport is profound and mysterious, beyond the measurement of words or symbols; its Way transcends the three voids, beyond the deliberation of the two vehicles; it surpasses the realm of numerical categories and cuts off the sphere of the conceptualizing mind. It is vast and boundless, non-active yet accomplishing all that is to be done; it is such that one knows not how it comes to be so, yet it is able to be so—this is the inconceivable.

Why is this so? For the sagely wisdom is without knowing, yet it illuminates all things; the Dharma-body is without form, yet it responds to all diverse manifestations; the ultimate resonance is without speech, yet profound scriptures are spread far and wide; the dark power is without deliberation, yet its movements coincide with the needs of affairs. Thus, it is able to govern and deliver all quarters, opening up things and accomplishing tasks; it appears beneficially throughout the world while remaining non-active within itself. Yet the deluded, seeing the cause of responsive illumination, call it "wisdom"; observing the manifested forms, they call them the "body"; encountering the profound scriptures, they call them "speech"; and witnessing the shifting changes, they call them "power."
Now, as for the ultimate limit of the Way, how could it be discussed through forms, words, or expedient wisdom within its divine realm?

Nevertheless, sentient beings have long remained in slumber; were it not for speech, they would not be enlightened. The Way does not operate in isolation, but is propagated by means of persons. For this reason, the Tathāgata commissioned Mañjuśrī from a distant region and summoned Vimalakīrti from another land, so that they might assemble at Vaiśālī to propagate this Way together.

What this sutra elucidates is as follows: when encompassing all practices, expedient wisdom is paramount; when establishing the foundation of virtue, the six perfections are the root; when rescuing the ignorant and deluded, compassion is foremost; and when speaking of the ultimate essence, non-duality is the gateway.
All these various accounts are the foundations of the inconceivable;

as for such things as borrowing a seat from the King of Lamps, requesting a meal from the Land of Fragrance, receiving the great trichiliocosm in one's hands, and encompassing the celestial phenomena within a single room—these are the traces of the inconceivable.
However, the profound gate is difficult to open, and the responses of the Sage vary.

It is not through the fundamental that traces can be manifested, nor is it without traces that the fundamental can be revealed. Although the fundamental and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability; therefore, he commanded his attendant to designate this as its name.

The Celestial King of the Great Qin possesses a sagely spirit that transcends the world and a profound mind uniquely awakened; he has spread supreme governance over the myriad affairs of state and propagated the transformation of the Way for a thousand years to come. Whenever he seeks out and contemplates these scriptures, he regards them as the dwelling place for the enshrining of the spirit;

yet he laments that the principles translated by Zhi Qian and Zhu Falan are obstructed by their literary style, and he constantly fears that the profound mystery of the Esoteric Doctrine might fall into decline due to the limitations of the translators.
The destiny of the Northern Heaven has its time for fulfillment.

In the eighth year of Hongshi, under the stellar cycle of Chunchu (the Bird’s Fire), he commissioned the Great General, Duke of Changshan, and the Right General, Marquis of Ancheng, along with one thousand two hundred śramaṇas of the exegetical school, to invite Dharma Master Kumārajīva at the Great Monastery in Chang’an to retranslate the authentic text.

Kumārajīva, possessing a capacity that transcended the world, settled his mind in the realm of ultimate reality; having mastered the "center within the circle" (the Middle Way), he was also adept at local dialects. At times, he would hold the Sanskrit manuscript in hand while orally translating it himself. Monastics and laypeople alike were filled with devotion, repeating each word three times over. He refined and investigated with meticulous care, striving to preserve the sacred intent of the original. His prose was concise yet profound, and its meaning subtle yet manifest; thus, words that were previously obscure and distant became clearly evident through him.

In my ignorance and limited capacity, I was permitted to listen in the assembly; though my thoughts lack the depth to penetrate the profound mysteries, I have roughly grasped the meaning of the text. I have thus composed these annotations according to what I heard, merely recording the perfected words as they were spoken rather than creating anything new of my own, so that gentlemen of the future may hear them together with me, though separated by time.
Regarding "The Teachings of Vimalakīrti," Kumārajīva said:
"Vimalakīrti is the Chinese term for 'Pure Name' (Jingming), and he was one of the five hundred youths."

Having come from the Land of Wondrous Joy to travel through this realm, he has now completed what was to be done and is about to return to his native land. Desiring to manifest his pure virtue to benefit all living beings, he realized that the manifestation of such traces to awaken the world must necessarily have its cause; therefore, he commanded those of like mind to go to the Buddha while he alone did not go.
That he alone did not practice the Dharma was because we knew his illness. How do we know this?
Five hundred like-minded companions together followed the Great Way; in advancing in virtue and cultivating goodness, they were invariably united in both movement and stillness.
The assembly for purifying the land is among the greatest of karmic undertakings; that it was not held concurrently with others clearly indicates that there was illness.
Because there was illness, there was an assembly for inquiring after one's health.
The assembly for inquiring after the illness originated from the gathering at the Pure Land, and the gathering at the Pure Land resulted from the skillful means of Vimalakīrti.
Thus, the very foundation upon which this sutra begins and ends truly resides therein.

If one observes it from the perspective of its own exposition, the various sages share equal merit; yet if one traces it back to its origin, that merit derives from Vimalakīrti. Since this identifies its source, it is called "The Teaching of Vimalakīrti."
Sengzhao said:
Vimalakīrti—whose name means "Pure Name" (Jingming) in the language of Qin—is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body.

His expedient path is boundless, and his traces of concealment and manifestation differ. He left that Land of Wondrous Joy to appear here in this Saha World, thereby harmonizing with the light of worldly dust while following the Way of the Teachings. He constantly travels together with Ratnākara as a companion in the city of the Dharma.
Once his teaching mission was concluded and he was about to return to Abhirati, he intended to manifest his divine virtues to propagate the Tathāgata’s path of inconceivable liberation.

He then commanded Ratnākara to go alone to Śākyamuni while he himself remained behind to manifest illness; thus, the occasion for inquiring after his illness arose and the beginning of these subtle words was established. Since this sublime proclamation originated with him, it is said that he spoke them.
Zhu Daosheng said:
"Vimalakīrti" means "Stainless Fame" (Wugoucheng) in this language.

He concealed his traces within the five desires yet remained transcendent and untainted; as his pure reputation spread far and wide, he was given this title. Those who value names for their correspondence with reality will surely hold his teachings in high esteem.

This explains the fundamental to manifest the reality; if one values this, one will ultimately attain what is sought. Because of this close connection, there is that which surpasses the words of the Sage.
The Sūtra.
Zhaò said:
"Sūtra" means "constant.

Although the past and present differ, the Way of Awakening does not change; it cannot be thwarted by the various heterodoxies, nor can it be altered by the multitude of sages. Therefore, it is called "constant."
It is called "Inconceivable Liberation.
Kumārajīva said:

It is also called *samādhi* and also called "supernatural power" (*ṛddhipāda*). Because it can cause the long and short to change their dimensions, or allow the large and small to contain one another, manifesting transformations according to one's will and possessing mastery over all phenomena with unimpeded liberation, it is therefore called "liberation."
The capable ones can indeed do so, yet sentient beings do not know how they do it; therefore, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
It is also said that the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas respond in accordance with thoughts as they arise, without needing to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) before being able to act.
The mind attains mastery and is no longer bound by incapacity; therefore, it is called "liberation.

If one were to directly clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it would contradict habitual practice and provide no basis for conviction. Therefore, one manifests that objects transform according to the mind to demonstrate that objects have no fixed nature. Since objects have no fixed nature, their nature is empty.
Because the Bodhisattva attains this lack of fixedness, he causes all things to revolve according to his mind; thus, the inconceivable is a clear proof of emptiness.
To manifest the fundamental principle of the school, it is taken as the title of this scripture.
Sengzhao said:
"Subtle, remote, profound, and deep—it cannot be fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles; this is 'inconceivability' (acintya).
Exercising mastery without obstruction, such that worldly entanglements cannot constrain it—this is 'liberation' (vimokṣa)."

This sutra begins with the Pure Land and concludes with the Dharma-offering; although what is elucidated therein varies, its inconceivable liberation is one and the same, and thus it is given this general title.
The former titles the sutra after a person's name, while this one titles the sutra after the Dharma.
To title a sutra after the Dharma is to manifest its ultimate purpose;
to title a sutra after a person is to propagate the Way by means of that individual.
Daosheng said:
"The designation 'Stainless' (Vimala) may refer merely to outward traces; since this is not necessarily the case regarding the mind, he further speaks of its liberation as yet another name."
That which is inconceivable is of two kinds:
first, the emptiness of principle, which cannot be grasped by deluded sentiments;
second, the marvelous and supernatural, which cannot be measured by shallow understanding.
If one realizes the principle of emptiness, then one is liberated from the delusions of conceptual thought.
Once such delusions are shed, one's actions become unfathomable.
Since Vimalakīrti now manifests wonders in both movement and stillness, he must have certainly been liberated from all delusions.

Liberation from delusion resides in the realization of emptiness; it is taught that emptiness is that which is to be realized. Thus, the name "Stainless" (Amala) is not merely a designation but possesses empirical verification.
When a name is indeed verified by reality, one's pursuit of it becomes ever more profound.
When one reaches those who seek [the Way], what worry is there that they will not attain awakening?
Chapter One: On the Buddha-land (Buddhakṣetra). Master Shi said:
Since the beginning and end of this sutra depend upon the Pure Land, the title "On the Buddha-land" is placed at the head of the fascicle.
"So it is. Zhao said:
" 'So it is' (rúshì) is a phrase expressing faithful compliance."
Now, when there is faith, the principles of what is spoken flow smoothly; when they flow smoothly, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
Whether the scriptures are extensive or concise, they are not transmitted without faith; therefore, I have set forth these words accordingly.
"I heard.
Kumārajīva said:
"If you had not said 'I heard,' then it would have been as if the Dharma were my own."
If I possess a fixed doctrine, my mind will have attachments; where the mind has attachments, contention and turmoil will inevitably arise.
If one says, "I have heard," then I have no fixed doctrine and nothing to which I am attached; gain and loss, right and wrong, all return to what has been heard.
Since I have no attachment and they have no contention, when there is neither attachment nor contention, from what cause could dispute arise?
Furthermore, it is said that there are two kinds of craving:
first, craving for the five sensory desires; [the second is craving for existence].
2. Attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
Non-Buddhist renunciants are able to sever attachment to sensual desires but cannot sever attachment to dharmas; therefore, their minds harbor attachments.
Disciples of the Buddha eliminate both types of attachment; once attachment to dharmas is exhausted, all contentious clinging completely ceases.
The opening phrase "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) exists for this purpose.
Zhaodao said:
Those who produced the scriptures [used this] to clarify that they personally received the Sage’s instructions, ensuring there was no error of hearsay.
At one time,
Kumārajīva said:
"It is time to expound the sutra."
Zhaò said:
"This is the time when the Dharma King inaugurates his auspicious reign and gathers [his followers].
The Buddha was in Vaiśālī."
Kumārajīva said:
"It is based on the region where the Buddha resided.
'Vi' refers to the suitability of the land for growing rice."
Vaiśālī means "Extensive Adornment," for its ground is level, vast, and magnificent.
Zhaò says:
Vaiśālī is the name of a kingdom; in the language of Qin (Chinese), it means "Extensive Adornment."
The land was level, vast, and magnificent; it was named for these qualities.
There was an Āmra grove.
Kumārajīva said:
The āmra tree bears fruit that resembles a peach but is not a peach.
Zhaò says:
Āmra is the name of a fruit-bearing tree; its fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach.
The aforementioned reference to the Nāga clan is found in another sutra.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus.
Zhaò said:

"Bhikṣu" is, in the language of Qin, sometimes called "Pure Beggar for Alms," sometimes called "Destroyer of Afflictions," sometimes called "Pure Upholder of Precepts," and sometimes called "One Capable of Terrifying Māra.
In India, a single term encompasses these four meanings; since there is no single term in the language of Qin to translate it, the meaning-based name has been retained.
Another version states: "The great assembly of bhikṣus numbered eight thousand. Kumārajīva said:
"These are the people who heard the sutra together.
He cites these three matters—time, place, and persons—to authenticate what was heard."
*Mahā* means "great" in the language of Qin; it also means "superior" and "abundant.
Because he is the most supreme among all beings and is venerated by both devas and humans, he is called "Great."
Because he is able to prevail over ninety-six kinds of disputations, he is called "Victorious.
Because their number is eight thousand, they are called "many.
Bhikṣu: in the language of Qin, this means "Destroyer of Afflictions," and it also means "Almsman."
Because they eliminate the five kinds of wrong livelihoods while sustaining the Dharma-body, they are called "alms-seekers" (bhikṣu).
As for why the bhikṣu and the bodhisattva are not counted together: it is because all bhikṣus are exclusively physical bodies, whereas most bodhisattvas are Dharma-bodies; thus, their bodies differ.
If a bodhisattva in a physical body has not yet attained the correct position of realization, their mind remains distinct [from that of an arhat];
for these two reasons, it is improper to speak of them as being the same as a bhikṣu.

The reason why Arhats are mentioned first and Bodhisattvas later is that people assume Bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and their wisdom is not yet complete, whereas Arhats have already exhausted the three outflows and achieved perfection in wisdom; this sequence is merely established according to what people infer based on their own perspectives.
There were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas.
Zhaò says:
"Bodhisattva" is the correct pronunciation for *bodhisattva*.
*Bodhi* is a name for the Buddha-way.
*Sattva*, in the language of Qin, means "a being of great mind.
One who possesses a great mind and enters the Buddha-way is called a *bodhisattva*.
There is no corresponding translation in the *Wu zhengming* (The Correct Names).
An alternative version states: "Thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained great supernatural powers.

Kumārajīva remarked: "There are generally three kinds of mahāsattvas: first, those who have left the household life; second, those who remain in the household life; and third, those who have come from other directions."
Furthermore, there are two types of bodies: first, the body of karmic bonds; second, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Among these, the Bodhisattva is for the most part the Dharma-body; nevertheless, his manifested form responds to conditions and shares the same traces as other beings. Because beings may perceive him as their equal and thus give rise to inferior conceptions, he first cites a general enumeration and only then proceeds to describe his virtues.

The Sanskrit text states: "The fundamental practices of supernormal powers and wisdom have already been performed. The various dharmas of the six perfections are the causes of supernormal powers and wisdom; these causes of supernormal powers and wisdom are precisely what is meant by "fundamental practices" (pūrvayoga).
He was known by all. Zhaò said:
"When a Great Being dwells in the world, it is like the sun and moon rising in the sky; among those with eyes, who would not know and recognize him?"
Another edition reads "revered and admired by all," but Kumārajīva said:

"The Sanskrit original says 'one of great knowledge and wide learning. Because his virtues manifest in accordance with the times, all people know him; because all people know him, those who revere him are many—this is the meaning that emerges [from the original]."
The fundamental practices of great wisdom are all fully accomplished.
Zhaò says:
"Great wisdom" refers to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
This wisdom takes the six perfections, the six supernormal powers, and various practices as its foundation;
all great beings have already perfected these foundational practices, which are established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas.
Kumārajīva said:
"The 'establishment through the Buddha's majestic spiritual power' refers to what the Buddha has in mind.
That which is protected by the Buddha's intention cannot be thwarted or destroyed; it is just as fish eggs, when protected by the mother, are certain to reach fruition."
Zhaò said:
"The moisture of Heaven is impartial, yet it does not nourish withered wood;
though the Buddha's majesty is universal, it does not take root where there is no foundation."
"Those who establish themselves in this way will surely have deep roots in the Way.
They shall protect the city of the Dharma and uphold the True Dharma.
Kumārajīva said:
The "Dharma-city" refers to the Dharma of true reality (*dharmatā*).
It is called "protection" because it causes sentient beings to have no divergent views.
Furthermore, all sūtras and teachings are termed the "Dharma-city," as they are upheld, proclaimed, and disseminated so that they shall not be destroyed.
There are those capable of upholding the True Dharma, and he likewise protects them as well.
Zhaò says:
"Externally, he acts as a city wall for the protection of the Dharma; internally, he possesses the firmness of receiving and upholding it."
He is able to roar the lion’s roar.
Zhaò says:
"The lion’s roar is the sound of fearlessness."
In all that he speaks, he does not fear the various heterodoxies and false teachings; his discourse is like the lion’s roar, by which all other beasts are cowed.
The lion’s roar refers to the beautiful exposition of the Dharma.
"His fame resounds throughout the ten directions.
Kumārajīva said:

"When it is said that he is 'widely known and well-acquainted,' it means that his traces appear in two regions and his transformation extends through a single country; thus all beings receive his bounty and recognize him as such."
The present statement, "renown throughout the ten directions," means that the fragrance of the Way spreads far and wide, and his name is heard everywhere.
Zhaò says:
When one's practice fills the world, there is no place where its reputation is not universal.
The people did not invite him as a friend, yet he remained with them in peace.

Kumārajīva said: "There are two kinds of benefit: that of this life and that of future lives. Because worldly matters involve seeking mutual profit, one acts only after being invited; because the Sage responds out of compassion, he goes without being petitioned. Wherever he goes, he necessarily brings intimacy; where there is intimacy, he necessarily provides protection. Therefore it is said: 'He remains in peace as a friend who was not invited.'"
Zhaor said:
"A true friend does not wait to be invited, just as a compassionate mother hastens to her infant.
Such a person can cause the Three Jewels to flourish and ensure they are never severed."
Sengzhao said:
"To continue the lineage of the Buddha causes the Three Jewels to flourish.
An alternative version states: "To cause the Three Jewels to flourish so that they may not be severed. Kumārajīva said:

This does not merely refer to manifesting the Three Jewels and proclaiming the circulation of the sutras and the Dharma; it means that one can accumulate goodness and build up merit to personally attain Buddhahood.
Once Buddhahood is attained, there is the Dharma, and with the Dharma, there is the Sangha; the meritorious work of ensuring these do not cease shall continue into future kalpas.
If it is said now that [the lineage] shall not be severed, then one must certainly be capable of this.

Furthermore, within this interval, one practices it oneself and transforms others; once I have transformed others and those others also transform beings, both beings and self will achieve fulfillment, and the Three Jewels will flourish ever more.
Because sentient beings are inexhaustible, the Three Jewels likewise shall never cease.
He subdued the enmity of Māra and restrained the various non-Buddhists.
Kumārajīva said:
Regarding the Māras, there are four Māras.
Because one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and afflictions are forever severed, one subdues the Māra of desire (*kleśamāra*).
Because one attains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), one no longer obtains a [physical] body; thus, one subdues the Māra of the body (*skandhamāra*).
Without a body, there is no death; thus, he subdues the Māra of Death.
Without the three Māras, Pāpīyān finds no opportunity; thus, he subdues the Māra of Heaven.
He subdues non-Buddhists, as when he caused Śāriputra to debate with a non-Buddhist for seven days and seven nights before finally achieving victory.
This is of that same category. Zao says:
"Māra" refers to the four Māras.
"Non-Buddhists (tīrthika) refers to the ninety-six kinds of paths.
[He] has already completely purified them and is forever free from the hindrances and entanglements.
Kumārajīva said:
There are three kinds of freedom from the entanglements of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-bandhana*): first, when the precepts are pure, the entanglements of the hindrances do not arise;
second, through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), they are severed, yet because they are not yet exhausted, their non-arising at that time is also termed "freedom";
third, within this [supramundane state], one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is freedom through total extinction.
Zhaò says: "The 'five' refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
The 'entanglements' (*paryavasthāna*) refer to the ten entanglements, though there are also immeasurable entanglements."
When the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are entirely purified, then the hindrances and entanglements cannot burden one.
The mind constantly dwells in unimpeded liberation.
Kumārajīva said:
Inconceivable liberation is precisely of this nature.
Because there is no obstruction regarding phenomena, it is called "unobstructed"; because it is unobstructed, it is liberation.

Whether regarding a single phenomenon up to hundreds of thousands, or from a single land up to lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one attains thorough penetration and sovereign mastery within them without obstruction.
It is not yet as unimpeded in all respects as that of the Buddha.
Zhaò says:
"This liberation is that which is attained at the seventh stage."
Having attained this liberation, one penetrates all phenomena without obstruction; therefore, the mind dwells in constant tranquility.
Mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, and eloquence remain uninterrupted.
Zhaò says: "Nian" (念) means right mindfulness;
"ding" (定) means right concentration.
Dhāraṇī means maintaining the good so that it is not lost and maintaining the evil so that it does not arise.
To maintain without any leakage or forgetting is called dhāraṇī.
There are two kinds of maintenance: maintenance associated with the mind and maintenance dissociated from the mind.
" Eloquence" refers to the seven forms of eloquence.
These four are the essential requisites of a Mahāsattva; therefore, they are never interrupted.
An alternative version reads: "His mindfulness is not cut off even for a moment, up until the accomplishment of eloquence. Kumārajīva said:
"Mindfulness" refers to mindfulness of the unsurpassed path.
"Uninterrupted" means not being cut off midway.
The meaning of "uninterrupted" extends throughout and permeates the three subsequent dharmas.

When Bodhisattvas attain these four dharmas, they enter deeply and become firm; their practice continues without loss throughout successive lives, becoming ever more radiant through the kalpas. Therefore, it is said that they are "uninterrupted.
They are fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means.

Kumārajīva said: "The preceding passage speaks of the uninterrupted mindfulness of the Way; only after the mindfulness of the Way is uninterrupted can one fully practice the six perfections. Once the six perfections are complete, one's own task is finished. When one's own task is finished, one uses skillful means to deliver others. There is nothing more vast for delivering others than supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); once these are possessed, one transforms sentient beings."
The sequence is as described later in the "Pure Land" chapter.
Zhaò says:
"Complete" refers to the practice of signlessness (*animitta*).
From the seventh stage upward, the mind and wisdom are quiescent; because the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no virtue that is not practiced.
Thus, while generosity reaches its ultimate in generosity, it is never truly giving; while precepts reach their ultimate in precepts, they are never truly observing them.
When the seven virtues and extraordinary merits possess no difference in their characteristics, they are termed "complete.
Expedient means (*upāya*) is simply a distinct function of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Wisdom penetrates the profound and exhausts the subtle, definitively determining the characteristics of phenomena; to be without knowing yet without not knowing is called wisdom.

Although one has realized the characteristics of dharmas, one is able to refrain from realizing [nirvana]; dwelling in existence without losing non-existence, and being in non-existence without abandoning existence, one merges with emptiness while preserving virtue, thereby providing succor to both sides—hence it is called "skillful means" (upāya).
He attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas through non-apprehension.
Kumārajīva said:

"Since the beginning of consciousness, I have never seen a dharma; only now have I first attained the ability to believe and accept it. To endure without fear and to abide peacefully without wavering—therefore, it is called 'patience' (kṣānti)."
Zhaò says:
"Kṣānti (patience/endurance) is precisely the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because it is able to endure and accept the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of reality, it is named 'kṣānti'."

Having attained this patience, one neither grasps nor acquires anything regarding phenomena, and the characteristics of the mind are forever extinguished; therefore, it is called the "patience of non-attainment and non-arising.
One is thus able to accord with and turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Zhaò said:
"The Way of non-arising has neither gain nor loss; it does not regress.
Its flowing and evolving are perfectly pervasive and are not restricted to a single person; this is the wheel."
Since the Buddhas have turned this wheel, the great beings (mahāsattvas) are likewise able to turn it in accordance with them.
An alternative version states, "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma" (*avaivartika-dharmacakra*). Kumārajīva said:
"The wheel of Dharma is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
One bestows an object by means of a wheel; because the recipient obtains this wheel, it is called "turning.
Because the giver attains it and does not lose it, it is called "non-retrogression.
That one's own vehicle turns forward and progresses is also termed "turning."
He skillfully understands the characteristics of dharmas and knows the faculties of sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
There are no distinct characteristics among all dharmas that he does not understand, and there are no diverse faculties among the multitude of living beings that he does not know.
Regarding the phrase "covering the great assembly," Kumārajīva said:
"The Sanskrit original says 'the assembly cannot be covered.'"
The multitude cannot obscure it; this clarifies its transcendence.
To say now that it "overshadows the multitude" is to say the same thing.
It has attained fearlessness.
Kumārajīva said:
"Bodhisattvas possess their own four fearlessnesses; these are not the fearlessnesses of a Buddha.
Fear arises from a sense of insufficiency; because there is no insufficiency, there is no fear."
To be able to speak but unable to practice is also a cause for fear; now, because one can both speak and practice, there is no fear.
To be able to speak and able to practice is what is called the Dharma.

Zhaò says: Bodhisattvas have four distinct forms of fearlessness: first, attaining the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining; second, knowing the faculties of sentient beings; third, seeing no one capable of challenging them such that they would be unable to answer; and fourth, being able to answer according to questions and skillfully resolving the doubts of the multitude.
Possessing these four virtues, he is thus able to outshine the great assembly.
Since the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths each have their own followers, the term "various" (*zhū*) is used.
Having cultivated his mind through merit and wisdom, his physical form is adorned with the primary marks and secondary signs, making his appearance supreme.
Kumārajīva said:
"One who is fully endowed with these virtues is therefore without fear.
Sengzhao said:

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who sat encircling him as he preached the Dharma. At that time, there was a son of a householder in the city of Vaiśālī named Ratnākara. Zao said:

Now, as for my coming alone with the villagers to visit the Buddha, it was intended to provide the occasion for inquiring after his illness and to open the gateway to this scripture.

Together with five hundred sons of elders, they each brought a parasol made of the seven precious gems to the place where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves at his feet and each offered their parasol as a collective供养 (offering) to the Buddha.

Kumārajīva said:

they then see and hear all the Buddhas therein preaching the Dharma.
Zhaò said:
"Since the divine transformations of the merging canopy have already been seen and are unfathomable;

and now, within it, the lands of the ten directions and the various Buddhas preaching the Dharma appear, such that the entire assembly in this Sahā world perceives and hears them from afar—this is even more rare."
The Dharma-King’s power of the Dharma surpasses that of all living beings; he constantly bestows the wealth of the Dharma upon all.
ZHAO said:
A secular king uses secular power to overcome his subjects, and thus his grace can extend throughout a single nation.
The Dharma King transcends all by means of the power of the Dharma; thus, he is able to provide spiritual succor to boundless realms.
He is able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena.
Zhaò says:
One is able to skillfully discern the distinct characteristics of all phenomena.
From this point down to the phrase "karma does not perish," the text entirely extols the gift of Dharma.
One remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Sengzhao said:
"The 'Ultimate Truth' (paramārtha) refers to the meaning of the single characteristic (ekalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena.
Although one distinguishes the diverse characteristics of phenomena, this does not contradict their single characteristic; this is the unsurpassed path of the Dharma King."
"Movement" means to deviate.
Having already attained mastery over all phenomena, one therefore bows one's head to this Dharma King.
Zhaò says:
A worldly king exercises sovereignty over his subjects; a Dharma-king exercises sovereignty over the Dharma. The Dharma has no fixed characteristic;

it is distinguished according to what is appropriate. For those who prefer diversity, he distinguishes diversity without contradicting unity; for those who prefer unity, he distinguishes unity without contradicting diversity. Though diversity and unity are distinguished separately, both accord with the characteristics of the Dharma; thus, he attains mastery.
The teaching of the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent.
Zhaò says:
If one wishes to say it exists, existence does not arise of itself.
If one wishes to say it is non-existent, its form manifests as soon as conditions converge.
That the manifestation of form is not called "non-existence" does not mean it is "existence," for it is neither self-originated nor is it called existence.
Furthermore, because there is existence, there is non-existence; if there were no existence, what would there be that is non-existent?
Because there is existence, there is existence; if there were no non-existence, what would exist?
Thus, that which exists inherently does not truly exist, and that which is non-existent inherently does not truly not exist—this is the correct teaching of the Dharma King.
"Because of causes and conditions, all phenomena arise.
Zhaò said:
"Existence does not arise from conditions, nor does non-existence arise from conditions; because phenomena are neither existent nor nonexistent, they arise through causes and conditions."
The treatise says:
Because dharmas arise from conditions, they do not exist; because they arise dependently, they are not non-existent.
There is no self, no agent, and no experiencer.
Sengzhao said:
"All phenomena arise solely from conditions; there is no separate, true sovereign entity, and therefore there is no self.
It is precisely because of the existence of a self that one is able to create good and evil, and receive the laws of calamity and fortune."
Since there is no self, there is neither an agent nor a recipient [of karma].
Nevertheless, the karma of good and evil does not perish.
Zhaò said:
If there were no creator and no experiencer, then performing good deeds to obtain merit or committing evil acts to incur calamity would not be possible.

Yet, the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings are transmitted from one to another, giving rise to beauty and foulness; the way of retribution follows in a continuous chain, just as sound harmonizes with its echo and a straight form produces a straight shadow. This is a natural principle that does not deviate by even a hair’s breadth—so why further rely upon a permanent self to preside over it?
"At the very beginning, beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power.
Zhaodao said:
"How could the armies of Māra possibly oppose that which is constrained by the power of the Way?"
From this point down to the "Ocean of Rituals," he praises the merits of the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of enlightenment.
He attained the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta-nirodha*).
Kumārajīva said:
The Sanskrit text says, "Nirvāṇa-ambrosia.
Nirvāṇa-ambrosia is precisely the Dharma of the true mark (dharmatā).
Thus, the Way of Awakening is accomplished.
Sengzhao said:
"The Way of Great Enlightenment is quiescent extinction and signless; its supreme flavor harmonizes with the spirit and is like ambrosia.

At the Bodhi tree, he first subdued external demons, and thereafter perfected the Way of Great Enlightenment—quiescent extinction and ambrosia—whereby the internal demons of habitual tendencies were forever extinguished."
"Since there is already no mind or intention," Kumārajīva said,
"there is no separate intention."
"Without feeling, perception, or mental formations.
Kumārajīva said:
"Without feeling, perception, or mental formations."
Zhaò said: What is the mind?
It arises because of defilement.
What is it that receives? It is suffering and pleasure that constitute conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
The Perfected Person merges with the Truth and abides in quiescence; their breast is empty and void. Although they reflect all phenomena simultaneously, the mind has never possessed anything.
Suffering and pleasure are mere pathways, yet they are not to be grasped; when self and objects are eternally quiescent, how could the mind possibly experience them?
As for "grasping," it refers to the three types of sensation: the sensation of suffering, the sensation of pleasure, and the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
"And he completely subdues all non-Buddhists.
Zhaò says:
"When the mind is without intent to subdue things, there are no things that are not subdued."
"He turned the Wheel of Dharma three times throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Zhaò said:
"This refers to his initial turning of the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times for Kauṇḍinya and others at the Deer Park throughout the great trichiliocosm."
That wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure.
Zao said:
"The Wheel of Dharma is eternally pure, like empty space."
Although the ancient and the modern differ and times change while customs shift, the sages have transmitted one another so that their Way remains unaltered.
That celestial beings and humans attain the Way serves as its testimony.
Kumārajīva said:
"This proves that the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma.
Zhaò said:
When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, the five disciples including Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devas attained the Way; this is the clear evidence of eternal purity.
Thus, the Three Jewels appeared in the world.
Sengzhao said:
"Once the realization of the Way is accomplished, there is the Jewel of the Buddha;
once the Wheel of Dharma has been turned, there is the Jewel of the Dharma."
The five men who left the household life and attained the Way constitute the Jewel of the Sangha;
thus we speak of its beginning.
By means of this wondrous Dharma, one delivers all living beings; once received, there is no regression, and one remains eternally tranquil.
Sengzhao said:

"Among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths, even the superior ones can sever the fetters and be reborn in the formless heavens; however, because their path is not true, they will inevitably fall back into the three miserable realms."

The Buddha delivers sentient beings of the three vehicles by means of the wondrous Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; there are none who, having received it, fall back again into birth and death. Therefore, it is said that once received, one does not regress, and having forever completed the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), one is eternally tranquil.
"The Great King of Physicians who delivers [beings] from old age, sickness, and death.
Zhaò says:
"Birth, old age, sickness, and death are among the most grievous of afflictions; because he rescues [beings] with the medicine of the Dharma, he is the preeminent King of Physicians."
"One should pay homage to the boundless ocean of Dharma-virtue.
Zhaò said:
"The wheel of Dharma is profound and vast, difficult to fathom; the flow and moisture of the ocean of Dharma are limitless; therefore, its virtue is boundless."
Unmoved by defamation or praise, like Mount Sumeru.
Zhaò says:
The winds of the eight worldly dharmas—gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and ridicule, suffering and pleasure—cannot move the Tathāgata, just as the four winds cannot shake Mount Sumeru.
Regarding good and evil alike, one maintains loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Zao said:
"One does not grieve when a hand is severed, nor does one rejoice when a hand is offered; for good and evil belong to others, while the covering of loving-kindness remains non-dual."
The mental activity is equal and impartial like empty space.
Zhaò says:
"Now, where there is mind, there is limitation; where there is limitation, there is no universality."
Because the Sage’s mind is no-mind, it is as equal as empty space.
Who, upon hearing of the "Jewel of Humanity," would not reverently receive it?
Zhaò said:
Among the gods he is a treasure of the heavens; among humans he is a treasure of humanity.
That he is a treasure for both gods and humans—how could this be something achieved by gods or humans alone?
Therefore, there is nothing that all beings do not reverently receive from him.
"Now I offer this humble parasol to the World-Honored One.
Kumārajīva said:
"I rejoice that what I have offered was small, yet I behold such a great transformation."
Zhaò said: "Wei" means small.

Within this [smallness], he manifests my three-thousandfold world system, the palaces where the devas, nāgas, and spirits dwell, as well as those of the gandharvas and yakṣas; all that exists in the world is seen, for the One of Ten Powers compassionately manifests these transformations.
Sengzhao said:
"That which is venerated is most subtle, yet that which is perceived is most vast; this is the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s compassion.
The 'Ten Powers' (daśabala) is merely another designation for the Tathāgata; because he is fully endowed with these ten powers, they are used as his name."
Apart from these ten titles, all other designations are merely of this same class.
When the multitude beholds such rare wonders, they all praise the Buddha; now I prostrate before the Honored One of the Three Realms.
Zhaò said:
Beholding the auspicious omen within the canopy:
the Great Sage, the Dharma King to whom all turn;
those who contemplate the Buddha with a pure mind are without exception filled with joy.
Each person sees the World-Honored One before them.
Zhaò said:
"The Dharma-body responds universally and perfectly, just as when the single moon rises in the sky, its reflection appears in a hundred bodies of water."
This is the supernatural power that is not shared with others. Zhaò says:
"It is not shared with those of the Two Vehicles."

The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind; all say that the World-Honored One speaks in their own language—this is a supernatural power, a unique quality not shared by others.
Sengzhao said:
"The secret mouth has but a single sound, yet beings of different species understand it differently.

When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each comprehend it according to their own capacity; they all universally receive and practice it to obtain its benefits. This is the extraordinary dharma of his supernatural power."
Sengzhao said:

"The Buddha preaches a single Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each receive and understand it according to their own inclinations. Those who favor giving hear teachings on giving; those who favor morality hear teachings on morality. Each receives differently, practices differently, and attains their respective benefits."
Just as a single sound varies according to its recipient, so too does this single Dharma vary according to its recipient.
When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, some feel fear, some rejoice, some develop weary detachment, and some sever their doubts; such is his inconceivable, unique spiritual power.
Zhaò said:

"When sentient beings hear of the retribution of suffering, they feel fear; when they hear of the wondrous fruit, they rejoice; when they hear of impurity, they feel weary detachment; and when they hear of the characteristics of dharmas, their doubts are severed."
I do not know what is being expounded by this single sound that causes ordinary beings to feel both joy and fear; how could this possibly be shared by those of the Two Vehicles?
I prostrate to the One of Ten Powers, the Greatly Diligent.
Zhaò says:
From here on, each [phrase] praises his virtue and pays him homage.
"I bow my head" refers to having already attained the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Zhaò said:
"This refers to the four fearlessnesses.
I prostrate myself before those who abide in the unshared dharmas."
Sengzhao said:
These are the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
I bow my head to all the Great Teachers; I bow my head to those who can sever the bonds of all fetters; I bow my head to those who have already reached the other shore.
Sengzhao said:
"The 'other shore' refers to the shore of Nirvana.
How could that Nirvana possess literal cliffs or shores? It is because we are different from it that we metaphorically borrow the term 'we' to refer to it."
I prostrate to the one who can deliver all the worlds; I prostrate to the one who has forever left the path of birth and death, fully knowing the signs of the coming and going of sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"He fully knows how the forms of sentient beings travel back and forth among the six realms of existence, and how their minds gallop toward what is right and wrong."
One who is skillful regarding all phenomena attains liberation.
Zhaò said:
"Because I am defiled by all phenomena, all phenomena bind me."
When my mind is unstained, then all myriad fetters are liberated.
Unattached to the world like a lotus flower, I constantly and skillfully enter the practice of emptiness and stillness.
Zhaò said:
Entering and exiting with mastery yet not deviating from stillness, he thus constantly enters skillfully.
He penetrates the characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction.
Zhaò said:
The myriad dharmas are profound and mysterious; who can know their limits?
Only the Buddha is unimpeded, and thus alone is called "Attained.
I prostrate to the one who is like space, having no dependence.
Zhaò said:
"The Sage’s mind has no dwelling place, just as space has no support.
At that time, after the elder’s son Ratnākara had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One!
These five hundred sons of elders have all already resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they wish to hear about attaining the purity of a Buddha-land.
Sengzhao said:
"Anuttara" means "unsurpassed" in the language of Qin;
"samyak-saṃbodhi" means "right and universal knowledge" in the language of Qin.
The Way is nothing greater than this; it is unsurpassed.
Its Way is true and correct, such that there is no dharma it does not know—this is "Right Universal Knowledge" (samyak-saṃbodhi).

Although these sons of noble families have long since resolved upon the Unsurpassed Mind, they have not yet cultivated the Pure Land. Therefore, as Ratnakūṭa and the others all arrived together, the Tathāgata manifested the canopy to stimulate their nascent potential.

Having already seen within the canopies the various excellent and distinct features of the buddha-fields of all the Buddhas, and with my mind set upon reverently practicing them, I therefore wish to hear about the specific excellences of the pure lands attained by the Buddhas.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the practices for purifying the buddha-fields of all bodhisattvas.
Sengzhao said:
"As for the reason why a field is pure, how could it be achieved through mere technical embellishments?"
Purification must necessarily arise from practice; therefore, I request that you explain practice.

Since all practice must reside within the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*), this question of the Bodhisattva is precisely the subtle purport of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the canopy and the fundamental intent behind the arrival of Ratnākara.
An alternative version states: "The Practice of Purifying the Buddha-land. Kumārajīva remarked:
"In the Sanskrit original, it says 'the characteristics of purity.
Since the subsequent passage speaks of sentient beings as being the Buddha-land, these characteristics are manifesting now, so that the events shall correspond to them later."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Ratnākara!
You are indeed able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the practice for purifying the buddha-field for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Thereupon, Ratnākara and the five hundred sons of the elders received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"Baoji! The various classes of sentient beings are the buddha-field of a bodhisattva."
Kumārajīva said:
"Ratnakūṭa asked about the characteristics of the Pure Land; therefore, I answered with its pure characteristics.
These pure characteristics are precisely the causes and conditions for the Pure Land, and there are three matters regarding these causes and conditions."
First, the merit of bodhisattvas; second, sentient beings; and third, the merit of sentient beings.
When these three causes are purified, one attains a pure land.
What is now referred to as "sentient beings" is a case of speaking of the effect within the cause.
In the subsequent explanation of the meaning, these three causes and conditions are fully present.
Zhaò said:
"The Perfected Person is empty and void, without form; yet they take shape in response to things."
Since even physical forms lack a permanent essence, how much more so can the lands of a realm possess constancy?

For sentient beings are manifold and their karmic actions differ; as these diverse transformations and distinct influences result in varying retributions, the pure are met with jewels and gems, while the defiled are met with sand and pebbles.
Beauty and ugliness originate from others; for me, they have no fixed nature. That land which is without fixed nature is called the true land.
Thus, the purity or defilement of a land depends upon sentient beings; therefore, it is said that the categories of sentient beings constitute the Buddha-land of a Bodhisattva.
If some were to claim that the purity or defilement of a land depends upon sentient beings, then that would be a land of karmic retribution for sentient beings, not the land of the Tathāgata.
This is likely because they have not yet understood the distinct nature of lands of retribution.
Let me attempt to discuss this.
Now, the Pure Land cultivated by the Tathāgata takes non-locality as its essence; therefore, it causes sentient beings of mixed conduct to perceive it differently according to their own views.
Because of divergent views, purity and defilement arise;
because there is no fixed direction, the true land manifests its form.
As for grasping at purity and defilement, these are the retributions of sentient beings.
To take its root in the absence of fixed direction is the true nature of a Buddha-land.

How could one say that the distinction between purity and defilement is only realized through separate regions and distinct locations, or by positing two lands—one for ordinary beings and one for sages?
Sheng said:
For a practitioner of the Pure Land, practice leads to the attainment of the Pure Land; it is not something created.
Those who create a land belong to the category of sentient beings.
Fearing that such creation might lead to confusion, one must first clarify the fundamental nature of creation to manifest the meaning of "attainment," and only then discuss practice.
"Why is this? Because a bodhisattva takes on a buddha-field according to the sentient beings he intends to transform.
Kumārajīva said:
From this point onward, the following two chapters enumerate the three causes to explain the meaning of "is.
The Sanskrit text states, "according to how many sentient beings are transformed," which seems to imply that the size of a land corresponds to the number of people transformed through teaching.

The meaning is this: whichever dharmas are used to transform sentient beings—whether it be giving, precepts, or others—each according to their respective practices, they will be reborn in that land; furthermore, the differences in the perfection and purity [of the land] are established according to the depth or shallowness of these three causes.
If one upholds the precepts, then that ground will be level and even;
if one practices generosity, then the seven treasures will be fully present.
These two dharmas are cited briefly; all others are to be understood in this same manner.
Zhaò says:
The following explains why sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-land.
The Buddha-land is nothing more than the reflection and shadow of sentient beings.
Now, when a form is long, its shadow is long; when a form is short, its shadow is brief. How could it be that the sun and moon cause this to be so?
It is simply the nature of the form itself.
Therefore, according to the number of sentient beings being transformed, one takes on the vastness or narrowness of a Buddha-land.
Therefore, Buddha-lands are sometimes composed of four continents, sometimes of a trichiliocosm, and sometimes of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Sheng said:
"A land is the domain of a sentient being's territory; that which is free from impurity within it is called pure."
Absence of defilement is non-existence; the establishment of boundaries is existence. Existence arises from delusion, while non-existence arises from understanding.
Once that understanding is perfected, delusion is finally exhausted.

At the beginning, the understanding that this bodhisattva’s original transformation is naturally responsive constitutes the initial stage; at the end, once [the practice] is perfected, it becomes a unified whole.

Since there are traces of the Buddha’s presence within the realm, one accords with the fundamental principle by following those who are transformed, taking that realm as the object of focus according to its meaning.
Since it is said that one "takes" from them, this does not mean they were created by oneself; if they were created by oneself, there would be nothing to govern them.
If no sentient beings exist, what could possibly be accomplished?
He takes up a buddha-field according to the beings he is to discipline.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the Sanskrit original, it is called 'vinaya'."
Vinaya means "skillful governance.
It skillfully governs sentient beings, causing them to abandon evil and practice good.
According to the extent to which they abandon evil and the depth to which they practice good, their realm is established.
"Subduing" (調伏) has the same essential meaning as [the previous term], but its phrasing is obscure; therefore, I have retained the original.
Zhaò says:
"According to the depth or shallowness of the sentient beings to be subdued, one takes up the excellence or inferiority of the Buddha-land."
Daosheng said:
"Although transformation already encompasses [all things], the name belongs to the beginning.
Since that [beginning] cannot do without subduing, it is appropriate to clarify this."
"If they were not tamed, there would be no land of the seven treasures.
One takes up a buddha-land according to which realm various sentient beings should enter into the Buddha's wisdom.
Kumārajīva said:

When cultivating a pure land, one should first contemplate the minds of sentient beings regarding their future lives, observing which realm they ought to see in the future in order to attain liberation. Having first assessed the superior or inferior qualities of the lands during that future kalpa, one then, together with those sentient beings, gathers the three causes to establish that land, so as to enable them to be reborn there.
"Encompassing" refers to that which was previously intended; this refers to the Buddha’s wisdom.
The subsequent mention of "the faculties of the bodhisattvas" clarifies that there are varying degrees of depth among those who will receive transformation in the future.
Sengzhao said:
"Among sentient beings, there are those who see purity and, out of admiration, advance in their practice; there are also those who see defilement and, out of aversion, advance in their practice.
Their preferences differ in direction, and I have merely spoken of them in brief."
Although the causes differ, their entry into the Buddha-wisdom is one and the same; therefore, they each take up a buddha-field according to what is appropriate for them.
Sengsheng said:
"While it is understood that [the fields] follow the transformations [of the Buddhas], there is still a risk of confusing their boundaries; thus, it is further necessary to clarify this."
If there were any confusion, one would be identical to those delusions and would certainly be unable to bring them to completion.
According to the various sentient beings, one takes up a Buddha-land by means of that particular land through which they should give rise to the roots of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"The preceding refers to entering the Buddha-wisdom.
Buddha-wisdom is the wisdom of non-arising attained at the seventh stage; it now constitutes the faculty of the bodhisattva."
The "Bodhisattva faculties" refer to the bodhicitta from the sixth stage downward.
Sengsheng said:
"Entering the Buddha’s wisdom also encompasses these."
However, as the name pertains to the initial entry [into the path], its manifestation lacks profound depth or vastness; therefore, it is further necessary to clarify this.
If there were no profound depth or vastness, then the land of the One Vehicle would not exist. Why is this so?
The Bodhisattva takes up a pure land solely for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said:
This explains why he first establishes the excellence or inferiority of the land, and only thereafter undertakes his practice.
If one were to establish a state for my own sake, it should be accomplished according to whatever circumstances arise;
however, since I now act for the benefit of sentient beings, I establish the state in accordance with what is appropriate for them.
Sengzhao said:
"The Dharma-body has no fixed location; how could there be any particular country?
Beauty and ugliness are external; what purity could there be to grasp?"
Those who take up the Pure Land do so solely for the sake of others; therefore, they take it up according to what is appropriate for them.
Sheng says:
"The reason" refers to the preceding four phrases.
If one has no territory of one's own to establish, nor resides within another's borders, only then can one bring sentient beings to maturity.
It is like a person who wishes to build a palace on empty ground; they may do so as they please without obstruction.
Kumārajīva said:
"The Sanskrit original says, 'To construct palaces within emptiness with sovereign ease and without obstruction.
Emptiness cannot be used as a palace; likewise, one attains a pure land without departing from sentient beings."
It is further said:
"One may construct a palace within space, yet one cannot use space itself as the palace; one must employ timber before it can be completed.
Likewise, although a Bodhisattva understands emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they cannot attain their realm through the mind of emptiness alone; they must accomplish that realm by means of the three causes."
Furthermore, because the underlying intent differs, the scriptural passages are not the same.
Sengsheng said:
"The construction of palaces and halls is a metaphor for bringing sentient beings to spiritual maturity."
An empty space is a place free from obstruction; it is like taking up something that is not defiled, for defilement constitutes an obstruction.
If one were to attempt this in empty space, it could never be accomplished.
Daosheng said:
Regarding empty space, it means there is no substance that can be used to construct a palace.
For example, it is like building a country oneself where there are no sentient beings to inhabit it.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva makes a vow to take up a Buddha-land for the sake of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment.
Dharmarakṣa said:
"It is a place of non-obstruction.
Those who wish to take up a Buddha-land do not do so within emptiness."
Zhaò said:
"The Pure Land must arise from sentient beings; it is like how the establishment of a palace must depend on the ground.
Without the ground, there are no sentient beings, and without sentient beings, the palace and its land cannot be formed."
The followers of the Two Vehicles clarify their spirits within the void and do not rely upon sentient beings; therefore, they have no Pure Land.
Daosheng said:
"It is not that there are no sentient beings."
"Ratnakūṭa!
You should know that the straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò said:

The purity of the land must necessarily arise from sentient beings, and the purity of sentient beings must necessarily depend on various practices; thus, the purity of the land was explained by directly citing sentient beings.
Now, all these various practices are fully enumerated to clarify the reasons for that purity.
Now, when conduct is pure, sentient beings are pure; when sentient beings are pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
This is an inevitable principle that cannot be otherwise.
Since there is no defilement or crookedness in the land, it arises from the rectitude of the mind; therefore, it is said that the straightforward mind is the Bodhisattva’s pure land.
This is a case of speaking of the effect within the cause, like pointing to gold and calling it food.
"Direct mind" means being honest and straightforward without guile.
This mind is the foundation of all practices; thus, it is mentioned in the *Banzhou sanmei jing*.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from flattery will come to be born in his land.
Zhaò says:
"Freedom from flattery" and "straightforward mind" are different names for the same single practice.
Since the Bodhisattva’s mind is upright, he transforms others to become like himself;
since his own land is perfected, he causes those who practice in concert to gather there.
This clarifies that because the conditions for transformation reach one another, their karmic retributions are linked; thus, the meaning of a Buddha-land is made manifest.

From here on, the two lines contrast with one another; they may be different names for the same thing expressed in sequence, or the former may be brief while the latter is detailed, or the former may be the cause while the latter is the effect—these are all analogous to the practice of causes.
There are two kinds of wholesome conduct:
first, the practice of goodness; second, the fruition of goodness.
From this point downward, all that is practiced by sentient beings is the fruition of goodness.
Śāriputra said:
"The principles for bringing about a pure land have already been fully set forth previously; now, I shall simply clarify that various practices are the foundation of a pure land.
This can readily be understood, which is why it says, 'Ratnākara, you should know,' where 'know' is as explained before."
In answering their questions, I have specifically relied on the manifestation of purity through deeds to demonstrate a heart that is truly free from defilement.
This is the very foundation of virtuous conduct; therefore, it is elucidated first.
Not being sycophantic toward sentient beings is one matter of purity.

When Bodhisattvas speak of their practices and sentient beings speak of their retributions, they do so in response to clarify that sentient beings received this transformation in the past and now possess this fruit.
When the bodhisattva’s practice is perfected, responding to it belongs to the Buddha.
Because he already presides over the realm in anticipation, it is said that [the result] arises in the next life.
The profound mind is the pure land of the bodhisattva.
Zhaò said:
"Because the tree of the mind and its manifold virtues are deep and firm, it is difficult to uproot that profound mind.
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are fully endowed with merit come to be born in his land."
Zhaò said:
"Because of the profound mind, virtue is complete.
The Mahāyāna mind is the pure land of the Bodhisattva."
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings of the Mahāyāna will come to be born in his land.
Zhaò says:
"To ride upon the eighty thousand practices, carrying all under heaven together without leaving out a single person—this is the mind of the Mahāyāna."
The three preceding states of mind constitute the sequence of initial practice for one who would study.
Now, those who wish to propagate the Great Way must first rectify their minds;
once the mind is truly upright, they can then enter into practice with depth.
Once one's practice has entered deeply, one can then transport [beings] extensively across the boundless.
This is the sequence of these three minds.
Having fully equipped oneself with these three minds, one then proceeds to cultivate the six perfections.
Another version reads: "The straightforward mind, the profound mind, and the bodhicitta. Kumārajīva said:
"The straightforward mind is the sincere mind.
At the very beginning of generating the resolve [for enlightenment], one begins with sincerity."
When the recognition of the Way becomes increasingly clear, it is called the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*).
When this profound mind expands and broadens, correctly tending toward the Buddha-wisdom, it is called the bodhicitta.
These are all the minds of those who receive transformation.
Those who undergo transformation through practice reach the Pure Land, and others are born there as well; through these causes and conditions, the Bodhisattva-land is established.
There are two kinds of goodness:
first, goodness through practice; second, goodness through birth as a result of retribution.
Generally speaking, when it is said that those who come to be born in that land will be fully endowed with goodness, this refers to being reborn as a result of having cultivated goodness.
Generosity is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, all sentient beings capable of renunciation will come to be born in that land.
Sengzhao said:
"To renounce national wealth and one's own life externally, and to renounce greed, attachment, stinginess, and jealousy internally, is called 'the ability to relinquish everything.
Maintaining the precepts is the pure land of the Bodhisattva."
"When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who have fulfilled their vows by practicing the ten paths of wholesome action will come to be born in his land.
Kumārajīva said:

"Regarding the mention of 'fulfilling vows' specifically in relation to upholding the precepts—it is because the precepts are difficult to practice and yet simultaneously encompass all other virtues that one's vows are thereby fulfilled."
Sengzhao said:
"The ten wholesome acts are the Bodhisattva precepts; there are also immeasurable precepts, of which these ten are merely mentioned briefly.
When the precepts are complete, there is no wish that cannot be attained; therefore, it is said they are 'fulfilled'."
"Patience is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings adorned with the thirty-two marks will come to be born in his land.
Zhaò says:
"Because patience results in a serene countenance, it is linked here to the physical marks; yet how could it be merely a matter of physical retribution?"
Diligence is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have diligently cultivated all merits will come to be born in his land.
Meditative concentration is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who have gathered their minds and are free from distraction come to be born in his land.
Wisdom is the pure land of a Bodhisattva;
when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who dwell in right concentration come to be born in his land.
Sengzhao said:
"To attain right wisdom and the definitive characteristics of dharmas among the three categories of sentient beings is what is called the 'group of those fixed in rightness' (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
The four immeasurable minds are the pure land of the bodhisattva."
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who have perfected loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity will come to be born in his land.
Zhaò says: Because these four mental states are all-encompassing and boundless, they are called "immeasurable."
The four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) are the pure land of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"To gather sentient beings by means of the four methods of equality is what constitutes the four integrations."
First is generosity, consisting of the two gifts of material wealth and the Dharma, given according to what others require.
Second is pleasant speech, which consists of harmonious words spoken with a loving heart, adapted to suit others.
Third is beneficial speech (*arthacaryā*): according to what is beneficial for others, one skillfully benefits them. Fourth is cooperation (*samānārthatā*):
encountering evil, one acts as if sharing in that evil in order to sever it; encountering good, one acts as if sharing in that good in order to advance it; therefore, it is called "cooperation."
"When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who have been liberated and gathered by him come to be born in his land.
Kumārajīva said:
"There may be those who see the Buddha yet do not attain liberation; this is because their merit and wisdom are shallow."
One who is able to practice the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) must possess profound wisdom and significant merit; therefore, they attain liberation in the presence of the Buddha.
Furthermore, because the four means of integration can enable sentient beings to attain liberation, the practitioner subsequently achieves the principle of liberation.
Zhaò says:
Liberation is the unconditioned fruit accomplished through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Because they practice together, all sentient beings are encompassed by this fruit.
Skillful means (*upāya*) is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess unimpeded skillful means regarding all phenomena will come to be born in his land.
Zhaò says:
Expedient means (*upāya*) refers to skillful wisdom.
By accumulating small virtues, one attains great merit; yet though the merit is accomplished, one does not realize [the ultimate fruit].

Abiding in existence without deviating from quiescence, dwelling in non-existence without losing transformation—acting without effort yet accomplishing all that is to be done—such is the unimpeded nature of expedient means.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the bodhisattva’s pure land.

When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who practice the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of spiritual power, faculties, powers, and the path of awakening will come to be born in his land.
Zhaò says:
"Mindfulness" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
"right effort" refers to the four right efforts.
The bases of psychic power are the four bases of psychic power.
The faculties are the five faculties.
The powers are the five powers.
Enlightenment refers to the seven factors of enlightenment;
the Path refers to the eightfold noble path.
Combined, these constitute thirty-seven [factors], the meaning of which is found in other sutras.
The mind of dedication is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"The two vehicles and the triple world each have their distinct practices; if one’s disposition lacks superior aspiration, then one receives retribution according to those practices."
The Great Being sets his mind upon the Buddha-way; therefore, he is able to dedicate those various practices toward the Single Vehicle.
This is the mind of dedication.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, he shall obtain a land of sovereign virtue, fully endowed with all perfections.
Zhaò says:
"When one encounters the good and dedicates it [toward awakening], what virtue is not perfected?
Although the following three phrases do not explicitly mention sentient beings, by mentioning the 'kingdom,' they are already included."
It is said that the removal of the eight difficulties constitutes the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, there shall be no three evil realms or eight difficulties in his land.
Zhaò says:
To preach the Dharma for the removal of the eight difficulties means that in such a land, the eight difficulties do not exist.
To personally maintain one's own observance of the precepts and refrain from criticizing the deficiencies of others is the pure land of a Bodhisattva.
When this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, there will be no mention of the transgression of prohibitions in his land.
Zhaò said:
"To violate prohibitions and incur an evil reputation arises from criticizing others while failing to maintain self-restraint.
The ten wholesome deeds are the pure land of the bodhisattva."
"When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, their life is not cut short prematurely.
Kumārajīva said:
"Dedication (pariṇāmanā) means skillfully directing [merit] toward the Buddha-way; therefore, it is called dedication."
Dedication involves benefiting both oneself and all sentient beings; therefore, it is said that one is "endowed with merit.
Being endowed with merit means being free from the eight difficulties; hence, it is further stated that one "eliminates the eight difficulties."
To eliminate the eight difficulties is the practice; therefore, one receives the retribution of being free from difficulties.

Since there are no eight difficulties, there are no manifold evils; since there are no manifold evils, there is no transgression of prohibitions; thus, next, the absence of violating the precepts is explained.

The previous discourse on the "Crossing by Means of Precepts" (śīla-pāramitā) now returns to the term "precepts," yet the meaning does not reside in the precepts themselves. Rather, it seeks to clarify through the precepts that one should not criticize the deficiencies of others.
Because one does not criticize the deficiencies of others, their deficiencies remain unknown; because their deficiencies remain unknown, they bear no reputation for violating prohibitions.
Because one practices this, one obtains this as the fruit; because one obtains this as the fruit, all evils are completely stilled; therefore, the ten wholesome actions follow next.
Zhaò says: "This is the retribution for not killing."
"Great wealth.
Zhaor said:
"This is the retribution for not stealing."
Brahmacarya.
Zhaò says:
it is the retribution for abstaining from sexual misconduct.
"What is spoken is truthful.
Zhaò said: "This is the retribution for not engaging in false speech."
He always used gentle speech.
Zhaò said: "This means not responding with harsh words."
One's retinue does not separate from them, and they skillfully reconcile disputes and litigation.
Zhaò says: "This is the retribution for not engaging in double-tongued speech."
"His speech is invariably beneficial. Zhaò said:
"This is the retribution for not engaging in frivolous speech."
Beings who are free from envy and anger and possess right view will be born in that land.
Zhaò says:
"Envy, anger, and false views are the most grievous afflictions of the mind; therefore, three specific virtues are established to counter them."
Vimalakīrti said:

"To cultivate the ten wholesome actions is to bring the various practices of the higher realms to fulfillment, thereby achieving purity of body, speech, and mind; this is the foundation of the Pure Land.
Thus it is, Ratnākara!"
When a bodhisattva follows their straightforward mind, they are able to initiate practice.
Zhaò says:
"Now, when the mind is straightforward, faith is firm; once faith is firm, one can then set forth and undertake practice."
Thus, that which begins with the myriad practices can only be the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*).

This chapter clarifies the gradual sequence of practice, wherein the subtle and the manifest are causally dependent; this is sufficient to begin with the straightforward mind and culminate in the Pure Land (*śuddhāvāsa*).
It is like planting a seed as fine as a hair or a silk thread, which eventually grows to a girth of a hundred spans.
By planting the sprout of a straightforward mind, all practices are thereby accomplished; hence it is said that [the result] follows [the cause].
Tanyao said:

"The preceding section only clarified that various practices are each causes for a pure land, yet it was not known how they are so obtained; therefore, I have arranged their meanings in sequence to explain them."
"Thus" refers to the aforementioned practices being like the aforementioned intention.
It means that by following the momentum of the straightforward mind, one is naturally able to carry out various practices;
as one carries out these practices accordingly, one attains the profound mind.
Zhaò said:
"Once one is able to initiate practice, the aspiration for the Way becomes ever more profound.
As that profound mind develops, the will is accordingly subdued."
Sengzhao said:
"When one's affinity for the Way is profound, the mind will be free from coarseness and wildness.
To tame oneself according to the mind is to practice as one preaches."
Zhaò said:
"Once the mind is disciplined and subdued, one is able to put into practice what has been heard.
By acting in accordance with what has been taught, one is able to dedicate [the merit]."
