Sengzhao said:
"If one can put what has been heard into practice, then one can turn that practice toward the supreme realm as the object of the mind.
According to such dedication, there arises skillful means."
Zhaò said:
"Since one is already able to dedicate [merit] toward the Mahāyāna, this is the source from which great skillful means arise.
According to these skillful means, one brings sentient beings to fulfillment."
Zhaò said:
"That which is established through skillful means has as its aim the maturation of sentient beings.
As one matures sentient beings accordingly, so does the Buddha-field become pure."
Zhaò said:
"Since sentient beings are already pure, the land is without defilement.
As the Buddha-land is pure, so too is the teaching of the Dharma pure."
Zhaò said:
"Since one dwells in a pure land, there is pure teaching.
As the teaching is pure, wisdom is pure."
Sengzhao said:
"Since there is pure teaching, pure wisdom arises.
As wisdom becomes pure, the mind becomes pure accordingly."
Sengzhao said:
"Once pure wisdom has arisen, the pure mind becomes increasingly luminous.
As the mind becomes pure, all merits and virtues likewise become pure."
Kumārajīva said: "A straightforward mind is one that is sincere; it is a mind that has faith in the Buddha-dharma.

Once faith is established, one is able to practice various virtues. As various virtues accumulate, the mind becomes increasingly profound. When the mind becomes increasingly profound, it no longer follows after various evils. To abandon evil and follow good is what is called 'taming' (dāmyati)."

When the mind is thus disciplined, one acts upon encountering what is wholesome; acting upon encountering what is wholesome, one is able to perform what is difficult to perform; because one is able to perform what is difficult to perform, one is able to act in accordance with what has been taught.

If one practices according to what has been taught, then all myriad virtues will be possessed; because all myriad virtues are possessed, one is able to dedicate them toward the Buddha-way. To progress further as one dedicates is the power of skillful means (*upāya*).
The essentials of skillful means are threefold:

first, being adept at one's own practice without grasping at signs; second, not grasping at realization; and third, being adept at transforming sentient beings. Having fulfilled these three, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity.
When sentient beings are brought to maturity, the three causes are fully perfected; when the three causes are fully perfected, one attains a pure land.
Once the land is pure, sentient beings become purely refined; when sentient beings are purely refined, one does not preach mixed teachings, and thus it is said that the teaching is pure.

If one receives the Dharma, one possesses the three lower purities; possessing these three lower purities means sharing the same virtues as the transformation master (nirmāṇa-adhipati). Therefore, it is said that "all are pure.
Although the previous chapter extensively explained the practice for purifying the land, it did not clarify the progressive stages of that practice.

This chapter clarifies that the ultimate goal is profoundly deep and vast, such that it cannot be transcended instantaneously; rather, there must be a path to seek and an orderly sequence to follow. Therefore, it is taught that the beginning of setting forth on this journey starts with a straightforward mind, while the perfection of its culmination consists in universal purity.
Sengzhao said:
"One who accumulates virtue without ceasing does so desiring to purify the mind; once the mind is purified, there is no virtue that is not pure.
Sengsheng said:
"Merit" refers to the sublime fruit.
It is named according to its origin;
therefore, O Ratnakūṭa!
If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, they should purify their own mind; as their mind becomes pure, so too will the buddha-field become pure.
ZHAO says:
This concludes the exposition on the meaning of the pure land.
The Pure Land is merely the reflection of this mind.
Now, if one wishes for an echo to be harmonious, one must harmonize one's voice; if one wishes for a shadow to be upright, one must rectify one's form. This is the fixed law of karmic retribution.
At that time, Śāriputra received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*anubhāva*).
An alternative version reads "received the Buddha’s holy intent" (*śrī-ājñā*), but Kumārajīva said:

"Holy intent" corresponds to *ṛddhi* (spiritual power) in the Sanskrit original; it is through the transformation of such spiritual power that those who were free from doubt are caused to give rise to doubts.
He had this thought:
"If it is said that when a bodhisattva’s mind is pure, the buddha-field is pure, then when our World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva, was his mind not pure?
Yet this buddha-field is as impure as this."
Zhaò said:
"The purity or defilement of a land is certainly beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles.

Since the Tathāgata intends to clarify that the Buddha-land is eternally pure and that beings of both noble and base character are born therein, he employs his majestic spiritual power to provoke their doubts and provide a basis for discourse; thus, it is said that they 'receive' [the teaching]."
Sheng said:

"Once one has heard that affairs are pure, one immediately becomes fixated on those affairs; thus, one again falls into obscurity regarding the absence of defilement. Because one considers stones and sand to be inconsistent with practice, [the Master] demonstrated the difficulty of reaching a definitive resolution."

Śāriputra was indeed one to whom nothing remained unpenetrated; yet, because he occupied a position of perceived insufficiency, he could be regarded as not fully awakened. Therefore, this thought was formulated to express the sentiments of the assembly.
Acting in accordance with the capacities of beings, these [teachings] originally emerge from the Buddha’s wisdom.
Now that they have been shown to be non-self, how could they be in vain?
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, immediately addressed them, saying:
"What do you think?
Are the sun and moon not pure?
Yet the blind do not see them."
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One."
"This is the fault of the blind, not the fault of the sun or the moon.
Śāriputra, it is because of the transgressions of sentient beings that they do not see the majestic purity of the Tathāgata’s buddha-field; it is not the fault of the Tathāgata."
Sengzhao said:
"Are the sun and moon not bright?
That they are not seen is simply due to blind eyes."
"Is the Buddha-field not pure?
It is because of one's own sinful defilements that it is not seen.
Śāriputra said:
The illumination of the sun and moon leaves no form unmanifested, yet the blind do not see it; is this the fault of the sun and moon?
It is the same with the Buddha.
In the past, he practiced his conduct to transform sentient beings, leaving no place where there was not ground free of sand and stones.
However, because sentient beings have committed offenses, they receive this defilement;
it is simply that you do not see it, which is not the fault of the Buddha.
Śāriputra, my land is pure, yet you do not see it.
Zhaò said:
"Just now, because I gave rise to doubt regarding this land, I have therefore clarified its purity right here.
Shēng said:
Since it has been clarified that impurity resides with sentient beings while the principle of purity belongs inherently to the Buddha, it is said, "My land is pure.
Śāriputra, however, based himself on the defilement he perceived and thus harbored doubt, failing to see this reality.
The phrase "yan er" expresses a sigh of lamentation.
At that time, the Brahma King Śikhin said to Śāriputra:
"Do not harbor such a thought as to consider this buddha-field to be impure."
"Why is this? I see that the land of Śākyamuni Buddha is pure, like the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Kumārajīva said:

The purity of Buddha-fields varies in degree: some are like those of the Four Heavenly Kings, up to those of the six heavens of the desire realm; some are like the Brahma heavens, up to those of the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens, or even surpassing the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Those who transcend the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens are only Bodhisattvas in their final birth who are born in this land.
Because [the Buddha] accords with the inclinations of all beings, the manifestations of the land differ.
That what was seen by Śikhin was like the palace of the Lord of Freedom (Īśvara) was merely what he was destined to see; it did not yet exhaust the full extent of its purity.
The subsequent statement, "For example, the land of the Buddha Ratnavyūha," refers to the true land of retribution and response purified by Śākyamuni.
This pure land is located within this very world, as explained in the "Life Span" chapter (*Juryōbon*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This purity and impurity occupy the same space without being intermingled, just as there might be two kinds of food in a single vessel intended for two types of sentient beings.
Zhaò said:

"Those with similar sounds harmonize with one another, and those with similar views accord with one another. The Brahma King is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body; because he relies on the pure wisdom of the Buddha, all that he perceives is pure, and it is by virtue of what he perceives that [others] realize it."
Furthermore, the Buddha-field is truly pure and transcends the three realms; how could it be merely like the celestial palaces of the mundane world?
This is likely said only from the perspective of what [beings] perceive.

Śāriputra, while among humans, saw only earth and stone; the Brahmā King, dwelling in the heavens, saw it as a celestial palace; and what others saw likewise differed according to their respective perceptions.
The suitability of a Buddha-field lies precisely in this meaning.
Daosheng said:

"The Brahma King Śikhin remains within the cycle of birth and death; through erroneous reasoning, he assumes that because he and others alike receive blessings within the triple world, it constitutes purity. He knows that those who lack such blessings naturally perceive this as defilement, and thus he views Śākyamuni’s land as no different from a celestial palace. To take Śāriputra’s failure to understand as evidence of extreme delusion is [a misinterpretation]."
Śāriputra said:
"As I behold this land, it is filled with mounds, ravines, pits, thorns, gravel, stones, and various mountains, abounding in impurities and filth."
Sengzhao said:
"Each takes what they perceive as proof.
Sengsheng said:
Although he had heard the preceding words, he still clung to his perception of impurity; therefore, he spoke again of what he himself saw to express his doubt.
The Brahma King Śikhin said:
"Virtuous one, because your mind possesses high and low [distinctions] and does not rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom, you see this land as impure."
Zhaò said:
"The myriad things and myriad forms are all produced by the mind; because the mind has heights and depths, hills and mounds arise.
Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva regards all sentient beings with complete equanimity, possesses a profoundly pure mind, and relies upon the wisdom of the Buddha, they are then able to perceive this buddha-field as pure.
Sengzhao said:
"If one can regard all living beings with an impartial mind and penetrate deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom, then since their pure karma is identical, what they perceive will not differ.
Sengsheng said:
Those whose minds harbor high and low [distinctions] harbor doubts based on stones and sand; thus, they judge according to the superior or inferior nature of sentient beings.
Furthermore, this is not to rely on the Buddha’s wisdom as the path of response; rather, it lies in the state of necessary awakening, and for this reason, one perceives only impurity.
If one removes the principle of evil, then sentient beings in stones and sand are no different from those in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, because this is observed through the wisdom of the Buddha, there is nowhere that is not pure.

Thereupon, the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately this trichiliocosm was adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels, like the land of the Tathāgata Ratnavyūha, adorned with the immeasurable merits of jewels.
The entire assembly marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, and each saw themselves sitting upon a precious lotus flower.
Zhaò remarked:
"The Buddha-land is eternally pure; how could it require transformation before being adorned?"
As for the pressing of the earth, it was likely what was perceived by the multitude due to their own transgressions.
The Land of Precious Adornments is the most excellent of pure lands; therefore, it was taken as an analogy.
Jizang said:
"The transformation of the earth through spiritual power is intended to clarify that what is defiled can be made pure.
It is like stones and sand, which, though filthy, do not differ when they reach a place free from impurity."

Furthermore, he manifested this transformation to demonstrate that there is no fixed characteristic, thereby dispelling feelings of attachment to impurity and leading one to grasp the principle of purity.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Observe for a moment how adorned and pure this buddha-field is."
Tanhui said:
"As for 'provisional observation,' this means that one provisionally relies on the description of purity and adornment to clarify the absence of defilement.
When it is manifested in reality, there is, in fact, no such thing as a Pure Land."
Śāriputra said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
That which was never before seen and never before heard now appears entirely within the adorned purity of the Buddha-land."
Zhaò said:
"To manifest the Pure Land where it had not been heard is like opening the eyes and ears of the deaf and blind to forms and sounds.
Shēng said:
Having realized its meaning, he reflected that his own previous state was the fundamental basis; thus, he said, "Fundamentally, I had neither seen nor heard [of this].
Since he attained realization from what he had previously neither seen nor heard, the Buddha-lands appeared to him as entirely beautiful and pure.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"My buddha-land is always pure like this.
It is only because I wish to deliver those of inferior capacity that I manifest this land of manifold evils and impurity."
Kumārajīva said:
"If one were to attain purity or defilement solely according to one's own karma of merit and demerit, it would not be what is meant by 'manifesting.
To speak of 'manifesting,' however, carries the sense of demonstration."
The Buddhas are able to manifest the pure for sentient beings while concealing the impure; however, to manifest the pure while concealing the impure would be of no benefit to sentient beings.
To allow both to appear without concealment signifies that their meanings are shown to be identical.
Zhaò said:
"From the perspective of the Buddha himself, he is thus eternally pure; yet because he externally accords with those who are inferior, he appears impure in the same manner as them.
Shēng said:
Since it is said that they are identical, they are no different from those [higher realms];
yet, because he condescends to those of inferior capacity, he manifests as if impure.
It is like when the various devas eat from the same precious vessel; according to their respective merits, the color of the food differs.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
If a person’s mind is pure, they will see the adornments of the merits of this land.
Zhaò said:
When those newly born in heaven wish to test and know the extent of their respective merits, they agree to eat celestial food together from a single precious vessel.
When the heavenly banquet arrives, it is so pure that nothing white in this world can serve as a metaphor for it.
Those with great merit, when they lift the rice toward their mouths, the color of the rice remains unchanged;
those with little merit, when they lift it toward their mouths, the color of the rice changes.
While its color is uniform within the vessel, it differs when held in the hand.
How could there be any difference in the rice?
The difference arises from heaven itself.
It is only by the fact that the Buddha-fields are not the same that this can be known.
Daosheng said:
"This is a metaphor for Brahmā and Śāriputra.

When the mind of wisdom is bright and pure, one perceives the adornment of merit; because they grasped it with a darkened mind, it was called 'filth,' but it is not that the Buddha-land itself is so."

When the Buddha manifested this land in its majestic purity, all five hundred sons of elders brought by Ratnākara attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and eighty-four thousand people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Sengzhao said:
"The flourishing of the Buddha-land is precisely for this purpose.

'Endurance of the non-arising' (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is the same as the aforementioned 'endurance of the non-arising of dharmas' (anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti); this endurance is simply the nature of wisdom."

Because one perceives that all phenomena are unarisen, and the mind and intellect are stilled such that one is capable of receiving non-retrogression, it is called "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and this world was restored to its former state.
Zhaò said:
"That which is not one's proper lot cannot be maintained for long; therefore, he returns to what he ought to perceive, seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka."
Sengzhao said:

"The realization of the Way through the Lesser Vehicle is not that of a Pratyekabuddha; it must rely on a teacher before its completion, and is therefore called the Śrāvaka-yāna, also known as the Disciple-yāna."

Thirty-two thousand devas and humans, realizing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely impermanent, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*).
Sengzhao said:
"The land is defiled yet can be purified; having been purified, it becomes defiled again. Through this, one awakens to impermanence and thereby attains the purity of the Dharma-eye."
The purification of the Dharma-eye is the path of the *srotāpanna*.
Because one first perceives the traces of the Path, it receives the name "Dharma-eye.
"Dust and grime" refers to the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Eight thousand bhikṣus did not grasp at any dharmas; their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated.
Zhaò said:
"The Way of Non-attachment involves neither grasping nor defilement regarding dharmas."
The exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*): when the ninety-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) and outflows are exhausted, one attains liberation through intentional mastery and becomes an Arhat.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll One.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Compiled by Shi Sengzhao of Later Qin.
Chapter Two: On Expedient Means (II). Master Kumārajīva said: This chapter, which introduces the virtues of Vimalakīrti, was not the intention of the compiler of the sutra.
The World-Honored One has always praised his skillful means and eloquence; therefore, the compilers of the sutras have recorded his virtues based on what they heard.
At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was an elder named Vimalakīrti, who had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.
Kumārajīva said:
"In order to set forth his virtues, one must first clarify the origins from which those virtues were cultivated.
He planted the roots of goodness deeply."
Kumārajīva said:
"It is the karma of meritorious virtue.
Sengzhao said:
The former sages cultivated virtue first, and thus the roots of goodness were deeply planted.
This scripture originated with Vimalakīrti, and its subtle words and profound teachings are fully contained within the subsequent text.
The translator of this scripture, wishing to preserve the person’s memory for posterity and to propagate his teachings, has thus recorded his virtues in their entirety in this chapter.
Regarding [his attainment of] the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
Kumārajīva said:
Wisdom is the activity of illumination.
Since the Tathāgata has already exhausted [all afflictions], he is named after wisdom (*jñāna*).
The Bodhisattva, though having seen [the truth] but not yet exhausted [afflictions], is able to endure them without retreating; therefore, he is named after patience (*kṣānti*).
Sengzhao said:

"The reason why the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of non-arising is uniquely termed 'patience' (kṣānti) is that, because their great enlightenment is not yet perfected and their power of wisdom is still weak, although they have realized non-arising, they are merely able to endure it; they have not yet the leisure for detached mastery, and thus it is called patience."
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of wisdom; he possesses mastery over all dharmas and is always in a state of leisure, and thus there is no longer any need for the name "patience.
His eloquence is unimpeded.
Kumārajīva said:
Having already perfected these two types of karma, one preaches the Dharma with eloquence to transform sentient beings.
Zhaò says: "This refers to the seven forms of eloquence."
He played with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Kumārajīva said:
"One expands the merit of one's transformative work through supernatural powers, and by the power of supernatural faculties, one also realizes one's eloquence."
For example, when Nāgārjuna was debating with a non-Buddhist, the non-Buddhist asked:
"What is the deity doing now?
He replied:
"The gods are now at war with the asuras.
He asked again,
"How is this proven?"

The Bodhisattva immediately manifested his realization; at that moment, he shattered their spears and broke their blades, causing the asuras’ heads and bodies to fall from the sky. Furthermore, he saw the devas and asuras arrayed in battle formation, facing one another in the void.
Once the non-Buddhists had witnessed this, they were subdued by his eloquence.
Such is the nature of the realization of supernatural powers through debate.
Zhaò said:

The Sūtra states that "the Bodhisattva attains the five supernatural powers," yet elsewhere it says he "possesses the six supernatural powers. Because he has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the fetters of the three realms have been exhausted, he is compared to those of the two vehicles; thus, it speaks of six.
However, when compared to the Tathāgata, his residual habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted;
therefore, it speaks of five.
He attained the various *dhāraṇīs*.
Kumārajīva said:
"Wisdom is able to maintain the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); it is also called 'maintaining' (*dhāraṇī*)."
The remaining dhāraṇīs are as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Sengzhao says:
"The meaning of 'total retention' (*dhāraṇī*) is the same as above."
The Sūtra says, "There are five hundred dhāraṇīs," and it also says, "Immeasurable dhāraṇīs.
One thereby attains fearlessness.
Sengzhao says:
This is the Bodhisattva’s four kinds of fearlessness.
It subdues the demons, toils, and enmities. Zao said:
The four māras weary me; therefore, they become my enemies.
I enter the profound dharma-gate.
Zhaò says:
The profound meanings of all dharmas have immeasurable gateways, all of which he enters skillfully.
He is adept in the Prajñāpāramitā and has thoroughly mastered expedient means.
Zhaò said:
Reaching the further shore of true wisdom is the perfection of skillful knowledge (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Its application is without fixed direction; this is the mastery of skillful means (*upāya*).
Thus, the great vows are fulfilled.
Kumārajīva said:

"At the time when one first generates the aspiration for enlightenment, that vow may not yet be great; or it may be great but not yet fulfilled. Only those Bodhisattvas who have attained the Great Dharma-patience (mahādharmanidhyānakṣānti) have vows that are both great and fulfilled."
The forty-eight vows of Amitāyus are of the same category as these great vows.
Zhaò says:
"Great Vows" refers to comparing them with the vows of Amitāyus.
He clearly understands the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"The myriad forms of living beings have different mental inclinations; he understands them all completely."
Furthermore, he was able to discern whether the faculties of others were sharp or dull.
Zhaò said:
"The sharpness or dullness of the faculties among those of the three vehicles is difficult to distinguish, yet he could discern them skillfully."
Having long practiced the Buddha-way, their minds have already become pure and mature, and they are resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
Zhaò says:
"It is only from the seventh stage (bhūmi) upward that one first attains such resolution."
"In all that one does, one is able to exercise skillful deliberation.
Zhaò says:
"In whatever actions of body, speech, or mind are performed, wisdom is always present beforehand; therefore, there is no failure in what is done."
He abides in the majestic deportment of a Buddha. Zao says:
"In his every movement and pause, he does not fail to maintain the sacred demeanor."
An alternative version states, "Possessing the majestic deportment of a Buddha. Kumārajīva said:
This means that he is able to transform his body into that of a Buddha, such that every movement and gesture is exactly like those of a Buddha.
His mind is as vast as the ocean.
Kumārajīva said:
"The ocean possesses three virtues: first, it is deep, vast, and boundless; second, it is pure and does not admit impurities; third, it stores up immeasurable treasures."
The three virtues of a Bodhisattva are identical in meaning to those of the ocean.

Zhaò said: "The ocean possesses five virtues: first, it is clear and pure, refusing to accept corpses; second, it produces many wondrous treasures; third, when great dragons pour down rain with drops as thick as axle-trees, it receives them without overflowing; fourth, neither wind nor sun can exhaust it; and fifth, its abyssal depths are difficult to fathom."

The mind of the Great Being is pure; it does not receive the corpse of one who breaks the precepts, it produces the jewel of the light of wisdom, it receives the great Dharma-rain of the Buddha without overflowing, and it cannot be diminished by the winds and suns of Māra’s evil. Its wisdom is profound and deep, beyond the reach of measurement; therefore, it is said that his mind is as vast as the ocean.
Praised by all Buddhas and revered by his disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the lords of the world, he dwells in Vaiśālī through skillful means for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Zhaò said:
"What joy could there be for those praised by all Buddhas and revered by humans and devas?
It is because they wish to deliver sentient beings that they manifest their residence in Vaiśālī."

With immeasurable wealth, they gather in the poor; with pure observance of the precepts, they gather in those who violate them; with the practice of patience, they gather in those who are wrathful; with great diligence, they gather in those who are indolent; with single-minded meditative stillness, they gather in those whose minds are distracted; and with definitive wisdom, they gather in those who lack knowledge.
Sengzhao said:
"The Perfected One does not manifest active practice;
those who manifest the practice of the six perfections do so merely to subdue the six corruptions."
Although he was a layman, he upheld the pure monastic discipline of a śramaṇa.
Zhaò said:
"Śramaṇa" is the general designation for those who have left the household life.
In the language of Qin, "yi" (義) is taught as "diligent practice"; diligent practice leads toward nirvana.
Although one may dwell at home, one does not cling to the three realms.
Zhaor says:
He is the dwelling place of the three realms.
Though he appears to have a wife and children, he constantly cultivates the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Zhaò said:
The purity of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is the practice of desirelessness.
Though one currently has a retinue, one always delights in seclusion.
Zhaò says:
Whether in a house or in the wild, he is thus said to be "distantly removed.
Although he wears precious ornaments, he adorns his body with the marks and signs of excellence.
Zhaò says:
Though they wear precious ornaments on the outside, within they are adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
Although they partake of food and drink, they take the joy of meditation as their true flavor.
Zhaò said:
While partaking of worldly food externally, he internally relished the flavor of the joy of dhyāna.
Whenever he arrived at places of gambling or games, he would immediately use them as a means to save others.
Sengzhao said:
"Cease your jesting with jesting," he said,
as he accepted various heterodox teachings.
Kumārajīva replied:
He currently practices the teachings of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika),
yet he does not disparage his correct faith.
Zhaò says:
To say that "the same is identical to the different" merely intends to make the different identical to oneself; how could this possibly destroy one's correct faith?
"Receiving" refers to receiving and studying the teachings of heterodox paths.
"Though he was well-versed in the secular classics, he always delighted in the Buddha-dharma.
Sengzhao said:
"Though he had fully mastered the secular classics, what he delighted in was the True Dharma."
"He is revered by all, making him the foremost among those who receive offerings.
Kumārajīva said, "Those who possess virtue are able to attract offerings; that those who can attract offerings, in turn, offer worship to this worthy man is why he is considered the most excellent."
Sengzhao said:

"Among those with teeth, there is none who does not revere [them]; among those who maintain purity, there is none who does not make offerings to them. Therefore, they are called the foremost of all objects of offering.
By upholding the True Dharma, they guide both the elderly and the young."
Sengzhao said:
"In the various districts of foreign lands, all establish 'Three Elders' (sānlǎo). Those with virtue serve as law-enforcers to adjudicate local disputes and oversee the elderly and the young."
Vimalakīrti manifests adherence to conventional dharmas, thereby attaining penetration into the path-dharmas.
In all his worldly occupations and social dealings, although he may obtain secular benefits, he does not feel joy therein.
Zhaò said:
"The Dharma-body Bodhisattva regards rubble as nothing but precious jade.
If this were so, people would not value his benevolence."
Therefore, though he appears to seek profit in common with others, how could there be any personal joy in it?
He wanders through the four crossroads to benefit sentient beings.
Zhaò said:
At the crossroads where all paths meet and people converge, he benefits them according to their needs.
He enters into the governance of the True Dharma to rescue and protect all beings.
Zhaò said:
To administer the True Dharma is the duty of the judicial official.
To guide by means of the True Dharma so that the people are free from partiality and injustice is to provide protection for all.
Upon entering places of discourse and debate, one guides them with the Mahāyāna.
Sengzhao said:
"In India, there are many heterodox paths, each claiming its own superiority; therefore, that country established separate halls for debate, intending to distinguish their relative merits.
Those wishing to clarify their own doctrine would strike a drum to assemble the multitude and go to the hall to seek debate; the victor became the teacher, while the vanquished became the disciple."
Vimalakīrti, having ascended this hall, subdued the non-Buddhists and subsequently guided them with the Mahāyāna, acting as their teacher.
He entered various schools of learning to entice and enlighten the ignorant youth.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is like when the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni entered the schoolhouse to teach the Sanskrit script; the Brahmā Heaven descended to bear witness, and all people believed and accepted it.
This is of that same category."
Zhaò says:
"The school" refers to the elementary school for teaching children to read and write.
"Inducing and opening [the mind]" is like the example of the Crown Prince entering school and being shown the Sanskrit script.
He entered various brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire.
Kumārajīva said:
"In a foreign land, there was a woman whose body was golden in color."
There was a son of a householder named Dāmatāla who, having pledged one thousand *niṣkas* of gold, entered the Bamboo Grove and traveled there together with them.
On the way, Mañjuśrī transformed his body into that of a layman, wearing precious robes that were exceedingly magnificent and beautiful.
When the woman saw this, a covetous mind arose within her.
Mañjuśrī said,
"If you wish to obtain the garment, you must give rise to the bodhicitta."
The woman asked,
"What is the bodhicitta? He replied:
"It is your own body. He asked,
"In what way is it so?"
He replied, "The nature of bodhi is empty, and your body is likewise empty; it is for this reason that it is so.
This woman, having previously planted roots of goodness and cultivated wisdom under Kāśyapa Buddha, immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas upon hearing these words.

Having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he intended to demonstrate the faults of desire; thus, he returned with the son of the elder to enter a bamboo grove.
Once they had entered the forest, he manifested his own body as dead, bloated, and putrid.
Upon seeing this, the son of the elder was struck with great terror and went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he too attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Such are the benefits shown by demonstrating the faults of desire.
Sengzhao said:

"In foreign lands, those who indulge in lust have established separate settlements; even those among the ranks of scholars do not so much as cast a glance their way. Yet the Great Being (Mahāsattva) conformed to their desires before demonstrating their faults."
He was able to establish his resolve even when entering wine shops.
Zhaò said:
"Wine leads to the loss of resolve and opens the gate to dissipation."
"If he is among the elders, he is the most honored among them, and for him he preaches the supreme Dharma.
Kumārajīva said:
"The 'elders' (gṛhapati) are like the noble clans of the four castes today."
The Śrāvaka is superior to the ordinary person; thus, proceeding in this manner through successive stages, the Buddha-dharma is the most supreme.
Zhaò said:

"Ordinary people are easily moved to compliance by awe, but difficult to follow through principle; therefore, the Mahāsattva always occupies a position of honor in order to propagate a transformative influence that bends others like the wind."
The Elder was of noble lineage and held great prestige; he largely adhered to worldly teachings and did not propagate the supreme Dharma that transcends the world.
Yet, among lay practitioners, he was the most honored.
Kumārajīva said:
"In foreign lands, those laypeople who possess great wealth and enjoy prosperity are called *gṛhapati* (householders).
[This term] refers to those who have severed their greedy attachments."
Zhaò said:
"If he accumulated a hundred million coins and entered the quarter of lay devotees (gṛhapati), his treasures would flourish even more, and thus his greed and attachment would become even deeper.
If he were among the Kṣatriyas, he would be the most honored among them."
Kumārajīva said:
"The Sanskrit term contains two meanings: first, 'patience' (kṣānti), and second, 'wrath' (krodha).

It refers to a person who possesses great power and can manifest great wrath, yet endures suffering and pain with such fortitude that he is difficult to subdue; it is for this reason that it serves as a clan name."
He taught him patience.
Zhaò said:
"Kṣatriya" refers to the royal caste; in the language of Qin, it means "lord of the fields."
At the beginning of the kalpa, humans consumed the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa); subsequently, they ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice.

Later, as human sentiments gradually became deceitful and each person began to claim exclusive ownership over their lands, they eventually established those of virtue to divide and apportion the fields.
This was the beginning of kingship; thus, it has been handed down as its name.
Their nobility and sovereignty are accompanied by much violence and resolute intent, such that they are unable to practice patience or harmony.
"If one is among the Brahmins, he is the most honored among the Brahmins.
Kumārajīva said:
"One who studies extensively and seeks heterodox paths, relying on his own wisdom to be arrogant and self-willed, is called a Brahmin."
He eliminated his pride.
ZHAO said:
"Brahman" means "external intention" in the language of Qin.
This lineage possesses its own scriptures, which have been transmitted from generation to generation; they take the study of the Way as their vocation.
Whether remaining as householders or leaving the home life to practice asceticism, they mostly rely on their own spiritual arts and treat others with arrogance.
If he is among the ministers, he is the most honored among the ministers, instructing them with the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
ZHAO said:
"The True Dharma refers to the laws and methods of governance."
He was instructed to govern the state with rectitude and assist the times through the Way.
If he were among the princes, he would be the most honored; thus, he was shown loyalty and filial piety. Zao said:
"The position you have inherited is one of great responsibility; you ought to prioritize loyalty and filial piety.
If you serve within the inner court, you are the most honored among those officials, charged with transforming and rectifying the palace women.
Kumārajīva said:
This is not like the eunuchs of the present day.

According to the laws of foreign lands, those who have been loyal and virtuous through successive generations, being elderly and possessed of great merit, are appointed as inner officials to transform and rectify the palace women.
Zhaò said:
"Seductive charms and perverse adornments are the natural inclinations of women; therefore, they are instructed in uprightness and integrity.
If she were among the common people, she would be the most honored among them, leading them to cultivate the power of merit."
Kumārajīva said:
"Once there was a lowly man who entered a city and saw another person whose attire was magnificent and pure, riding a great horse and holding a precious parasol. The lowly man cried out:
'This is not good!'"
This was repeated up to three times.
That person, finding it strange, asked:
"I have adorned and purified [this place] in such a manner; why do you say it is not good?"
The lowly man said, "Your Majesty,
having cultivated the roots of virtue in past lives, you have obtained this karmic retribution.
Your majestic power and noble attire are such that all people look up to you with reverence."
"In the past, I did not plant roots of merit, and thus I am as base and ugly as this.
Comparing myself to you, I am like a mere beast; therefore, I simply said that I do not like it, but I was not disparaging you."
The lowly person was moved by this to feel a sense of urgency and extensively cultivated meritorious deeds.
When one’s physical presence inspires others to awaken, the benefit is already vast; how much more so when one transforms people through the Dharma!
Zhaò said:
"Because the power of his merit was slight and shallow, he was born among the common people.
Had he been in the Brahma Heaven, he would have been the most honored among the Brahmās, instructing them with supreme wisdom."
Kumārajīva said:
"In the Hīnayāna, there are three kinds of the first Brahma realm; in the Mahāyāna, there are four kinds. It is the same for the remaining three higher realms.
Although the Brahmā kings possess concentration and wisdom, these are not the definitive liberation; because they are instructed in the Buddha’s wisdom, it is said that [the latter] is superior."
Zhaò said:
"Brahmā is largely attached to the blessings of dhyāna and does not seek the transcendent, supreme wisdom.
As for Śakra, he is the most honored among the Śakras; [the Buddha] manifested his impermanence to him."
Kumārajīva said:
"Because the Brahmā gods have thin defilements and shallow attachments, I manifested supreme wisdom for them.
Because the Śākya people have deep love and profound attachments, I manifested impermanence for them."
Zhaò said:
"The Heavenly Emperor dwells in the Trāyastriṃśa Palace, delighting himself in the five desires; looking eastward, he forgets the west, and for the most part does not contemplate impermanence.
If he is among the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), he is the most honored among them, protecting all sentient beings."
Kumārajīva said:
"The World Protectors (Lokapālas) are the Four Heavenly Kings.
When various evil ghosts and spirits prey upon sentient beings, the Four World-Protecting Kings guard them, ensuring they are not harmed."
Now it is said that the Venerable One is protected by the power of his Way, extending even to the ten directions.
Zhaò says:
"The Four World-Protecting Kings each govern one direction; they protect their respective domains, ensuring that malevolent spirits and ghosts cannot cause harm."
The Elder Vimalakīrti benefits sentient beings through such immeasurable skillful means.
Zhaò says:
"The Dharma-body responds perfectly and its traces are without end; therefore, it is called 'immeasurable'."
The above is merely a brief account.
Regarding his manifesting illness through skillful means,
Kumārajīva said:

The aforementioned skillful means employ giving and precepts to gather people; when giving and precepts gather people, they respond with gratitude for his kindness. When many inquire after his illness, his transformative influence becomes vast.
For this reason, he extensively manifested skillful means and subsequently took up residence in illness.
Because of his illness, kings, ministers, elders, householders, brahmins, and others—including princes and their various attendants—numbering many thousands, all went to inquire after his health.
Sengzhao said:

"Although the manifestations of his transformative responses were directed toward various regions and his wondrous traces were manifold, this sutra originated from his manifesting illness; therefore, the author provides a separate preface to recount that specific event."
Regarding his past life, Vimalakīrti used his own physical illness as an occasion to expound the Dharma extensively.
Kumārajīva said:
"This was intended to clarify that even one who treads the Path cannot avoid such afflictions; how much less can those without virtue preserve themselves from them?"
Sengzhao said:

"Those who agree with me are easy to convince; those who differ from me are difficult to follow. Therefore, taking his own physical illness as an occasion, he extensively elucidates the afflictions inherent in having a body.
O virtuous ones!"
"This body is impermanent.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is the constant dharma of all Buddhas that they must first arouse the minds of people through seven matters, and only then preach the Four Noble Truths."
What are the seven?
First, generosity;
second, ethical discipline; [and so forth].
Third, the retribution of rebirth in the heavens;
fourth, the discourse on "flavor," which refers to the flavor of pleasure;

fifth, the faults and perils of that retribution: although there is a small measure of pleasure, the various sufferings are immeasurable. Sentient beings are deluded by this slight pleasure and fail to perceive the manifold sufferings, just as when a mustard seed is placed atop a mountain, one sees only the mustard seed and does not behold the great mountain.
Sixth, teaching weariness with and detachment from the world;
seventh, praising the merits of *nirvāṇa*.

Now, rather than explaining these seven dharmas, he speaks directly of impermanence because, in this assembly, their accumulated virtues have already reached maturity and their wisdom and discernment have been cultivated to clarity.
Furthermore, impermanence is the primary characteristic of emptiness; since one intends to explain emptiness, impermanence is established first.
The reason only the body is discussed and not other phenomena is that attachment arises only slightly toward other phenomena.
"Powerless and without solidity.
Kumārajīva said:
"There is no power capable of acting."
"Without solidity" means that its substance is not real.
"The law of rapid decay" means it cannot be relied upon.
Zhaoruo said:
The body is fragile and precarious; even great strength cannot preserve it. Who can believe it to be eternally firm?
This is the meaning of impermanence.
It is suffering and affliction.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, affliction arises.
It is the gathering place of all maladies."
Zhaò says:
"Suffering" refers to the eight sufferings, yet there are also immeasurable sufferings.
"Affliction" refers to the nine afflictions, yet there are also immeasurable afflictions.
"Sickness" refers to the four hundred and four types of illness;
this is the meaning of suffering.
O virtuous ones!
Such a body is not to be relied upon by the wise.
This body is like a mass of foam; it cannot be grasped or rubbed.
Zhaò says:
Rubbing and squeezing a mass of foam to reveal its lack of substance serves as a metaphor for contemplating the body’s falsity.
From this point down to the metaphor of lightning, the meaning of emptiness is clarified.
This body is like a bubble; it cannot endure for long.
Zhaò says:
"Not long" seems to clarify the meaning of impermanence.
However, a bubble on water does not endure because it is hollow within and lacks substance; this is merely the meaning of emptiness.
This body is like a mirage, born from craving.
Zhaò said:
"One sees a shimmering heat haze in the distance and is deluded into thinking it is water."
The four great elements, through the views of craving, are delusively taken to be the body.
This body is like a plantain tree; within it there is no solidity.
Zhaò says:
The plantain tree has only leaves and no trunk.
This body is like an illusion, arising from perversion.
Zhaò said:
To perceive illusions as persons and the four great elements as a body is entirely inverted.
This body is like a dream, a false perception.
What is falsely seen in a dream is not real upon waking.
"This body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma.
Kumārajīva said:
"When a physical form obstructs sunlight, the light cannot reach that spot; thus, a shadow appears there."
Because ignorance obstructs true wisdom with the three types of karma, there is this body.
This body is like an echo, belonging to various causes and conditions.
Zhaò said:
The arising of the body from karmic causes is like the production of form and sound from shadows and echoes.
This body is like a floating cloud, changing and perishing in an instant.
Kumārajīva said:
In an instant their colors change, and in a brief moment they vanish.
The body is likewise: in the space of a blink, it undergoes the transformations of youth, old age, sickness, and death.
From being like foam to being like lightning, all serve as metaphors for impermanence.
Whether by way of being insubstantial, or by way of not lasting long, or by way of being unreal, or by way of depending on causes and conditions, he clarifies why things are impermanent.
The following four analogies regarding the four elements illustrate emptiness and non-self.
This body is like lightning; it does not abide for even a single thought-moment.
Sengzhao says:

To say that it changes and perishes without abiding explains impermanence (*anitya*). However, all [these explanations] take its falsity and lack of reality as the reason for its rapid extinction and non-abiding; this is still an explanation of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"This body has no master; it is like the earth.
Kumārajīva said:
"The earth has no permanent master; it belongs to whoever is stronger."

The body likewise has no master; it changes according to circumstances. When illness arrives, it suffers; when death arrives, it perishes. Its aggregation and dispersal follow conditions, and it cannot attain autonomy.

Sengzhao said: "Now, all things and all forms are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). When they exist externally, they constitute earth, wood, mountains, and rivers; when they exist internally, they constitute the four limbs and hundred members. They aggregate to form life and disperse to form death. Life is internal and death is external. Although the internal and external differ, their 'greatness' is no different. Therefore, by using the analogy of the internal and external four great elements, one clarifies the absence of self (*anātman*)."
Just as with external lands, which according to tradition from ancient times until now are occupied by the strong and thus have no permanent owner, so it is with the body.
It is composed of manifold conditions: when conditions combine, it arises; when conditions disperse, it dissolves. How could there be a true sovereign who acts as its eternal master?
"Lord," "Life-force," "Person"—these are four names established for the single meaning of a self.
This body is without self, like fire.
Kumārajīva said:
Burning through forests and wilds with a formidable and fierce reputation, it is like a valiant warrior arraying his forces to achieve victory;
yet, when sought in reality, there is no enemy.
The body is likewise: its movements, actions, and myriad undertakings appear, from the perspective of delusion, as if governed by a master; yet when one traces their origin, there is no self.
Sengzhao said:
To act with unrestrained freedom is called "self.
Yet, externally, the arising and ceasing of fire depends upon fuel; the fire is not self-sufficient.
Fire is not sovereign; fire has no self.
Since external fire lacks a self, the same is true for internal fire.
This body has no life-span; it is like the wind.
Kumārajīva said:
"Though it flutters, fans, and beats, coming and going, it is merely the movement of accumulated breath; there is no enduring life or vitality therein.
The body is also like this: breathing in and out, moving about, and speaking are all activated by means of breath; they possess no vitality."
Zhaò said:
That which exists eternally and does not change is called longevity.
Yet external winds accumulate and blow, causing movement and stillness to be without constancy.
Movement and stillness are impermanent; wind has no life-span.
Since external wind lacks a life-span, the same can be known for internal [winds].
This body is without a self (pudgala) and is like water.
Kumārajīva said:

"To be pure, clear, and limpid is to wash away defilement; to be curved, straight, square, or round is to adapt to the circumstances of the moment. Yet, when sought with sincerity, who is it that acts?"

The body is likewise: its knowing, seeing, advancing, and halting shift in accordance with circumstances; it functions through the conjunction of conditions and proceeds by means of numerical factors. When one examines its causes in detail, there is no person therein.
Sengzhao said:
That which is honored above all things and remains unchanged from beginning to end is called "human.

Water, however, externally benefits all forms; it conforms to squareness or roundness according to the object, and its depth or height varies according to its environment, yet its essence has no fixed form.
Since the substance is not fixed, water has no person.
As there is no person in external water, the same can be known for internal water.
This body is unreal; the four great elements constitute its abode.
Zhaò says:
The four "non-constants" conclude with the preceding section.
From here on, it specifically clarifies the falsity of the body and the various defilements and calamities.
"The four great elements assemble provisionally to form the abode of the spirit; it is not a real home.
This body is empty, being devoid of 'self' and 'what belongs to self.
Kumārajīva said:
Detaching from the self is the emptiness of sentient beings;
detaching from what belongs to the self is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma*).
The preceding four lines provide metaphors for emptiness and non-self; these [lines] state the actual meaning of emptiness and non-self directly.
Sengzhao said:
"The 'I' is the subtle master of the body.
As for 'what belongs to the I,' beyond the self, the body, the state, wealth, wife, children, and all things are entirely what belongs to the I."
The wise person contemplates the body as empty and tranquil within; both [the self and the body] are abandoned.
This body is without cognition, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles.
Kumārajīva said:
To attain knowledge through conceptual synthesis is not true knowledge.
To seek knowledge and fail to find it is to be like a mere shard or pebble.
Zhaò said:
Although the body is capable of contact, it lacks cognition; although internal consciousness is capable of cognition, it lacks contact.
When sought by way of their own intrinsic nature, both are devoid of cognition.
Since they are said to be without cognition, how do they differ from bricks and pebbles?
"This body is without agency; it is moved by the power of the winds.
Kumārajīva said:
"That which has no agent yet performs actions is that which is moved by the winds."
From "ignorance" to "non-action," this further explains the meaning of emptiness and non-self.
Zhaò says:
"All movements and activities are caused by the power of the wind; who is it that acts?"
"This body is impure.
Kumārajīva said:
"Although a srotāpanna has seen the Four Truths, he still remains deluded regarding pure form; therefore, after the four aspects of impermanence, impurity is explained next."
Furthermore, what was previously taught were impermanence, suffering, and non-self; this present teaching concerns the gateway of impurity.
To dismantle the four inversions, these four types of contemplative practice are taught.

Having practiced these contemplations, one is subsequently able to remain unattached to the body; once unattached to the body, one is then able to study the Dharma-body. Therefore, the teaching on revulsion comes first, followed by the teaching on the Dharma-body.
It is filled with filth and impurity. Zao said:
"Thirty-six substances fill its body."
"This body is a deceptive illusion; though it is provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, it will inevitably return to decay and extinction.
Kumārajīva said:
"This clarifies that which is destroyed by impermanence, and is therefore suffering."
From this point downward, all that is said constitutes metaphors for suffering.
It refers to the suffering of calamities and illness.
The section beginning with "the dilapidated well" serves as a general metaphor for the immeasurable sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Sengzhao said:
"Even if one bathes in fragrant water and clothes oneself in the finest garments, if it is not the True, how can it endure for long?
This body is a calamity, a source of a hundred and one ailments and afflictions."
Sengzhao said:

"When one of the four great elements increases or decreases, one hundred and one diseases arise; when all four great elements increase or decrease, four hundred and four diseases manifest simultaneously. Therefore, the body is a confluence of calamities."
"This body is like an abandoned well.
Kumārajīva said:
"An 'abandoned well' (qiūjǐng) refers to a desolate mound and a dried-up well."
In the past, there was a man who committed an offense against the king. Fearing punishment, he fled; the king then ordered a drunken elephant to pursue him.
In his desperate terror, the man threw himself into a dry well.
In a half-well, he found a piece of withered grass and grasped it in his hand.

Beneath it, an evil dragon spat venom toward him; beside him, five poisonous snakes likewise sought to harm him; two rats gnawed at the grass until it was nearly severed; and a great elephant approached from above, intending to seize it.

That person was in extreme suffering and great terror; above him was a tree from which drops of honey occasionally fell into his mouth, and because of the attachment to that taste, he forgot his fear.
The dried-up well is birth and death;
the intoxicated elephant is impermanence;
the venomous dragon is the evil realms.
The five venomous snakes are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The decaying grass is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The two rats, black and white, are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight.
The drop of honey represents the pleasures of the five desires.
One who obtains the drop of honey and forgets their fear is a metaphor for sentient beings who, having obtained the drop of honey that is the five desires, do not fear suffering.
"Pressed by old age.
Zhaor said:
"The spirit dwelling in the body is pressed by old age and death, just as a person in a precarious well is pressed by dragons and snakes."
The source is in another sutra.
This body has no fixed permanence.
Kumārajīva said:
One should reflect that there is the lot of death, for which no fixed time is set;
it is certain that one must die.
Zhaò said:
Although the span of life is not fixed, one cannot avoid undergoing death.
This body is like a venomous serpent.
Zao said:
The four great elements are like four snakes;
they are like enemies and bandits.
Zhaò said:
The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are likened to five thieves;
they are like an empty village.
Kumārajīva said:

In the past, there was a man who offended a king. Desiring to kill him secretly, the king placed four venomous snakes in a chest and ordered him to guard them; furthermore, five hostile bandits drew their swords and stood watch over him.
The spiritual friend told him to run, and the man immediately departed; he entered an empty village and took up residence there.
The spiritual friend spoke again:
"This place is where wicked bandits dwell; if you stay here, in a mere moment the bandits will arrive, and you will lose your life and forfeit your wealth."
"You should quickly abandon it, and you shall attain peace and security.
The man followed these instructions and immediately left it behind.
He then saw a great body of water and bound together a raft to cross over.
Having crossed over, one is secure and free from further afflictions.
The king is a metaphor for Māra;
the casket is a metaphor for the body.
The four snakes are the four great elements (mahābhūta).
The five hostile robbers are the five aggregates (skandha).
The empty village is the six sense bases (āyatana).
The "evil bandits" are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
The "river" is birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

When the good spiritual friend instructs one to run away, it means that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach sentient beings to distance themselves from evil Māras, abandon the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*), and relinquish the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Sentient beings follow the teaching; although they abandon the afflictions of the three evil realms, they have not yet emerged from the various villages and thus remain subject to wicked bandits. Therefore, he further instructs them to board the raft of the Eightfold Noble Path to cross the current of birth and death.
Having crossed over the stream of birth and death, one becomes serene and non-active, free once more from all afflictions.
Zhaò says:
"The six sense-faculties are likened to an empty village; there are authentic proofs for this, and the metaphors appear in other scriptures."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Contemplate the body as being like four poisonous snakes.
This body is impermanent and is constantly being devoured by immeasurable worms."
This body is foul and impure, a prison bound by craving and desire.
This body is terrifying, like a dead dog.
This body is unclean, with its nine orifices constantly discharging filth.

This body is like a city: flesh, blood, sinews, bones, and skin wrap around it; the hands and feet serve as watchtowers and battlements for repelling enemies; the eyes are the apertures; the head is the palace hall; and the king of the mind dwells within.

Such is the city of the body, abandoned by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, yet constantly relished and attached to by foolish ordinary people; within it dwell the rākṣasas of greed, lust, anger, and delusion.
This body is not solid; it is like a reed, an eranda tree, a bubble on the water, or a plantain tree.

This body is impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment, like a flash of lightning, a torrential flood, or a mirage; it is also like drawing on water, where as soon as one draws, it immediately vanishes.
This body is easily destroyed, like a great tree standing on the edge of a steep riverbank.
This body will not last long; it shall be devoured by tigers, wolves, owls, crows, eagles, vultures, and hungry dogs.
What wise person would take pleasure in this body?
It would be easier to contain the waters of the great ocean within the hoofprint of an ox than it would be to fully describe the impermanence, impurity, and foul stench of this body.

One might as well gather the great earth and make it like a jujube fruit, gradually reducing it in size to that of a *ting-li* seed, even down to a single atom; yet one could never fully describe the faults and afflictions of this body. Therefore, one should abandon it as one would discard mucus or spittle.
It is a composite formed by the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas).
Zhaò says:
"Aggregates" refers to the five aggregates.
The elements (dhātu) are the eighteen elements;
the bases (āyatana) are the twelve bases.
These three factors combine provisionally to form the body, which is like an empty village where there is nothing whatsoever to rely upon.
"O virtuous ones!
This [world] is to be weary of and loathe; you should instead delight in the Buddha-body.
Zhaò said:
"We share this same affliction; it has been a source of weariness for us for a long time. We ought to joyfully seek the Buddha-body together.
Why is this? Zhaò said:"
Those who observe superficially claim that the Buddha’s body is merely the excellence of physical form; yet, since it cannot avoid the afflictions of birth and death, cold and heat, why seek it?
This is intended to clarify the ultimate and most wondrous essence of the Dharma-body.
"The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body.
Zhaò says:
"The scripture states that the Dharma-body is the body of empty space."

It is neither born nor unborn, neither has form nor is it without form; it transcends the realm of the three worlds and cuts off the sphere of the conscious mind. It is not encompassed by the aggregates or sense bases, nor can it be reached by words of praise. Cold and heat cannot cause it affliction, and birth and death cannot transform its essence.

Therefore, as for this entity: it is subtle and wondrous, devoid of form, such that it cannot be said to exist; yet it fully responds to the myriad shapes, such that it cannot be said not to exist. It encompasses the eight directions, such that it cannot be called small; it penetrates the finest interstices, such that it cannot be called large. Thus, it is able to emerge from life and enter death, penetrating the transformations of the infinite; it manifests in diverse regions, responding to endless requests.

This is what the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot deliberate upon and what those in their final birth before Buddhahood cannot perceive; how much less could ordinary people, devoid of the eye of wisdom, dare to apply their minds to its midst?
I have merely relied on the sincere words of the sutras to roughly indicate its profound ultimate.

If that is so, then the Dharma-body appears as a celestial being among the heavens and as a human being among humans; how could one possibly abandon the sixteen-foot form nearby while seeking the Dharma-body afar?
Daosheng said:
"As for the Buddha-body, its physical substance is that of the sixteen-foot form."
The body sixteen feet tall emerges from the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Because it is designated by the name of that from which it emerges, it is said to be identical to the Dharma-body.
"Dharma" here carries the sense of being non-contradictory to the ultimate truth.
That which is devoid of non-Dharma meaning is precisely the reality of signlessness (*animitta*).
The "body" (*kāya*) is the essence of this meaning.
While the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is true and real, the sixteen-foot response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is provisional; by what means, then, can this be clarified?

To realize the Dharma is to exhaust delusion forever and eliminate even its semblance; it is wondrously transcendent beyond the three realms and its principle is darkly merged with the formless realm.
Since form is already non-existent, it can manifest as all forms;
since the three realms are utterly severed, it can encompass all realms.
There is nothing that does not manifest form; it is solely through resonance that the response occurs, for the Buddha is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).
As for the magnitude or minuteness of forms, and the length or brevity of lifespans, these are all but shadows and traces used to engage sentient beings; they are not the Buddha’s true reality.
If sentient beings lack the capacity for resonance, then [the Buddha] will not manifest.
It is not that the Buddha does not wish to receive them; rather, because sentient beings do not arrive, they sever their own connection.
If he were to manifest for those who have not arrived, such a thing has never occurred.
It is like the sun shining in the sky while its reflections appear in various vessels; the myriad reflections and myriad forms are all taken up by the vessels—how could it be the sun that does so?
If the vessel lacks water, the reflection will not appear.
It is not that [the Buddha] does not wish to manifest; rather, because the vessel is not yet ready, he simply withdraws himself.
Thus, whether it be the sixteen-foot or the eight-foot form, both are Buddhas within the water of the sentient beings' own minds.
The Buddha is eternally formless; how could there be duality?
Since all prior afflictions arise from having a body, [the teaching] leads one to delight in the Buddha-body.
Nevertheless, as the traces of the Buddha-way intersect with the realm of existence, although there is a distinction between the refined and the coarse, they should not differ regarding impermanence.
To cause them to delight in this, one should clarify its meaning.

Since it is said that this is itself the Dharma-body, it is not merely to make them know that there is no suffering of a physical body; rather, it is the means by which all the illnesses of sentient beings are severed.

This further leads them to delight in the Dharma; the practice of delighting in the Dharma is the cultivation of the lower dharmas. Therefore, those who practice the Dharma attain the Buddha-body, which is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom.
Sengzhao said:
"A body of ultimate subtlety must arise from causes of ultimate subtlety.
Merit and wisdom are the two activities of a Mahāsattva."
These two karmic hindrances are the initial gateway to the myriad practices and the essential passageway to Nirvana; therefore, they are proclaimed as existing.
From this point downward, although various practices are listed separately, they are all practices that are unconditioned and signless.
Because one practices the signless and the unconditioned, the Dharma-body that is thereby accomplished is likewise signless and unconditioned.
It arises from ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Zhaò said:

"The fivefold Dharma-body arises from kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; it arises from generosity, ethical discipline, patience and gentleness, diligent application of energy, meditative concentration, liberation, and samādhi."
Zhaò says:
"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas;
"samādhi" refers to the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).
Liberations refer to the eight liberations;
samādhis refer to the three samādhis.
These are all specific practices of the perfection of dhyāna.
"Extensive learning and wisdom give rise to the various *pāramitās*.
Zhaò says:
"The 'various' refers to the six perfections mentioned above."
Pāramitā, in the language of Qin, means "reaching the other shore.
The other shore is the shore of true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
After attaining non-arising, all the various practices cultivated are entirely in accord with true reality; their essence is no longer subject to differentiation.
It arises from skillful means and arises from the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Zhaò says:
"From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one possesses the six supernormal powers."
Were it not for the six supernormal powers directing their boundless transformations, one could not achieve the ultimate body.
It arises from the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*). Zao said:
The divine eye, the knowledge of past lives, and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows constitute the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā).
They arise from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and from tranquility and insight (śamatha-vipaśyanā).
Kumārajīva said:

When first practicing contemplation, fixing the mind on a single point is called *śamatha* (calm abiding); when stillness reaches its peak, clarity arises, and this clarity is precisely *prajñā* (wisdom), which is termed *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Zhaò says: "Calm abiding is concentration; insight is wisdom."
It arises from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; it arises from the abandonment of all unwholesome dharmas and the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas.
Zhaò said:
"The resolve to certainly sever [defilements] and the aspiration to certainly accumulate [merit]—these two states of mind are the primary pillars of practice.
They arise from truthfulness and arise from non-negligence."
Zhaò said:
"The true roots of goodness from which [virtue] arises, and the meritorious deeds of non-negligence by which it is accomplished—these two states of mind are the essential requisites for practice."
The body of the Tathāgata is born from such immeasurable, pure dharmas.
O noble ones!
Those who wish to attain the Buddha-body and sever all the illnesses of sentient beings should resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Sengzhao said:
"To give rise to the unsurpassed mind is not merely to eliminate one's own afflictions, but also to rescue the afflictions of all beings.

Thus, the Elder Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma to those who had come to inquire after his illness according to their needs, causing countless thousands of people to all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Chapter Three: On Disciples (2–3), Part One. At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself as he lay ill upon his bed:
Sheng said:
"To 'think of one's own illness' means to feel self-pity regarding the thought of being ill.
Now, to have a body is to have illness; this is simply the constant nature of the world."
For one who has realized this, what harm could there be?
Nevertheless, the sons of the wealthy elders of Vaiśālī all went to visit the Buddha and listen to the Dharma.

Since Vimalakīrti’s situation was likewise the same, it would have been reasonable for him to be grieved by his illness; thus, he used the pretext of honoring the Dharma to invite the Buddha to inquire after his ailment.
The World-Honored One possesses great compassion; how could he fail to bestow his pity?
Zhaò said:

"The highest goodness is like water; thus it follows the contours of the low and high. Because it accords with goodness and benevolence, it can accomplish all things through its adaptability without any stinginess."
The time for active goodness has arrived; thus, one meets with the subtle契机 (qí) without missing the mark.
By dwelling in what the multitude detests, one is able to share their same urgency.
The World-Honored One, in his great compassion, will surely deign to inquire after us; through this, the Way shall be propagated, and those rescued will be many.
This was the underlying purpose of manifesting this illness.
Daosheng said:
"That you were prevented from attending to the sublime teachings due to your illness is truly lamentable."
This person is truly pitiable and ought to be approached;
as for this matter of compassion, it is fitting to dispatch someone to offer words of consolation.
Yet the Buddha’s great kindness encompasses all beings universally; since there is currently no messenger, will you not surely take pity on them?

This is likely because ordinary sentiment expects the dispatching of an envoy; how could it be said that one preserves oneself? Rather, it is by distancing oneself from the self that one reaches others.
If the Buddha were to dispatch an envoy, the malady of the aforementioned illness would suddenly transform into great rest.
Is it not likewise the way to return to the natural state?
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately told Śāriputra:
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Kumārajīva said:
"Within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the various Arhats surpasses the mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas;
within the Mahāyāna Dharma, both matters are superior."
Now, because the Śrāvaka teachings are used here to clarify the distinction between the Great and the Small Vehicles, he first summons his disciples.
Among his disciples, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom; therefore, he summons him first.
He appointed those he knew were incapable in order to manifest the extraordinary eloquence of Vimalakīrti and inspire the assembled multitude.
Furthermore, he appointed others so that each might proclaim their own excellence, thereby clarifying that his responsive eloquence and wisdom are versatile and boundless.
The following section concerns "sitting in quietude" (*yànzuò*), which the Sanskrit original calls "restraining body and mind. Zhaò says:

"The Perfected Man suspends his mind and communicates silently; he does not precede his words with physical gestures, for his profound mechanisms respond latently. Thus, he was commissioned to inquire after [the Buddha's] illness."
Śāriputra, because you are the foremost among the five hundred disciples in supreme wisdom, I have first commanded you.

That the Tathāgata knows these people are incapable [of this task] yet still appoints them is intended to manifest the inexhaustible virtue of Vimalakīrti and to inspire a sense of awe and longing within the assembled multitude.
Śāri is the name of his mother;
"putra" (弗) means "son" in the language of Qin.
In India, it is common to name a son after his mother's name.
Zhu Sheng said:
"One who understands the intention grasps the underlying purpose.

That today’s envoy was assigned to return to Mañjuśrī while other persons were appointed for the rest was done by relying on the customary protocol for dispatching envoys, desiring thereby to manifest the virtue of Vimalakīrti through a metaphorical display."
As for virtue being manifested through this: since our encounter took place in the past, you must now highly esteem it. If such esteem is grounded in reason, then that reason is indeed noble.
If you have already submitted to virtue and rely on hearing the principles as being noble, then how could you fail to awaken when the occasion of discussing illness arises?
Now, the principle of dispatching an envoy must proceed from those closest at hand to those further away; therefore, the disciples are mentioned first, followed by the Bodhisattvas.
Since Śāriputra was foremost among those who received the Buddha's teachings directly, he was the first to be commanded.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
Sengzhao said:
"In carrying out the mission of the Buddha, one ought to employ a person of great stature.
The Great Being Vimalakīrti possesses immeasurable wisdom; he is not someone that a mere disciple can match."
Furthermore, since I was once rebuked by you and remained silent, unable to respond, how could I dare lightly accept this mission and incur the reproach of negligence?
Sengsheng said:

"As for the wondrous vehicle, there is no coarse capacity to which it does not reach. What you have now struck upon is precisely its response to the immediate needs of sentient beings; how could there ever be a time when it is incapable of responding to Śāriputra?"
The reason for this inability truly lies herein.
Now, if one wishes to manifest this reality, it must necessarily have a medium through which to be expressed.
Vimalakīrti’s traces reside in his eloquence and quick-wittedness, such that he is feared by the entire kingdom.
In the past, there were principles for engaging in debate, wherein even Śāriputra once showed his defeat before them, considering himself incapable;
who would say this was false? Why is this so?
I recall that once, while I was sitting in meditation beneath a tree in a forest, Vimalakīrti came to me and said:
"O Śāriputra! It is not necessarily this kind of sitting that constitutes 'sitting in meditation'."
Zhaò said:
"The traces of non-bestowal have already been demonstrated previously.
Once, while I was sitting in meditation beneath a grove, Vimalakīrti came by and remarked that my manner of sitting was not correct."
Daosheng said:
"There was a reason for his words; it was not a refusal of the command.
He employed the pretext of not refusing the command in order to draw out and extol the excellence of Vimalakīrti."
To say "it need not necessarily be this" does not mean to say "it is not this," but merely that it need not necessarily be this.
That one does not say "it is not this" means that, in reality, it can serve as a "trap" (筌) for seeking meditative concentration.
It is not necessarily this that causes illness; there are other ways in which illness arises.
If one does not fall ill where one ought to be ill, how can one not be censured?
Śāriputra truly has nothing further to rely upon.

It is fitting that one should guide others through one's own conduct; yet what one practices is precisely what the other is afflicted by. Since Vimalakīrti dwells in a state of insufficiency, it is certainly appropriate to entrust him with this censure.
In that case, Śāriputra’s reputation for being a man of few words has been eclipsed.
As for "sitting in quietude," it refers to the manner of dwelling in seclusion.
Now, one who sits in quietude does not manifest body or mind within the three realms; this is what constitutes sitting in quietude.
Kumārajīva said:
"This chapter clearly elucidates ultimate concentration (*samādhi*) as instruction for those who have not yet attained it; it does not merely clarify emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
