When a Bodhisattva settles the mind in the true realm, consciousness no longer wanders outward, and thus the [dualistic] mind does not manifest."
The body of the Dharma-transformation transcends the triple world; it is the state where both body and mind are entirely hidden, the ultimate pinnacle of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Although the Śrāvaka can conceal the mind within the true Dharma, he is unable to remain unseen by his own body; as long as the body is perceived within the triple world, one remains burdened by external objects.
Therefore, for something to remain hidden while still being manifest is not considered a skillful means of concealment.
It is also said:

at that time, Śāriputra entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), which was able to hide his mind while his body remained visible; it was for this reason that he was criticized.
Sengzhao said:

As for the meditative sitting of the Dharma-body, both form and spirit are extinguished; the Way transcends ordinary realms and lies beyond the reach of sight and hearing. How could it possibly manifest itself within the three realms or cultivate the mind to achieve concentration?

Śāriputra still possesses a physical body born of worldly retribution as well as the mental faculty (manas) born of worldly retribution; therefore, he regards the human world as a source of disturbance and sits in meditation beneath the forest trees. Because he has not yet reached the state where both form and spirit leave no trace, he is subject to this reproach.
Whenever censure arises, its intent lies in providing great benefit; how could it have as its core concern the distinctions of self and other, or right and wrong?
Sheng said:
"To examine the reason why one sits in meditation within the forest is to conceal one's physical form."

If one does not conceal [the mind], it will inevitably be moved by external affairs; therefore, one conceals it to cause it to remain detached from affairs as a means of seeking stability, yet the one who conceals suffers from the fact that their physical form is not concealed.
If one holds that the fault lies in not concealing [one's intentions], yet those who do conceal them are still disturbed by those who do not, then this is not what is meant by "concealment.

One who conceals their form fundamentally desires to hide their intent; if the intent is not hidden, it will inevitably be dragged away by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Therefore, one conceals it so as not to see what is desirable, thereby gaining the means to still desire; however, for the one who conceals, there remains the affliction of the intent not being hidden.
If one clings to the notion that non-concealment is a source of affliction, yet that which is concealed is still disturbed by non-concealment, then it is not truly for the purpose of concealment.

If one can perceive within the three realms that there is no place of non-secrecy or non-concealment, then one will no longer be disturbed by it; this is precisely what constitutes the true meaning of concealment.
To manifest without concealment or hiding, yet to manifest without necessarily emerging from the three realms—this is why it is said that one does not manifest body or mind within the three realms.
To manifest various dignified postures without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—this is true sitting in meditation (*yansuo*).
Kumārajīva said:
"This means that although he has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), he is able to manifest immeasurable transformations to respond to sentient beings.
Sengzhao said:
When those of the Lesser Vehicle enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), their bodies remain like withered wood, devoid of the capacity for movement or function.

When a Great Being enters the meditative absorption of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇasamādhi*), although mental consciousness is eternally extinguished, the body pervades the eight directions; acting in accordance with the capacities of beings, responding to assemblies in infinite ways, and maintaining dignified decorum in every movement and posture—such is the ultimate form of *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation).

The former passage states that he does not manifest body or mind within the three realms, while this passage speaks of manifesting all dignified demeanors (*īryāpatha*). Now, because there is no manifestation, he is able to manifest everything; this absence of non-manifestation is precisely the essence of non-manifestation itself.
I hope that gentlemen who participate in the profound mystery will thereby understand that which unites them and harmonize that which differentiates them.
To manifest the affairs of ordinary people without abandoning the Dharma is what constitutes "sitting in repose."
Sengzhao said:
"The adherents of the Lesser Vehicle are obstructed by the cycle of birth and death, and thus cannot harmonize with the light of the world;

the Great Being (Mahāsattva), however, regards beauty and ugliness as having the same ultimate purpose and views the sacred and the secular as one. Therefore, though he appears as an ordinary person all day long, he is in fact the Dharma all day long."
That Vimalakīrti maintained a household was precisely such a case.
Daosheng said:

"Once one has retired to the forest, one ought to seek meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The method for seeking concentration is first to rectify the body so that it does not move; because it does not move, one does not deviate from concentration, and because the body is rectified, one does not contravene the Way. This is a sublime art for seeking the concentration of the Way."

If one seals [the mind] with what is not correct, such that one moves to rectify it while violating the Way, or remains stationary while being at odds with stillness, one will once again be disturbed by incorrectness and movement; this is not the principle of rectifying the person through immobility.

If one who has not emerged from the meditative absorption of cessation were to manifest various modes of deportment, then the manifestation of deportment would be distinct from the absorption; since there is no such distinction, they do not contradict one another.

Dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) refers to movement; "extinguishing concentration" (*nirodha-samādhi*) refers to the extinction of the mind and its mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). This concentration is the ultimate opposite of the manifestation of movement; therefore, it is singled out for discussion.
If one does not abandon the dharmas of the Path yet manifests the affairs of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), then one does not perceive that the affairs of an ordinary person differ from the Path.
The affairs of an ordinary person are precisely the lack of rectitude in the body.

Regarding the fact that matters concerning the deportment of ordinary persons appear in the subsequent phrase: the point of contention lies here, and therefore they are drawn forward by what precedes.
That the mind dwells neither within nor without—this is called "sitting in meditation" (*yansan*).
Kumārajīva said:
"The sages and saints who collect their minds are called 'internal,' while ordinary people whose thoughts run wild are called 'external.
To say that there is neither internal nor external means that one regards the internal and external with an equal mind."
Sengzhao said:
"The body is an illusory dwelling; why dwell within it?
All phenomena are empty; why regard them as being external?"

Those of the Lesser Vehicle bind their minds within to guard against distracting thoughts; ordinary people scatter their reflections outward because they seek much; the Great Beings observe with equanimity, thus having no reliance on either the internal or the external.
Dongsheng said:
"Once the body is upright and motionless, one should next collect the mind.
As for the method of collecting the mind: if the object of focus wanders away, one should immediately collect it and bring it back."
To think of departing to engage with external objects is called "roaming outward"; to restrain oneself and return to the self is called "abiding within.

If one regards roaming outward as distraction and abiding within as concentration, one is once again being driven by the internal and external; this is not the intended meaning of collecting the mind.
When the mind does not abide within, there is no interior wherein it may abide.
Nor does it exist without; there is no exterior wherein it may dwell.
Only then does it cease to roam.
"Unshakable amidst all views.
Kumārajīva said:
"If one takes views as being movement, then that view itself is a state of dwelling."
To practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is what constitutes "sitting in meditation.
Zhaò says:
"Various views" refers to the sixty-two kinds of false views.
Generally, those who perceive views as views must first abandon all views in order to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

However, the Mahāsattva perceives that the true nature of all views is itself the factors of enlightenment; therefore, he does not abandon views at one extreme while cultivating the factors of enlightenment at the other.
Sheng said:
"The meaning of gathering the mind in mindfulness requires that one attain its Way.
What is this Way?"
It lies in right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Right contemplation is precisely the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
This contemplation of the thirty-seven factors is the intention for perceiving principle; because one perceives through conformity to principle, the mind can abide therein.
If one values the contemplation that attains the principle, yet is instead deluded by that very contemplation, then one loses the principle; this is not true contemplation.

If one remains unmoved amidst all views, this is precisely what it means to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. In this way, one does not perceive the thirty-seven factors as distinct from these views, and thus there is no further delusion.
To be immovable is to not depart.
"Various views" refers to false views.
To enter nirvana without severing the afflictions—this is true sitting in meditation.
Kumārajīva said:
"Afflictions are themselves nirvāṇa; therefore, one does not wait for them to be severed before entering it.
Sengzhao said:
The seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) afflict and disturb sentient beings; therefore, they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*).

The true nature of these afflictions is itself *nirvāṇa*. Those whose power of wisdom is strong perceive that the afflictions are themselves entry into *nirvāṇa*, without waiting for them to be severed before entering it.
Daosheng said:
"If one has already contemplated the principle and attained its nature, then bondage should have been exhausted and nirvana achieved.
If you must regard nirvana as something precious and desire to grasp it, then you will once again be bound by nirvana."
If one were to enter *nirvāṇa* without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), then one would not perceive *nirvāṇa* as distinct from the afflictions, and thus there would be no bondage.
These two preceding lines are also subject to the same fault mentioned below; they are drawn upward by what follows.
If one can sit in this manner, it is what the Buddha has authorized.
Zhaò said:
"This is the seat of the Dharma of equality, authorized by the Buddha."
"How can this compare to the seated meditation of the benevolent one, which relies upon conditions?
At that time, our World-Honored One heard these words and remained silent, unable to offer a reply.
Sengzhao said:
The principle has emerged beyond expectation, and I do not know how to respond to it.
Therefore, I am unable to venture to visit him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
Kumārajīva said:
"Maudgalyāyana is a Brahmin surname; his personal name is Kolita.
Kolita is the name of a tree deity; because he was obtained through seeking that deity, he was named after it."
From birth he possessed great wisdom; therefore he was named Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Zhaò said:
Maudgalyāyana was the foremost in supernormal powers among the disciples; he was born of the Brahmin caste.
His clan name was Kauṇḍinya and his personal name was Kolita.
"Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness," [the Buddha] said.
Śāriputra replied:
Now, individuals possess varying strengths and weaknesses, and their capabilities differ.
While Śāriputra himself was incapable, why must it necessarily be so for others?
Therefore, he did not suppress [the truth] but simply did not inform him.
Furthermore, this serves as a means to further propagate the excellence of Vimalakīrti.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, when I entered the great city of Vaiśālī, I was preaching the Dharma to the laypeople in the midst of the streets and alleys.
Śrī said:

"The layman possesses wisdom and sharp faculties; he should have heard directly of the true nature of reality (dharmatā). However, Maudgalyāyana had not yet discerned the layman's faculties and, relying on conventional methods of teaching, first used the seven matters of giving and precepts to awaken him."

When a layperson hears that practicing giving and observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven and the enjoyment of blessings, they give rise to the notion of a "sentient being. Once this notion of a sentient being has arisen, they falsely produce various conceptual marks regarding all phenomena. Therefore, one first establishes the teaching to clarify that there are no sentient beings, and subsequently destroys these various marks; only then can one return from what was deluded and respond to one's fundamental consciousness.
Zhaò says: The scripture does not record what was said therein.
Judging by the subsequent tone of reproach, it must have been a discourse on conditioned wholesome dharmas, such as the categories of giving and precepts.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me:
"O Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
When preaching the Dharma to lay householders, you should not preach as the Venerable One has just done."
Sengzhao said:

"Vimalakīrti observed that the laymen present were ready to hear the meaning of emptiness; however, Maudgalyāyana failed to properly discern their spiritual capacities and instead guided them with teachings concerning existence. It was for this reason that Vimalakīrti rebuked him."
Daosheng said:
"The purpose of preaching the Dharma is fundamentally to lead others to value the Dharma, not to eliminate it.
Since they have come to value it, they have become attached to it and thus delight in the Lesser Vehicle."
Those who delight in the minor [teachings] desire exclusively to escape suffering, yet they contravene its fundamental basis.
Those who are dogmatically attached deviate from the principles of the Dharma; such deviation truly arises from their own subjective sentiments.
Furthermore, those who preach the Dharma may incur the suspicion of having dull faculties, and there is also the appearance of preaching in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma.
Since laypeople do not possess the practice of seeking the Way, it would be fortunate if one did not preach the principles for abandoning the secular world, thereby injuring their fundamental nature.

A layperson harbors greed and attachment; they cannot be made to see the nobility of the Dharma so as to shift their attachments. Therefore, it is said that one should not preach the Dharma to white-robed laypeople as you have done.
Now, one who preaches the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma.
Sengzhao says:
"Dharma" refers to the true Dharma of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
This follows the text where the meaning of the Dharma is naturally established.
"The Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilements of sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said:
The defilements of sentient beings refer to the twenty kinds of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Through false views they grasp at signs, yet phenomena ultimately possess no signs; since the principle contradicts such views, it is said that they are "detached" from them.
The chapter begins by clarifying ultimate emptiness through two meanings:
first, being free from characteristics; second, being free from views.
Because those who are deluded claim that there are characteristics, it is explained that there are no characteristics by means of being free from characteristics.

Although the deluded give rise to false views, within each and every dharma there is no such view; therefore, by means of "leaving behind views," it is clarified that those characteristics perceived by false views do not exist.

From this point onward, whenever it is said that there is "no name and no description," or that one "leaves behind consciousness and leaves behind contemplation," these cases are analogous to "leaving behind views."
Sengzhao said:
From this point onward, the true meaning of the Dharma is elucidated.
For if one clings to sentient beings, one defiles the true Dharma; if one realizes that the Dharma has no sentient beings, then that defilement naturally departs.
Because sentient beings habitually cling to and overvalue the self, this treatise first clarifies its non-existence.
[The Master] says:
From here on below is the fundamental principle of the Great Treatise (*Mahā-śāstra*).
The Dharma is of two kinds: the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Although the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena is truly not different, there are differences in the ease or difficulty of attaining awakening for those who are deluded; therefore, they are distinguished.
Sentient beings, by means of their collective aggregation, form a physical body; since this unreal nature is readily perceptible, [the teaching concerning it] is easy.
Dharmas, being independent, largely approach the realm of ultimate reality; therefore, [the teaching concerning them] is difficult.
Now, first, the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) is clarified.
Regarding the phrase "the dharma has no sentient beings," it means that the dharma is characterized by the absence of sentient beings.
The phrase "because it is free from the defilements of sentient beings" is the explanation thereof.
To say that sentient beings spontaneously give rise to attachments is not in accordance with principle.
When the emotions do not follow principle, they are called defilements.
If one attains the vision of principle, these defiled emotions will necessarily be exhausted.
By verifying this through the realization of freedom from defilement, one knows that there are no sentient beings.
"Sentient beings" arise from the convergence of manifold phenomena; they are designated as a single sovereign master by means of names.
Phenomena possess no self, for they are free from the defilement of self.
Vimalakīrti said:
"The 'self' is simply the Lord of Sovereignty.
Phenomena have no life-span, for they are free from birth and death."
Sengzhao said:
"Birth and death are merely the beginning and end of life.
Once the beginning and end are transcended, then life and its duration cease to exist."
The various terms for "detachment" (li) are all alternative names for emptiness (śūnyatā).
Daosheng said:

"To exist in the world is called 'life' (ming), and to live for a hundred years is called 'longevity' (shou); thus, those who possess these are also given the names 'one with life' and 'one with longevity.'"
Life-span is the retribution of past karma and the law of birth and death.
Where there is the defilement of life-span, there is the burden of birth and death.
To be free from such burdens and thereby verify the absence of life-span is what constitutes clear understanding.

The reason for not speaking of "life-span" but rather of "birth and death" is that life-span is what human sentiment cherishes; if one were to hear of being separated from it, one would certainly find no joy.
Birth and death, however, are what human sentiment loathes; if one hears of being separated from them, one will surely rejoice. Thus it is.
In the Dharma there is no person, for the past and future limits are severed.
Zhaò says:
Heaven produced the myriad things, and among them it holds humanity most precious.
That which remains unchanged from beginning to end is called a "person" (*pudgala*).
Therefore, non-Buddhists take the person to be the self (*ātman*), claiming it is unchanging from beginning to end.

If a phenomenon were severed at its prior and subsequent limits, it would be ever-new and never the same; if it were ever-new and never the same, there would be nothing that does not change. If there were nothing that does not change, then the "person" would no longer exist.
Sheng said:
"A human being is that which possesses spirit beyond the designation of wood or earth; it is that which comes and goes between life and death.
While coming and going are indeed endless, when these cycles are severed, one becomes all the more joyful."
"The Dharma is eternally quiescent, because it extinguishes all marks.
Zhaò says:
"Now, where there are marks, there are divergent forms; once divergent forms have taken shape, right and wrong arise. Once right and wrong have arisen, how can there be quiescence?"
When all marks have ceased, there is nothing that is not tranquil.
Sengsheng said:
"The first four lines refer to the emptiness of sentient beings."
The following twenty-six phrases refer to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
"Quiescent" (*jiran*) signifies the meaning of being tranquil and devoid of activity.
"Characteristics" (*xiang*) refers to the appearance of activity.
Sentient beings are easy to understand; when they become attached to them, their delusion is heavy, and thus one clarifies it by means of the defilements within.
The Dharma is difficult to awaken to; when one becomes attached to it, the delusion is light, and thus one manifests it by means of what is deluded about externally.
The Dharma is free from marks because it has no object of perception (*ālambana*).
Zhaò says:
"Perception" refers to the mind's perception.
Marks are the reflections of the mind.
Indeed, because there are conditions, there are marks; without conditions, there are no marks.
Dharmas have no names, for they transcend all speech and language.
Zhaò said:
"Names arise from speech; when speech is cut off, who provides the name?
Dharmas have no verbal expression, for they are free from vitarka and vicāra."
Sengzhao said:
"Vitarka and vicāra are coarse states of mind and the foundation of speech.
Because the true Dharma is without marks (animitta), vitarka and vicāra naturally depart; once vitarka and vicāra have departed, there is no further verbal expression."
From the second dhyāna upward, because there is no vitarka (applied thought) or vicāra (sustained thought), it is called the "silent sagehood" of the noble ones.
Since dharmas have no form or characteristics, they are like empty space.
Zhaò said:
The myriad dharmas have myriad forms; the myriad forms have myriad characteristics.
Dharmas are free from frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), for they are ultimately empty.
Zhaò said:
The true realm is beyond words; all verbal discourse is merely empty play.
It transcends the realm of speech and is ultimately empty.
Phenomena possess no "mine," for they are free from the notion of "mine."
Sengzhao said:
The preceding passage directly clarifies non-self; this passage clarifies non-mine.
All dharmas other than the self are termed "mine."
Dharmas are without discrimination, for they are free from all consciousnesses.
Zhaò says:
"Discrimination arises from consciousness."
Dharmas have no counterpart, because they do not exist in mutual dependence.
Zhaò says:
All dharmas arise through mutual dependence, just as length and shortness are defined in relation to one another.
The Dharma does not belong to causes, nor does it reside in conditions.
Kumārajīva said:
"That which possesses superior power is the cause; that which is submerged by power is the condition."
Zhaò says:
That which precedes and follows one another in mutual production is the cause (*hetu*).
That which manifests and assists one another in mutual completion is the condition (*pratyaya*).
All phenomena (dharmas) are established only by depending upon conditions and mutual reliance.
If one observes that a phenomenon does not exist within its conditions, then that phenomenon does not belong to its causes.
Sengsheng said:
"Condition" (*hetu*) refers to that which previously lacked the thing itself, yet arises from it.
"Conditioning cause" (*pratyaya*) refers to that which originally possessed its own constituent part, yet arises from it.
Since "condition" fundamentally takes "arising" as its meaning, if it now cannot fail to arise, how can it be said to be "capable of arising"?
In this case, the cause would fail to function as a cause.
Because causes are proximate, they are difficult to understand; because conditions are remote, they are easy to comprehend.
Now, by explaining the difficult through the easy, it becomes easy to understand.
Because it is proximate, it is said to "belong to"; because its conditions are remote, it is said to "reside in.
The dharmas are identical to the dharma-nature, for they enter into all phenomena.
Zhaò says:
Suchness (tathatā), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—these three emptinesses are of one and the same reality.
However, because there are differences in the depth of their contemplative application, they are established with three distinct names.
When one first perceives the reality of dharmas—just as seeing a tree from a distance and knowing for certain that it is a tree—it is called "suchness."
When one's vision of the Dharma becomes increasingly profound—like approaching a tree and knowing that it is a particular kind of wood—it is called the *dharmatā*.
When one exhaustively realizes the true nature of phenomena—like fully knowing the number of a tree’s roots, trunk, branches, and leaves—it is called the *bhūtakoṭi*.
These three have never failed to be trees; it is only due to perception that they appear as distinct.
The True Dharma spoken of is identical to these three kinds of emptiness.
As for "entering all dharmas," who could possibly enter the diverse characteristics of all dharmas?
"That which universally enters all phenomena—is it not solely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?
Daosheng said:
"The nature of phenomena is the fundamental constituent of all phenomena."
That which exists by virtue of conditions is a provisional existence; that which is provisionally existent does not exist by way of its own nature.
Since existence is not inherent in its nature, this is precisely its fundamental state.
Thus, the phenomena (*dharma*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are identical in principle though different in name; therefore, they are said to be the same.
Since their nature ought to be the same, they are described as being identical.
While all phenomena are distinct, when they enter into the realm of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), they are unified and integrated as one.
To unify the multitude through the One is the means by which they accord with the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The Dharma conforms to Suchness (*tathatā*), for there is nothing to which it conforms.
Zhaò says:
The Dharma is itself without-dharma; who then could follow Suchness?
Because there is nothing to follow, it is called "following Suchness.
Sengsheng said:
That which is "as it is" (tathatā) is such that there is nothing it does not accord with.
If there were anything to follow, it would be different; thus one could not truly follow it.
Only when there is absolutely nothing to follow can one truly follow.
It is precisely because names differ while the reality remains the same that the term "conformity" (suí) is employed.
Just as it is appropriate to speak of "conforming," one therefore uses the word "conformity.
The Dharma abides in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Another version states: "The Dharma is identical to Suchness, the Dharma-nature, and the Reality-limit. Kumārajīva said:
"These three are one and the same reality.
Because there are degrees of depth during the time of contemplation, they have these three names."

When one first perceives its reality, it is called "suchness" (tathatā); as it becomes increasingly profound, it is called "nature" (prakṛti); when its limits are fully exhausted, it is called "the limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi).

Because those who are newly trained are led astray by the six sense-faculties and their minds change according to external objects—perceiving sameness during contemplation but perceiving difference upon emerging—it is clarified that all dharmas share these three characteristics.
"Because it is unmoved by any extremes.
Kumārajīva said:
"Therefore, existence and non-existence are not the middle; in reality, they constitute the extremes."

To say that something exists when it does not exist, and to say that something does not exist when it does exist—despite the arising of all peripheral defilements, these cannot turn it into something else; therefore, it is said that the various extremes do not move it.
Zhaò said:
"Because there is a limit, there is movement; if there were no limit, what would there be to move?
The limit of the limitless is called the 'limit of reality' (bhūtakoṭi); this is where the true Dharma abides."
Dongsheng said:
"The extremes of existence and non-existence cannot alter the dharma-nature to cause it to change; thus, it is boundless.
The limit of the boundless is called the 'actual limit' (bhūtakoṭi)."
That which is immovable is that which abides herein.
Phenomena are without fluctuation because they do not rely upon the six sense objects.
Zhaò said:
Sentient emotion relies upon the six sense objects, and thus there is the movement of restlessness; the Dharma is fundamentally without reliance, and thus there is no agitation.
Sengsheng said:
"The six sense objects each have their respective counterparts, and as these phenomena compete and vie with one another, there is the principle of agitation."
Once it has already been moved, it becomes something else; it is not its true reality.
Dharmas have no coming or going, for they never abide.
Sengzhao said:

If dharmas were eternally abiding, then as they pass from the future to the present and from the present to the past, these dharmas would traverse the three periods of time and thus possess coming and going.
Because phenomena do not abide permanently, phenomena have neither coming nor going.
Phenomena accord with emptiness.
Sengsheng said:
To cling to existence is to deviate from principle and distance oneself from it; therefore, one should accord with emptiness and conform to signlessness.
Sengsheng said:
Emptiness appears as if it possesses the characteristic of existence.

However, if emptiness were to exist, then emptiness would become a form of existence, which would not be what is meant by "emptiness"; therefore, it is said to be "without characteristics" (animitta).
Since one has already conformed to emptiness, one should accordingly follow signlessness and accord with non-action.
Zhaò said:
This is the same as the three types of emptiness.
Daosheng said:
"To 'dispel' [the notion of] accomplishment is to have a semblance of intentional activity; since intentional activity is irrational, it is called 'non-activity' (wu zuo)."
Having already conformed to emptiness and followed signlessness, one should then mysteriously accord with this.

Phenomena transcend beauty and ugliness; phenomena have no increase or decrease; phenomena have no arising or ceasing; phenomena have no place of return; phenomena surpass the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Sengzhao said:
"Transcending the ordinary realm, it is beyond the reach of the six sensory faculties.
The Dharma has no high or low; the Dharma eternally abides, unmoving."
Sengzhao said:
"The true Dharma abides eternally; even sages and worthies cannot alter it.
The Dharma is detached from all contemplative practices."
Zhaò said:
"The Dharma is fundamentally without marks; it is not something seen through the practice of contemplation. Is it not only through non-contemplation that one sees it?
O, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
