Knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings, one gives Dharma teachings as appropriate, thereby initiating the activity of wisdom (*jñāna-karman*).
Zhaò says:
"The myriad practices of the Mahāyāna are divided into two types of activity; since wisdom serves as the hallmark of practice, the activity of wisdom is established separately."
Because all conditioned phenomena follow one another, merit and virtue are established as a whole.
Whatever is cultivated and established is not accomplished by a single karma alone;
yet, in various sutras, the characteristics of cultivating a pure land are linked with merit and virtue.
Knowing that the teaching of the Dharma is bound to the activity of wisdom—
this merely emphasizes the predominance of its function, yet it has never been devoid of the other activities.
Knowing all dharmas as neither to be grasped nor abandoned, one enters the gate of the single mark and gives rise to the activity of insight.
Zhaò said:
"To decisively examine and investigate the principles is called wisdom (jñāna); to direct the mind toward discernment is called insight (prajñā).
One first resolves the state of sentient beings and stabilizes the contemplation of the characteristics of all dharmas, and only then preaches the Dharma; therefore, this is linked with wisdom."
Now, by constructing the mind to discern the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa) so as to enter through a single gate, one is bound to wisdom (prajñā).
An alternative version reads "the karma of knowledge (jñāna) and the karma of wisdom (prajñā)," to which Kumārajīva remarked:
"Between these two types of karma, wisdom is superior in its clarity; therefore, there are these two kinds of discernment."

To personally perceive the Dharma within is called wisdom (*prajñā*); to know the mental characteristics of external sentient beings with certainty and without doubt, and to preach the Dharma for them, is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
This brings about the severance of all afflictions.
Kumārajīva said:
"This is precisely the karma that obscures wisdom.
It constitutes all manner of hindrances."
Śīkṣānanda said:
"Returning to the two karmas of merit and wisdom—when these two karmas are complete, all obstacles of sin are eliminated.
The latter two lines also summarize these two karmas."
All unwholesome dharmas give rise to all wholesome karma.
Zhaò says:
"There is no good that is not cultivated; therefore, there is no evil that is not severed."
"Because one attains all wisdom and all wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood.
Kumārajīva said:
"The Buddha-dharma is of two kinds: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane."
That which transcends the world is called the dharma that assists the path to Buddhahood.
Zhaò says:
"All wisdom is the activity of knowledge (jñāna-karman), and all wholesome dharmas are the activity of virtue (guṇa-karman)."
The dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood are the various untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of the Mahāyāna.
The two activities of wisdom and merit are not accomplished by means of what is tainted; those who accomplish them must necessarily do so by means of the dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood.
Śāriputra said:
"If all wisdom and all wholesome dharmas are taken as the factors that assist the path to Buddhahood, then this Dharma-giving assembly will surely be accomplished.
It is thus, son of good family!"
This constitutes the assembly for the gift of Dharma. Zao said:

"If one can fully embody the aforementioned dharmas, then their dark, moistening influence will be boundless. Such an assembly does not limit itself to a single direction; such a gift does not limit itself to the physical form. Because it does not limit itself to the physical form, its wondrous preservation extends to the spirit; because it does not limit itself to a single direction, the assembly encompasses all. This may be called the Great Gift and the Great Assembly."
If a bodhisattva abides in this assembly of the gift of Dharma, they are a great donor.
Śāriputra said:
"There is nothing that such a one does not give to the ultimate degree."
They are also fields of merit for all the world.
Kumārajīva said:
"If one practices the giving of material wealth, one is merely called a donor; one is not called a field of merit."
If one practices the gift of Dharma, they are called both a donor and a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Sengzhao says:

A "field of merit" means that when people plant blessings within me, I am free from the weeds and tares of defiled conduct; thus, others obtain immeasurable retributive fruits—this is what constitutes a field of merit.
Huisheng said:
"It is easy to be a donor, but difficult to be a recipient of offerings.
One must possess virtue that is truly capable of bringing about blessings; only then is it so."
“World-Honored One!
When Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, two hundred people from among the assembly of brahmins [attained realization].
Kumārajīva said:
Since they employ their ritual laws and possess merit, virtue, and wisdom, they are appointed as the presiding masters of the assembly.
All of them have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, my mind attained purity.
Zhaò said:
"All mental burdens were entirely removed, and one attains pure faith."
Exclaiming that it was unprecedented, he prostrated himself at Vimalakīrti’s feet and offered him a necklace worth hundreds of thousands of coins.
Vimalakīrti said,
"If this object remains after seven days of giving, it shall be considered most precious."
As for the aforementioned Vimalakīrti, he manifested a disposition that highly esteemed the gift of the Dharma and was unwilling to accept [the offering].
Kumārajīva said:
"Originally, my intention was to preach the Dharma, and furthermore, I wished to censure the giving of material wealth; harboring these two thoughts, I did not accept it.
I said: 'Householder!'"
"I pray that you will surely accept it and give it as you wish.

Vimalakīrti then accepted the necklace, divided it into two portions, took one portion and gave it to the lowliest beggar in this assembly, and took the other portion and offered it to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.
Zhaò says:

"The preceding section describes advancing directly through the gift of Dharma, yet has not yet reached the state where the mind of giving is equalized. Therefore, it describes the giver reaching the highest while exhausting the lowest to clarify that the mind of giving must be impartial; thus, the intention of giving lies in accomplishing virtuous merit."
The entire assembly saw the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa of the land of Prabhāsa.
Kumārajīva said:

"Because that Buddha’s majestic virtue is preeminent and his land is pure, he intends to inspire the assembly to give rise to a superior aspiration; therefore, he first offers a gift and subsequently causes them to see [the land]."
Furthermore, he saw pearl necklaces above that Buddha transform into a jeweled pavilion supported by four pillars.
Kumārajīva said,
"This is the manifestation of the wondrous future retribution for Śubhavyūha."
The four sides are magnificently adorned without obstructing one another.
Master Sheng said:
"To divide it into two parts is intended to clarify their equality."
He manifested supernatural powers to verify the gift of Dharma.
He transformed it into a precious four-pillared terrace; how could such a thing be accomplished by the gift of material wealth?
This is the nature of the assembly for the gift of Dharma; therefore, there is nothing it cannot encompass.
When Vimalakīrti had manifested these supernatural transformations, he spoke as follows:
"If a donor gives with an impartial mind to even the lowliest beggar, it is equivalent to the field of merit of the Tathāgata."
Kumārajīva said:

"One gives to the Buddha because the field is supreme, and thus the mind is profound; one gives to the poor because their condition is one of suffering, and thus compassion is deep. Therefore, although the fields of merit have different characteristics, the resulting retribution is the same."
To be without discrimination and equal to great compassion, seeking no karmic reward—this is what is called being fully endowed with the gift of Dharma.
Zhaò said:

"If one can treat the honorable and the humble as equal and act with a single intent toward rewards, practicing giving through impartial compassion, only then is one fully endowed with the gift of Dharma."
Sheng said:
"To apply one's mind in this way is not the giving of material wealth;
it is precisely how one fulfills the assembly for the gift of Dharma."
The most lowly beggar in the city, seeing this supernatural power and hearing what was said, all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.

In this manner, each of the bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words spoken by Vimalakīrti, and all said, "I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
Zhaò says:
"The thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas all spoke of the conditions for their inability [to go], but the text does not record them in full.
(Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Volume Four)
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Five, composed by Śramaṇa Shi Zhaoyao of the Later Qin.
Chapter Five: Mañjuśrī Inquires after the Illness. Chapter Five: Mañjuśrī Inquires after the Illness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī.
Zhaò said:
"Mañjuśrī" means "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) in the language of Qin.
The Sūtra says: "He has already attained Buddhahood; his name is the Honored One Dragon-Species (Nāga-jāti).
Mañjuśrī, go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That superior man is difficult to respond to.
Kumārajīva said:
Your words surpass even mine, let alone those of the various worthies.
This is likely due to the depth of your long-standing affection; how could it be anything more than that?
Zhaò said:
Why must thirty-two thousand not be capable? Why must Mañjuśrī alone be the foremost?

My view is that the Supreme Person employs strategies without fixed form; his traces differ whether hidden or manifest. Thus, he alternately appears as long or short, merely responding to the conditions of sentient beings.
Who would dare to determine their relative superiority or inferiority, or to discern their strengths and weaknesses?

Mañjuśrī, intending to harmonize the minds of the assembly and fulfill his mission, first extolled the virtues of Vimalakīrti to inspire the multitude with the thought that such a person is difficult to encounter.
"That person is a venerable leader among men; it would be difficult to offer him a response. I shall instead receive the Buddha’s sacred instructions and go to inquire after his illness.
He has profoundly penetrated the reality of suchness (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Zhaò said:
"The true nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is difficult to fathom, yet he was able to penetrate it deeply and skillfully expound the essential points of the Dharma.
Kumārajīva said:

This phrasing is not convenient; according to the original sūtra, it should state that "he expounds the Dharma with essential words," meaning that concise and essential speech can resolve complex principles.
Zhaoluo said:
"He is skilled at using brief words to present many meanings; this praises his excellence in grasping the essential purpose of expounding the Dharma."
His eloquence was unimpeded and his wisdom was unhindered.
Zhaò said:
"His verbal eloquence responded perfectly and without obstruction; his wisdom was all-pervasive and without hindrance."
"He fully knows all the ritual methods of the bodhisattvas.
Kumārajīva said:
"This refers to supernatural transformations and various modes of dignified conduct."
"There is no secret treasury of the Buddhas that one cannot enter.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is as stated in the *Guhyakapada Sūtra*: it refers to body, speech, and mind."
Sengzhao said:
"Nearing the knowledge of the Bodhisattva's ritual protocols, one enters far into the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
'Secret treasury' refers to the secret treasury of the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind."
"Subduing the various māras.
Zhaò says:
"The various māras" refers to the four māras.
Regarding "wandering through supernormal powers" (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*), Kumārajīva said:
"Supernormal transformations constitute 'wandering'; because they attract sentient beings toward oneself and are not ultimate reality, they are called 'play' (*krīḍā*)."
Furthermore, although supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are great, those capable of them may easily master them; for me, they are no difficulty, being like a mere play.
It is also said that within these supernatural powers, one is skillfully able to enter, abide in, and emerge from them with sovereign mastery and without obstruction.
Sengzhao said:
"Those who roam through and penetrate the transformative teachings take them as their own delight.
Their wisdom and skillful means have already attained liberation."
Sengzhao said:
"To exhaust the application of wisdom and bring the path of skillful means to its ultimate end is what is called 'deliverance' (*tuo*).
Nevertheless, one should follow the holy intent of the Buddha and go there to inquire after his illness."
Sengzhao said:
"His virtue is such that I am not fit to face him.
I must await the Buddha’s sacred instructions before proceeding."
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others within the assembly all thought to themselves:
"Now that these two great beings, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, are conversing together, they will surely discourse upon the sublime Dharma."
At that moment, there were eight thousand bodhisattvas and five hundred śrāvakas.
Kumārajīva said:
"The other śrāvakas focused their minds solely on escaping suffering and did not seek the profound Dharma; therefore, they were not included in this enumeration."
Five hundred disciples had deeply penetrated wisdom and delighted in hearing the profound Dharma; this was why they traveled together.
Hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all wished to follow them.
Zhaò said:
Since the Great Being’s supreme assembly must surely contain wondrous teachings, I wish to join you in presenting them.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the various bodhisattvas, the great disciples, and the hosts of devas and humans, entered the great city of Vaiśālī, surrounded by those who paid him respectful homage.
Zhaò said:
"The Āmra Garden is outside the city, while the chamber of Vimalakīrti is inside the city.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself:"
"Now Mañjuśrī has arrived with a great assembly.
He then used his supernatural powers to empty the room and remove everything within it.
Kumārajīva said:
Desiring to clarify the fundamental principle, he manifests the appearance of emptiness to inspire awakening.

In the utmost reverence and presentation of offerings, one must accord with what [the recipient] finds most at ease; since Mañjuśrī delights in the stillness of the void, he responds to him with emptiness.
Sengsheng said:
"The one who gives rise to this thought does so because an empty room is used to demonstrate a disposition of receptive openness.
Since 'existence' departs, there is emptiness; thus, by subtly employing this, the fundamental tenet is indicated."
Those who manifest supernatural powers are the servants of mindfulness,
as are all the attendants.
Sheng said:
If one fears that it might interfere with those already attending upon him, it must be taken separately.

Furthermore, as for the essence of our doctrine, its fundamental purpose is the lack of abandonment toward all living beings; if one does not forsake them, there are none who are not being attended to.
He prepared only a single couch and lay upon it as if ill.
Sengzhao said:
"The manifestation of illness arose because the matter required it at this time."
He went to an empty room to attend to Huiyuan with words of inquiry, the evidence for which will appear later.
He provided only a single bed, which was the origin of the practice of borrowing seats.
Huiyuan said:
The rooms are numerous and small; even the beds would be an obstruction.
Furthermore, sitting, reclining, walking, and standing are fundamentally suited to the human body's needs; one should provide for them as required—why must they be prepared in advance?
If one removes it by this means, how could it be said that [the teaching] is not extended?
It is precisely because there are guests for whom it is intended.
As for establishing it in reality to await those who require it, it is to manifest spiritual power as an expression of the merit of explaining the principle.
Since his merit was beyond measure, it was verified that what he had said was true.
When Mañjuśrī entered his house, he saw that the room was empty and devoid of all possessions, with only a single bed for him to sleep upon alone.
Śāriputra said,
"Those who see him grasp his essential meaning.
At that time, Vimalakīrti spoke:
"Welcome, Mañjuśrī.
Kumārajīva said,
"If I remained silent and spoke no word, then the roles of host and guest would not be harmonized."
The words of praise, "Welcome," clarify that when a guest arrives for a meeting, the host receives them with open-minded receptivity.
It is to come without the appearance of coming; it is to see without the appearance of seeing.
Sengzhao said:
This is intended to clarify that the movements and postures of a Mahāsattva of the Dharmakāya do not deviate from the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Although the true mark does not come, it comes by means of this; although the true mark is invisible, it is seen through its marks by means of this.
To come without coming and to see without seeing—such is the Dharma-body; what excellence could surpass this!
Sengsheng said:
"Since you take the realization of the principle as your concern, when you come, it is manifested as the coming of that which possesses the characteristic of non-coming."
"There is that which comes with the characteristic of not coming; this is the ultimate excellence of the good.
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is."
"Householder!
That which has come does not come again; that which has gone does not go again. He said:
"Thus" refers to the aforementioned principle. "If" means "even if.
"Coming" cannot manifest itself as "not coming."
Since it has already come, it does not come again; thus, the fact that coming is itself the mark of non-coming is manifest.
As for its essence being without merit, how could I possess any goodness? Why is this so?
That which comes has nowhere from which it comes; that which goes has nowhere to which it goes.
Sheng said:
"Coming fundamentally arises from non-coming. If that which comes has no place from which to come, how much less can that which has already come come again?"
This clarifies the characteristic of "coming" by means of its contrast with "going.
That which has been seen can no longer be seen. Zhaò says:
To clarify that there is no characteristic of coming or going is to fulfill what is praised by the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti).
Indeed, the perception of the characteristics of coming and going is merely a provisional designation based on causes and conditions.
That which has not yet come does not come, and that which has already come does not come again.
Since that which has already departed and that which has not yet arrived cannot come or go, how could there be coming or going?
The same applies to seeing.
As for the various subtle arguments concerning this, one should seek them in the various treatises.
Dongsheng said:
"Since the preceding text has already provided a full account, I shall not elaborate further.
Let us set this matter aside for now."
Sengzhao said:
"Although I longed for his subtle words, my mission had not yet been fulfilled; therefore, I temporarily suspended my discourse to inquire after his illness. Layman!"
"Is this illness bearable?
Kumārajīva replied,
"If the illness is severe and difficult to endure, then one's religious practice will be abandoned."
"I inquire after the severity of your illness: is it bearable?
Is there improvement from your treatment, and has it not worsened?
The World-Honored One sends his inquiries most earnestly and in measureless abundance."
"Layman! From what cause does this illness arise?
Kumārajīva replied:
The scriptures of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) know only three great diseases, yet they do not understand the earth element (pṛthivī-mahābhūta).

Within the Buddha-dharma, the four great diseases are taught; the arising of these diseases is produced by the increase or decrease of the four great elements. Since the increase or decrease of the four great elements must necessarily have its own causes, one therefore inquires into the origin of those causes.
"How long has it been since its arising?
How shall it be extinguished? Zhaor said:
The mission having been proclaimed, he therefore asked again about the origin of the illness:
"From what cause does this illness arise?
How long has it been since its onset?"
"How can it be extinguished?
Sheng replied:
"Your question seeks the traces of actual illness in order to grasp the meaning of a provisional sickness."
Vimalakīrti said:
"My illness arises from ignorance and craving.
Daorong said:

Because sentient beings undergo ignorance, they possess craving; because they possess craving, they receive a body; once they receive a body, they become ill. Because they are ill, my own illness arises.
That my illness arises because sentient beings are ill clarifies that I have manifested this *vaimātra* (illness) for the sake of all beings.
Because it has long been for the sake of sentient beings, one knows that it is not something near at hand.
The subsequent statement, "When their illness is extinguished, my illness is extinguished," clarifies that the arising of this illness does not restrict itself to sentient beings alone.

Newly initiated bodhisattvas have not yet been able to dwell long within the cycle of birth and death; because this gives rise to illness in all beings, it is clarified that the Great Being possesses a vast mind while dwelling in sickness.

If one traces back to the prior limit, the beginning is the initial generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); if one seeks the subsequent limit, it coincides with the extinction of all sentient beings. When newly initiated practitioners hear this, their narrow minds become expansive.

Regarding the two phrases on the arising and ceasing of illness, although the words concern illness, the intent is to clarify great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); therefore, it speaks only of the arising and ceasing, and the duration or brevity of the illness.
Once duration and brevity are clarified, great compassion is naturally revealed; for this reason, the arising and ceasing are answered first, followed by the arising of great compassion.
This collection takes the elucidation of the essential doctrine as its foundation; yet, it first explains great compassion because there are two gateways for entering the Buddha-dharma:
first, great compassion, and second, wisdom.
From the shallow to the deep, there is a gradual progression in its propagation; therefore, Great Compassion is taught first, and the True Mark (*tathatā*) is taught afterward.
Master Kumārajīva composed this explanation of emptiness:
"Ignorance has no prior limit; since there is no prior, there is likewise no middle or end."
Illness is likewise; there is no distinction between long-standing and recent.
Since this context does not resemble the meaning of "emptiness," I have separately recorded my private understanding as above.
Zhaò said:
The answer is: It has been some time.
Why is the Bodhisattva so ill?
He is ill because he gives rise to compassion for them.
The maladies of sentient beings have ignorance and craving as their root;
the maladies of Bodhisattvas have great compassion as their source.

For greatness arises from what is lowly, and illness is born of compassion. Thus, while the emergence of compassionate illness stems from ignorance and craving, ignorance and craving are without beginning and their source cannot be known; the duration of my own illness is rooted in the same source as theirs.
This clarifies the beginning of his compassionate illness; it need not be spoken of solely in terms of himself.
Sengsheng said:
"The purpose of manifesting this illness is to uproot the ignorance and craving of sentient beings from time immemorial and to exhaust their infinite source."
Although I have a present birth, in reality there is no "I" who has this present birth; my intention lies in that past meaning, yet that is precisely the sickness of the past.
Thus, the sickness arose at the time of deluded craving, not merely now.
The reason I did not speak of it in terms of "all" is that my current response concerns long-standing illness; the meaning does not lie in universality.
Nevertheless, when one speaks generally of ignorance and craving, universality is already included therein.
Furthermore, the reason he does not speak of them as "sentient beings" is that the Bodhisattva no longer possesses delusion or craving, yet remains naturally bound by affinity.
Because all sentient beings are ill, therefore I am ill;
if the illness of all sentient beings is extinguished, then my illness is extinguished.
Zhaò said: "The answer is 'extinction.
The illness of the Great Being arises because of that [object]; once that illness has been extinguished, what further cause for affliction remains for me?"

However, because sentient beings are boundless and ignorance and craving are limitless, that which is encompassed by great compassion is equal in measure to them; thus, the former compassion is inexhaustible, taking ignorance and craving as its limit, while the latter compassion is infinite, perishing together with all sentient beings.
This is because it is reached through compassion; it clarifies that the cessation of suffering through compassion is not something remote.
Daosheng said:
"Delusion and craving are the source of sentient beings' defiled illness; once the source is exhausted, the illness is also eliminated."
The root of the Bodhisattva’s illness lies herein; yet, once that illness has been cured, would it not cease to exist?

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s illness takes universal salvation as its primary aim; if there are sentient beings who do not receive its benefits, they simply do not respond to the transformation, which is not due to any partiality on his part.

Thus, although it is said that when one person’s illness is cured, the Bodhisattva is cured, this is precisely so that all sentient beings may attain freedom from further illness; only then does the Bodhisattva’s own illness cease.
Speaking in terms of sentient beings, even the companions of a bodhisattva fall ill; thus, one cannot fail to distinguish [the bodhisattva] from them.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva enters into birth and death for the sake of sentient beings, and where there is birth and death, there is illness.
If sentient beings attain freedom from illness, then the Bodhisattva will likewise no longer have illness.
Zhaò says:
"The Dharma-body is without birth; how much more so, then, is that which possesses form?"
Since there is no physical form, how could illness arise?
Yet, because one undergoes birth for their sake, one cannot be without form.
Since there is form, one cannot be without affliction; therefore, according to the duration [of that life], one shares in the same ailment.
If they are free from illness, the Bodhisattva is no longer ill.
It is like an elder who has an only son: when the son falls ill, the parents also fall ill;
when the son’s illness is cured, the parents are also cured.

In this way, the bodhisattva loves all sentient beings as if they were his own children; when sentient beings are ill, the bodhisattva is ill, and when the illness of sentient beings is cured, the bodhisattva is also cured.
He asked again,
"What is the cause from which this illness arises? Zhi said:
The question was presented first and the answer follows later; thus, it is so designated.
The reason the answer is not given first is that the cause of the illness is manifested through arising and ceasing.
The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion.
Zhaò says:
"The sickness of a bodhisattva takes great compassion as its root; it arises because of this."
This answers the first question.
Sheng said:
"Were it not for great compassion, such illness would not arise groundlessly."
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder,
why is this room empty and devoid of attendants?"
Sengzhao said:
"The significance of the 'empty room' lies herein.
[The Master] asked why the room was empty and why there were no attendants; the absence of attendants will be answered separately later."
Huisheng said:
"Having finished inquiring about his illness, you next asked about the meaning of the room being empty.
As for a person’s dwelling, there ought naturally to be the necessities of life."
Now, all is vast emptiness; what is the reason for this?
Furthermore, those who are ill ought, by principle, to have attendants.
Yet I know not where they are, nor why they are absent.
As for the inquiry regarding two matters, it was because the attendant had departed while remaining in emptiness.
Vimalakīrti said:
"The buddha-fields of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty."
Sengzhao said:
"The principle of equality leaves no dual traces; there is not a single land throughout the ten directions that is not empty. Why, then, do you ask specifically about the emptiness of a single room?"
Sengsheng said:
"That which exists can now be departed from; it is manifestly not real. This clarifies that although the lands of the Buddhas appear serene and peaceful, they too are empty."
"Buddha-fields" refers to the lands where Buddhas reside.
To cite this as an example is truly because even a Buddha who has attained sovereign mastery cannot cause his own land to exist [as a fixed entity], let alone other matters!
Furthermore, because this is what human sentiment values, it is designated as the point of awakening.
Again, he asked:
"By what is emptiness defined?"
Kumārajīva asked:
"If one considers a room empty because it contains no objects, by what principle is a world-system considered empty?
Sengzhao replied:
A room is considered empty because it contains no objects; by what, then, is a Buddha-field empty?
This is intended to clarify the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Sengsheng said:
One regards the preservation of the state as existing, yet fails to realize that it is likewise non-existent.
Now, when you speak of their commonality, on what basis do you alone perceive this?
I reply:
[The interlocutor] said, "By means of the emptiness of emptiness. Kumārajīva replied:
"It is not that something is empty because there is no substance; rather, it is empty because the nature of the land is empty, which is precisely ultimate emptiness."
Sengzhao said:
"Existence arises from the mind, and the mind is triggered by existence.
The city of 'is' and 'is not' is where deluded conceptualization resides; thus, divergent arguments concerning existence and non-existence arise in chaotic contention."

If one can empty the mind and settle the spirit within the true realm, maintaining that wondrous contemplation of both being and non-being within the cycle of existence, then although wisdom encompasses all things, it has never begun to be "existent," and though its profound discernment reflects nothing, it has never begun to be "non-existent. Thus, one can align heaven and earth under a single principle without contradicting reality; by mirroring all phenomena through profound penetration, self and others become one. Because self and others are one, wisdom performs no act of illumination; because it does not contradict reality, every thing is inherently identical.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The noble wisdom is without knowing, taking emptiness as its characteristic.
All phenomena are unconditioned, equal in measure to it.
Thus, that which is emptied of existence by means of the wisdom of emptiness is empty of itself within existence; how could it require the deliberate removal [of things] before becoming empty?
The emptiness above is the emptiness of wisdom; the emptiness below is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*).

One directly clarifies that since phenomena are empty, there is nothing by which to grasp at meditative concentration; therefore, one inwardly invokes true wisdom and outwardly realizes the emptiness of phenomena.
Sheng said:
"The upper emptiness is the emptiness of the wisdom of emptiness; the lower emptiness is the emptiness of the preceding principle.
One must employ the wisdom of emptiness for it to truly become empty; if one does not employ the wisdom of emptiness, it will never become empty."
"How can it be said that I am not empty?
He asked again:
"What is the use of emptiness being empty?"
Kumārajīva said:
"If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were inherently empty, then it should remain empty by its own nature simply as it is.
Why, then, would the various noble sages further employ the wisdom of emptiness to empty all phenomena?"
Sengzhao said:
"The former [line] refers to the emptiness of dharmas; the latter refers to the emptiness of wisdom.
Since the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is itself empty, why rely on the emptiness of wisdom for them to become empty?"
Daosheng said:
"If principle is indeed empty, what need is there for the wisdom of emptiness before it becomes empty?
There is an inherent wisdom of emptiness that brings about understanding; this emptiness is precisely what is produced by that wisdom."
This is not reasonable; how can one claim that the principle itself is empty only after it has been emptied by the wisdom of emptiness?
The answer is:
it is empty because it is the emptiness of non-discrimination.
Kumārajīva said:
"The 'upper emptiness' is the wisdom of emptiness; the 'lower emptiness' is the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Although the nature of phenomena is inherently empty and does not depend upon the wisdom of emptiness, if that wisdom were absent, then [phenomena] would be perceived as existent by me."
By means of this non-conceptual wisdom of emptiness, one attains emptiness; thus, for the self, there is emptiness.
Zhaò says:
"The arising of wisdom begins with conceptual discrimination, yet because all dharmas are without marks, wisdom is without discrimination."
Wisdom that is non-conceptual is the emptiness of wisdom; all phenomena that are signless are the emptiness of phenomena.
Because wisdom does not conceptualize phenomena, one thereby knows that phenomena are empty.
How could there be a separate wisdom that uses emptiness to empty phenomena?

Rather, when wisdom does not differentiate phenomena, at that time wisdom and phenomena are both identical to the same emptiness, and there is no further distinct emptiness. Therefore it is said that because non-discrimination constitutes the emptiness of wisdom, wisdom knows that phenomena are empty; it is not that there is a separate wisdom-emptiness used to empty phenomena.
Sheng said:
"The 'wisdom of emptiness' mentioned previously does not refer to a wisdom that discriminates and constructs emptiness; it refers merely to attaining awakening by following the principle.
If one considers following the principle to be awakening, and only after obtaining this does one attain emptiness, would it not be the case that the principle itself is already empty?"
He asked again:
"Can emptiness be conceptually differentiated?
Kumārajīva replied:
This question concerns the wisdom that realizes emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).

Although it was previously clarified that this wisdom does not perceive the distinction between emptiness and existence, it has not yet been clarified that the essence of this wisdom itself is empty and without distinction; therefore, the question is asked: can this wisdom of emptiness be differentiated?
Sengzhao said:
"The preceding [passage] takes non-discrimination as the emptiness of wisdom; therefore, one knows that the emptiness of dharmas is no different from this [wisdom-emptiness].
Although it is said there is no difference, the mark of difference has already manifested; once the mark of difference has manifested, discrimination arises."
If one knows that phenomena are no different from emptiness, on what basis can it be said that one knows phenomena are empty by means of non-conceptual wisdom being empty?
Therefore, the question is asked: Can the emptiness of wisdom and the emptiness of phenomena be differentiated?
Since both wisdom and dharmas are empty, a single mention of emptiness is sufficient.
Daosheng said:
"The very term 'emptiness' appears to possess characteristics; once there are characteristics, it becomes distinguished from other things."
If emptiness were merely conceptual discrimination while wisdom were non-discriminative, then emptiness and wisdom would be distinct.
Since emptiness would thus differ from wisdom, it would furthermore not arise from wisdom.
He replied,
"Discrimination is also empty.
Kumārajīva said:
If wisdom were different from emptiness, it would be conceptual discrimination; yet although there is discrimination, its nature is also empty.
Sengzhao said:
"What was just stated refers merely to making a distinction within non-discrimination."

If one can engage in discernment without a mind of conceptual discrimination regarding that which is non-conceptual, then although one may continue to discern throughout the entire day, one has never truly discerned; therefore, it is said that even discernment is empty.
Sengsheng said:
"As for those who speak of emptiness, even the characteristic of emptiness is empty.
If the characteristic of emptiness were not empty, then emptiness would be a form of existence."
If emptiness is already existent, how could existence not be so?
Thus, if all things were existent and not empty, then even the analytical discernment [of them] would be empty only after they have been so analyzed.
He asked again:
"Where should emptiness be sought?
Sengzhao replied:

The Master, having previously clarified emptiness through correct wisdom, feared that those who are deluded might think the meaning of emptiness resides in the correct and not the erroneous; therefore, he asks where the meaning of emptiness lies, in order to demonstrate that there is no distinction between the erroneous and the correct.
Sheng said:
"I have already exhausted my sincere words; yet those who are deluded are still unable to believe them fully. Therefore, I request to offer this discourse once more in order to enlighten them."
The preceding reasoning shows that substantiality is ultimately empty and that conceptual discrimination is also empty; being empty, it is signless (*animitta*).
If one were to take this signless emptiness as a reality, where could one seek it to find such a thing?
He replied:
"One should seek it among the sixty-two views.
Kumārajīva said:
The preceding section clarified ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), wherein there is no phenomenon that is not empty.

Nevertheless, when one directs the mind toward seeking liberation, there must necessarily be a ford; and in the essential pursuit of this ford, there must necessarily be points of delusion. The arising of such delusions is born from perceiving differences, and among the most extreme forms of difference, none surpasses that between the heterodox and the orthodox.
There is nothing that more thoroughly distinguishes the extreme limits of the heterodox and the orthodox than this;
therefore, when asked where one should seek [the truth], he answered with two methods. Zhaò said:
Now, the false arises from the true, and the true originates from the false; if one examines their fundamental nature, that nature is non-dual.
Therefore, those who seek the emptiness of right wisdom should seek it within wrong views.
Sheng said:
"Now, those who harbor conceptualizations do not transcend the sixty-two views.
Such views are erroneous, yet they are absent herein; is it not the case that even 'emptiness' itself is empty?"
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the sixty-two views?
Daosheng replied:
If the sixty-two views are considered erroneous because they maintain the existence of marks, then where else should one seek that which is so?
The answer is:
One should seek it within the liberation of the Buddhas.
Zhaò said:
"Abandoning false views is called liberation; turning one's back on liberation is called false view.
If this is so, then false understanding and its manifestations are intertwined—what is their origin?"
As for its origin, it is but one.
Therefore, when seeking [the truth] amidst false views, one must take liberation as the fundamental basis.
Sheng said:
Liberation means being liberated from fetters and bonds.
If one maintains the perception of marks without deviating into error, one cannot depart [from them].
Since these do not exist within liberation, we know that the principle of all views is necessarily so.
Regarding the term "all Buddhas," it clarifies that their wondrousness must be identical.
Again, he asked:
"Where should one seek the liberation of all Buddhas?"
Jīvaka asked:
"If the liberation of all Buddhas is the liberation from fetters and bonds, then in what else could one seek that which is so?
He replied:
"One should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"The mental activities of sentient beings are precisely the activities of bondage; these activities of bondage are that from which liberation arises."

Furthermore, the heterodox and the orthodox share the same root, and liberation is a single gate; when one traces back to their true nature, they have never been different. Therefore, if one seeks the liberation of a Buddha, one should seek it within the mental activities of sentient beings.
Daosheng said:
"To act according to the mind means not to take principle as one's guiding concern.
One who takes what is contrary to principle as their concern will be entangled in birth and death, unable to escape them."
If there were no liberation within the mental activities of all sentient beings, then one would know that liberation is what liberates.
Mental activities are likewise nothing but the sixty-two views; however, because their meanings differ, they are categorized as "this" or "that."
If one does not clarify that the liberation of all Buddhas is the liberation from fetters, it will still be insufficient to verify that the sixty-two views are erroneous;
and if one does not clarify that the sixty-two views are erroneous, it will likewise be insufficient to verify that emptiness is the reality.
Therefore, the subsequent inquiry is clear. An alternative version states:
"The sixty-two views, the liberation of all Buddhas, the intentions and practices of sentient beings. Kumārajīva said:
"The two views are the root of existence and the ultimate of perversion."
Liberation is the ultimate end of existence and the subtle perfection of correctness.
The mental activities of sentient beings lie between two views.
These three aggregates of phenomena are where the common mind is obstructed; they are determined to perceive them as distinct.
Indeed, the grasping of marks and the arising of delusion originate from this; conversely, seeking the ultimate source while remaining in confusion must also lead to this very point.
Since the three natures reach the same destination, they mutually interpenetrate one another.
Furthermore, regarding what you asked concerning why there is no attendant:
all the various Māras and heterodox teachers are my attendants.
Sengzhao said:
In the world, an attendant is one who merely shows reverence, obeys orders, and provides for whatever is required; such a person is called an attendant.

A Bodhisattva’s attendant, however, is one who—regarding those who are arrogant, disobedient, or contrary to the Way as being in great discord with them—harmonizes through profound compliance and serves to nourish the Dharma-body; such a person is called an attendant. This is why the various Māras and heterodox teachers serve as the foremost among those who provide service.
Why is this? The various Māras delight in birth and death, yet the Bodhisattva does not abandon birth and death.
[The Devī] asked:
Māra delights in birth and death, and thus dwells therein.
If one does not conform to transformation, one will remain forever alienated from it; how then could one be made to awaken to the fundamental principle of existence?
Those of external paths delight in various views, whereas the Bodhisattva remains unmoved amidst all views.
Kumārajīva said:
"The words do not reveal any sign of difference.
Sengzhao said:
Māra delights in the five desires and does not seek transcendence from the world; therefore, he binds them with birth and death.
Although those of other teachings seek transcendence from the world, they cling to their own paths; therefore, he binds them with false views.
The Great Being contemplates birth and death as identical to nirvana, and thus is able not to abandon them;
he contemplates false views as identical to right view, and thus is able to remain unmoved.
Because he is neither moved nor does he abandon, he is able to serve as an attendant by means of this very state.
Dongsheng said:
"Nor do I abandon any views.
Māra and the non-Buddhists represent the ultimate deviation from principle; yet once one has attained their fundamental tenets, what further can be said beyond this?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"Householder, what are the symptoms of your illness?
Kumārajīva replied:
Observing the matter as it is: if one says there is illness when there is none, yet has not yet perceived its characteristics, one therefore seeks those characteristics.
Sengzhao said:
"Having already known the origin from which the illness arises, he further asks about the specific symptoms of the illness produced thereby."
The four hundred and four diseases each have their own distinct characteristics; what, then, are the characteristics of the illness of Great Compassion?

To clarify that the formless Great Compassion gives rise to illnesses in response to sentient beings, although it manifests illness throughout the day, it remains entirely without characteristics throughout the day.
Dongsheng said:

"The state of 'inquiry into illness' ought to pertain to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Previously, by answering according to reality (*yathābhūta*), I obstructed the intent of the question regarding emptiness.
Furthermore, since the meaning of emptiness has already been clarified, its state is thereby made manifest."
Vimalakīrti said:
"My illness is formless and invisible.
Zhaò said:

Great compassion has no object of focus, yet there is nothing it does not take as its object; because there is nothing it does not take as its object, it can respond to things by manifesting illness. To manifest illness in response to things means that, within itself, it never becomes ill. Because it never becomes ill, it can share in the characteristics of all illnesses without contradicting the Way of formlessness.

Why is this? Great Compassion is without conditions; being without conditions, it is without marks. Because this sickness arises from that which is without marks, the sickness itself is also without marks. Therefore, it is said: "My illness has no form and cannot be seen."
Sheng said:
"Illness is a physical phenomenon; in principle, it must be observable, yet it lacks substantial reality—this is why I spoke thus.
He asked again:
"Is this illness conjoined with the body or conjoined with the mind?
Kumārajīva said:
"The previous answer that it is formless and invisible is precisely a statement of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)."
Regarding these words, it seems as though there is a flaw in their perception; thus, this question arises. Zhaò says:

"Perhaps those who heard that illness cannot be seen assumed that mental illness is invisible because it has no form, or perhaps they thought that physical illness is invisible because it is subtle; it is for such reasons that they pose this question."
With what thing do the ailments of body and mind conjoin that one says they cannot be seen?
Sheng said:
"The body is the basis for receiving illness, and the mind is the master of perceiving pain; when the illness conjoins with these, it becomes formless."
Therefore, I have used this as a pretext for inquiry, so that you may clarify that the illness has no locus, and subsequently exhaust all forms.
He replied:
"It is not joined with the body, because the characteristics of the body are detached."
Kumārajīva said:
"Because there is no body, there is no illness.
Furthermore, it is not a matter of the mind merging [with the body], for the mind is like an illusion."
Kumārajīva said:
"Because the mind has no reality, it is without affliction.
Sengzhao said:
When the physical form is detached, it is no longer the body; when the mind is like an illusion, it is no longer the mind.
Since both body and mind do not exist, with whom would the illness conjoin?
Because there is no conjunction, there is no illness; because there is no illness, it cannot be perceived.
Daosheng said:
"The body originally manifests distinct forms; therefore, it is said to be devoid of characteristics.
The mind moves without fixed direction; therefore, it is said to be illusory."
Since both body and mind do not exist, with what could they possibly combine?
He asked again:
"Regarding the four great elements—the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element—which of these great elements is afflicted by disease?"
Kumārajīva said:
"This is intended to clarify the origin from which illness arises.
The origin of illness does not stem from a single factor; it must arise from the temporary conjunction of the four great elements."
If illness arises through conditional conjunction, then illness has no intrinsic nature; since illness has no intrinsic nature, it is likewise unobservable as described above.
Although this clarifies the causes from which illness originates, it thereby clarifies why there is ultimately no illness.
Zhaò says:
"The arising of the body is constituted by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Previously, I examined the body as a whole; now, I examine the four great elements individually, seeking their fundamental source in detail."
Huisheng said:
"The body and mind are originally formed by the combination of the four great elements.
While the body and mind may be absent, the four great elements may still exist."
Furthermore, as each of the four great elements gives rise to one hundred and one various ailments, these can be acknowledged as such; therefore, they have no substantial form.
You may again take this as a point of inquiry to clarify that because illness arises from the four great elements, it possesses no real form.
The answer is:
This illness is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element; the water, fire, and wind elements are likewise so.
Zhaò said:

The fundamental nature of the four great elements is inherently free from affliction; it is only when various conditions assemble that they undergo increase and decrease and mutually inhibit one another, whereby affliction arises.
If one wishes to say there is illness, its fundamental nature is inherently non-existent;
if one wishes to say there is no illness, it exists through the mutual dependence of conditions.
Therefore, illness is neither the earth element nor is it separate from the earth element; the other great elements are likewise.
Yet the illnesses of sentient beings arise from these four great elements.
Śāriputra said:
"It is truly because of him that I am ill;
since he has an illness, therefore I am ill. Zhaò said:

The four great elements are fundamentally non-existent, and thus illness likewise does not exist; yet the illusory ailments of sentient beings arise from these four great elements, and so I manifest illusory illness in response to their illness.
Tracing back to their origin, both "self" and "other" lack substantial reality; yet you wish to contemplate their forms and characteristics—why is this?
Sengsheng replied:
"This too is a condition, not a real illness."
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"How should a bodhisattva console a sick bodhisattva? Zhaò said: [This refers to the inquiry regarding the method of consolation.]
Although it was Mañjuśrī who should have initiated the inquiry regarding the illness, the fact that he instead questioned Vimalakīrti was because the minds of those assembled were focused on him.
Furthermore, by taking the one who was ill as his witness, he thereby ensured that the assembly would be thoroughly consoled and instructed.

This is intended to clarify the path of non-attainment in the Mahāyāna, in order to console bodhisattvas who have recently begun their practice and are currently afflicted by illness; thus, this question arises.
Daosheng said:
"To offer consolation to those who are ill is fundamentally the work of those who are themselves without illness."
Since Vimalakīrti was already free from such things, he followed this by posing the question.
Although one may be a bodhisattva, if one has not yet escaped illness, one cannot help but be afflicted by it; because of this, one clings to life and fears death.
If there is any lingering attachment to life or fear of death, it will inevitably increase the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, those who share the same Way should offer mutual consolation; the method for such consolation is to eliminate these very sentiments.
"If this attachment is eliminated, birth and death will almost cease.
Vimalakīrti said: "One speaks of the impermanence of the body, but does not speak of wearying of or seeking liberation from the body."
Kumārajīva said:

"In general, there are three kinds of dharmas: namely, worldly dharmas, supramundane dharmas, and the dharma of the śrāvakas, which involves contemplating impermanence and thereby feeling revulsion for the body; the dharma of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), which involves attachment to the body and not contemplating impermanence; and the dharma of the bodhisattvas, which involves contemplating impermanence yet not feeling revulsion for the body."
Now, for the sake of the sick, I shall expound the Dharma of the Bodhisattva; by dwelling thus amidst illness, the mind will not be distracted.
Zhaò says:

The method of consolation and exhortation should consist in explaining to the sick that the body is impermanent so as to remove their greedy attachments; one should not expound upon wearying detachment (nirveda) to cause them to seek realization.

Those who do not contemplate impermanence and do not feel weary detachment are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); those who contemplate impermanence and feel weary detachment are followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyānika*); those who contemplate impermanence yet do not feel weary detachment are Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, one should console and encourage the beginner, causing them to settle their mind within illness to save all sentient beings—neither wearying of birth and death nor delighting in nirvana.
This is the method by which a Mahāsattva offers consolation and encouragement.
Sheng said:
"Now, that which craves life is the sentiment of attachment to the self; once one has such a sentiment, there is no end to this craving.
If, however, it is truly impermanent, how could it be worthy of such love and attachment?"
If one can follow through with awakening, there is no need to expect the dispelling of delusions, for they will vanish of their own accord.

For one whose delusions have vanished, there is no longer a self; though the delusions are already gone and the self is absent, one ultimately does not grasp at principles. By not grasping at principles, one is necessarily able to exhaust them; when principles are exhausted and nature is fully realized, the natural course leads to universal salvation.

As for the time when one is still deluded, one ought indeed to be distressed by delusion and seek its transcendence; yet the aspiration to seek transcendence must involve a weariness with the body through the realization of impermanence.
Thus, this weariness with the body arises from a state of delusion; it is not a disposition held within the midst of correct principle.
It is said that the body possesses suffering, yet it is not said that one finds joy in nirvana.
Daosheng said:
"If, according to principle, [the self] were impermanent, then one would experience affliction due to the loss of what is loved."
One must skillfully refute [such views].
This accumulation of the eight sufferings is especially not to be clung to.
Previously, while in delusion, one felt weary of and sought to leave behind impermanence; now, one likewise takes up suffering and seeks the bliss of Nirvana.
Speaking from the perspective of ultimate principle, how could this be so?
[The Buddha] taught that the body is without self, yet he also spoke of instructing sentient beings.
Daosheng said:
Generally, the love of one's body arises from attachment to a self.
If this [body] is indeed impermanent and suffering, how could there be a ruler within it?
If there is no ruler within, what cause would there be for such longing?
Furthermore, based on the afflictions that delude people, he employs [these teachings] solely for his own perfection.
Since these are held within his enlightened mind, they are called "instruction.
He explains that the body is empty and quiescent.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is according to their sharpness or dullness of faculties that the teachings are spoken in either extensive or abbreviated form.
For example, a great tree cannot be toppled by a single axe; since its roots have been deepened through accumulation, they cannot be removed by a single dharma."
There may be those who, although they hear of impermanence, claim it is not suffering; for them, one then explains suffering.
Once they have heard of suffering, they may then claim there exists a master of suffering and pleasure; therefore, one explains non-self and emptiness.
He does not speak of ultimate quiescence.
Zhaò says:

Although he perceives the suffering of the body, he does not delight in the bliss of nirvāṇa; although he knows there is no self, he does not omit instruction because of the emptiness of sentient beings; although he understands the emptiness of the body, he does not grasp at the path of ultimate nirvāṇa; thus, he is able to dwell peacefully within saṃsāra and share the same afflictions as sentient beings.
Therefore, when offering consolation, one should speak of what ought to be practiced; one should not speak of what ought not to be practiced.
[The disciple] said:
"Since there is no one who can act as a sovereign, what existence does my body possess?"
If there were no body, from what would attachment arise?
What is called "emptiness and stillness" clarifies that there is no substantial reality; it does not mean non-existence.
Furthermore, these four propositions follow a sequence according to their meaning, and together they exhaustively encompass the principle.
He spoke of repenting for past transgressions but did not speak of entering the past.
Kumārajīva said:
"Those of sharp faculties can immediately attain composure without confusion upon hearing these four preceding phrases."
From this point onward, the teaching is intended for those of dull faculties; it employs direct and urgent language to instruct their minds.
Since today’s ailment must stem from prior transgressions, he teaches them to repent of those past sins.

Since it has already been stated that there are prior offenses, this would imply that offenses possess a permanent nature that enters into the past; therefore, it is taught that they do not enter the past in order to eliminate the notion of permanence.
Sengzhao said:
The teaching instructs the sick bodhisattva to repent for past transgressions.
Although past transgressions bind the person, it is not said that these transgressions possess a permanent nature; they proceed from the future to the present, and from the present into the past.
Sheng said:
"Those who cherish life and fear death do so because they dread committing transgressions.
If one can reform and repent, one will transcend that realm; what, then, is there left to fear?"
Therefore, one teaches and exhorts them regarding their prior transgressions in order to eliminate their fear.
This is merely based on conditions; it does not claim that there is any substantial reality.
One takes pity on the suffering of others by means of one's own suffering.
Kumārajīva said:
"This is to cause him to extend his own feelings to pity all things.
He should reflect and say:"
"I now have a slight ailment, yet my pain is still so great;
how much more so for the sentient beings in the evil realms who undergo immeasurable suffering.
Zhaò said:
"Exhorting those who are ill" means to take one's own illness as a measure to feel compassion for the illnesses of others.
It is said:
"If even I, who possess wisdom, still suffer from the pain of illness, how much more so must it be for those who have not yet attained realization?"
"To extend one's own compassion to others is the sentiment of universal salvation; how could one then fear death for oneself?
One should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas from past lives.
Sengsheng said:
"Throughout incalculable kalpas, you have undergone immeasurable suffering; how can you suddenly forget it all at once?
You should instead keep in mind the benefit of all sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said:
Throughout incalculable kalpas, one has undergone immeasurable suffering without ever practicing the Way.
To undergo suffering for the sake of the Way will surely yield great benefit.
Having thus exhorted oneself, one should further contemplate bringing benefit to all sentient beings so that they may likewise attain this benefit.
Zhaò said:
"One should reflect that in past lives one has endured immeasurable suffering; compared to this, the present suffering is but a fleeting moment—why should it cause such grief?
One need only exert oneself to rescue others from their suffering."
Sheng said:
"One who intends to benefit all sentient beings enters the cycle of birth and death; such a person must not harbor fear.
One should simply recollect the merit one has cultivated."
Kumārajīva said:
"According to the customs of foreign lands, every meritorious deed performed from birth until death is recorded one by one.
When the time of death arrives, those nearby recite these accounts for the dying person, enabling them to rely on their merit so that their mind is free from sorrow and fear."
Zhaò said:
"I fear that newly initiated bodhisattvas may be disturbed by illness; therefore, I urge them to recollect the merit they have cultivated to gladden their spirits.
Shēng said:
"If one possesses merit, one's future rebirth will surely be superior; what, then, is there to fear?
One should be mindful of pure livelihood.
Kumārajīva said:
"Pure livelihood" (śuddhājīva) is precisely right livelihood (samyag-ājīva).
He reflects: "From birth until now, I have always practiced right livelihood; I shall certainly go to a happy destination.
What, then, have I to fear?"
Zhaò said:
"Do not, for the sake of curing bodily ailments, give rise to wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
'Wrong livelihood' refers to the flattery and adornment practiced for the sake of one's life, seeking profit and preserving existence."
Huisheng said:
"When practicing goodness, the original aim is to attain the Way and transcend the world; one never seeks profit, clothing, or food.
One does not even fear being dragged by the cycle of birth and death, much less the sufferings of sin."
"Do not give rise to sorrow or distress.
Sheng said, "To grieve is of no benefit; it serves only to bring about further affliction."
He constantly gave rise to diligence.
Kumārajīva said:
"Though his body passes away and his life ends, his intention does not abandon it."
Sheng said:
"Laziness arises because of illness; once one is lax, anxiety increases all the more.
When one strives to compete with fate, one is constantly plagued by the fear of failing to reach the goal; how, then, could there be any room for vexation?"
"You should become a King of Physicians to treat and cure all manner of illnesses.
Kumārajīva said,
"Let him, through his illness, give rise to the Great Vow."
Since there is no one capable of curing such various illnesses, one should employ the method of Dharma to treat all ailments.
Zhaò said:
"One should become a Great King of Physicians of the Dharma to heal the maladies of all living beings."
"Why should you worry about your own illness?

Sheng replied, "I shall only strive diligently to seek out remedies so as to encompass all beings; do not give rise to anxiety or distress, for it is merely a source of suffering that yields no benefit."
"A bodhisattva should console a sick bodhisattva in this manner, causing them to rejoice.
Mañjuśrī said, "Householder!"
"How should a sick bodhisattva discipline his mind?
Zhaò said:
"The preceding question concerned the propriety of consolation and encouragement; the present question concerns the method for disciplining the mind."

With skillful exhortation outwardly and skillful self-discipline inwardly, one is then able to traverse the cycle of birth and death alongside all sentient beings, sharing their afflictions; though undergoing every kind of bitterness and hardship, one does not regard them as suffering.
This is precisely the reason why Vimalakīrti dwells in illness.
He raised this question in order to demonstrate to beginners the way of dwelling in illness; thus, he spoke as follows:
Śāriputra said:

Now, the mind rushes toward objects and there is no evil it will not commit; it is like a runaway horse that is difficult to restrain. Therefore, one drifts with the current through birth and death, unable to escape its realm.
If one wishes to extricate oneself [from suffering], it is essential to subdue and harmonize [the mind].
There must be a way to achieve this method of subduing and harmonizing.
It is like training a horse with a galloping course; how could it fail to comply?
Only after one has attained the Way can one truly submit.
As for a Bodhisattva who has not yet escaped illness, they will inevitably be dragged by the urgency of their afflictions, making it all the more difficult to exercise self-restraint.
Therefore, he asked him again. Vimalakīrti replied:
"A sick bodhisattva should reflect thus: 'This illness of mine arises entirely from the delusions, inversions, and various afflictions of my past lives.'"
Sheng said:
"If one is truly constrained by what is perceived as illness, one cannot help but investigate the nature of that illness.
Since the nature of illness is non-existent, how could it possibly constrain me?"
That which arises from conditions is already non-existent in itself; how much more so that which is produced by deluded thoughts and inversions?
Since there is no real dharma, who is it that suffers from illness?
Sengzhao said:
"The method for dealing with illness requires first knowing the root cause of the disease.
The arising of such illnesses is entirely due to the delusions and inversions of previous lives."
Because of deluded thoughts and inversions, afflictions arise; once afflictions have arisen, one cannot be without a body, and having a body, one cannot be without suffering.
If one traces back to its origin, it is found to be empty, false, and unreal. Since the origin is not real, who is there to suffer from illness?
This clarifies that a beginner first practices the contemplation of non-self.
Sengsheng said:
"Furthermore, there is nothing to be afflicted by."
Since there is nothing that is ill, illness itself is also non-existent.
Why is this so? Because the body is a provisional name for the conjunction of the four great elements, and these four great elements have no master.
Kumārajīva said:
"The four great elements are the basis of the body; since that basis has no master, the body likewise has no self.
The body, too, is without self."
Sengzhao said:
This explains the meaning of non-self.
The four great elements combine and aggregate, and are merely conventionally designated as a "body."
Since the four great elements have no master, how could "body" or "self" arise?
It is like a single grain of sand having no oil; even a heap of sand has none.
"Master" and "self" are merely different names for the same thing.
Sengsheng said:
"Regarding those who calculate the self, some take the body itself to be the self, while others claim that the self exists within the body.
Now, if we investigate the body through principle, it is composed solely of the four great elements; there is no further distinct dharma."
The four great elements have no master, and the body likewise has no self.
The four elements are four, while the self is one; if one were to claim that it dwells within them as a master, yet since there is no master, the self has no center.
The body is one, and I am also one; if you say that the body is indeed "I," yet there is no self, then "I" am not identical to it.
If the self truly does not exist, what is there to be afflicted by?
Furthermore, this illness arises entirely from attachment to a self.
Kumārajīva said:
"The arising of illness has a single cause."
First, because of past attachment to a self, one extensively generates fetters and karma; as for the fruit of these fetters and karma, one undergoes suffering.
Second, because of present attachment to a self, the mind is afflicted; due to this affliction of the mind through attachment to a self, illness increases.
Therefore, one should not give rise to attachment toward the self.
Zhaò said:
"If this self were real, why would it give rise to illness?"
Sheng said:
"Furthermore, this illness is fundamentally empty; that there are those who fall ill is entirely due to attachment to a self.
If one can remain unattached to a self, how could illness exist?"
Having identified the root of the illness,
Kumārajīva said:
"It is this attachment to 'self'."
He immediately eliminated the notion of a self and the notion of sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said:
"These three cases are identical in fact, yet differ in their underlying meaning."
Zhaò says:
"The root of affliction is precisely the aforementioned deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Because of the existence of deluded conceptualization, the self and sentient beings manifest."
"If one awakens to the inversion of deluded thoughts, then there is no self and no sentient beings.
Sheng said:
"Since you know that the illness arises from attachment to the self, you should eliminate it immediately."

Although sentient beings are indeed myself, I shall now proceed to demonstrate that within the synthesis of all phenomena there is no self; therefore, I apply this [analogy] to substantiate and manifest this meaning.
One should give rise to the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
Kumārajīva said:
"This is using a provisional dharma to dispel the self, just as a person nourishes this anger to extinguish that anger.
Sengzhao said:
I considered that my affliction was grave; therefore, I eliminated the notion of a self (*ātman*) and gave rise to the notion of dharmas (*dharmasaṃjñā*).

This notion of dharmas is a malady with respect to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), yet it is a medicine with respect to the self. Since these two—ascension and descent—are mutually dependent, I provisionally employed it as a remedy.
Sheng said:
"What is the purpose of removing them?
It is to give rise to the perception of phenomena (dharmasaṃjñā)."
To give rise to the perception of phenomena (dharmasaṃjñā) does not mean to be attached to phenomena.
One should form this thought:
"This body is merely composed of a collection of various phenomena."
Dongsheng said:
"The 'various dharmas' refer to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas).
'Combining to form a body' clarifies that these serve as its causes."
The term "only" (but) means that there is no self within the causal conditions;
arising is merely the arising of dharmas, and ceasing is merely the ceasing of dharmas.
Sengzhao said:
This explains the concept of "dharma-thought" (*dharmasaṃjñā*).

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and all phenomena (*dharma*) assemble provisionally to form the body; their arising occurs only through the common arising of all phenomena, and their cessation occurs only through the common cessation of all phenomena. There is no separate, true sovereign that presides over their arising and cessation.
Having eliminated the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*), one perceives only the dharmas of dependent origination; therefore, this is called the "notion of dharmas" (*dharma-saṃjñā*).
Daosheng said:
"That which arises and ceases is the fruit."
The term "only" (mātra) indicates that even within the fruit there is no self.
Furthermore, these phenomena do not cognize one another.
[Vasubandhu] says:
The following two lines further clarify that cause and effect are not the self.
When various phenomena combine, they arise through mutual conditioning;
as for arising through mutual conditioning, it is impossible for them not to arise.
It is not that the characteristic arises as the agent.
If it were the case that the characteristic arose as the agent,
there would necessarily be a cognition of the arising of that characteristic.
Yet that which is known resides in the other and not within oneself;
through repeated mutual cognition,
this constitutes the meaning of "self" as autonomous.
When arising, it does not say, "I arise"; when ceasing, it does not say, "I cease. Zhaò said:
"The myriad things are in chaotic profusion; who is it that brings about their gathering and dispersal?"
When conditions conjoin, things arise; when conditions disperse, they depart. Since their gathering and dispersal are not predetermined, phenomena do not know one another.
Sheng said:
"That which arises from conditions cannot but arise from them; it does not arise from something else."
If there were something from which [cognition] arises, there would necessarily be a cognition of that source of arising.
However, since the object of cognition resides within oneself and not in that external thing, there is no principle of mutual cognition between them.
This also constitutes the meaning of "self" as sovereign mastery.
Regarding that sick bodhisattva who seeks to eliminate the notion of dharmas,
Kumārajīva said:
Previously, one was dispelled by means of the Dharma; from this point onward, one is dispelled by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One should form this thought:
"This perception of dharmas is also a perversion (*viparyāsa*); perversion is a great affliction, and I should abandon it."
Zhaò said:
"Although the conception of dharmas has been eliminated, the self [conception] remains a perversion even with respect to the Truth.
Since one has not yet escaped from affliction, one ought to abandon it."
Sheng said:
"If one eliminates the notion of a self by means of the notion of dharmas, how could there still be attachment arising toward dharmas?
Because delusion arises regarding the traces of words, they are subsequently eliminated."
Furthermore, one may also consult the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* to fully exhaust its meaning.
What is meant by "detachment"?
It is detachment from the self and what belongs to the self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
Sengzhao said:
"I am the master of all things, and all things are my possession.
If one is detached from 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' then there is no phenomenon that is not detached."
Sheng said:
"When the sentiment of 'self' arises, one regards all external phenomena as belonging to oneself.
That which belongs to oneself is a phenomenon that stands in opposition to the self."
Since the self no longer exists, how could that which belongs to it remain alone?
How does one become detached from "self" and "what belongs to self"?
It means becoming detached from these two phenomena.
Sheng said:
"Previously, I simply spoke of two matters; now you say that one must depart from these two matters. They are 'two' only when they are in opposition, and only then is there departure.
How does one depart from these two dharmas?"
This means not dwelling on internal or external phenomena, but practicing equanimity. Zhaò said:

"When there is 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' the duality of phenomena naturally arises. Once this duality arises, the internal and external take form. When the internal and external have taken form, phenomena acquire diverse names. With the diverse naming of phenomena, right and wrong begin to oppose one another. When right and wrong oppose one another, all manner of afflictions come into being."

If one can refrain from conceptualizing internal and external phenomena and practice with a mind of equanimity, one then enters the practice of emptiness, free from the affliction of the notion of dharmas.
"Internal and external" refers to the subjective mind and its sensory objects.
Dongsheng said:
"The internal is the self; the external is all phenomena. These constitute a duality through their mutual opposition.
To not dwell upon them and to act within equanimity is what is meant by 'detachment'."
What is meant by "equality"?
It refers to the equality of the self and nirvana.
Zhaò said:
To view all things from the highest to the lowest with equal contemplation is precisely what accords with equality.
Daosheng said:
"Although nirvāṇa is not non-existent, it is a dharma that indicates non-existence; therefore, among external dharmas, this one instance is cited to clarify my point regarding equality."
Why is this so? Both "self" and "nirvāṇa" are empty.
Zhaò said:
In phenomena, there is nothing that is not different; in emptiness, there is nothing that is not one.
By what is it empty?
It is empty merely by virtue of names.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Beneath a name there is no reality.
These two dharmas lack any determinate nature."
Sengzhao said:
Because one turns one's back on nirvāṇa, it is called "self"; because one abandons the self, it is called "nirvāṇa.
Since these two dharmas exist in mutual dependence, names arise; yet when their intrinsic nature is examined, that nature has no fixed determination, and thus both are empty.
Dongsheng said:
"It is simply that there is no fixed nature.
When this equanimity is attained, there is no further affliction, except for the affliction of emptiness itself."
Sengsheng said:
"It is also by means of verbal traces that one eliminates them.
Because their meanings range from coarse to subtle, it is said thus."
"Even the sickness of emptiness is empty.
Kumārajīva said:

"The preceding [passage] clarified that there is no self and no dharmas, yet it had not yet eliminated emptiness itself. If emptiness is not eliminated, then emptiness becomes a burden; being a burden is precisely what constitutes a 'sickness. Therefore, it is clarified here that even the sickness of emptiness is empty."
Sengzhao said:

"The habitual attachments and burdens of sentient beings are so profound that they cannot be abandoned all at once; therefore, one gradually eliminates them through successive stages until there is nothing left to eliminate.
