First, one uses the Dharma to eliminate the self; next, one uses emptiness to eliminate the Dharma; now, by using the ultimate emptiness (atyanta-śūnyatā) to empty that very emptiness, one reaches the pinnacle of being free from affliction."
Sengsheng said:
"The principle of emptiness is not the illness; rather, it is the attachment to emptiness that constitutes the illness.
Speaking from the perspective of this illness, one therefore refers to emptiness as the illness."
This sick bodhisattva experiences all sensations by means of non-appropriation.
Kumārajīva said:
"Sensation" refers to the three sensations of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
If one can understand and accept the non-existence of sensation, then one can take birth for the sake of sentient beings and endure the three types of sensation.
Sheng said:
"The various sensations" refers to the three sensations.
Once one contemplates that illness is empty, the three types of sensation are all absent.
One who can be without these three sensations finds them naturally eliminated.
This is not because of a deliberate desire to abandon them; rather, there is the compassionate intent of entering into sensation for the sake of transformation.
One does not yet possess the Buddha-dharma, nor does one extinguish sensation to attain realization.
Zhaò said:

"Those who skillfully regulate themselves dwell amidst existence without being stained by existence, and abide in emptiness without being stained by emptiness; this is the ultimate state of non-sensation."

Because the mind is without reception, there is nothing that it does not receive; because there is nothing it does not receive, it is able to eternally share in all sensations with all sentient beings.
These "sensations" refer to painful sensations, pleasant sensations, and sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant.
As long as the Buddha-dharma is not yet fully realized and sentient beings are not yet delivered, one does not merely extinguish the three types of sensation to attain realization.
Sheng said:

"Based on the affliction of the emotions of sensation, those who seek that which is not subject to extinction must take that which is sufficient to eliminate affliction as the ultimate excellence, and no longer hope for the exhaustive realization of principle."
This is precisely the realization of the Middle Way that is free from extremes, wherein one comes to rest.
Even if one’s own body experiences suffering, one should contemplate sentient beings in the evil realms and give rise to great compassion.
Kumārajīva said:
"If even my body of merit and wisdom suffers such pain, how much more so must the sentient beings of the evil realms suffer immeasurable agony?
Thinking thus, he immediately gave rise to a heart of compassion, vowing to uproot their suffering.
Huisheng said:
"Previously, there was the sentiment of entering [the world] to receive [beings], which is the mind of great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
What is this great compassion?"
Even if one experiences physical suffering, one should contemplate sentient beings in the evil realms and rescue them.
Although one previously contemplated that illness is empty—which can indeed prevent the mind from being deluded by suffering—one has not yet attained the realization that it is truly non-existent.
If one contemplates the principle for a long time until it becomes clear, then rebirth will no longer occur; this is why it is said that "one's own body may be subject to suffering.

As for the thought of sentient beings in the evil realms: I am currently among humans, possessing both merit and the clarity of wisdom, yet I still experience such suffering as this; how much more so must it be for those in the three evil paths who lack both merit and wisdom?
As for those who contemplate the evil realms, since no one within the cycle of birth and death can escape them, this serves as the condition for giving rise to great compassion.
Having been tamed myself, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings.
Sengzhao said:
"The essential point is to share in the suffering and joy of all living beings together.
Sengsheng said:
Unless one is tamed and disciplined, one cannot avoid the three evil realms.
One should only eliminate the illness without eliminating the dharma.
Kumārajīva said:
This refers to the dharmas of permanence, bliss, purity, and so forth, as perceived by those with false views.

The reason it is said that these do not exist is not because one uses the non-existence of bliss and purity to eliminate them; rather, it is solely for the purpose of eliminating the disease of deluded conceptualization.
There is no dharma that can be removed; therefore, one is able to abide within it without removing that dharma.
Sengsheng said:
"To subdue means to remove what is clung to as delusive existence, not to remove the existence of dharmas."
He instructs them in order to sever the root of illness. Zhaò says: "All dharmas arise through conditions;
their gathering and dispersing are not of themselves. They take form when they assemble and vanish into formlessness when they disperse. Dharmas are simply natural; what do they have to do with me?"
The arising of affliction is due to my own deluded conceptualization regarding phenomena; it is I who create affliction for myself.
How could phenomena cause me to give rise to deluded conceptualization?
Thus, deluded conceptualization is the root of illness, while phenomena are not the source of my affliction.
Therefore, the rise of instruction and guidance merely removes the root of the illness; it does not remove the phenomena (dharma).
Sheng said:
"Only after the root of the illness is severed is the illness removed."
"What is called the root of illness?
It is said to be the presence of攀缘 (pān-yuan, clinging/conditioning).
Śāriputra asked:
The characteristic of that which is grasped constitutes the object of attachment (*ālambana*).
"Existence" means that it exists;
from the existence of such an object of attachment, it becomes the root of affliction.
Kumārajīva said:
"The previous discourse explained how a bodhisattva seeks the root of his own illness and settles his mind through principle; thus, he can remain undisturbed while facing sickness.

Now, it clarifies that for the sake of severing the illnesses of sentient beings, one must first investigate the causes and origins of those diseases, and only then respond to what is appropriate for them."

When the spiritual mechanism subtly moves, the mind becomes attached; this attachment of the mind is called "clinging" (ālambana). To grasp at signs through clinging is the beginning of deluded movement and the root of all affliction.
Sengzhao said:
"To 'cling to conditions' means that deluded thoughts subtly stir and cling to all phenomena.

Once deluded thoughts have taken these as objects, beauty and ugliness are already distinguished; once beauty and ugliness are distinguished, hatred and love blaze forth together. Thus, myriad fetters are vexed within, and ten thousand ailments arise without."

From the time of his own cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) onward, skillful calculation could not record it; its origin is merely a subtle thought, hence it is said that "clinging to conditions" (*ālambana*) is the root.
Sengsheng said:
"What was previously called 'existing' is now said to have 'just begun to exist.'"
What is it that serves as the object of attachment?
It is called the three realms.
Zhaò said:
This clarifies the objects of攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective conditions).
Dharmas outside the three realms are untainted and unconditioned; these dharmas are without marks and cannot be taken as objects of攀緣 by means of deluded thoughts.
That which can be taken as an object of cognition is merely the three realms.
Sengsheng said:
"The dharmas of the three realms are but conventional phenomena; they are not ultimate reality."
"How does one sever the攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective conditions/dependencies)? Zhaò said:
"Since one already knows its root, by what means does one sever it?"
Regarding "by means of non-attainment," Sheng said:
"It is by means of the principle of non-attainment that one cuts it off."
If there is nothing to be attained, then there is no objective support for clinging.
Zhaò says:
"The reason one clings to objective supports is that the mind harbors the intent to grasp."
Thus, there is grasping because the mind harbors the notion of attainment.
If one can know that dharmas are illusory and deceptive, such that there is neither grasping nor attainment, then the攀緣 (pān-yuán; clinging to objects) will naturally cease.
"What is meant by 'non-apprehension'?
It means being free from the two views.
Daosheng said:
Second, the non-apprehension of views.
What are the two views?
They are the view of the internal and the view of the external; these are non-apprehensible.
Sengzhao said:
"Internally there is deluded thought, and externally there are all phenomena; these two are false and illusory, and ultimately nothing can be attained.
Sengsheng said:

Second, although one initially holds the view that internal and external phenomena exist as objective realities, when wisdom contemplates them, one realizes that in principle there is no such distinction between internal and external; subsequently, these two views can no longer apprehend anything as internal or external.
Mañjuśrī! This is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines his mind.
To sever the suffering of old age, illness, and death—this is the bodhi of that bodhisattva.
Dongsheng said:
"Bodhi takes the salvation through reality as its path.
If a bodhisattva can act in this way, although they have not yet attained it, it is already present."
If it were not thus, that which one has cultivated and refined would be devoid of wisdom and benefit.
Zhaò said:

"If one can skillfully harmonize the mind so as not to harbor divergent thoughts, and dwells eternally within birth and death while severing that suffering—this is the path to Bodhi for a Bodhisattva."
If one cannot do so, then that which they practice is not yet sufficient to constitute wisdom within, nor sufficient to constitute benefit without.
Sheng said:
"Without wisdom, there is no benefit for things."
For example, one may be considered brave only after having conquered an enemy.
Daosheng said:
"When both oneself and those close to one have no further enemies, that is true bravery."
One who thus simultaneously eliminates old age, sickness, and death is what is meant by a Bodhisattva.
Sheng said:

"A Bodhisattva regards sentient beings as no different from their own kin; if he does not eliminate the enemies of old age, sickness, and death for them, he has likewise failed to eliminate his own enemies."
That sick bodhisattva should further reflect:
"Just as this illness of mine is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
Kumārajīva said:
Understanding that illness is not real, one is therefore able to dwell within it without being disturbed.
If one were to say that illness truly exists, then illness could never be eliminated;
sentient beings are boundless, and thus illnesses would likewise be inexhaustible.
If the nature of inexhaustible illness truly exists, how can it be transcended?
At that moment, one becomes confused and the mind turns back toward retreat.
If illness were not real, it would be easy to eliminate; then compassion would arise, and one would give rise to great vows to save all beings.
Sheng said:
"Furthermore, one gives rise to great compassion through this very thought.
'As for my illness, it is neither real nor existent'—this means that he has already attained realization."
As for the statement that "the illness of sentient beings is neither real nor existent," this means that they have not yet awakened to it.
This is intended to instruct them so that they may come to know this Dharma.
However, since the cultivation of the great compassionate heart has already been fully detailed in the preceding text, what is clarified here is merely mindfulness.
When performing this contemplation, if one gives rise to a great compassion based on attachment or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it.
Kumārajīva said:

"This means that one has not yet deeply entered the true reality (bhūtatathatā); seeing sentient beings as existing entities, the mind gives rise to attachment, and from this, compassion is produced—this is called 'great compassion based on attachment and views.'"
A great compassion born of attachment and views is false and impure; because it can cause others to give rise to thoughts of weariness and aversion, it should be abandoned.
Zhaò says:

"If one is to discipline oneself, one should first contemplate that the illnesses of oneself and of all beings are formed through causes and conditions, being provisional and without reality; it is appropriate to give rise to compassion with such a mind."
If this contemplation is not yet pure, and one gives rise to compassion upon seeing sentient beings with feelings of attachment, it is called "compassion born of attachment and views.
Although this compassion is wholesome, it is mixed with the objective realm of attachment and views; thus, it cannot avoid being a burden and should therefore be relinquished.
Dushun said:

"When one gives rise to great compassion through the two aforementioned contemplations, if within those contemplations there is a mind of attachment and affection, or if one perceives sentient beings and desires to rescue them out of such [attachment], this constitutes 'great compassion born of attachment and views.'"
"Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas eliminate adventitious afflictions.
Kumārajīva said:
The mind is fundamentally pure and free from defilement; it is through the encounter with the conditions of defilement that they arise, serving as adventitious dust upon the mind.
Thus, he gives rise to great compassion. Zhaò says:
When the mind encounters external conditions, afflictions arise abruptly; therefore, they are called "adventitious dust.
It is the dharma of a bodhisattva to eliminate this adventitious dust and give rise to great compassion.
If attachment and views are not severed, afflictions will proliferate all the more; therefore, one should abandon them.
Daosheng said:
"Attachment and views arise from deluded perceptions and are but adventitious defilements; only by eliminating them can one give rise to great compassion.
One who possesses attachment and views within their compassion will harbor a sense of weariness and aversion toward birth and death."
Kumārajīva said:
"If one gives rise to views because of attachment and feels compassion, there will be weariness and fatigue.
If one can remain free from these, there will be no weariness."
Sheng said:
"If one attempts to pull it out by means of craving, one will inevitably abandon it.
Since one has already seen it yet does not eliminate it, how can one achieve complete transformation?"
"Wherever one is born, one will not be obscured by craving or views.
Kumārajīva said:
"If one can eliminate craving and views, one immediately abandons the karma of fetters and undergoes dharma-birth, which is sovereign and unimpeded."
Sengzhao said:

"Now, wherever there is something seen, there must be something obstructed; wherever there is something loved, there must be something hated. This is the way of the finite—how could it possibly bring about the function of the infinite?"

If one can depart from these, then the Dharma-body is born through transformation, being neither present nor absent; birth and death are endless, yet one does not perceive them as distant. How, then, could there be the obscuration of craving and views, or the exhaustion of weariness?
Śāriputra said:
"It is because those who are born everywhere do not experience weariness or aversion; how could they be thus shrouded by craving and views?
That which is born is without bondage, and it is able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings to untie their bonds."
Zhaò said:
"Once attachment and views are eliminated and the Dharma-body is established, then that which is born will be without bondage, and one will also be able to liberate others from their bonds.
Shēng said:
Since Great Compassion arises without being obscured by attachment or views, it does not further bind one to birth.
As the Buddha has said:
"If one is bound oneself, it is impossible for one to release the bonds of others."
If one is oneself unbound, it is possible for one to untie the bonds of others;
therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bondage.
What is meant by "bondage"?
What is meant by "liberation" (*jie*)? Zhaò says:
It refers to the meaning of internal harmony achieved through the unraveling of bonds.
"Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is a bond for a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna presents two obstacles: it obstructs both nirvāṇa and the bodhisattva path."
Sengzhao said:
"Rebirth within the three realms and the attainment of realization by the two vehicles both result from attachment to the flavor of dhyāna; this is why they constitute bonds.
Sengsheng said:
If one practices dhyāna with craving for its retribution, then one finds flavor in that practice.
Once one finds flavor in the practice, one will surely be deluded by its retribution.
Now, those who are deluded by retribution are bound to rebirth.
"Taking birth through skillful means is the bodhisattva's liberation.
Zhaò says:

"Since he himself is already free from birth, yet takes birth for the sake of sentient beings through skillful means, then there is no bondage between self and others; this is why it constitutes liberation."
Sengsheng said:
"Those who take birth for the sake of saving all living beings do so as a skillful means (upāya).
Because they originally did not act for their own sake, there is no delusion regarding their karmic retribution."
Furthermore, there is bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means, and liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means;
there is bondage through skillful means lacking wisdom, and liberation through skillful means accompanied by wisdom.
Zhaò said:

Skillfully accumulating manifold virtues is called *upāya* (expedient means); directly penetrating the characteristics of phenomena is called *prajñā* (wisdom). Only when both practices are fully possessed does one attain liberation.
If one possesses wisdom but lacks expedient means, one cannot avoid being bound.
"If one possesses skillful means but lacks wisdom, one likewise cannot escape bondage.
Sengsheng said:
"This further expands upon the meaning of bondage and liberation."

Skillful means are of two kinds: first, performing practices with merit that ultimately leads to the wondrous fruit; second, employing them as a transformation so that [the goal] is necessarily accomplished.
Wisdom is also of two kinds: first, contemplating principle to subdue the mind; second, exhausting the fetters through contemplation.
Contemplating principle to subdue the mind is common to all three vehicles; however, if one is biased and attached, one is bound within the Lesser Vehicle.
If it is employed as a skillful means for transformation, then one will not be bound.

Regarding the attainment of results through the practice of meritorious deeds: if one possesses fetters, one will inevitably receive retribution within the three realms, thereby remaining bound in birth;
however, if one attains the wisdom that exhausts all fetters, then one is liberated.
What is meant by being bound by wisdom lacking skillful means?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity, yet seeks to discipline himself within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is called being bound by wisdom lacking skillful means.
Kumārajīva said:
"To contemplate emptiness without grasping and to engage with existence without attachment—this is called skillful means (*upāya*).

Now, it is clear that those who have returned from the six realms of rebirth are not yet free from obstruction. When they contemplate emptiness, they have nothing to grasp or attach to; however, when they emerge from contemplation to manifest in pure lands and transform sentient beings, they give rise to views, grasping at signs, and hearts of craving and attachment."
It is clumsy in engaging with movement, yet subtle in still contemplation.
The wisdom that contemplates emptiness does not grasp at signs; although this is a skillful means (*upāya*), it receives its name from wisdom (*prajñā*).
Here, however, we take only the non-attachment while engaging with existence as the skillful means; therefore, it is said that there is no skillful means, but only wisdom.

From the seventh stage upward, their minds are constantly in a state of concentration, remaining unchanged whether in motion or stillness; therefore, it is said that they possess "expedient wisdom. Zhaò says:

From the sixth stage downward, the mind is not yet purely unified; when dwelling in existence, one abandons emptiness, and when dwelling in emptiness, one abandons existence. One is thus unable to engage with both existence and non-existence through the impartial true mind. Consequently, when adorning the lands and transforming sentient beings, one mixes these practices with attachment and views.
This is not what is meant by practicing virtue through skillful means; therefore, it lacks expedient means.
Yet, because one self-regulates by means of the three emptinesses, it possesses wisdom.
What is meant by liberation through wisdom accompanied by expedient means?

That is to say, one does not adorn buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity with a mind of craving or attachment; rather, one disciplines oneself within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, without weariness or fatigue.
Sheng said:
"When one contemplates the principle and subdues the mind, one will inevitably loathe birth and death.
One realizes that these are merely produced through the expedient means of transformation."
This is called liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means. Zhaò says:
From the seventh stage upward, one is fully endowed with both practices; because one traverses birth and death without weariness or fatigue, this constitutes liberation.
What is called "the bondage of lacking skillful means through wisdom"?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, while abiding in afflictions such as desire, hatred, and wrong views, plants the roots of various virtues; this is called "the bondage of lacking skillful means through wisdom."
Kumārajīva said:
"From the seventh stage downward, there are also differences in degree of superiority and inferiority.
This clarifies that those who are newly learning do not cultivate correct contemplation and do not restrain their afflictions; therefore, it is said that they lack wisdom."
Yet, being able to cultivate virtue and dedicate it while looking up toward the great fruit, one is said to possess skillful means (*upāya*).

If one can cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) to eliminate the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), this is called the wisdom that is free from afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa-prajñā*).
Furthermore, being skillfully able to dedicate [merit] such that the mind does not regress is the skillful means for seeking [enlightenment].
Although those from the sixth stage downward still generally remain within the realm of bondage, if they can possess these two dharmas, they are liberated even amidst bondage.
The aforementioned wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*) and the skillful means of engaging with existence without attachment—these two gates are supramundane dharmas (*lokottara-dharma*).
The present discussion of wisdom with signs (*sanimitta-prajñā*) and the skillful means capable of seeking [the truth]—these two gates are mundane dharmas (*laukika-dharma*).
Sengzhao said:
Not cultivating the wisdom of emptiness to eliminate afflictions constitutes wisdom;
yet encouraging the accumulation of manifold virtues constitutes skillful means.
What is meant by liberation through wisdom and skillful means?
It refers to planting the roots of all virtues while remaining free from all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and wrong views, and then dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Dushun said:

"Although one may be exempt from the bonds of birth by means of being without fetters, it is still possible to rely upon this to accomplish the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, one must speak of dedication (pariṇāmanā).
This is called 'liberation through wisdom and skillful means.'"
Zhaò says:

Above, there was the liberation through the wisdom of skillful means; now, there is the liberation through the skillful means of wisdom. Although the resulting liberation is the same, the sequence of practice differs.

Among those who first practice, some first accumulate merit through skillful means and subsequently cultivate the wisdom of emptiness, while others first cultivate the wisdom of emptiness and subsequently accumulate merit. Each follows what is appropriate for them, yet their liberation does not differ.
To leave behind afflictions is the capacity for self-discipline through the three gates of emptiness;
to accumulate merit toward Bodhi belongs to the stream of adorning the lands and transforming sentient beings.
These preceding and succeeding divergent teachings each fully exhaust their own excellence.
Mañjuśrī! That sick bodhisattva should contemplate all dharmas in this manner.
Zhaò said:
"From 'not real' downwards is the contemplation of non-binding.
Furthermore, contemplating that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self is called wisdom.
Kumārajīva said:

The preceding four lines spoke of the worldly and world-transcending wisdom and skillful means in combination; now, these four lines specifically clarify the world-transcending wisdom and skillful means.

They are also described as "superior unification through wisdom and skillful means. This principle clarifies that by employing wisdom and skillful means within the midst of illness, one is thus able to realize enlightenment without extinguishing the physical body.
If one regards the body as existing, then when illness arrives, one is distressed.
If one knows that the body is not real, then one remains undisturbed even in the midst of sickness.
World-transcending wisdom also has degrees of depth and shallowness; since "impermanence" is the initial characteristic of the statement "all is empty," impermanence is taught first.
The realization of impermanence is the mundane, shallow wisdom.
Although one’s body may be afflicted by illness, to remain constantly within the cycle of birth and death to benefit all beings without weariness is called skillful means.
Kumārajīva said:
"Birth and death are things to be loathed, yet one is able not to loathe them; because one skillfully dwells amidst perils and difficulties, it is called 'expedient means' (upāya).
Sengzhao said:
The Mahāyāna contemplation of the four marks of impermanence is itself the contemplation of equality and reality; therefore, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To dwell in the world with an impartial mind without weariness is therefore called skillful means (*upāya*).
The discourse on consolation and encouragement refers precisely to this matter.
Furthermore, one contemplates the body: the body is not separate from illness, and illness is not separate from the body.
Kumārajīva said:
When separated from the body, there is no illness; therefore, they are not separate.
Furthermore, it is said that the body and the illness share a single characteristic, and thus they are not separate.
This illness and this body are neither new nor old.
Kumārajīva said:
"This clarifies that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of bodily illness has neither newness nor antiquity; it speaks of supramundane profound wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is what is called wisdom."
Even if one assumes that the body has an illness, it does not undergo permanent extinction.
Sheng said:
"Although it is said that there is wisdom within skillful means, within skillful means there is no further wisdom."
Regarding "one who creates through skillful means possesses wisdom," there is further skillful means within that wisdom.
Therefore, having clarified this, I shall now expand upon its meaning.
This is called skillful means (*upāya*).
Kumārajīva said:
"Because one does not grasp at the characteristics of that which can be extinguished, one is able to remain unextinguished; this is the power of skillful means (*upāya*).

To engage with existence while appearing to grasp at characteristics yet actually not grasping them—when one does not grasp at characteristics, the principle is severed from existence—and yet one is able to engage with existence with such mastery over difficult matters, it is therefore called 'skillful means.'"
Sengzhao said:

The designations "new" and "old" arise from the concepts of "prior" and "subsequent. However, there is no illness apart from the body, and no body apart from illness; since both are produced by a multitude of conditions, which is prior and which is subsequent?
Since there is neither priority nor posteriority, there is neither new nor old; as there is neither new nor old, one enters the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and thus it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Possessing this wisdom, yet proceeding with the same speed as others without grasping at nirvana, is termed skillful means (*upāya*).
The initial teaching on self-discipline refers precisely to this matter.

Consoling and encouraging oneself through self-discipline is, in brief, skillful means and wisdom; since skillful means and wisdom are the pivotal essentials of this sutra, they are mentioned here in conjunction.
Mañjuśrī! A sick bodhisattva should thus discipline his mind. He said:
Having observed gain and loss, he was likewise tamed;
yet he did not abide therein.
Sheng said:
If one wishes to eliminate what is undisciplined, one must certainly take discipline as one's primary concern.
Furthermore, one should not abide in an undisciplined mind.
Zhaò said:

The practice of the Mahāyāna is wordless and signless; yet, words for the sake of subduing [sentient beings] have been employed to manifest the preceding text. Now, in order to clarify the meaning that lies beyond words, both [words and signs] are non-abiding.
That neither abides in either is the fundamental intent of "provisional speech," and the fundamental intent of provisional speech is the ultimate of "subduing.
Sengsheng said:
"It is simply that one does not take subduing as one's primary concern; it is not that one does not subdue."
Why is this? To abide in an undisciplined mind is the way of fools;
to abide in a disciplined mind is the way of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abide in either a disciplined or undisciplined mind; to be free from these two dharmas is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Sengzhao said:
The designation "undisciplined" originates from the foolish, while the name "disciplined" originates from the śrāvakas.

The Mahāyāna practitioner fundamentally possesses neither names nor marks; if one were to say they are undisciplined, they would be the same as ordinary people, and if one were to say they are disciplined, they would be the same as the Śrāvakas. Only by remaining free from both extremes does one accord with the middle-way practice of a Bodhisattva.
To remain within birth and death without being defiled by conduct, and to abide in nirvana without entering final extinction—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Sengzhao said:
If one wishes to say they are in birth and death, birth and death cannot defile them; if one wishes to say they are in nirvana, they do not enter ultimate cessation.
One might wish to say that they dwell in nirvana, yet they do not pass into extinction.
Therefore, those who practice by abiding in the Middle Way neither remain in saṃsāra nor dwell in nirvana.
"This is not the practice of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Kumārajīva said:
"The practices of ordinary persons are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable (*āniñjya*) practice."
"Immovable conduct" refers to the conduct of the realms of form and formlessness.
Because the lifespan in these two upper realms lasts for many kalpas, non-Buddhists consider it to be permanent; this is the meaning of "immovable."
The Buddha is also named according to what is designated by the world;
it is not the practice of the worthy and sages.
Kumārajīva said:
This means practicing the three liberations without realizing them;
this is the bodhisattva’s practice.
It is neither a defiled practice nor a pure practice; this is the bodhisattva’s practice.
Zhaò said: It is that which cannot be named.
Although it transcends the conduct of Māra, it manifests the subduing of all Māras; this is the practice of a Bodhisattva.
Zhaò said: That which cannot be said to exist and cannot be said to not exist—this can only be the practice of the Mahāyāna. Why is this so?
If one wishes to say that it exists, it is without characteristics and without name;
if one wishes to say that it does not exist, the myriad virtues are fully operative.
Because the myriad virtues are fully operative, although it is non-existent, it exists.
Being without marks and without names, things exist yet are non-existent.

Thus, to speak of existence does not contradict non-existence, and to speak of non-existence does not contradict existence. For this reason, this chapter sometimes speaks of "active practice" (yǒngxíng) and sometimes speaks of "non-active practice" (wúxíng); although existence and non-existence differ, their ultimate aim is no different.
The practices of Māra refer to the four practices of Māra.
Having long since transcended them, he manifests the subduing of Māra merely to demonstrate that there is something to be overcome.
Although he seeks all-knowledge, he does not seek it at an improper time; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"To seek the fruit of ultimate fulfillment when one's meritorious practices are not yet sufficient is called seeking at the wrong time.
Sengzhao said:
To seek realization midway before all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) has been perfected is called seeking at an improper time.
Although one contemplates that all phenomena are unarisen, not yet entering the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"To contemplate non-arising is to take up the dharma of realization.
Not entering the stage of right determination clarifies that there is no realization."
Sengzhao said:
"The 'correct position' refers to the stage of attaining realization.

While those of the three vehicles equally contemplate non-arising, those with weak power of wisdom cannot emerge from it on their own, whereas those with strong power of wisdom transcend it without realizing [a fixed state]."
"Though one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, yet enters into various false views—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"To contemplate dependent origination is the way to sever false views."
That one can instead align with those of false views—how could this be possible for those of the Two Vehicles?
Although they embrace all sentient beings, they do so without attachment; such is the practice of a Bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is the Dharma of the Four Means of Integration (catvāri saṃgrahavastūni).
The Four Means of Integration are the methods for cherishing sentient beings; here, it clarifies that one cherishes them without becoming attached."
Zhaò said:
"The four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu) gather others; they are the ultimate expression of loving-kindness and benevolence.
To regard others as oneself and yet remain free from attachment—this is the height of compassion."
"Though one delights in seclusion, not relying on the exhaustion of body and mind—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"The cessation of mental consciousness is called 'seclusion'; seclusion is the meaning of emptiness."
"Not relying" means being clear regarding emptiness and not grasping at signs.
Zhaò says:
"Small detachment is to leave behind clamor and bustle; great detachment is to exhaust both body and mind."
Although the Bodhisattva delights in great detachment, he does not rely upon it;
although he traverses the three realms,
Kumārajīva said:
To manifest within the three realms without destroying the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
To dwell therein without confusion.
Zhaò says:
"The three realms are themselves the dharma-nature; how could dwelling within them cause any destruction?"
Although one practices within emptiness, one plants the roots of manifold virtues; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
One practices emptiness with the desire to eliminate existence, yet simultaneously plants the virtues of existence.
"Though practicing signlessness, one delivers sentient beings; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"By practicing signlessness, one seeks to eliminate the grasping at the signs of sentient beings, and only then does one deliver them."
Although they practice non-action, they manifest the reception of a body; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Sengzhao says:
"To practice non-action means desiring not to create birth and death, yet still manifesting the reception of a body."
Although one practices non-arising, one gives rise to all wholesome practices; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"Practicing non-arising" means that while desiring to extinguish all minds of arising, one is simultaneously giving rise to all wholesome practices.
"Though practicing the six pāramitās, to thoroughly know the minds and mental factors of sentient beings is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:

"The six perfections are dharmas for one's own cultivation; once one's own cultivation is complete, one then transforms others, and it is through transforming others that one comes to know the minds of sentient beings."
Although one practices it oneself now, one is already able to know that [other] person.
Furthermore, in the sixth perfection, one contemplates the signlessness of phenomena; without being hindered by signlessness, one is also able to know the minds of sentient beings.
Sengzhao said:
"The six perfections are practices of signlessness (*animitta*).
In signlessness there is no cognition, yet one thereby universally knows the mental activities of sentient beings."
Although they practice the six supernormal powers, they do not exhaust their outflows; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"Though they possess the six supernormal powers, they do not engage in the practice of exhausting the outflows."

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva contemplates outflows (*āsrava*) as being themselves non-outflows (*anāsrava*), he is able to dwell eternally within birth and death while sharing in those same outflows; how could he, by means of the exhaustion of outflows, make himself distinct from them?
"Though one practices the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), not being greedily attached to being reborn in the Brahma world is the bodhisattva practice.
Kumārajīva said:

"The practice of the four immeasurables should lead to birth in the stages of the four dhyānas; that it specifically mentions the Brahma [world] here is because sentient beings take the Brahmā deity as their primary object of veneration, and thus he cites that which they revere."
Furthermore, the stages of the four dhyānas are collectively termed "Brahma.
Although one may practice meditative concentration, liberation, and samādhi,
Kumārajīva said:
Dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas;
samādhi refers to the four formless attainments;
and liberation refers to the eight liberations.
The samādhis are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Yet not being reborn according to these dhyānas is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
To take up the cause while not taking up the fruit can be called acting with mastery.
Although one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, not permanently departing from body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—this is the bodhisattva practice.
Kumārajīva said:
"Although one contemplates these four dharmas, one does not realize their ultimate extinction.
Sengzhao said:
The practitioners of the Lesser Vehicle observe the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, attaining realization by becoming detached from them.
Although Bodhisattvas likewise observe these four, they do not attain realization through permanent detachment.
Although they practice the four right efforts, they do not abandon physical and mental diligence; this is the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"Vigorous effort" refers to the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).
Because one does not grasp at them, they are called "detachment."
Zhaò said:
"The practitioners of the Hīnayāna cultivate the four right efforts; once their merit is accomplished, they relinquish them and enter into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although Bodhisattvas practice these same deeds, they do not relinquish them in the same way."
"Though he practices the four bases of psychic power, he attains mastery over supernatural faculties; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Kumārajīva said:
"Though he manifests the study of the supernormal powers, he has in reality already attained mastery over supernatural faculties."
Zhaò said:
"Although they equally practice the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) of the Hīnayāna, they have long since attained the sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the Mahāyāna.
The bases of psychic power are the cause of the supernormal powers."
Although they practice the five faculties, they discern the sharpness or dullness of the various faculties of sentient beings; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Zhaò says:
"The followers of the Lesser Vehicle cultivate only their own faculties and are not skilled regarding the faculties of others."
Although a bodhisattva practices in common with others, they skillfully understand the faculties of beings so that both self and others may be brought into accord.
Although they exercise the five powers, they joyfully seek the ten powers of a Buddha; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although they practice the seven factors of enlightenment, they discern the wisdom of a Buddha; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although they practice the eightfold noble path, they delight in practicing the immeasurable path of the Buddhas; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Kumārajīva said, "He has fully clarified the manifestation of shallow dharmas, yet inwardly he has truly entered the profound dharma.
Sengzhao said, "Although his faculties, powers, and path of awakening are the same as those of the śrāvakas, the object of his aspiration always lies in the practice of a Buddha."
Although he practiced both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), Kumārajīva said:
"Initially fixing the mind upon an object is called *śamatha*; that which corresponds to this fixation is called *vipaśyanā*."
To practice the dharmas that assist the Path without ultimately falling into quiescent extinction is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Zhaò says:
"To bind the mind to its objects is called *śamatha* (calm abiding); to discern and penetrate deeply is called *vipaśyanā* (insight)."
Śamatha and vipaśyanā are the essential methods that assist toward nirvāṇa.
The bodhisattva practices by means of them, yet does not follow them by falling into nirvāṇa.
Although he practices all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, he adorns his body with the primary and secondary marks; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Sengzhao said:
Those who cultivate the practice of non-arising and non-ceasing and signlessness do so fundamentally to extinguish signs, yet they adorn their bodies with the primary and secondary marks.
Although they manifest the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they do not abandon the Buddha-dharma; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Sengzhao said:
"Though they manifest the deportment of the Hīnayāna, they do not abandon the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
Though they accord with the ultimately pure characteristics of all phenomena, they manifest their bodies according to what is appropriate; this is the practice of a Bodhisattva."
Sengzhao said:
"The principle of ultimate purity has no form or appearance, yet it manifests various images according to what is appropriate for each being.
Although one contemplates that all Buddha-lands are eternally quiescent like space, yet manifesting various kinds of pure Buddha-lands—this is the practice of a bodhisattva."
Zhaò said:
Emptiness is fundamentally non-manifesting, yet it manifests for others.
Although one attains the Buddha-way, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvana, one does not abandon the path of the bodhisattva; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Sengzhao said:

Although he manifests the attainment of Buddhahood, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvana, he does not remain in eternal quiescence, but returns to the cycle of birth and death to cultivate the bodhisattva path.
As listed above, how could these be within the capacity of the followers of the Two Vehicles?
They are the practice of the Bodhisattvas alone.
When these words were spoken, among the great assembly led by Mañjuśrī, eight thousand devaputras all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Five;
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Compiled by Shi Sengzhao of the Later Qin.
Chapter Six: The Inconceivable (Ṣaṣṭhaḥ acintya-parivartaḥ).
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that there were no seats within this room, had this thought:
Kumārajīva said:
"The Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body possess neither physical nor mental fatigue.

As for Śrāvakas, whose forms are bound by karma, although their minds delight in the Dharma, their bodies experience weariness and exhaustion; therefore, they give rise to the thought of cessation and rest."

Among the disciples, Śāriputra was the most senior in years and physically frail; therefore, he was the first to conceive this thought, wishing not to manifest his own accumulated traces of weariness.
Furthermore, because Vimalakīrti would surely have already anticipated his mind, Śāriputra simply thought it over without speaking.

Upon examining the subsequent statement, "Where should the great beings sit? it appears that he inferred his own fatigue to observe the physical condition of the assembly, conceiving this thought out of concern that they might require rest.
"Where should these bodhisattvas and the assembly of great disciples sit?
Śāriputra said:
"The seats were previously removed in anticipation; therefore, Śāriputra gave rise to the thought regarding the hair."
The elder Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir, have you come for the sake of the Dharma? Kumārajīva said: [The following is the translation of the subsequent dialogue].

He did not directly criticize [the questioner] but instead questioned him, wishing to demonstrate that his underlying thoughts were contrary to reason and that he was trapped in a state of defeat whether advancing or retreating.
[The questioner asked,] "Are you seeking a seat? Zhaò said:
The purport of "sleeping alone on the bed" is manifested here.
Śāriputra silently grasped the underlying mechanism; thus, he struck upon the opening of the discourse.
Vimalakīrti was about to elucidate the Way of Non-seeking, and therefore he questioned him by means of that [statement].
Sheng said:
"The thought of seeking a seat implies a desire for something; such desire contradicts the Dharma and is not the purpose for which you have come.
Śāriputra replied:
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Indeed, Śāriputra!"
Regarding "one who seeks the Dharma," Kumārajīva said:
"Not grasping at the characteristics of dharmas, but comprehending the principle within the Dharma, is called seeking the Dharma."
If one grasps at marks and gives rise to attachment, the mind will diverge from the Dharma; this is not the seeking of the Dharma.
One does not covet even body or life, much less a seat.
Indeed, the seeker of the Dharma does not seek in terms of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Sengzhao says:
"If one seeks the Truth, one does not seek even the Dharma, much less the implements for securing the body.
From this point downward, the text applies universally to all phenomena to clarify the meaning of non-seeking.
There is no seeking after the realms (dhātu) or bases (āyatana).
ZHAO said:
"Realms" refers to the eighteen realms.
"Entry" refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
It is not a seeking after the realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
Zhaò said:
There is no seeking within the three realms. O Śāriputra!
Indeed, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha, does not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and does not seek by clinging to the Saṃgha.
Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek by seeing suffering, does not seek by abandoning the origin [of suffering], and does not seek by realizing cessation or cultivating the path.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one says, "I shall see suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path," this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), not the seeking of the Dharma.
Zhaò said:
Where there is seeking, there is proliferation; where there is proliferation, there is no true seeking. Thus we know that true seeking is non-seeking.
"O Śāriputra! The Dharma is named 'quiescence.
If one practices with arising and ceasing, one is seeking arising and ceasing, not seeking the Dharma."
The Dharma is called "stainless.
If one becomes stained by the Dharma, even up to nirvāṇa, this is attachment and not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no place of practice.
If one practices within the dharma, this is merely practicing within its sphere; it is not the seeking of the dharma.
The dharma is without grasping or abandoning.
If one grasps at or abandons the dharma, this is grasping and abandoning; it is not the seeking of the dharma.
The Dharma has no location.
If one clings to a location, this is clinging to a place, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named "signlessness."
If one pursues consciousness according to its characteristics, this is to seek characteristics rather than to seek the Dharma.
The Dharma cannot be dwelled upon;
if one dwells in the Dharma, this is to dwell in the Dharma rather than to seek the Dharma.
The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.
Zhaò says:
The six consciousnesses are briefly designated by four names.
"Seeing and hearing" refers to the visual and auditory consciousnesses;
"perceiving" refers to the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses;
and "cognizing" refers to the mental consciousness.
If one engages in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, this is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma is named the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If one engages in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is seeking the conditioned; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
Therefore, Śāriputra,
those who seek the Dharma should have no seeking toward any phenomena.
Zhaò says:
The characteristics of dharmas are such as these; how can they be sought?
If one wishes to seek them, only non-seeking is true seeking.
Daosheng said:
Now, those who seek the Dharma do not truly "seek"; they seek by means of having no further seeking.
When these words were spoken, five hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Zhaò said:
"The Mahāyāna Dharma-eye is pure.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

"O Benevolent One, you travel through immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya lands; in which Buddha-field is there a lion throne endowed with excellent, sublime, and perfected merits?"
Kumārajīva said:
"To ask while already knowing the answer is intended to inspire confidence among the assembled multitude.
There are two meanings to the phrase 'borrowing a seat in that country':"
First, he wished to manifest the pure and adorned merits of all Buddhas by providing an extraordinary seat, thereby deepening the aspirations of bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice.
Second, he wished to utilize the traces of his coming and going so that his transformative influence might flow through two lands.
Zhaò said:
"The Great Being Mañjuśrī travels and transforms beings without limit; he must have seen the exquisite seats of various kingdoms.

Vimalakīrti wished to inspire a spirit of reverence and faith among those present at the assembly, and therefore he inquired before taking [the seat], demonstrating that he examined the matter with care."
Śāriputra said:
"The reason I asked first was to clarify that what follows is indeed the truth.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Householder!
To the east, beyond thirty-six Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a world named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa; its Buddha is named Sumeru-dīpa-rāja, and he currently resides there."
The body of that Buddha was eighty-four thousand yojanas in height.
Zhaò said:
"Yojana" is the name for a unit of distance in India.
The superior yojana is sixty *li*, the middling yojana is fifty *li*, and the inferior yojana is forty *li*.
His lion throne is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, its adornments being unsurpassed.

Thereupon, the elder Vimalakīrti manifested his supernormal powers; immediately, that Buddha dispatched thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, broad, majestic, and pure—which entered the room of Vimalakīrti.
Zhaò said:
"Although Vimalakīrti went to fetch [the Buddha] by means of his supernormal powers, that Buddha would not have sent him, nor would there have been any way for him to arrive.
This was something never before seen by the various bodhisattvas, the great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings."
The chamber was vast and spacious, fully accommodating thirty-two thousand lion thrones without any obstruction.
Neither the city of Vaiśālī nor the four continents of Jambudvīpa were cramped; all appeared exactly as they had been before.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī,
"Please take your seat upon the lion throne.
Sit together with these superior bodhisattvas, and you should manifest your own body so that it conforms to the form of that seat."
The bodhisattva who had attained supernormal powers immediately transformed his body to a height of forty-two thousand yojanas and sat upon the lion throne;
the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples were all unable to ascend it.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra,
"Please take a seat on the lion throne.
Śāriputra replied:
"Householder!
This seat is high and broad; I cannot ascend it.
Kumārajīva said:
Vimalakīrti, through his supernatural power, intended to demonstrate to the assembly that the difference between the Great and Small Vehicles is as vast as this.
It is also said that these are the seats of the merits of all Buddhas, and not something upon which those lacking merit may ascend.
Principle is inherently profound and pure;
it is not something that can be constrained. Vimalakīrti said: "O Śāriputra!..."
"Only by prostrating before the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja can you sit.

Thereupon, the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved upon enlightenment and the great disciples immediately prostrated before the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja, and they were then able to sit upon the lion thrones.
Śāriputra said:
"Householder,
this is truly unprecedented!"

Thus, this small room accommodates these high and vast seats without obstructing the city of Vaiśālī; furthermore, it does not crowd the villages, towns, and cities of Jambudvīpa, nor the palaces of the devas, nāga kings, ghosts, and spirits throughout the four continents.
Vimalakīrti said: "O Śāriputra!
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'inconceivable.'"
Sengzhao said:
"If there are inconceivable traces manifested externally, there must be inconceivable virtues manifesting internally.
If one traces back to their source, they are simply expedient wisdom."
Why is this so? Wisdom illuminates nothing that is obscure, and expedient means cultivate nothing that is not virtuous.
Because there is nothing obscure it does not illuminate, there is no principle it does not exhaust; because there is no virtue it does not cultivate, there is no achievement it does not accomplish.
Merit lies in non-attainment, and thus it is perfected through unity;
principle reaches its ultimate in non-extremity, and thus it is made pervasive through emptiness.

Therefore, wisdom encompasses all things yet remains without illumination; expedient means accumulate myriad virtues yet remain without merit; one is darkly quiescent and non-active, yet there is nothing that is not done—this is the pinnacle of the inconceivable.
The large and the small accommodate one another; diverse forms respond in unison. Is this merely a coarse record for the ears and eyes, sufficient to speak of it in its entirety?
Nevertheless, by means of the derivative to indicate the fundamental, and relying on the coarse to manifest the subtle, I have thus borrowed this seat to briefly reveal the matter.
This sutra begins with the Pure Land and concludes with the Dharma-offering; the Mahāyāna path contained therein is nothing other than the inconceivable Dharma.
Therefore, he entrusts [the teaching], saying: "This sutra is named the Dharma-gate of Inconceivable Liberation; you should uphold it.
This chapter receives its distinct title because it manifests external traces.
Liberation is the dharma of a sovereign mind.

Having attained this liberation, whatever one undertakes—whether internal practice or external response—is performed with sovereign freedom and without obstruction; this is beyond the capacity of the followers of the Two Vehicles to deliberate upon.
One attains this liberation only upon reaching the Dharma-body from the seventh stage upward.
An alternative version reads "liberation through the samādhi of psychic power," to which Kumārajīva remarked:
"These are different names for the same essence."
If one desires to act but is unable to do so, that constitutes bondage; to act in accordance with thought is immediately liberation.
To have no incapacity is what is called liberation.
Being able to act while remaining unaware of how it is so accomplished is therefore termed "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

If a bodhisattva abides in this liberation, they can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed without any increase or decrease; the original appearance of Sumeru, the king of mountains, remains as it was before.
Kumārajīva said:
"Sumeru is the quintessence of the earth."
This earth is great; what is explained below—water, fire, wind, and earth—are its four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Those who are deluded claim that these four great elements possess a spirit (*ātman*), asserting that they are the greatest and eternal. Now, by means of the power of the Way (*mārgabala*), we shall demonstrate that they are not spiritual entities.
That something as minute as a fine mote is contained within suggests that clarity is not large;
that the vast and the minute can coexist suggests that things have no fixed substance and that clarity is not constant.

All of this serves to overturn what has been confined, to extract what is obscured and stagnant, and to eliminate habitual attachments, thereby providing a path for returning to the fundamental source.

The Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven neither perceive nor know that they have entered [the mustard seed]; only those who are ready for deliverance see Mount Sumeru enter within the mustard seed. This is called the inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation.

Furthermore, he causes the waters of the four great oceans to enter into a single pore without disturbing the fish, turtles, crocodiles, alligators, or any other aquatic creatures; yet the original appearance of those great oceans remains as it was before. The dragons, spirits, and asuras do not perceive or know where they have entered, nor is there any disturbance to these beings.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can seize the trichiliocosm as if it were a potter’s wheel and place it in his right palm; he may then cast it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet the sentient beings therein remain unaware and unknowing of where they have gone. He may then return it to its original location without causing anyone to perceive the thought of coming or going, and this world remains exactly as it was before.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there may be sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world and can be delivered; for them, the Bodhisattva manifests seven days as a single kalpa.
Kumārajīva said:
Alternatively, it may also be said that time is an eternal dharma, yet by causing its duration to be altered, it demonstrates that it is not eternal.
Thus, for those sentient beings, it is made to be perceived as one kalpa.

Or, for those sentient beings who do not wish to dwell long but are ready to be delivered, the Bodhisattva immediately shortens one kalpa to seven days, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as seven days.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can gather the adornments of all buddha-fields into a single land and manifest them to sentient beings.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva may take the sentient beings of a single buddha-field and place them upon his right palm, flying to the ten directions to display them everywhere, yet without moving them from their original location.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The articles of offering used by sentient beings throughout the ten directions to serve the Buddhas, the Bodhisattva causes them all to be seen within a single pore.
Furthermore, all the suns, moons, and stars existing in the lands of the ten directions, he causes them to be universally seen within a single pore of his own.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All the winds that exist throughout the worlds of the ten directions, a bodhisattva is able to inhale and draw into his mouth without his body being harmed, and even the trees outside do not break or snap.

Furthermore, when the kalpas of the worlds in the ten directions are consumed by fire at their end, he places all those fires within his belly; yet the functions of the fires remain as before, and they do no harm.

Moreover, from below, passing through Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he takes a single Buddha-land and lifts it up to a region above, passing through countless worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as easily as one might pick up a jujube leaf with the point of a needle, without causing any disturbance.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernormal powers, manifest the body of a Buddha, or manifest the body of a pratyekabuddha, or manifest the body of a śrāvaka, or manifest the body of Śakra, or manifest the body of Brahmā, or manifest the body of a world-protector, or manifest the body of a wheel-turning monarch.

Furthermore, all sounds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether superior, middling, or inferior—he is able to transform them all into the voice of the Buddha, causing it to produce the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Furthermore, the various teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions are all universally made available for hearing therein. Śāriputra!
I have now briefly described the power of the bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation; were it to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard the exposition of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation dharma-gate, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to Śāriputra:
"It is like a person presenting various forms and images before one who is blind; they are not seen by that person."
It is just like this: when all the śrāvakas hear this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, they are unable to understand it.
When the wise hear this, who would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"Why have we forever severed our roots, becoming like withered seeds regarding this Mahāyāna?
Upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, all Śrāvakas should wail and weep, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm."
Zhaò said:
"Because the point of divergence is profound, I have merely used words to suggest that one should weep aloud.
If those of the Two Vehicles, whose sorrow and grief are forever eliminated, do not even shed a single tear, how much less could they cause the three thousandfold world-system to tremble?"
All Bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crown of their heads.
Zhaò said:

"Kāśyapa intends to clarify the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, thereby elevating one and suppressing the other for the sake of the audience. Thus, those for whom it is not their lot should shed tears of despair, while those for whom it is their lot should harbor joy as they receive it upon their crowns."
If there are bodhisattvas who believe in and understand this inconceivable gate of liberation, all the hosts of Māra can do nothing against them.
Zhaò says:
"If one can merely believe and understand it, even Māra cannot disturb them; how much more so for those who practice in accordance with it!"
When Mahākāśyapa had spoken these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa:
"O Virtuous One!"

Those who act as Māras in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are for the most part bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation, who manifest as Māras through the power of skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings.
Zhaò said:

According to Kāśyapa, those with faith and understanding who are inconceivable cannot be disturbed by Māra; yet there are also bodhisattvas in the ten directions with faith and understanding who are disturbed by Māra. This is intended to clarify that the actions of the inconceivable Mahāsattva are sovereign, and because he wishes to advance those who have only recently begun their studies, he manifests as a māra-king—this is not something that the power of Māra can achieve.
This clarifies the inconceivable and also fulfills the intent of Kāśyapa’s words.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!

There may be immeasurable bodhisattvas in the ten directions, from whom someone might beg for hands, feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, blood, flesh, skin, bones, villages, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, pearls, conch shells, clothing, or food and drink.
Such beggars are mostly bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who, through the power of skillful means, go to test them so as to make their resolve firm.
Kumārajīva said:

"A Bodhisattva whose karmic bonds are being exhausted has nearly completed the perfection of giving but has not yet reached its ultimate limit. Therefore, an inconceivable Bodhisattva forcibly solicits from him, so that he may be made to exhaust his lack of parsimony and fully perfect his firm resolve."
It also causes sentient beings to know its steadfastness, and it causes them to know their own steadfastness for themselves.
Zhaò says:
"Generally, the arising of testing occurs when things have not yet been distinguished."
The inconceivable Great Being has already perfected his supernormal powers and perceives the faculties of others in advance;
how could there be any need for testing? Nevertheless, in order to strengthen their resolve, he sought what was not required.
To seek what is not required is identical to the traces of demonic trials; thus, it is described as "trial.
How could one wait for a trial before knowing [the truth]? Why is this so?
Bodhisattvas who dwell in the inconceivable liberation possess the power of majestic virtue; therefore, they practice coercion to demonstrate such difficult matters to all sentient beings.
Ordinary persons of inferior capacity lack such power and influence, and thus cannot coerce a bodhisattva in this way.
Zhaò said:

"To amputate a person's hands and feet, to separate them from their wife and children, or to forcibly seize their national wealth, generates grief and sorrow; yet although there is minor suffering in the present moment, it leads to great peace for eternal kalpas."

This is because one must deeply observe the capacities of people's faculties and weigh their relative gravity; it is not within the power of one who sees the near but fails to see the far to perform such a task.
It is like the trampling of a dragon-elephant, which is not something a donkey can endure.
Zhaò says:
"The ability or inability serves as an analogy.
The superior among elephants is called a 'dragon-elephant' (nāga)."
This is called the gate of wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva who dwells in inconceivable liberation.
Zhaò says:

Wisdom reaches far and through, while skillful means guides from near; they are the reason for the manifestation of diverse traces and the means by which the multitudes are perfected. Since things do not exist without causes, yet none can fathom them, these two gates of provisional wisdom and [true] wisdom constitute the foundation of the inconceivable.
Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings (6). At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?"
Kumārajīva said:
"If sentient beings possessed a truly fixed and determinate nature, then the inconceivable Great Being (Mahāsattva) would not have needlessly traveled to test them and cause them to suffer."
Because it is not real and is easily accomplished, one practices harassment and oppression.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of Buddha-dharma:
first, existence; second, emptiness.
If one constantly dwells in existence, one is burdened by attachments and conceptualizations; if one constantly contemplates emptiness, one abandons the roots of goodness.
If emptiness and existence are employed alternately, the two aforementioned faults will not arise, just as the sun and moon alternate in their functions to bring all things to completion.
Since it has already been stated that [beings] exist, we now clarify the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One should contemplate sentient beings as being thus.
"Sentient beings," "spiritual self" (*puruṣa*), and "self" (*ātman*) are merely different expressions for the same meaning.
It is like a foolish man traveling along a road who encounters a discarded chest containing a large mirror.
Upon opening the chest and looking into the mirror, he sees his own reflection; thinking it to be the owner of the chest, he bows his head in apology and departs, leaving it behind.
It is likewise with sentient beings who, upon entering the precious mirror of the Buddha-dharma treasury, grasp at signs and calculate a self, only to cast it aside and depart.
It is also like a blind person walking along a road who encounters the prince of a kingdom and clings to him firmly, refusing to let go.
In a short while, the king’s officials arrived; they inflicted extreme pain and coercion to forcibly seize it, and only then did they release it.

It is just like sentient beings with wrong views who perceive a self where there is no self: when impermanence and suffering arrive, and things disintegrate according to conditions, they finally realize it is not a self; it is exactly like this.
Like clouds in the sky, they vanish when approached.
When one observes the emptiness of all phenomena with true compassion, that is true wisdom; within true wisdom, the arising of unconditioned compassion is called "true compassion."
It also takes loving-kindness as its foundation; preaching the true Dharma for others is called "true loving-kindness.

Furthermore, it takes loving-kindness as its foundation, and subsequently, various practices such as giving are designated by names—either named after their intrinsic nature or named after their causes.
From this point onward, the examples may be sought accordingly.
Zhaò said:
"The contemplation for self-regulation by the Great Being who is distressed with compassion, and its subtle words and profound purport, are also fully contained in the preceding text."
However, the characteristics of dharmas are empty and profound, beyond what the mind can perceive;
true contemplation is dark and silent, beyond what words can distinguish.

How could it be otherwise? That he does not realize nirvana but shares the same afflictions as all living beings, and that he manifests inconceivable traces without fixed origin—sometimes appearing as a māra king to pressure beginners—all these are the deeds of a Great Being who has mastered himself.

When one observes oneself and others as both being empty, the analogy for this matter becomes even more profound; yet it causes those who aspire to the ultimate truth to be bewildered by the reach of "wordless speech," while those who cling to themselves increase their view of a sentient being. Thus, the Way that transcends words is difficult to express in words.
By drawing near upon various metaphors and reaching far to illustrate true contemplation, one removes the burden of worldly people’s attachment to words; for this reason, this question arises.
Daosheng said:
"The aforementioned 'inconceivable' refers to the traces of responding to and transforming sentient beings."
He responded without fixed direction, as if he possessed the sentiments of a sentient being.
Since one who possesses the sentiments of a sentient being cannot perform transformation, it was necessary to question him.
Vimalakīrti said:
For example, just as a magician views the illusory person he has conjured, so does a bodhisattva view sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"The magician views the illusion and knows it is not real."
The Great Being’s observation of sentient beings is also like this.
Sengsheng said:
"It is not that there are no illusory persons; it is simply that there are no real persons."
Since there is no real person, one who realizes that even the illusory person lacks reality likewise finds no reality.
If the illusory person is not real, how could sentient beings alone be real?
They are like the moon seen in water, like the reflection of one's face in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like an echo, and like clouds in the sky.
Zhaò said:
"From afar one sees form, yet up close there is no image.

It is like a mass of foam, like a bubble on the water, like the solidity of a plantain tree, like lightning persisting for long, like a fifth great element, like a sixth aggregate, like a seventh sense-organ, like the thirteen bases, and like the nineteen realms."
Sengzhao said:
The scriptures have a fixed number [of categories].
This is how the Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings.

It is like form in the formless realm, like the sprout of scorched grain, like the view of a self in the body of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), or like the entry into a womb by a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Zhaò said:
"Although a non-returner may temporarily regress, they will certainly not undergo rebirth."
It is like the three poisons in an Arhat.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the Mahayana teachings, it is said that they merely exist as slight traces beyond the three realms."
"Even for a Bodhisattva who has attained *kṣānti* (receptivity), greed, anger, and the violation of precepts [do not arise].
ZHAO said:
"One attains the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* at the seventh stage (*bhūmi*); since the fetters of the mind are forever eliminated, how much more so the coarse matter of violating precepts?"
"As for the Buddha’s residual habits of affliction (*kleśavāsanā*)," Zhaò said:
"Only the Tathāgata has completely exhausted all fetters and residual habits."
It is like a blind person seeing forms, or like the inhalation and exhalation of one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Zhaò said:
"The mind stirs within and the breath moves in and out without; once the mental conceptions have ceased, there is no longer any coming or going of the breath."

It is like the tracks of a bird in the sky, like the son of a barren woman, like the afflictions of an illusory person, like what is seen in a dream after one has awakened, or like the taking up of a body by one who has entered parinirvāṇa.
Sengzhao said:
"There has never been one who enters nirvana and yet again receives a body;
it would be like a fire without smoke."
Zhaò said:
"Fire must depend on material substance.
The Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as being like this."
Mañjuśrī said: "If a bodhisattva practices contemplation in this manner, how does he practice loving-kindness? Zhaò said:
[This refers to the following:]...
Loving-kindness takes sentient beings as its object; if there were no sentient beings, upon what would the mind of loving-kindness rely?
This is intended to clarify that true loving-kindness is without an object yet is not divorced from objects, thereby fulfilling the meaning of the aforementioned "true loving-kindness without marks."
Sheng said:
"Since one has realized that sentient beings lack substantial reality, one must necessarily extend oneself to others;
thus, there is compassion (*maitrī*). Yet, it seems as though no additional compassion is being applied; therefore, he asks again."
Vimalakīrti said:
"Once a bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he reflects to himself:
'I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.'"
Dongsheng said:
"The Principle is always as luminous as this, yet sentient beings have been at odds with it for kalpas on end.
Since the Bodhisattva has already awakened to it, how could he not manifest it to all?"
This is a provisional mental application established for the purpose of contemplation; it is not a real recollection.
This is precisely true loving-kindness.
Zhaò said:
Sentient beings are fundamentally empty, yet they are unable to awaken to this themselves; therefore, I preach this Dharma so that they may realize it for themselves.

How could there be "I" and "them"? If one can contemplate the emptiness of sentient beings, then mental activities are also empty. To practice compassion within emptiness by means of this mind of emptiness is what is called true, signless compassion.
"If one harbors thoughts toward sentient beings while practicing loving-kindness, this is merely a deceptive compassion; how could it be deemed sufficient?
[Dao]sheng said:
'It must be able to provide actual relief, not merely a hollow thought.'"
He practices the compassion of quiescence (*śānti-maitrī*), because there is nothing that arises.
Kumārajīva said:
