"Knowing that all phenomena (*dharma*) are quiescent and non-arising, one gives rise to compassion on this basis without losing that quiescence; therefore, it is named 'quiescence.'"
Sengzhao said:

After attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at the seventh stage, all the myriad practices one performs are signless and objectless, sharing the same essence as non-arising.
To share the same essence as non-arising is to be without discrimination.

True compassion is without conditions and devoid of mental characteristics; since mental characteristics are absent, it is placid and eternally quiescent. It has never been non-compassionate, yet it has never possessed compassion; therefore, it is said that practicing the compassion of cessation means there is nothing produced.
From this point downward, the text extensively clarifies the practice of signless compassion (*animitta-maitrī*) in order to establish the meaning of reality.
Although the names of these practices differ, they all emerge from the essence of compassion; therefore, they are all designated by the name "compassion."
Dongsheng said:
"To explain it by saying that sentient beings are like illusions is precisely 'illusion-like compassion.
Whatever may be called compassion is without exception thus; therefore, I have generalized and named it in this way, rather than describing its specific variations."
That [the nature of things] is like an illusion has already been clarified by me previously; there is nothing further to explain.
Since there is no further clarification below, how could there not be an explanation?
One practices the "unheated" compassion because one is free from afflictions (*kleśa*).
Zhaò says:
The arising of afflictions stems from craving and views; since compassion is free from craving and views, it is devoid of burning distress.
Compassion that is equal in practice is so because it treats the three periods of time as equal.
Zhaò said:
"Compassion extends through the three periods of time, yet one does not perceive any difference between these three periods.
This is because when practicing the compassion of non-contention (*araṇā-maitrī*), there is nothing that arises."
Kumārajīva said:
"To perceive that dharmas arise is to contend with dharmas.
Sengzhao said:
Since self and others are equally empty, how can disputes arise?
One practices non-dual compassion because the internal and external do not meet.
Kumārajīva said:
"Internal and external" refers to the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*).
Internal and external constitute duality; their mutual relation constitutes conjunction.
Zhaò says:
Internal compassion and external conditions are both empty and without conjunction.
One practices indestructible compassion because it is ultimately exhausted.
Zhaò says:
"Conditionless true compassion has its compassionate aspect forever exhausted; what thing could destroy it?
One practices firm and steadfast compassion because the mind cannot be ruined.
Zhaò said:
The preceding section clarified that there is nothing external capable of destroying [it]; this section clarifies that there is nothing internal that can destroy it of its own accord.
One practices pure compassion because the nature of all phenomena is inherently pure.
Zhaò said:
True compassion is signless, sharing the same purity as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It practices boundless compassion because it is like empty space.
Zhaò said:
There is no intentionality in concealment, yet there is nothing that the mind does not conceal.
This is because one practices the compassion of an Arhat, thereby destroying the thieves of the fetters.
Kumārajīva said:
In the language of Qin, it means "to slay the thieves that are the fetters.
This name arises from its production through the elimination of the fetters;
it is so named because it is capable of eliminating the fetters as well. Thus, it receives its name based on this capacity.
Sengzhao said:
"Arhat" means, in the language of Qin, "one who has destroyed the thieves of the fetters.
Since the afflictions and fetters such as envy, anger, depravity, and doubt are extinguished through compassion, one may be named an Arhat.
One practices the compassion of a bodhisattva for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
The title "bodhisattva" arises from the pacification of sentient beings; because one uses compassion to pacify sentient beings, one may be called a bodhisattva.
One practices the Tathāgata’s compassion because one has attained the mark of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Sengzhao says:
The title "Tathāgata" arises from attaining the mark of suchness; since compassion accords with the mark of suchness, it may be called "Tathāgata."
"Practicing the compassion of a Buddha for the sake of awakening sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said: "The multitudes of living beings have long been in deep slumber; the Bodhisattva awakens them.
Sengzhao said:
To awaken oneself and to awaken others is what is called a Buddha.
Since compassion involves both self-awakening and the ability to awaken others, it may be termed "Buddha.
One practices spontaneous compassion because it is not obtained through causes.
Kumārajīva said:
"The absence of cause is spontaneity; spontaneity is the meaning of having no teacher.
Sengzhao said:
The Way of the Mahāyāna is accomplished without a teacher; it is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*).
The true compassion of a Bodhisattva likewise comes about without cause—can this not be termed "spontaneous"?
He practices the compassion of Bodhi because it is of one equal flavor.
Kumārajīva said:

"Only the Bodhi of the Buddha can understand that all dharmas have a single characteristic and a single flavor. Now, by generating compassion from within the realization of signlessness, it is therefore distantly identical to Bodhi."
Zhaò says:
The path of equality, single flavor, and signlessness is called bodhi.
Signless, true compassion is likewise of equality and single flavor, and may thus be named bodhi.
He practices peerless compassion because he has severed all attachments.
Kumārajīva said:

"If an ordinary person practices compassion while still bound by the fetter of attachment, they may be considered equal; however, no one can be equal to one who practices compassion with all attachments severed."
Sengzhao said:
"Those of the Two Vehicles and those below the sixth stage all give rise to loving-kindness out of attachment to others.
If one can give rise to loving-kindness without a mind of attachment to others, this loving-kindness is transcendent and may be called peerless."
He practices the compassion of great pity because he guides others by means of the Mahāyāna.
Zhaò says:
"To rescue others from suffering and distress and to guide them by means of the Mahāyāna—this is the capability of great pity."
To desire the happiness of others through loving-kindness and further guide them by means of the Mahāyāna may be called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This is because one practices tireless loving-kindness while contemplating emptiness and non-self.
Sengzhao said:
The sentiment of weariness arises from the preservation of a self.
One who practices compassion with a mind of emptiness and non-self will reach the end of birth and death, never again experiencing weariness.
One practices the compassion of the gift of Dharma because there is no withholding or begrudging.
Zhaò says:
"There has never been one who has attained true compassion yet is stingy with the wealth of the Dharma; such may be called the gift of Dharma."
One practices the compassion of observing the precepts in order to transform those who violate the prohibitions.
Zhaò says:

"There has never been one who attains true compassion yet fails to transform others through the dual practice of abstaining from killing and stealing; such a person may be called one who observes the precepts."
"Practice the compassion of patience (*kṣānti*), for it protects both others and oneself.
Kumārajīva said:
"If one can practice patience, then internally one does not burden oneself and externally one does not harm others; therefore, it is said that it protects both others and oneself."
In all these instances, the characters for "superior practice" (*shangxing*) do not exist in the Sanskrit original.
Zhaò says:
"There has never been one who attains true compassion yet fails to protect others, thereby causing anger and strife; this may be called patience (*kṣānti*)."
One practices the compassion of diligence because of bearing the burden of sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
There has never been one who attains true compassion without bearing the burden of sentient beings; this may be called diligence.
One practices the loving-kindness of meditative concentration because one does not relish its flavor.
Zhaò says: "There has never been one who attains true loving-kindness yet receives the flavor of the five desires with a distracted mind; this may be called meditative concentration."
One practices the compassion of wisdom because there is nothing for which one does not know the proper time.
Kumārajīva said:
"To seek the fruit before one's practice is complete is called 'not knowing the proper time.'"
Zhaò said:
There has never been one who attains true compassion yet remains ignorant of the timing of practice; this may be called wisdom.
One practices the compassion of skillful means because it manifests in all ways.
Zhaò says: There has never been one who attains true compassion without manifesting through skillful means to respond universally; this may be called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
One practices unhidden compassion because the straightforward mind is pure.
Kumārajīva said:
"His mind is upright and straightforward; he must repent for his transgressions and never conceal his faults—these are the two karmas.
Zhaò said:
There has never been one who has attained true compassion yet whose mind remains crooked, concealed, or impure;
such a person may indeed be called "without concealment," for they practice the compassion of the profound mind and are free from mixed conduct.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the direct mind there are still lingering fetters; now, having entered deeply into the Buddha-dharma, there are no mixed thoughts.
Sengzhao said:
There has never been one who attains true compassion yet intersperses it with shallow practice; this may be called the "profound mind.
It practices non-deceptive compassion because it is not false or artificial.
Kumārajīva said:
Physical action is upright and correct, not deceiving others.
Zhaò says:
"There has never been one who attains true compassion yet remains false and insubstantial; this may be called 'non-deception'."
He practices the compassion of peace and happiness in order to enable others to attain the bliss of Buddhahood.
Kumārajīva said:
"The Sanskrit original says 'abiding in the bliss of nirvāṇa.'"
Sengzhao said:
"There has never been one who attains true compassion without causing both others and oneself to obtain the bliss of Buddhahood; this may be called 'Peaceful Bliss.
Such is the nature of the Bodhisattva's compassion."
Sengzhao said:

"The various names mentioned above are all the true essence of compassion. Because this capacity exists inherently, these names exist; they do not rely on external, borrowed practices to constitute their own designation."
If true compassion is such as this, how could it be that sentient beings perceive it?
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"What is meant by 'compassion' (karuṇā)?"
The answer was:
"Whatever merits a bodhisattva performs, he shares them all with all sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said:
To bestow both merit and the fruits of that merit upon all sentient beings is the practice of giving to relieve suffering.

The three types of equality are fully explained within the context of giving; if explained extensively, they should also be understood as being like the four immeasurables, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Zhaò says: By means of observing the inquiry regarding loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he fully explains the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
Compassionating those who suffer for a long time, he does not take account of the manifold virtues accumulated by his own person, but vows to share them with all beings.
"To put others first and oneself last is the practice of great compassion.
Sheng said:
"Now, one who wishes to uproot suffering must necessarily relinquish their own happiness in order to rescue others."
Furthermore, this is truly compassion.
What is meant by sympathetic joy?
The answer is:
When there is benefit bestowed upon others, one rejoices without regret.
Zhaò says:
"To personally attain the benefits of the Dharma and share that joy with the multitude—experiencing the joy of the Dharma for both oneself and others—is called *muditā* (joy)."
Sheng said:
"Since compassion benefits them, there is only joy and no regret; this is also true joy.
What, then, is meant by equanimity (upekṣā)?"
He replied,
"The merit and blessings one has performed.
Kumārajīva said:
This also clarifies emptiness within the context of giving.
There is no expectation of reward.
Kumārajīva said:
In this present life one seeks no favor, and in the future one seeks no recompense.
When Śrāvakas practice the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), they cannot truly benefit sentient beings.
Now, when Bodhisattvas practice the four immeasurables, they are already truly able to benefit sentient beings; therefore, these four immeasurables are all termed "Great" (*mahā-*) [immeasurables].
Zhaò said:
"In the practice of great compassion and asceticism, sorrow arises from it;
in the practice of loving-kindness and joy, gladness arises from it."
Once sorrow and joy have been laid bare, love and hatred arise as their signs; therefore, the practitioner abandons suffering and cultivates bliss, viewing all sentient beings with equanimity.
In the right equanimity of the Mahāyāna, both action and its retribution are extinguished, and thus there is nothing to be hoped for.
The three grades are all without marks and without objects, and they proceed in conjunction with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Once the practice of loving-kindness is complete, the other types can be understood by analogy.
Sheng said:
To abandon hatred and attachment by means of conceptualizing sentient beings is not true abandonment.
If one can abandon them without looking for the reward of merit, that is the ultimate form of abandonment.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Upon what should a bodhisattva who fears birth and death rely?
Kumārajīva replied:

Having taken on a body for the sake of sentient beings, yet not having abandoned the fetters and karma, the substance of those fetters and karma cannot yet be free from fear; one must have something upon which to rely before being able to bring the great task to its ultimate conclusion. Therefore, he asks about that upon which he relies, so that his progress may not be abandoned or regressed.
Sengzhao said:
"Birth and death constitute fear; there is nothing greater than this fear.
Upon what does the Great Being rely, that he can dwell eternally within birth and death without regarding it as fear? Sengsheng replied:
Those whose practice is based on reality will inevitably enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Speaking from the perspective of birth and death, this is a state that should be feared.
If one has not yet attained liberation and might instead fall under its sway, what reliance could a Bodhisattva have to remain unafraid?
Vimalakīrti said:
"A bodhisattva, amidst the terrors of birth and death, should rely upon the power of the Tathāgata’s merit.
Kumārajīva remarked:
The merit of the Tathāgata is thus profound and subtle; I shall surely attain it. How could I give rise to weariness or aversion because of this slight suffering?
If one seeks the Buddha-way with a single mind, advancing directly without turning back, then all sufferings will naturally cease and all fears will be eliminated.
It relies both upon mindfulness and upon seeking the goal.
Zhaò says:
"The fear of birth and death is what the followers of the Two Vehicles find difficult."
Who, not relying on the power of the Tathāgata’s merit, could abide in this?
Śāriputra said:
"Those who enter into birth and death with equanimity must surely seek to deliver others from birth and death."
If one enters with the sole intention of achieving salvation, one will ultimately realize the fruit of Tathāgata-hood.
If one proceeds with such a profound sense of purpose, one ought not find even minor suffering difficult to endure.
Furthermore, since there is this karmic retribution in the unseen realm, how could the sufferings of birth and death possibly weigh upon one?
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits, where should they abide?
Kumārajīva replied:
If one wishes to rely upon and approach the merits of the Tathāgata, it is necessary to direct the mind toward a specific focus; therefore, he asks where [the Buddha] dwells.
Daosheng said:
"If one were to enter directly with the desire to save others, one might not necessarily be able to save them."
Since it is not necessarily able to provide salvation nor achieve the great fruit, he asks again where one should abide upon entering [the path].
He replied:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits should abide in the liberation of all sentient beings."

Sengzhao said: "To abide in the transformation of all things is for the mind to be vast and great; when the mind is vast and great, there is nothing difficult in where one goes. This is what is meant by abiding in the power of the Buddha's virtues."
Sheng said:
"One who enters through clarity and salvation must necessarily abide within deliverance.
He asked again:
"If one wishes to deliver sentient beings, what must be eliminated?
Daosheng replied:
"What is called 'deliverance' necessarily implies that there are those to be delivered and something from which they are to be liberated; it is for this reason that I ask."
The answer is: "To deliver sentient beings and eliminate their afflictions.
Sengzhao says: "Since one intends to seek out the root, one first speaks of its branches.
Sengsheng says:
One crosses the river of afflictions and is liberated from the bonds of afflictions.
He asked again:
"If one wishes to eliminate afflictions, what should one practice?"
Sheng asked:
"If sentient beings already possess afflictions, what practice should they undertake to eliminate them?
He replied:
"One should practice right mindfulness.
Daosheng said:
"As for the existence of afflictions, they arise merely from deluded emotions; one should therefore observe the principles of the Dharma to dispel them."

However, at the initial stage of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the principle is not yet clearly perceived and the mind does not abide in that principle; it is only through the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*) that one can attain contemplation.
Since mindfulness functions by means of non-forgetfulness, one is thereby able to maintain the contemplation.
Another version reads "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*). Kumārajīva said:

"Right mindfulness extends from beginning to end and encompasses both the refined and the coarse; generally, any thought that is not erroneous and does not contradict principle is termed 'mindfulness'."
He asked again:
"How does one practice right mindfulness?
Daosheng replied:
Question: "Is right mindfulness (samyak-smṛti) practice? This is a repeated question. Answer:
"One should practice non-arising and non-ceasing."
Zhaò said:

"Right mindfulness means correctly directing the mind to contemplate the Dharma, examining its goodness or evil; that which is good is increased and not extinguished, while that which is evil is extinguished so that it does not arise."
Sheng said:
"To practice by means of neither arising nor ceasing.
He asked again:
What phenomena do not arise?
What phenomena do not cease? Answer:
"Unwholesome states do not arise, and wholesome dharmas do not perish.
Kumārajīva said:
"When unwholesome dharmas arise, one must extinguish them; before they have even begun to arise, one must prevent them from arising."
Virtuous dharmas shall not perish, but shall be made to increase and expand.
Daosheng said:
"The power of mindfulness and contemplation constitute the beginning of establishing principle; this is precisely what restrains evil and brings one toward goodness."
He asked again:
"What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome?
Sengzhao replied:
Having realized that good can be produced and evil can be extinguished, one seeks the ultimate source by relinquishing both; thus, one traces back to their origin.
[The opponent] says:
"Now, one good and one evil alternate as the fundamental basis, and there is never a definitive separation between them."
One must seek its fundamental origin and contemplate it; only then will it be discerned.
He replied:
"The body is the foundation."
Kumārajīva said:
"The body refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Zhaò said:
"Good and evil deeds do not arise except through the body.
Sheng said,
"The reason one performs good and evil is for the sake of the body."
He asked again:
"What is the root of the body?
He replied:
Sensual desire is the root.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because the attachment to sensual desires is profound, one extensively generates fetters and karma."
It is also because of the moisture of craving that one undergoes birth;
therefore, among all the fetters (*saṃyojana*), desire and greed (*kāmarāga*) are singled out for mention.
Zhaò said:
Craving is the root of birth; it lengthens all fetters. Among all who possess a body, there are none who do not arise from it.
Birth said:
"Desire is the impulse of greed within me; therefore, I am one who receives a body."
He asked again:
"What is the root of sensual desire?
He replied:
"False conceptualization is the root.
Kumārajīva said:
"Dharmas have no fixed characteristics; characteristics arise from delusion, and through false conceptualization and discrimination, one judges them as good or ugly."
Once likes and dislikes have manifested, the mind of desire naturally arises; therefore, they constitute the root of desire.
Sengzhao says:
"Dharmas possess neither beauty nor ugliness; it is through false discrimination that one labels them beautiful or ugly. Once beauty and ugliness have manifested, greed and desire are born."
Vimalakīrti said:
"Because one falsely discriminates phenomena, there is that which can be greedily attached to.
He asked again:
What is the root of false discrimination?
The answer is:
inverted perception is its root.
Kumārajīva said:
"To perceive existence and non-existence as contrary to the true nature of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) is called perversion.
One first perceives existence and non-existence, and subsequently discriminates between the beautiful and the ugly."

Thus, the views of existence and non-existence are the root of delusive entanglements and the beginning of false conceptualization; therefore, they are given the partial and inverted names [of "existence" and "non-existence"].
Zhaò says:
"The Dharma is fundamentally not existent; it is through inverted thought that it is taken to be existent."
Once one has already conceived of things as existing, one then discriminates between their beauty and ugliness; this is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
Sheng said:
"When the deluded mind turns inward, it becomes inverted; only then does it falsely discriminate external phenomena."
He asked again:
"What is the root of inverted perception?
He replied:
"Non-abiding is the foundation.
Kumārajīva said:
"Dharmas have no intrinsic nature; they arise through the interaction of conditions."

When it has not yet arisen, one knows not where it is deposited; because one knows not where it is deposited, there is no place of abiding. Because there is no place of abiding, it is neither existent nor non-existent.

Being neither existent nor non-existent, it serves as the root of existence and non-existence. When there is no abiding, its source is exhausted and there is nowhere further from which it could emerge; therefore, it is called "rootless."
Being without a fundamental basis yet serving as the basis for all things, it is therefore said that it establishes all dharmas.
Zhaò says:
The mind is like water; when still, it possesses clarity; when stirred, it lacks reflection.
Turbid with delusion and craving, fanned by the winds of falsehood, surging and tossing like waves, it never rests for even a moment.
Observing phenomena through this lens, where could one go without falling into ruin?
It is like facing a gushing spring and demanding that it return to its original state; such a thing has never occurred.
The arising of inverted perceptions is rooted in non-abiding; this is where the meaning lies.

All phenomena arise as substantial entities through the convergence of multiple conditions; when conditions have not yet converged, phenomena have no locus. Having no locus, they have no abiding. Having no abiding, there are no phenomena.
Because it takes non-existence as its basis, it is able to establish all phenomena.
Daosheng said:
"What is called 'inversion' means that what is contrary to reality is regarded as unreal."
If one takes unreality as one's essence, this is itself non-abiding.
Since one does not abide in oneself, how could one abide elsewhere?
If there were something in which to abide, it could not be called perversion.
He asked again:
"What is the basis of non-abiding?
He replied:
Without abiding, there is no root.
Sengzhao said:
"If one takes the movement of the mind as the root, then because of this existence, the characteristic of arising comes into being."
The principle reaches its ultimate limit at the initial movement; there is nothing further that serves as its source.

If one were to take non-existence as the source, then existence would arise from non-existence; yet since non-existence itself has no cause, it likewise has no source. Thus, there is nothing further that serves as the source.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Non-abiding is precisely the principle of having no fundamental basis. Mañjuśrī!"
"All dharmas are established based on the root of non-abiding. Sengzhao said:

"Because there is no abiding, there is the inversion of perception; because of the inversion of perception, there is conceptual differentiation; because of conceptual differentiation, there is craving and desire; because of craving and desire, there is the body. Once there is a body, good and evil are presented together; once good and evil are presented, all phenomena arise."
From this point forward, words and numbers cannot fully express it.
If one properly grasps the root, then all secondary branches may be eliminated.
Sheng said:
All dharmas are without exception like this.
It is only because principle manifests within inversion that we take it from the perspective of inversion to clarify it.
If one contemplates in this way, can afflictions still arise?
At that time, there was a heavenly maiden in Vimalakīrti’s room.
Kumārajīva said:
"There is no fixed abode and no fixed spirit; the spirits vary in refinement or coarseness according to the excellence or inferiority of their respective householders."
Because it is an unprecedented chamber, the celestial maidens are taken as its deities.
Sengsheng said:
"In foreign lands, deities are also referred to as 'heavenly ones' (tian)."
Now, wherever there is a household of merit, the deities of fortune surely dwell therein; it is for this reason that the Bodhisattva has manifested himself among them.
This is a matter of entering the cycle of birth and death.
Upon seeing the great beings and hearing the Dharma they preach, he immediately manifests his body and scatters celestial flowers over the Bodhisattvas and the great disciples.
Kumārajīva said:

"The bodhisattvas above were dissatisfied with the emptiness of their chamber; the reason they now provide this offering is that the master of the house is ill, so his spirit has received their intent and brought forth these offerings."
Zhaò said:

"The heavenly maiden is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body who constantly propagates the inconceivable path of the Mahāyāna together with Vimalakīrti; therefore, she manifested as a household deity to share his quarters."
Seeing that the Great Being had assembled and heard the Dharma being preached, he manifested his form and scattered flowers, desiring thereby to initiate a discourse.
Daosheng said:
"The manifestation of a goddess scattering flowers demonstrates that even those of humble station revere the Dharma, thereby deepening one's aspiration for the Dharma."
He secretly desired to use this occasion to expound the principles, thereby demonstrating that he does not fear birth and death; thus, although he entered [the world], he remained untainted by it.
Had he feared it and sought to avoid it, he would have become even more deeply attached.
When the flowers reached the various bodhisattvas, they all fell away.
Daosheng said:
"Let them fall of their own accord."
When it reached the Great Disciples, they immediately accepted it without rejecting it.
Kumārajīva said:

"Because Heaven possesses this unprecedented chamber free from heterodox teachings, it disparages the Lesser Vehicle and extols the Great Way; thus, together they act as shadow and echo, illuminating the supreme goal."
Sheng said,
"Though it is said that this is caused by the power of Heaven, there must be something that invited it.
All the disciples exerted their supernatural powers to remove the flowers, yet they were unable to make them go."
Sengzhao said:
"Since I am about to distinguish between the Great and the Small, I have allowed the language to be thus ornate.
Sengsheng said:
Now, the purpose of fashioning and adorning oneself with finery is fundamentally to eliminate the desire for such things.
If one truly has no longing for ornamental display, even if one remains so adorned all day long, how could there be any transgression?
To employ supernatural power to remove the flowers because one dislikes them clinging to the body is merely a pretext for observing the precepts in their entirety.
This is intended to clarify that evil inevitably leads to good; yet, though one wishes to comply with the rules, one instead acts contrary to their true intent.
If that is so, then since it is by means of the very root of attachment that one eliminates it, how could it be discarded?
Therefore, by using this matter to clarify this principle, the logic is just like the matter itself.
At that time, Devaputra asked Śāriputra:
"Why have you removed the flowers?
Daosheng said,
"I was surprised, so I asked him."
He replied:
"These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, I have removed them.
Sengzhao said:
To have incense and flowers attached to one's body is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; therefore, he removed them.
According to one interpretation, if the flowers of the Dharma were scattered upon the body, one should fall [into saṃsāra]; that one does not fall indicates they are not merely worldly flowers.
Śakra said:
"It does not accord with the Dharma.
Brahmā said:
Do not say that these flowers are improper.
An alternative version reads "improperly discriminating," but Kumārajīva said:
"In the Sanskrit original it says 'impure. Since śramaṇas must renounce all ornamentation, flowers are considered impure."
"Why is this so? Because these flowers are without discrimination.
Kumārajīva said:
"The nature of the flower is fundamentally non-dual; therefore, there is no discrimination.
Daosheng said:
"The nature of the flower has no substantial reality; how could there be such discriminations as 'accordant with the Dharma' or 'not accordant with the Dharma'?"
"O Benevolent One, you have merely given rise to discriminative conceptions yourself.
Zhaò said:
"How could the flower have any intention regarding falling or not falling?"
"The notion of discrimination arises solely from you, O Benevolent One.
Daosheng said:
"Whether something accords with the Dharma or not accords with the Dharma is merely the product of deluded conceptualization; it is not that the profound principle itself is thus."

If one has left the household life within the Buddha-dharma and engages in conceptual discrimination, it is contrary to the Dharma; if there is no such discrimination, then it is in accordance with the Dharma.
Sengzhao said:
"Whether one is in accordance with the Dharma or not depends on the mind, not on outward form."
Dongsheng said:
"If one's substance embodies the principle that there is neither good nor evil, then one accords with the Dharma of the Vinaya.
Observe how the flowers do not adhere to the various Bodhisattvas; this is because they have already severed all conceptual discriminations."
Daosheng said:
"It is not only that they do not cause attachment; it is also impossible for them to make one attached.
It is like when a person is afraid: a non-human being cannot take advantage of them."
Kumārajīva said:
"Suppose a rākṣasa transforms himself into a horse, and a man mounts it without suspicion.
On the way, the horse asks the man:"
"Is this horse good?
The man drew his sword and showed it to him, asking,
"Is this sword good?"
Knowing that his mind was upright and fearless, [the non-human being] ultimately did not dare to inflict harm.
Had it not been so, the non-human being would have taken advantage of him.
Śāriputra said:
At a time of fear, one's mind has already become timid and weak; thus, those who find an opportunity gain the upper hand.
It is because the disciple fears birth and death that he speaks thus.
[The Master] said:
The pursuit of excellence through flowers and incense increases birth and death; yet, those who loathe them do so because they fear birth and death.
Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch find their opportunity therein.
Sheng said:
If one simply says, "I loathe it," then the desire for gain will cease.
Once one has already distanced oneself from what is feared, the five desires can no longer exert any influence.
Sheng said:
Once one has already distanced oneself from evil, even if the objects of the five desires are arrayed before one, they can no longer induce attachment.
When the residual habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers merely adhere to the body;
when the residual habits are exhausted, the flowers do not adhere.
Kumārajīva said: He asked:
"If a bodhisattva’s habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted, how is it that they do not become attached?"
The answer is:
There are two kinds of habitual tendencies: first, the habitual tendencies of the fetters; second, the habitual tendencies of attachment toward the Buddha-dharma.

When one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), the habitual tendencies of the fetters are entirely exhausted, yet the habitual tendencies of attachment toward the Buddha-dharma have not yet been severed.
It is also said that although Dharma-body Bodhisattvas possess residual habits (*vāsanā*), because their vessel is pure, these habitual tendencies do not arise.
Sengzhao says:
Whether one is attached or unattached depends solely on the internal; what concern is this for the flower?
Sheng said:
"If one merely rejects the external flowers, although this does not eliminate the underlying knots of affliction, it is nonetheless their habitual manifestation.
If even these habitual tendencies can cause flowers to cling to the body and cannot be removed, how much more so for the actual knots?"
Śāriputra said,
"How long has it been since the deva entered this room?
Kumārajīva replied:
The Sanskrit original says "for how long.
Zhaò remarked:
"To determine the duration of dwelling in the chamber of the Mahāyāna of the Vimalakīrti—how marvelous is such subtle eloquence!"
Sheng said:

"Since I have already yielded to him, I feel some resentment that he treats his own dwelling as heaven; yet, I do not wish to confront him with direct rebuke, so I have sent this inquiry under the pretext of a long-standing question."
The answer was:
"I dwell in this room as an elder dwells in liberation.
Sengzhao said:
To clarify the first point—that there is no distinction between long and short durations—he employs liberation as an analogy.
Liberation, in this context, refers to unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*).
Sengsheng said:
"To dwell in a chamber is to be bound.
As for liberation, it is clear that there is no real bondage.
Śāriputra said:
"Have you been here for so long?
Sengzhao replied:

"The Way of liberation is formless and signless; if one pursues it from the front, its head is not seen, and if one seeks it from behind, its tail is not seen. It is vast and boundless, leaving no trace—this is what is called liberation."
"If one stops at this point and liberation remains unknowable as to whether it is near or far, then it is indeed very far.
Sengsheng said:
"Although the intent of Śāriputra’s previous question was expressed in terms of 'stopping in the room,' the words themselves actually concern duration."
If one takes [the meaning] from those who do not understand, they will simply say that the previous answer was correct.
If one were to respond to their words, one would say: "It has been a long time since Śāriputra attained liberation."
"Śāriputra, it has indeed been a long time since you attained liberation; has your dwelling in the chamber not likewise been for a long time?
Since your dwelling in the chamber has already been for so long, you can no longer attain liberation in the same manner as before; therefore, I cannot help but ask about this duration."
The deity said,
"How long has it been since you, Venerable One, attained liberation?
Sengzhao replied:
He questioned him about what he had attained, intending to lead him to self-awakening.
"The unconditioned liberation you have attained, O Elder—can it truly be called 'long'?
Śāṇavāsa replied:
When it was said, "The liberation of the Elder has been long-lasting; what does it resemble?
Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
Zhaò said:
"You spoke of 'long duration' previously, yet now you demand that it be real in the end; therefore, I do not know how to answer.
Sengsheng said:
"Since you say that liberation has no duration, then its traces must truly be non-existent."
If liberation were truly characterized by non-action (wuwei), then its verbal expression would also be substantially real.
Since existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, how could words be used to explain liberation?
Therefore, one resorts to this silence to clarify that liberation is not a substantial nothingness.
Since liberation is neither truly non-existent, one must first bring one's speech to rest before one can attain certainty regarding their identity.
Tian said:
"How is it that you, an elder of great wisdom, remain silent?"
Sengzhao said:
"Among the five hundred disciples, you, O Benevolent One, are foremost in wisdom; why do you remain silent?
Sengsheng replied:
He remained silent as if there were something he had not yet understood.
[The Buddha] replied:
"Liberation is beyond all verbal expression; therefore, I do not know what could be said regarding it."
Sengzhao said:
Previously, when I heard the request for liberation, its beginning and end were difficult to discern, and it was described as being of long duration.
Yet the characteristic of liberation is not something known by the mind, nor is it reachable by words. To accord with the ineffable purport of liberation, there is nothing that can be said about it.
Sheng said,
"I do not know their meeting.
Tian said:
"Verbal expressions and written words are all marks of liberation.
Zhaò said:
"Śāriputra considered that speech had long been a source of error; therefore, he remained silent and spoke no words, believing this to be in accord with the true understanding."

Because they have not yet attained the state where speech and silence are of equal import, nor the unimpeded engagement with all things, Tian-shuo and others provide explanations to clarify their meaning.
Seng-sheng said:
"Is there not a point of convergence here?"
Why is this so? Because liberation is neither internal nor external, nor does it exist in between the two.
Śāṇavāsa said:
Now, as for liberation, it is my being released from bondage.
Since it does not reside exclusively within me, it is not internal;
nor does it reside exclusively in the bondage, so it is not external.
It results in liberation, yet it does not abide in duality.
Characters and words likewise are neither internal nor external, nor do they exist in between the two.
Daosheng said:
I am the internal;
that which is spoken of is the external.
The union of these two constitutes the intermediate space.
Therefore, Śāriputra, there is no liberation apart from words. Zhaò says:

The locus of the Dharma is ultimately comprised of three categories; yet when one seeks words within these three categories, liberation cannot be found anywhere. How, then, can one wish to speak of liberation separately, apart from words?
Dongsheng said:
"When Śāriputra previously stated that because liberation is ineffable one should remain silent, he was implying that speech is different from liberation.
Since it has now been clarified that there is no difference between them, he [the Buddha] therefore cautioned him."
Why is this so? Because all dharmas possess the characteristic of liberation.
Zhaò said:
Although the myriad dharmas differ from one another, none are not the mark of liberation; how could written words alone be an exception?
Sheng said:
"It is because there is nothing that is not the mark of liberation."
Śāriputra said:
"Is it not the case that liberation consists in being free from lust, anger, and delusion?
Zhaò said:
The two vehicles regard the extinction of fetters and the unconditioned as liberation.
Having heard this superior explanation, they find it inconsistent with their original orientation; therefore, they pose this question.
Daosheng said:
"I merely asked because the Buddha has said that freedom from lust, anger, and delusion constitutes liberation.
The deva replied,
"The Buddha spoke of freedom from lust, anger, and delusion as liberation for those who possess overweening pride."
Dongsheng said:
"Those with overweening pride harbor the notion that they have attained the Dharma, yet they cannot realize liberation through lust, anger, and delusion as they are.
Therefore, I tested them by speaking thus, so as to cause them to awaken."
If one is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the Buddha says that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is itself liberation.
Zhaò says:

One who deprecates birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and exalts their own path is called a person of overweening pride; for such a person, it is taught that liberation consists in being separated from the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

If one neither disparages birth and death nor exalts one's own path, then for such a person it is taught that the nature of the three poisons and all fetters is itself liberation; there is no liberation apart from them.
Although the followers of the Two Vehicles are free from fetters and pride, they still possess a semblance of pride and fetters because they disparage birth-and-death and exalt nirvana.
As for "pride," it arises when one has not yet attained the Way but claims to have attained it, thereby giving rise to arrogance.
Sheng said:
"One who takes non-attachment as their core concern does not wait for verification before attaining awakening.
Śāriputra then spoke:
Excellent, excellent,
O goddess!
What have you attained, and by what means have you realized it?
Kumārajīva said:
"Regarding conditioned fruits, one speaks of 'attaining'; regarding unconditioned fruits, one speaks of 'realizing.
Such is the distinction."
Sengzhao said:
"Since you excel in what you have explained beyond what I am capable of reaching, I asked about what path you have attained and what fruit you have realized; is your eloquence indeed such as this?
Sengsheng replied:
Since he has understood and mastered these words, he must have attained something and realized something before such eloquence could arise; therefore, I question him about it.
The deity said:
"I have neither attainment nor realization; therefore, my eloquence is such as this.
Kumārajīva said:
If one perceives that there is something attained or realized, then the mind becomes fettered; where there is a fetter, there is obstruction; and where there is obstruction, there is no eloquence.
It is precisely because there is nothing attained or realized that one is able to be thus.
Sengzhao said:
"A path that possesses limitations cannot give rise to unimpeded eloquence; unimpeded eloquence must emerge from an unimpeded path.
For one who has attained or realized the Path, there must necessarily be that which is not yet attained and that which is not yet realized."
Because the Way of the Mahāyāna involves neither attainment nor realization, there is nothing that is not attained and nothing that is not realized.
From this arises discernment; therefore, there is nothing that is not discerned.
Daosheng said:
"To take non-attainment as attainment and non-realization as realization—this is why I have distinguished it in this way. Why is that?"
If there were anyone who attained or realized [the Dharma], they would be characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Zhaò said:
"If one perceives that they themselves have something attained, they will necessarily perceive that others have not attained it."
Regarding this equal Dharma of the Buddha, such people are still those possessed of overweening pride; how then could they attain unhindered eloquence?
Daosheng said:
"If there were anyone who attained it, then it would not be attained."
To take what has not been attained as attained is the arrogance of overestimation (*adhimāna*).
Śāriputra asked the goddess:
"In which of the three vehicles do you aspire?"
Kumārajīva said:
"I have humbly listened to his virtuous voice and know that he is no ordinary man; yet, as I have not fathomed the vehicle upon which he rides, I have asked about his aspirations.
Zhaò said:
The Superior (Shangzhi) stated that there is neither attainment nor realization, yet it was not known which vehicle this referred to; therefore, he asked again.
Daosheng replied:
"The three vehicles equally take non-attainment as their underlying intention; thus, it is not known what specific aspiration [the Superior] holds."
The deva said:
"Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the śrāvakas, I am a śrāvaka;
because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of causes and conditions, I am a pratyekabuddha."
Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of great compassion, I am the Mahāyāna.
Sengzhao said:
"The Way of the Mahāyāna has neither 'riding' nor 'not riding. Since one rides for the sake of others, what vehicle do I myself have?"
Jiasheng said:
"I act in accordance with them; I have no fixed position. Śāriputra!"
It is like a person entering a campaka grove who smells only the campaka and does not smell any other fragrance.
Kumārajīva said:
"This does not mean that there are other fragrances which one does not smell; rather, it means that one is fully satisfied with what has been heard and no longer seeks elsewhere."
This can be understood through the meaning of the analogy.
Thus, if one enters this room, one perceives only the fragrance of the Buddha’s merits and takes no pleasure in smelling the fragrance of the merits of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Zhaò said:
"That which has neither vehicle nor non-vehicle is the Mahāyāna; therefore, the fragrant grove is used as a metaphor.
This clarifies that the room of Vimalakīrti is not mixed with the fragrance of the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha); how could those who dwell in this room smell anything else?"
By this, one may know what vehicle my intention rides upon.
Daosheng said:
"Vimalakīrti’s dwelling in this room and his responding to beings is the great illumination of the principle of the ultimate source."
Yet, the principle of the ultimate truth does not admit of limited meanings; this, then, manifests the external merit of the Buddha’s virtues. Śāriputra!

Should any Śakras, Brahmās, Four Heavenly Kings, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and others enter this room, upon hearing this superior person expound the True Dharma, they will all delight in the fragrance of the Buddha’s virtues and resolve their minds [upon enlightenment] before departing.

Śāriputra! I have resided in this room for twelve years, yet from the beginning I have never heard any teaching on the Dharma of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; I have heard only the inconceivable Buddha-dharma of the Bodhisattvas' great kindness and great compassion.
Sengzhao said:
"The teachings of the Mahāyāna are all termed 'inconceivable.
Since the Emperor’s question regarding the duration of his residence in the chamber was intended to initiate a philosophical discussion, [the Master] answered with the topic of liberation."
Now, by stating my actual age, I clarify that what I have heard is not mixed with anything else.
Sheng said:
"If even the devas and spirits who briefly enter this room invariably depart having awakened to the Great Meaning, how much more so for me, who have long heard the wondrous Dharma?"
Nevertheless, it is not that it cannot be made great, but rather that it is not something that can be made great. Śāriputra,
in this room there constantly manifest eight unprecedented and rare dharmas.
Jian sheng said:
"Having heard the wondrous Dharma and witnessed such unprecedented events, how could one not consider this truly great?
What are these eight?"
This room is constantly illuminated by golden light.
Sheng said:
"The Master’s lordship resides in compassion; how could there not be times when he shines his light?"
As for those who do not see it,
they have severed their own connection;
it is not that it is absent from the chamber.
Day and night are no different, for this room does not rely on the light of the sun or moon to be bright; this is the first unprecedented and rare quality.
Those who enter this room are not troubled by any defilements.
Kumārajīva said:
"His chamber is pure and free from offensive odors and malevolent spirits; because the conditions for defilement have been severed, defilement does not arise.
When malevolent spirits arise, it is like a ten-headed rākṣasa entering the body of a king—anger and harm immediately manifest; such is their nature."
Sengzhao said:
"Those who enter this room find their afflictions naturally stilled.
Sengsheng said:
This chamber constantly manifests the ultimate principle; to behold it is to enter therein.
Once one has truly gained entry, one will no longer be afflicted by any defilements.
This is the second unprecedented and rare dharma.
This room is constantly filled with Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and bodhisattvas from other realms, arriving in an unceasing stream; this is the third rare and unprecedented phenomenon.
In this chamber, the Dharma of the six pāramitās and the stage of non-retrogression is constantly preached; this is the fourth rare and unprecedented phenomenon.

In this chamber, the foremost music of devas and humans is constantly performed, with strings producing the sounds of immeasurable Dharma-transformations; this is the fifth rare and unprecedented phenomenon.

In this chamber there are four great treasuries filled with heaps of various jewels; they provide for the destitute and relieve the needy, such that one may obtain them without end. This is the sixth unprecedented and rare quality.

In this room, Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Akṣobhya Buddha, Ratnaguṇa, Ratnārcis, Ratnacandra, Ratnavyūha, Durjaya, Siṃhanāda, Sarvārthasiddha, and other such infinite Buddhas of the ten directions—all come whenever this superior person brings them to mind.
Sheng said:
"The principles of the Buddha are always present within one's mind; when one contemplates them, they immediately manifest.
He extensively expounded the secret and essential Dharma-treasures of all Buddhas, and having finished speaking, he departed. This is the seventh rare and unprecedented dharma."
Within this room, the palaces adorned by all the devas and the pure lands of all the Buddhas appear.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is like having a cubit-sized diamond; all forms and colors existing beyond stone walls for dozens of li will appear within it."
This room is brilliantly transparent; its significance is just like this.
This constitutes the eighth extraordinary and rare quality. Śāriputra!
In this room, eight unprecedented and rare phenomena are constantly manifested; who, having witnessed such inconceivable matters, would still take pleasure in the Dharma of the Śrāvakas?
Zhaò said:
"To manifest the extraordinary events of the chamber is to fulfill the meaning of the Fragrant Grove.
Śāriputra then spoke:
"Why do you not transform this female body?
Zhaò said:
"You possess unimpeded wisdom yet have received an impeded body; why do you not transform and abandon it?"
The goddess said:
"For twelve years now, I have sought the mark of a woman and have been unable to find it; what, then, is there to transform?
Zhaolun said:
Since coming to reside in this chamber, I have heard the True Dharma, yet I have not realized that a woman differs from a man; how then could there be any transformation?
Has the Heavenly One awakened to the female form in only twelve years?
To clarify that this chamber is characterized by a purely uniform teaching and lacks any discordant sounds, it is for this reason that the statement is made up to this point.
It was because the heavens manifested in female form that this discourse arose.
For example, suppose a magician conjures an illusory woman by means of his arts, and someone were to ask:
"Why does she not transform her female body?
Would that person be asking correctly?
Śāriputra said: "No.
An illusion has no fixed characteristic; how could it undergo transformation?"
The goddess said:
"All dharmas are likewise thus; they possess no fixed characteristics.
Why, then, do you ask why I do not transform out of this female body?"
Zhaò said:
"All phenomena are like illusions and possess no fixed characteristics; who is handsome and who is ugly that one would wish to transform them?
At that moment, by means of her supernatural powers, the goddess transformed Śāriputra so that he appeared as a goddess, while she herself manifested a body like that of Śāriputra, and asked:
"Why do you not transform your female body? Zhaò said:
"He intended to establish the principle that illusory transformations have no fixed nature; therefore, he manifested this change to question her, so as to lead her to self-awakening."
Śāriputra, appearing in the form of a goddess, replied:
"I do not know what has been transformed.
Kumārajīva said:
This is stated according to principle based on the perspective of liberation;
yet, he transformed into a female body.
Zhaor said:
"I do not know by what means I transformed myself into this body; how then could I wish to transform it again?
The Deva said, "Śāriputra, if you can transform this female body, then all women should likewise be able to transform theirs."
Sengzhao said:
"The benevolent one does not know why she transforms yet transforms into a female body; the multitude of women likewise do not know why they transform yet become women.
If the benevolent one has no intention regarding being female and yet cannot transform her female body, then the multitude of women are likewise unable to transform themselves."
How can one exhort others to transform their female bodies?
This clarifies that although a woman lacks a fixed nature, she is nonetheless formed by causes and conditions and cannot achieve mastery over her own transformation.
Just as Śāriputra was not a woman yet manifested in a female body, so it is with all women: though they manifest in female bodies, they are not women.
Zhaò says:
"Just as Śāriputra was in reality not a woman, yet now manifests this female form."
The multitude of women also manifest this female form, yet in reality they are not women.
Since there is no fixed characteristic for male or female, it can be known by analogy with oneself.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are neither male nor female.
Sengzhao said:
"How could the Buddha’s words be false!
At that moment, the heavenly maiden withdrew her supernatural power, and Śāriputra’s body returned to its former state."
The Deva asked Śāriputra:
"Where now is the physical form and appearance of your female body?
Zhaò said:
"Since I wish to inquire about where the marks of a woman's form reside, I have resumed my body to ask you.
Śāriputra replied,
"The marks of a woman's form neither reside anywhere nor do they not reside anywhere."
Sengzhao said:
If one wishes to say it exists, its marks are now seen to be non-existent;
if one wishes to say it does not exist, it previously possessed marks.
It is like a magical illusion, lacking any fixed nature and having no place where it can be found.
The Deva said:
"All dharmas are likewise thus—neither existing nor non-existing."
"That which neither exists nor does not exist" is what the Buddha taught.
Sengzhao said:
"How could this apply only to the marks of a woman? All dharmas are likewise so."
He spoke in accordance with what the Buddha had taught, clarifying that the principles cannot be altered.
Śāriputra asked the goddess:
"When you pass away from here, where will you be reborn?"
Sengzhao said:
"Since you already know that the manifested marks have no location, you now ask about the location of that which is to arise.
Tian replied:
"Born through the Buddha's transformation.
Kumārajīva said:

"He did not speak directly of non-arising, but spoke of arising because he wished to take the characteristics of arising as a basis to demonstrate that, in principle, there is neither birth nor extinction."
"I am born like that.
Zhaor said:
"Since the physical marks of this life are already like illusions and transformations, how could being born again after death be any different?"
He said, "That which is produced through the Buddha's transformation is not a matter of death and rebirth.
The deity said, "Sentient beings are likewise; there is no death and rebirth."
Sengzhao said:
"Is it that I alone am like an illusion, while all things are not?
Śāriputra asked the goddess:"
"How long will it be before you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Zhaò said:

"While the physical marks of the body may vanish and arise like illusions or transformations, the true path of *bodhi* must surely possess reality; therefore, he asks how long it will take to achieve it."
The deity said:
"If Śāriputra were to return to being an ordinary person, only then would I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Zhaò said:
"What you expect will certainly not happen.
Śāriputra said,
"That I would become an ordinary person— that is impossible."
Sengzhao asked:
"How could it be possible for a sage to return to the state of an ordinary person?
Tian replied:
That I should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is likewise impossible.
Zhaò says:
"That those sages [remain as] ordinary beings while I achieve the path to Bodhi—there is not a single instance where this is possible."
Why is this? Because awakening has no place of abiding, there is therefore no one who attains it.
Zhaò says:
The path to Bodhi is unconditioned and signless; since it has no place of abiding, who could possibly attain it?
Śāriputra said:
"Now, the Buddhas of the present have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and those who have already attained or will attain it are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—what do you mean by this?"
Sengzhao said:
"Based on what he has attained, he asks.
Tian said:
All these are spoken of as having the three periods of time merely because of the conventional designations of words; it does not mean that bodhi has past, future, or present.
Kumārajīva said:
"The nature of bodhi is empty, and therefore it transcends the three periods of time."
Since bodhi is empty, there is no attaining of Buddhahood; since there is no attaining of Buddhahood, there is likewise no bodhi.
They arise through the convergence of conditions, and in principle they are not separate; therefore, existence and non-existence should be regarded as identical.
Sengzhao said:
"In the conventional world, one speaks of numbers and thus attains the three periods of time; this does not mean that Bodhi—the supreme, true Way—has past, future, or present.
Tiantai said:
"Śāriputra! Have you attained the path of an Arhat?
Kumārajīva replied:

The Buddha-way is profound and subtle, the ultimate reality of existence; that which one has not yet attained, one still considers to be non-existent, whereas that which one has already attained, one realizes to be non-existent. Therefore, by asking this question, he is led to examine himself in order to awaken to the Buddha-nature.
Sengzhao said:

"When an Arhat enters the mind of outflowlessness (anāsrava-citta), he does not perceive the attainment of the Way; when he enters the mind of outflows (sāsrava-citta), he perceives that there is attainment.
Now I ask: at the time of self-realization and attainment of the Way through the ninth liberation, does he perceive that there is attainment?"
This is intended to lead one to realize for oneself the meaning of non-attainment.
It says:
"Because there is nothing to be attained, one attains."
Kumārajīva said:
"Because one understands that there is no attainment in the Dharma, one accords with the principle of the Dharma; therefore, based on this accord, it is conventionally designated as 'attainment.
Sengzhao said:
He answered by inferring from his own mind:
"Because there is no attainment, there is attainment; where there is attainment, there is non-attainment. This clarifies that true attainment lies precisely in non-attainment.
Tian said:
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this: they attain through non-attainment.
Kumārajīva said:

"The two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) are identical in that they take realization as their attainment yet find nothing to be attained; however, the Mahāyāna’s awakening to the Dharma is profound, and furthermore, it is free from the distinction of entering and exiting [the state of realization]."
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra:

"This goddess has already made offerings to ninety-two billion buddhas; she is able to sport with the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, her vows are fully accomplished, she has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, and she dwells in the stage of non-retrogression. By virtue of her original vow, she can manifest herself at will to teach and transform sentient beings."
Zhaò said:
"The preceding section merely discussed birth through words, without yet revealing the depth of that Way.
Vimalakīrti manifested its true reality from a different perspective, thereby inspiring the feelings of reverence and faith in the assembled multitude."
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Six;
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Compiled by Śramaṇa Sengzhao of the Later Qin.
Chapter Eight: On the Buddha-Way (7).
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"How does a bodhisattva penetrate the Buddha-way?"
Kumārajīva said:

"Because the preceding chapter describes how the goddess took on a body according to her vow to propagate the Buddha-dharma, this section extensively clarifies the efficacy of her unimpeded penetration by illustrating the traces of her perfect adaptation."
Sengzhao said:
The preceding passage stated that the Way of the Buddhas takes non-attainment as attainment; this Way is empty and profound, not something accessible through ordinary practice.
Since there must be a means by which it is accessed, he asks for the reason why it is accessed.
Śāriputra said:
"To manifest transformations without fixed direction is the Way of the Buddha; since you are able to embody this, you have attained thorough penetration.
Vimalakīrti replied:
"If a bodhisattva practices what is not the Path," Kumārajīva said, "there are three kinds of 'not the Path':
first, the retributive fruits of the evil realms; second, the karmic actions leading to the evil realms; and third, mundane wholesome karma and the retributive fruits of such wholesome karma."
Generally, anything that dwells in what is not its own fundamental reality is termed "non-Dharma.
By dwelling in non-reality without losing its fundamental essence, one is able to utilize non-Dharma to propagate the Way; thus, this penetration is true penetration.
It is like a skilled physician who touches upon things to create medicine; thus his medical art is put into practice, and whenever he encounters illness, it is cured.
This is what is meant by "thoroughly penetrating the Buddha-way. Zhaò said:

If one regards that which is the Way as the Way and that which is not the Way as not the Way, then love and hatred will arise together and defilements and entanglements will become manifest; how then can one penetrate the subtle purport of the mind and reach the Way of equality?
If one can neither regard the Way as the Way nor regard non-Way as non-Way, then right and wrong are severed within the mind; thus, upon encountering any thing, one may mount it.

Therefore, by dwelling in this state where there is no sentiment of "is" or "is-not," and riding upon that which is neither "not-is" nor "not-not-is," one is able to view beauty and ugliness with equanimity and tread through adversity as if it were constancy. By harmonizing one's light with the dust of worldly toil, one becomes ever more luminous the more one darkens; this may be called the unimpeded and equal path of the Buddha.
Jizang said:
"Those who manifest and act beyond the external form all do so through the process of transformation according to conditions (*nirmāṇa*).
Since the heavenly maiden was precisely such an instance, I have elaborated upon it here."
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva practice on what is not the path?
He replied:
"If a bodhisattva commits the five acts of immediate retribution yet remains free from affliction and anger," Kumārajīva said,
"the five acts of immediate retribution are sinful karmas."
From the hells up to the hungry ghosts, these are the retributive fruits of the evil destinies.
Zhaò says:
"The five heinous crimes necessarily arise from affliction and anger; once one has abandoned the body after committing such sins, one must enter the hells to undergo uninterrupted suffering."
The Bodhisattva manifests the practice of the five heinous crimes yet remains free from affliction or anger; this is because, by not regarding these crimes as crimes, he is able to accord with them.
If one regarded these crimes as crimes, who would dare to accord with them?
As for the hells, they are devoid of all defilements of sin.
Zhaò said:
"The defilements of sin are the cause of the hells."
He manifests the reception of its retribution, yet in reality there is no cause for it.
As for animals, they possess no faults such as ignorance or arrogance.
Zhaor said:
Those whose delusion and pride are particularly heavy mostly fall among the animals;
as for those who possess complete merit, they become hungry ghosts.
Zhaò said:
"Those who are stingy and greedy lack merit and mostly fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
As for practicing the paths of the form and formless realms, do not consider them superior.
Kumārajīva said:
The Sanskrit original states, "reaching the realms of form and formlessness. Ordinary beings who are born there consider it to be the foremost and most supreme nirvana;
however, since they are now born through conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), they do not regard it as supreme.
Zhaò said:
"Regarding the causes for receiving existence within the two upper realms, although their conduct is the same, one knows them to be base and inferior.

[The Buddha] manifests the practice of desire while remaining free from all defiled attachments; he manifests the practice of anger yet harbors no resentment toward sentient beings; he manifests the practice of ignorance while subduing his mind through wisdom."
Zhaò said: "He manifests the practice of the three poisons without contravening the three virtues.

He manifests the practice of stinginess and greed while relinquishing all internal and external possessions and not sparing even his own body or life. He manifests the practice of violating the prohibitions while abiding securely in pure precepts, feeling great dread even at the slightest offense. He manifests the practice of anger while remaining constantly compassionate and patient. He manifests the practice of indolence while diligently cultivating merit and virtue. He manifests the practice of distracted thought while constantly maintaining mindfulness of concentration. He manifests the practice of ignorance while attaining penetration into both mundane and supramundane wisdom."
Sengzhao said:
"This demonstrates the practice of the six corruptions without contradicting the six perfections;
it demonstrates the practice of flattery and hypocrisy while being skillful in means according to the principles of the various sutras."
Kumārajīva said:
"Although its outward form may resemble flattery, in reality it does not deviate from the correct; this is what is meant by 'skillful means' that accords with the meanings of the various sūtras.
Sengzhao said:
Outwardly he manifests flattery and hypocrisy in accordance with worldly custom, while inwardly he truly employs skillful means as taught in the sutras.
He demonstrates the practice of arrogance, yet toward sentient beings he is like a bridge.
Kumārajīva said:
To speak of his humility: though he was trampled upon by others, he endured it without pride, like a bridge.
Zhaò said:
"He allowed all beings to tread upon him; this is the ultimate degree of lowliness."
He manifests the practice of all afflictions while his mind remains ever pure.
Zhaò says:
"Afflictions are displayed outwardly, while the purity of the mind is maintained inwardly."
He manifests entry into the realm of Māra while remaining in accord with the Buddha’s wisdom and not following the teachings of others.
Zhaò says:
"Externally he conforms to heterodox teachings, yet internally he accords with correct wisdom."
He manifests entry among the śrāvakas to preach the Dharma unheard of to sentient beings.
Kumārajīva said:
"Abiding therein does not mean abandoning one's original nature; rather, as superior training becomes increasingly clear, one preaches without waiting to hear it from others."
Zhaò said:
"If a śrāvaka cannot awaken on his own without hearing from others, how much less could he explain to others what he has not heard?
[The Buddha] manifested entry into the stage of a pratyekabuddha to achieve great compassion and teach and transform sentient beings."
Zhaò said:
"The Mahāyāna Dharma of Great Compassion is not something that can be practiced by Pratyekabuddhas.
[The Buddha] manifests entry into poverty while possessing the merit of an inexhaustible jewel-hand."
Kumārajīva said:
"His hands can produce jewels, bestowing them extensively and inexhaustibly.
Sengzhao said:
From his hands he produces natural treasures that exhaust the needs of the destitute without end.

He manifests entry into physical deformity while remaining adorned with all the marks and signs of excellence; he manifests entry into lowly births while being born into the lineage of Buddhas, endowed with all virtues.
Kumārajīva said:

"The Buddha-lineage is precisely the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). To attain this profound patience is called 'the birth of the Dharma'; one has thereby transcended the lowly and entered the realm of the Buddha."
Zhaò says:
"To attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is necessarily to continue the lineage of the Buddhas; this is what is meant by being born into the Buddha-lineage.
He manifests entry into a state of weakness, inferiority, and ugliness, yet attains the body of Nārāyaṇa."
Kumārajīva said:
"The Heavenly Malla is one whose body is firm, solid, and upright;
he is one whom all sentient beings delight to behold."
Zhaò said:
Nārāyaṇa is the name of a celestial warrior; he is upright and exceptionally marvelous, with a will and strength that are fierce and powerful.
He manifests entry into old age and illness, yet has forever severed the root of disease and transcended the fear of death.
Sengzhao said:
"For a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, birth and death are forever exhausted; how much more so, then, old age and sickness?

He manifests the possession of the necessities of life while constantly contemplating impermanence and truly having nothing to crave; he manifests the presence of wives, concubines, and court ladies while always remaining far removed from the mire of the five desires."
Kumārajīva said:
"He is like Prince Mūkapangu.
He manifests as dull-witted and mute, yet achieves eloquence and dhāraṇī without loss; he demonstrates entering into heterodox paths, yet delivers others through the true path."
Kumārajīva said:
"The place where one crosses over is called 'ferrying' (ji).
It means to deliver all sentient beings."
Zhaò said:
"A place where a river or ford can be crossed is called a 'right crossing' (zhèngjì); a place that is dangerous and difficult is called a 'wrong crossing' (xiéjì).
The Buddha-way is called the right crossing, while external paths are called wrong crossings."
He manifests by entering all paths in order to sever their causal conditions.
Zhaò says:
"To enter various heterodox paths is not for the sake of seeking them out; it is merely to sever their causal ties."
He manifests in nirvana yet does not cease the cycle of birth and death.
Zhaò says:
He manifests his body in nirvana while precisely entering into birth and death.

All that has been listed above regarding the bodhisattva constitutes what is not the Way; yet to abide therein without obstruction is precisely what constitutes the Way. Therefore, it is said that one "penetrates and realizes the Buddha-way."
"Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva can practice in this way upon what is not the path, this is called penetrating the Buddha-path.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti questioned Mañjuśrī.
Kumārajīva said:
"Since we first met, Vimalakīrti has been the sole speaker; it seems as though the merit of his eloquence and wisdom has been attributed to him exclusively.
By now having him speak, I wish to manifest his virtue."
It is also said that one dedicates merit as an offering.
What constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata?
Kumārajīva replied:
"Seed," "root," and "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya) are one and the same meaning.

Because the Great Beings (mahāsattva), by following the various types of beings to transform them, penetrate the Buddha-way, we know for certain that sentient beings who have accumulated evil can give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta). Since the ability to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment constitutes the causal condition for the Buddha-way, he asks about the "Buddha-seed."
It is also said that the new learners desire to attain Buddhahood but do not yet know the causes for becoming a Buddha; therefore, they inquire about those causes.
Sengzhao says:
Having already clarified why the Buddha-way is pervasive, he now asks from whence that Way originates.
Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī alternately engaged in dialogue, responding to circumstances as they arose; who could discern the underlying cause?
Daosheng said:
"The 'seeds of the Tathāgata' is a metaphorical expression for grain seeds."
Previously, it was shown that all evils constitute the Buddha; now, it is clarified that actual evil constitutes the seed. Therefore, he next poses a counter-question.
Mañjuśrī said: "The body of existence (*satkāya*) is the seed."
Kumārajīva said:
"To have a body" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) which are subject to outflows (sāsrava).

[The commentator] explains that "having a body" should actually mean "the view of a self-body" (satkāya-dṛṣṭi); since the view of a self-body is the source of the three realms of existence and the root of all fetters and entanglements, he speaks directly of the view of a self-body.
The view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) conceives of a self; because it desires to obtain happiness, one is able to practice goodness, and thus it serves as the seed of the Buddha.
Sengzhao says:
"Where there is a body, there is the view of a self-body."

Now, the mind has no fixed location; it changes according to its objects. It is defiled when in the presence of the defiled and pure when in the presence of the pure; though the defiled and the pure differ, their underlying nature is not distinct.

Why is this? When the perverse is transformed into the correct and the evil is changed into the good, could it be that there exists some distinct "correctness" apart from the perverse or some "goodness" apart from the evil, which arises transcendentally without cause and is suddenly attained of itself?
Thus, since the correct arises from the deviant and the good is born from the evil, it is said that the various fetters and afflictions constitute the seeds of the Tathāgata.
Ignorance and craving are the seeds.
Kumārajīva said:
"What was previously stated as a general exposition is here divided into two gates.
Since all fetters belong to these two gates, I have specifically cited these two gates."
From this point onward, the following is a detailed and sequential exposition.
Greed, hatred, and delusion serve as seeds;
the four inversions serve as seeds.
The five hindrances are the seeds.
Kumārajīva said:
"The four inversions are the cause and the five hindrances are the fruit; these together are called the two wheels of birth and death."
Once the two wheels are complete, one wanders through the six realms of existence;
the six sense bases serve as the seeds.
Kumārajīva said:
The meaning of "yi" (義) is the craving of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Since craving is the root of birth, it is explained here with particular breadth.
The seven stations of consciousness (*saptavijñānasthiti*) serve as the seeds.
Śrīmitra said:

"Within the first dhyāna, excluding the Brahmā King at the beginning of the kalpa and the various minor Brahmās at the beginning of the kalpa, all subsequent beings together constitute the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

At the beginning of the kalpa, there was only the Brahmā King and no other Brahmās; the Brahmā King then conceived the desire for other Brahmās to exist. At that time, other Brahmās encountered the conditions for birth and came into being. Consequently, the Brahmā King gave rise to a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), claiming that he himself had created them, while the other Brahmās also claimed to have been born from the Brahmā King."

Although there is refinement or coarseness, their erroneous perceptions (*vitarka*) do not differ; this is called "different bodies with one perception," the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

In the second dhyāna, while the physical forms have no distinction of superiority or inferiority, the mind possesses various states; excluding the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*), there are diverse and differing thoughts.
