This is called "one form with different perceptions," the third station of consciousness.

In the third dhyāna, the body is free from coarseness and the mind is free from discursive thought; this is the so-called "single perception of bliss," which is the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Together with the first three stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), these are called the seven stations of consciousness.
The station of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*) means that consciousness attains stable abiding.
When consciousness is clearly mindful, free from affliction and harm, and indestructible, it is called a "station.

In the evil realms, there is destruction by suffering; in the four dhyānas, there is destruction by non-conception (*asaṃjñā*); and in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is destruction by non-perception (*naivasaṃjñā-nāsaṃjñā*).
Furthermore, because the mental images (*bhūmi-saṃjñā*) in those stages are subtle and dim, and mindfulness is not clear, consciousness does not abide securely there.
Question: Since the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) is also destroyed by the miserable destinies (*apāya*), why is it established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)?
Answer: One takes up the destruction of the *bhūmi* (planes), not the destruction of the *dhātu* (realms).

Within the desire realm, the evil destinies and the fortunate destinies differ in their planes; since their experiences of suffering and pleasure lead to distinct ends, they do not intersect in meaning, and thus they do not destroy one another.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that there should be seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
the eight wrong dharmas (*mithyā-dharma*) serve as their seeds,
and the nine bases of resentment (*āghāta-vastu*) serve as their seeds.
Kumārajīva said:
"Those who love me are my enemies; those who hate me are my friends; and those who afflict my own body are myself. In one lifetime there are three, and across the three lifetimes there are nine.
In meaning, these are called the 'nine fetters' (nava-saṃyojana)."
The ten unwholesome paths serve as the seeds.
To state it briefly, the sixty-two views and all afflictions are likewise the seeds of the Buddha.
Zhaò says:
Sentient beings amidst the dust and toil of affliction are themselves the realization of the Buddha-way; there is no other person who becomes a Buddha, for they are the very seed of Buddhahood.
Daosheng said:

"As for the awakening of the Mahāyāna, it fundamentally does not involve abandoning birth and death in this life to seek it further afar; rather, it consists in taking the reality within the midst of the affairs of birth and death as awakening itself."
If one remains within a given matter yet transforms its reality to achieve awakening from the very beginning, is this not because the sprout of the Buddha arises from the affairs of birth and death?
Once that awakening has grown long, the practice must necessarily become skillful; is this not the meaning of "planting"?

The reason why it begins with the possession of a body and culminates in all manner of afflictions is that the clarification of principle unfolds extensively until it reaches the realization of great awakening in its reality.
It is asked: what does this mean?
Sengzhao asked:
"If the Way that reaches the ultimate subtlety must necessarily have a cause that reaches the ultimate subtlety, why do you say that worldly afflictions (*rajas*) serve as its seed?
Sengsheng replied:
The Buddha is the ultimate wisdom, yet he takes all evils as his seed; since he cannot be solitary or isolated, he asks in this manner.
He replied:
"If one perceives the unconditioned and enters the stage of right determination."
Kumārajīva said:

"From the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the Arhat’s realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), all are termed the 'right position' (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

To speak of 'entering by means of the unconditioned' (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to entering the right position and attaining realization because one has abandoned the perception of signs (*nimitta-darśana*)."

Furthermore, it is said that one "sees the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). The unconditioned is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), and this truth of cessation is the realized dharma (*adhigamadharma*) which is definitively clear;
whereas when seeing the first two truths, although there is no opposing force, they are not yet definitively clear.
Speaking according to the point at which he has definitively attained realization,
he is unable to again give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāṇakavāsin said:
This is clarified by means of present phenomena.

To "see the unconditioned and enter the stage of right determination" means that once one has attained the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and above, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been severed; having reached that state, one begins to see it.
Because one originally desires to abandon birth and death in order to seek awakening, once awakened, one exists beyond birth and death.
Since there is nothing further to be abandoned, this is precisely the meaning of awakening; therefore, one cannot again give rise to the bodhicitta.

For example, just as lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, but rather in low, damp, and muddy swamps, so too those who perceive unconditioned dharmas and enter the stage of right determination can never again give rise to the afflictions within the mire of the Buddha-dharma; it is only among sentient beings that the Buddha-dharma arises.
Dongsheng said:
"This refers to entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It is like planting seeds: they can never sprout in empty space, but will flourish in soil enriched with manure."
"Thus, one who has entered the unconditioned state of correctness does not give rise to the Buddha-dharma, yet they give rise to a view of self as high as Mount Sumeru.
Kumārajīva said:
"This means that their view is both profound and lofty."
Zhaò said:
"My own mind is naturally lofty, like Mount Sumeru among all other mountains.
Yet it is still able to give rise to the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind and produce the Buddha-dharma."
Sheng said:
"The two metaphors illustrate the principle of non-action (wuwei).
These two metaphors clarify the manner in which things begin to sprout and develop."
Therefore, one should know that all afflictions constitute the seed of the Tathāgata.
Kumārajīva said:

This means that for incalculable eons, sentient beings have taken on bodies through afflictions and entered deeply into birth and death; by extensively accumulating the roots of goodness and simultaneously delivering sentient beings, they subsequently attain the Way of the Buddha.
This is why it is called a "seed.
For example, just as one cannot obtain a priceless jewel without descending into the great ocean, so too one cannot obtain the jewel of omniscience without entering the great ocean of afflictions.
Sengzhao said:

"Since those of the Two Vehicles have realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and dwell securely in the state of right position, their minds are empty, tranquil, and still; they are serene and at ease. Having no fear of birth and death, they possess the joy of the unconditioned; being pure and self-sufficient, they have neither hope nor seeking."
Who would be so resolute as to take the Mahāyāna as their core aspiration?

Ordinary beings are submerged in the five destinies, obscured by afflictions; they lack the joy of the unconditioned when advancing and harbor the fear of birth and death when retreating. Furthermore, with their own minds naturally arrogant and longing only for superiority, they are thus able to set out from the dust of worldly toil and fix their hearts on the Unsurpassed, planting their roots in birth and death to blossom forth the flowers of perfect enlightenment.

How could those who have not yet transcended being ordinary beings—those whose lives sink into the abyss and who wander and linger in the ocean of defilements—be able to attain this unsurpassed treasure?
For this reason, ordinary beings bear the reputation of "reversing and returning," while those of the Two Vehicles suffer the shame of "ruined faculties."
Jizang said:
"The priceless jewel is produced from the ocean;
likewise, the jewel of omniscience is produced from afflictions. One must enter the ocean of afflictions to seek it, and only then will one obtain it."
This parable clarifies that since one does not abandon conditioned existence (*saṃyojana-saṃskāra*), there is indeed a principle of re-entry.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Mañjuśrī! You have spoken these words well.
It is truly as you say: the host of afflictions constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata.

We are no longer capable of generating the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution can still resolve their minds to be born within the Buddha-dharma, yet we are now forever unable to do so; it is like a man whose sense organs are destroyed, who can no longer derive benefit from the five desires.
Thus, for those śrāvakas who have severed all fetters, there is nothing further to be gained within the Buddha-dharma, and they never again aspire to it.
Zhaò says:

Kāśyapa knew of himself that his own mind was weak and could not give rise to the aspiration for the Great Way; as for those who seek excellence, they are like people who have committed the five heinous crimes. Grieving that he was incapable, he thus approved of Mañjuśrī’s words.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
Ordinary worldlings may turn back from the Buddha-dharma, but the śrāvakas do not. Why is this?
Ordinary beings, upon hearing the Buddha-dharma, are able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and ensure that the Three Jewels are never severed.
Even if a śrāvaka were to hear of the Buddha-dharma, the powers, and the fearlessnesses for the rest of their life, they would never be able to arouse the intention for unsurpassed enlightenment.
Sengzhao said:
"If ordinary persons, upon hearing the Dharma, can continue the lineage of the Buddha, then their repayment of gratitude is reciprocal.
Śrāvakas, however, seek only their own benefit and do not propagate the Three Jewels; thus, in relation to the Buddha-Dharma, they lack reciprocity."
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that those of the two vehicles who have ceased [their practice] will ultimately and necessarily attain Buddhahood;
yet this sūtra uses the analogy of impaired faculties to show that they no longer possess the aspiration to seek it.
Now, Nirvana is the true essence of the Way and the ultimate pinnacle of the sublime.

Since those of the Two Vehicles have not yet exhausted their residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) and have not yet removed their obscurations of darkness, how can they seek the Way of the true and ultimate with a spirit still burdened by defilements?
Because their three realms of existence have been exhausted, they are provisionally granted *nirvāṇa*, though it is not actual *nirvāṇa*.

This sutra intends that once the two vehicles have grown weary of birth and death and their forward progress has ceased, they remain hidden in the unconditioned for a long, enduring time; compared to ordinary beings, this state is then considered eternal severance.

Furthermore, when suppressing or elevating [the teachings], one may hear of the base and inferior Hīnayāna; since the supreme person’s extraordinary responses to these teachings were not uniform, the various sūtras consequently contain differing explanations.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samantavabhāsavigraha who asked Vimalakīrti:
"Householder, who are your father and mother, your wife and children, your kinsmen and relatives, your officials and subjects, and your friends and acquaintances?"
"Where are the slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages?
Zhaò replied:

'Vimalakīrti’s skillful means are boundless; his concealment and manifestation are difficult to fathom. Outwardly he appears to have a family and kin, yet inwardly he takes the Dharma as his family.'"
Fearing that those who are deluded might see only the physical form and fail to reach its underlying Way, he raised this question.
Daosheng said:
"The universal manifestation of the form-body takes the thorough penetration of the Buddha-way as its trace."

The purpose of asking about this meaning is to clarify its underlying reality; since it must necessarily have a foundation that traces back to the ultimate nature of birth and death, one is thus able to penetrate all things without exception.
Therefore, at the conclusion of the *Śīla-varga*, it is stated that "the means employed are not fixed."
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti replied with a verse:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas. He said:
That which is called the Bodhisattva takes wisdom as its master; since wisdom functions through internal understanding, it possesses the significance of a mother.
Expedient means serve as the father.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because it exhausts the source of wisdom, it is called 'crossing over' (pāramitā).
Since the Sanskrit sound contains the meaning of 'mother,' it is therefore regarded as a mother."

It is also said that although Prajñāpāramitā has luminous illumination as its essence, in terms of its efficacy in accomplishing and bringing all practices to fulfillment, it does not equal Upāya; therefore, it is regarded as the mother.
Upāya is the father, for within the Sanskrit sound there is the meaning of "father."
There are two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*): first, to have a profound understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while not grasping at signs or seeking personal realization;

second, because the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is so profound that it cannot be believed or accepted [directly], one must employ skillful means to guide and attract sentient beings so that they may gradually awaken.
The meaning of skillful means (*upāya*) is profound and its merit is weighty; therefore, it is considered the father.
Zhaò says:

Wisdom is internal illumination, while skillful means is external application. It is that from which the myriad practices arise and by which all Buddhas emerge; thus, the Bodhisattva takes wisdom as mother and skillful means as father.
Daosheng said:
"To employ external salvation as a means is the meaning of being a father who establishes the path of the Bodhisattva.
No leaders of all beings arise except through this."
Kumārajīva said:
"Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas are collectively termed 'Guiding Teachers.
Because those who are newly trained are considered not yet free from the process of taking birth, they must have parents."
Now, wishing to manifest that he transforms beings through the Dharma and has severed the taking of further bodies, he answers with the Dharma.
[The interlocutor] says:
"From the Bodhisattva up to the Buddha."
He took the joy of the Dharma as his wife.
Kumārajīva said:

"Just as in the second dhyāna one gives rise to joy because of the personal delight in being detached from the lower stages, so too does one feel deep-seated love and delight for all wholesome qualities and the true Dharma, giving rise to great rapture; with this one amuses oneself, having no other source of joy besides it."
Joy serves as an instrument of pleasure, analogous to a wife.
Zhaò says:
"Dharma-joy" refers to the internal joy that arises from perceiving the Dharma.
Ordinary people find pleasure in the beauty of their wives, whereas Bodhisattvas find pleasure in the joy of the Dharma.
Sheng said:
"A wife takes her observance of chastity as her delight; she grieves when that chastity is lost."
This refers to one who delights in the Dharma.
Compassion is her female nature.
Kumārajīva said:
Their nature of compassion is weak; they follow external things and enter into existence, just as a woman’s nature is weak and she follows external things.
Zhaò says:
"The sentiment of compassion resembles the nature of a woman; therefore, they are likened to women."
Sheng said:
"Beyond compassion lies what is appropriately employed; therein lies the principle of the female.
A virtuous mind and sincerity constitute the male."
Kumārajīva said:
"A sincere mind is capable of discernment in affairs, just as a man possesses a nature of integrity and steadfastness to bring his family affairs to completion.
Sengzhao said:
Sincerity and uprightness are the nature of a man; yet there are those who commit evil while remaining sincere, which is why this is distinguished by the inclusion of "a virtuous mind.
Master Jing says:

"Since his mind is already virtuous and is further augmented by sincerity, he will surely be able to manage the affairs of the Bodhisattva family and accomplish great deeds; because he possesses the duties of a man, he is called a 'sincere man.'"
"Ultimate emptiness is the tranquil dwelling.
Kumārajīva said:

"Nothing provides better shelter against wind and rain than a house; nothing is more sublime for extinguishing manifold perceptions than emptiness. It can also sever all challenges and subdue the enmity of Māra, just as within a dense and deep-roofed mansion, the threat of bandits naturally vanishes."
It is also said that what exists is not the essential truth, as one wanders there only temporarily; emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taken as the fundamental principle and made one’s permanent abode.
Sengzhao says:
"Hall and chamber serve to shield against wind and frost; emptiness and stillness serve to block out defiled thoughts."
Sheng said:
"To exist in dependence upon conditions is to have external existence;
to lack intrinsic nature is to be internally empty."
"It can provide shelter from the winds and rains of unrighteousness and ward off the afflictions of the bandits of the fetters; this is the principle of a dwelling.
The disciples said, "We are beset by the manifold dust-labor of defilements.
Kumārajīva said:
The "multitude of dusts" refers to sentient beings burdened by afflictions (*kleśa*).
He transforms them so that they follow him, causing them to receive the Right Path.
Thus, he turns [them] according to his will.
Kumārajīva said:
"This means to cause others to transform according to oneself.
Sengzhao said:
Sentient beings burdened by worldly afflictions are transformed according to their inclinations; there are none who are not disciples.
Daosheng said:
"To transform the delusions of the various defilements into the clarity of wisdom—is this not the true meaning of transformation?"
Regarding the "Dharmapada-saṃnipāta" (The Collection of the Factors of Enlightenment) as "Good Friends," Kumārajīva said:

"The thirty-seven factors are common to all three vehicles; for Bodhisattvas, they are supplemented by the six perfections as their factors of enlightenment. Because these [factors] provide close support, protection, benefit, and accomplishment—sharing the same meaning as the 'three benefits'—they are categorized as 'good friends.'"
"By this, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Zhaò said:
"That which brings me benefit is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; can they not be called 'good spiritual friends'?"
Sheng said:
"To benefit me with the Way and thereby fulfill the meaning of a virtuous friend—
this is what the various pāramitās and dharmas do as my companions."
Kumārajīva said:
"There may be those who, though considered friends, are not necessarily companions for the end;
or there may be those who, though companions, do not act as friends."
Furthermore, it is said that having companions ensures a good beginning and a successful conclusion, leading inevitably to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Zhaò says:
"The six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are the essential practices of the Mahāyāna."
"One who resolves to take up the path as a companion and arrives together at the site of enlightenment is my true companion.
Śāriputra said:
"I originally desired to reach the other shore of all dharmas, and it was by relying on the various pāramitās that I attained it; you are indeed an excellent companion."
He compared the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to courtesans.
Kumārajīva said:
"The four means of attraction gather the multitude, just as a troupe of courtesans attracts people."
Sengzhao said:
"The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) delight the multitude; they correspond to the female entertainers.
Sengsheng said:
To win over people through delight is the principle of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
To sing and recite the words of the Dharma is to take this as music.
Zhaò said:
He would chant the words of the Dharma with his mouth to serve as music.
Daosheng said:
"For bringing delight to the ears and producing true music, nothing is better than this."
"Total Retention (Dhāraṇī) is a garden and grove.
Kumārajīva said:
"Total Retention broadly receives and encompasses all that is wondrous, forming a forest; its marvelous delights and entertainment for the mind are just like a garden and grove."
Dharmapāla said:
"To maintain all dharmas so that they do not scatter or perish is the meaning of 'grove' (ārāma).
The forest trees are the outflow-free (anāsrava) dharmas."
Sengsheng said:
"The dharmas of outflowlessness (anāsrava-dharma), having roots so deep they cannot be uprooted and principles so lofty and spreading, are like the image of a tree.
That the dharmas of outflow (sāsrava-dharma) can no longer intermingle among them is the meaning of a forest."
"Awakening Mind: Pure and Wondrous Flowers.
Kumārajīva said:

"As for the nature of flowers, if they remain closed, they are not wondrous; if they have already opened and passed away, they are ruined. Only when their opening and closing reach their proper measure do they fully manifest their wondrousness."

The harmonizing of the awakened mind is likewise so: if it is too high, it scatters; if it is too low, it sinks. When it attains the middle between high and low, one proceeds straight on with equanimity.
The characteristics of its opening and closing are like those of a pure flower.
Daosheng said:
"The seven factors of enlightenment take awakening as the Way and non-defilement as purity; these are the flowers of the Dharma.
Liberation and wisdom are the fruits."
Kumārajīva said:
"Liberation is the fruit of the unconditioned;
wisdom is the fruit of the conditioned."
Sengsheng said:
"The exhaustion of fetters is liberation.
Because it arises from wisdom, it is designated by that name; what is ultimately attained is the fruit."
"The bathing pool of the eight liberations.
Kumārajīva said:
"The utility of water is to remove dirt and dispel heat."
The nature of liberation likewise consists in the removal of attachments and the clearing away of obstructions.
Sengsheng said:
"Eight" is used to correspond to the eight directions.
Liberation means removing the stains of the mind;
thus, it carries the significance of a bathing pool.
The water of meditative concentration is serene and fills it completely.
Huisheng said:
"To cease [mental activity] is to be capable of reflection; this is the nature of water.
Once the mind is settled and satisfied, it becomes profoundly still and full."
He spread out the seven kinds of pure flowers.
Kumārajīva said:
"The first is purity of precepts; it is purity from beginning to end."

In their physical and verbal actions, they commit not even the slightest evil; their minds do not give rise to defilement; they neither grasp at signs nor aspire for rebirth; and in bestowing fearlessness upon others, they do not limit it to sentient beings alone.

Second is purity of mind: the minds of the three vehicles that subdue afflictions, the minds that sever fetters, and even the minds of the three vehicles that have exhausted outflows—these are called purity of mind.
Third is purity of view: seeing the true nature of phenomena without giving rise to delusive thoughts; this is called purity of view.
Regarding "crossing over doubt and purification" (*vicikitsā-viśuddhi*): if one's insight is not yet profound, although one may understand at that moment, doubt may later arise;
if one's insight is profound and doubt is severed, it is called "crossing over doubt and purification."

Fifth is the purity of discerning the path (*mārga-vibhāga-śuddhi*). Being well able to see what is the appropriate path to be practiced and what is not the path to be abandoned is called the purity of discerning the path.

Sixth is the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment through practice (*pratipad-jñānadarśana-śuddhi*). "Practice" refers to the four modes of practice: difficult with slow progress, difficult with quick progress, easy with slow progress, and easy with quick progress.
"Abandonment" refers to the severing of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

While on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), one has not yet been able to personally know for oneself what has been practiced and what has been abandoned; however, once one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one fully knows and sees for oneself what was practiced and what was abandoned with clear and distinct penetration. This is called the purification of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of practice.
The seventh is the purity of Nirvana. Sengsheng said: First, purity of precepts;

second, purity of mind; third, purity of view; fourth, purity through overcoming doubt; fifth, purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path; sixth, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the course of practice; and seventh, purity of knowledge and vision regarding cessation.
Since these seven [lotuses] take purity and excellence as their principle and emerge from the water of meditative concentration, they are figuratively "flowers in the water.
[They] bathe this stainless person.
Kumārajīva said:
One bathes to remove impurities, which serves to eliminate heat and attain comfort.
When a Bodhisattva enters the eight liberations while remaining free from fetters, it is outwardly for the sake of sentient beings and inwardly for the self-delight of the mind.
Zhaò said: "Dhāraṇī and powerful memory are the garden of myriads of virtues.

Within this garden, one plants the forest of outflowlessness (anāsrava), spreads the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga), and bears the fruit of liberation (vimukti). One adorns the pond of the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) and accumulates the waters of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), which are filled to the brim and serene. The flowers of the seven purities (saptaviśuddhi) are spread out, arrayed upon the water. Thereafter, the stainless gentleman wanders through this grove and bathes in this flower-pond; he rests in leisurely ease and frolics in play—this is the height of bliss."
How could it compare to the pleasures of the groves, waters, and forests of the mundane world?
"Factors of enlightenment" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
"Liberation" refers to the fruits, both conditioned and unconditioned.
"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the fruition.
Sheng said:
"By bathing in this, one will no longer have any defilements."
Regarding the phrase "elephants and horses gallop with the five supernatural powers," Kumārajīva said:

"It means riding the Great Vehicle, traveling freely and without obstruction throughout the ten directions, while simultaneously transporting all sentient beings together to the site of enlightenment."
Sheng said:
"The five supernatural powers are swift without being hurried; they are used to illustrate elephants and horses.
The Mahāyāna is taken as the vehicle."
Sheng said:
"He has mounted the Great Vehicle;
he guides and disciplines with a single mind."
Kumārajīva said:
"One-pointedness of mind" (ekāgratā) is called "harmony" (saṃprayoga) in the Sanskrit original.

Within the mental states of the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), there are three aspects: first, the arousal [of the mind]; second, the gathering of the mind; and third, that which is named equanimity (upekṣā).
If there is an excess of arousal, the mind becomes distracted; when distracted, one should collect it.
If there is an excess of collection, the mind sinks; when sunk, one should apply diligence to arouse the mind.
If movement and stillness reach their proper balance, one should allow them to proceed naturally; maintaining this state of poised equanimity in the center is called *upekṣā* (equanimity).
Renunciation is itself mastery; mastery is itself harmony. It is like a skilled charioteer:
if [the horse] is slow, he prods it; if it is fast, he restrains it. When its pace is appropriate, he releases it to go; thus, as it strides along a level path, it will surely reach its destination.
Sheng said:
"One mind" refers to equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If there are no longer distinctions of high or low, fast or slow, it is appropriate to let things be as they are, by means of one mind.
"Roaming upon the Eightfold Noble Path.
Zhaodao says:

"The five supernatural powers serve as the elephants and horses; the Mahāyāna serves as the superior carriage; and single-mindedness serves as the charioteer—thus one roams upon the Eightfold Noble Path."
Sheng said:
"The Eightfold Noble Path is the main thoroughfare, and he travels upon it.
His physical marks are complete to adorn his countenance, and the various secondary signs embellish his form."
Śīkṣānanda said:
"Adornment is sufficient within the body; it does not depend on the external.
Daosheng said:
The primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana) are the ornaments;
shame and remorse (hrī-apatrāpya) are the supreme garments.
Kumārajīva said:
The essential point is that it prevents wrongdoing and stops evil, just as clothing can ward off wind and cold.
Sengzhao said:
"Shame and remorse are the barriers against all evils; they are the supreme garment upon the Dharma-body."
Sheng said:
"Clothing obstructs the form so that one may feel shame at exposing its ugliness.
To feel abashment and refrain from committing evil deeds—this is what is meant by this."
"The profound mind serves as a floral garland.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because one possesses profound faith and delight, one is able to cultivate goodness."
To occupy the foremost position among the good is like a floral garland upon the head.
It is further said that the profound mind illuminates all virtues, just as a flower garland adorns the body and clothing.
Sengzhao says:
The profound mind is the supreme ornament upon the Dharma-body, just as a floral garland is worn upon the head.
Daosheng said:
"Since a floral garland is an adornment for the head, it is used to bind the hair so that it does not become disheveled."
"The profound mind is the beginning of the examination of conduct; therefore, it is used as an analogy.
It is 'rich' in the seven treasures.
Kumārajīva said:
These are faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and remorse.
When living as a householder, one is able to relinquish wealth; when leaving the household life, one is able to relinquish the five desires and the afflictions.

Because one upholds the precepts through faith in what is wholesome, and by upholding the precepts one ceases from evil; having ceased from evil, one proceeds toward all manner of goodness; proceeding toward all manner of goodness requires extensive learning; through hearing the Dharma one is able to renounce; and through the ability to renounce, wisdom arises. Therefore, these five matters are explained in this sequential order.
The five things are the treasures, and shame and remorse are the guardians. Since the guardian is also a treasure among riches, these seven things are collectively termed "wealth.
Sengsheng said:
"There are seven treasures; their principle is inexhaustible, and they represent the ultimate limit of wealth."

"To practice as taught and dedicate [the merit] for the sake of great benefit.
Kumārajīva said:
"Practice" refers to one's own practice.

Taking the seven riches as the foundation, benefiting both self and others, and further dedicating this merit toward the Buddha-way—when the seven riches thus increase ever more, that is the greatness of benefit.
Sengzhao said:
"The seven riches are faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and remorse.
Worldly people consider jade and silk to be abundant, whereas Bodhisattvas regard these seven riches as wealth."

To enter and emerge from the Dharma-treasure and share its benefits with others, while simultaneously instructing them in the methods for growth and prosperity, so that they may practice according to the teachings and dedicate their merit toward the Buddha-way—this is the greatest of benefits.
Sheng said:
"As for what has been taught, practicing in this way already secures external benefits; furthermore, because one can thereby easily obtain the Great Treasure, it constitutes a great benefit.
The four dhyānas serve as the bed and seat."
Kumārajīva said:

"When one speaks of the four dhyānas, they are likened to a bed or seat because they enable one to be free from three afflictions: first, freedom from venomous stings; second, freedom from defilement and dust; and third, freedom from dampness and cold."
The fourth dhyāna is likewise free from three afflictions: it is free from the poison of ill-will, the dust of sensual desire, and the chill of sloth-and-torpor.
Being free from these three afflictions, it is peaceful, secure, and blissful.
Zhaò said:
"Ordinary people, being afflicted by venomous insects and dampness, therefore cut down wood to make beds.
Bodhisattvas, being afflicted by the poisons and evils of the lower realms, therefore take the four dhyānas as their bed."
Sheng said:
"The four [legs] correspond to the four directions.
Chan represents the principle of peace and happiness; it is the symbol of the bed."
It arises from pure livelihood.
Zhaò says: "The high couch of the four dhyānas is that which is accomplished through the cultivation of pure livelihood.
Shēng says:
"Pure livelihood is the skillful practice for dhyāna;
extensive learning increases wisdom, serving as the voice of self-awakening.
Kumārajīva said:
As previously stated, one sleeps upon the couch and attains peaceful rest; since there is a proper method for awakening from that peaceful rest, the topic of music is explained next.
When nobles in foreign lands sleep, they first instruct musicians to play subtle strains of music at the moment the dawn star appears, after which they awaken.
Now, by means of the sound of the Dharma heard through extensive learning, one awakens from the slumber of meditative absorption.
Zhaò said:
"When the kings of foreign lands wish to rise from their reclining position, they play stringed and wind instruments."
The Bodhisattva Zizhiao (Self-Awakened) rested peacefully in the fourth dhyāna, awakening himself through extensive learning.
Sheng said:
"When nobles in foreign lands lie down and wish to awaken, they play music to rouse themselves."
"This refers to those who attain awakening through hearing.
It is the food of the nectar-like Dharma.
Kumārajīva said:

The various devas place diverse medicinal herbs into the ocean and rub them against a mountain of jewels to produce nectar; by consuming it, one attains immortality, and it is thus called the "medicine of deathlessness."
In the Buddha-dharma, Nirvana is the ambrosia that brings about the eternal severance of birth and death; it is the true medicine of immortality.
It is also said that at the beginning of the kalpa there was the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) ambrosia, by eating which one attains longevity.
Within the Buddha-dharma, the nectar of the true mark nourishes one's life of wisdom; this is the true nectar-food.
Sengsheng said:
"The food of the heavens has the flavor of nectar; by eating it one attains longevity, and thus it is called the food of immortality."
Nirvana is the dharma of immortality; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for this.
The flavor of liberation serves as the drink.
Kumārajīva said:

There are four kinds of flavors: first, leaving the household life to depart from the five desires; second, practicing meditation to depart from the confusion of afflictions; third, wisdom to depart from delusive thoughts; and fourth, nirvana to depart from birth and death.
There are also two kinds of liberation: first, liberation from afflictions; second, liberation from hindrances.
It is also said that the nature of craving, being untainted, is called "thirst"; when craving is severed, one attains liberation.
Liberation is called "gruel" (*pāna*) because it quells the thirst of craving; likewise, the four tastes are also called "gruel" because they eliminate the thirst of craving.
Sengzhao says:
"The untainted nectar (*anāsrava-amṛta*) fills its substance, while the dharma-gruel of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) moistens its body."
Sheng said:
"Craving is the root of bondage; to harbor it without satiety is like a parched person requiring water—it leads to great suffering.
For one who has attained liberation, the absence of craving serves as their drink, and the absence of suffering serves as their flavor."
"Cleanse the mind through bathing.
Kumārajīva said:
"When the mind is pure, there is no defilement; being free from defilement is itself bathing, which is also called 'wandering in the eight liberations.'"
Dongsheng said:
"To purify the defilements of the mind is bathing;
the category of precepts is the fragrant ointment."
Kumārajīva said:
"Pure precepts remove defilement; they do not depend on incense.
Sengzhao said:
A pure mind is the water for bathing; the observance of precepts is the incense for anointing the body.
Sengsheng said:
"The precepts reside outside the physical form, yet their merit serves as the incense for anointing the body."
"Destroying the thieves of affliction.
Kumārajīva said:
"There are two kinds of abandonment regarding afflictions: first, cessation through obstruction; second, eternal abandonment."
"Crushing and destroying" means to obstruct and sever.
"Descending and subduing" refers to the four māras; it means to sever them forever.
The preceding discussion concerned the nourishment of the four limbs; once the body is healthy and robust, one can extensively undertake various activities.
From this point onward, his activities are explained.
[The commentary] says:
"From this point onward, it clarifies that which he does and speaks."
"Brave and powerful, none can surpass him; having subdued the four Māras, he raises the banner of victory at the site of enlightenment.
Kumārajīva said:

"In foreign lands, when one defeats an enemy and achieves victory, one erects a banner of victory; likewise, at the site of enlightenment, the subduing of the Māras also manifests the sign of such victory."
Zhaò said:
"According to the customs of foreign lands, when one wins a battle and defeats the enemy, a banner is erected to signify victory.
When a Bodhisattva subdues the thieves of affliction and overcomes the four Māras, he establishes a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to manifest this sign of triumph."
Although he knows there is neither arising nor ceasing, he manifests birth for the sake of others; he appears in all lands, just as the sun is seen by all.
Zhaò said:
"Knowing there is no arising or ceasing, one attains the Dharma-body and is no longer subject to rebirth."
Because he gives rise to existence for their sake, there is nowhere he does not go to see them.
From this point downward, the text exhaustively praises the Bodhisattva’s virtue of transformative response.
Because he takes the Dharma as his home, he is able to act in such a manner.
He makes offerings to the immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions; yet toward these Buddhas and his own self, he harbors no thought of discrimination.
Zhaò says:
"He has never perceived any difference between 'them' and 'himself.'"
Although they know that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, they constantly cultivate pure lands and transform the multitudes of living beings.
Zhaò says:
"Knowing emptiness yet not abandoning existence; this is why they always abide in the Middle Way."
Regarding all classes of sentient beings—their forms, voices, and modes of conduct—the Bodhisattva of Fearless Power can manifest them all at once.
Aware of the various deeds of Māra, he demonstrates compliance with their ways; through his wisdom of skillful means, he can manifest anything according to their inclinations.
"Or he may manifest old age, sickness, and death.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is like when the Buddha, wishing to convert King Puṣya, intentionally manifested himself as an old bhikṣu."
It is also like the transformations manifested at the four city gates.
He brings all sentient beings to fulfillment, understanding them to be like illusions and transformations, attaining unimpeded penetration.

Sometimes he manifests the conflagration at the end of an eon, where heaven and earth are utterly incinerated; for those sentient beings who harbor the notion of permanence, he illuminates them so they may realize impermanence.
Kumārajīva said:
"It may be a real fire, or it may not be a real fire.
As for that which is not a real fire, when two days have passed, or even on the third or fourth day at sunrise, sentient beings see the appearance of burning and immediately realize impermanence."
This also includes those who do not burn [the house].
Countless billions of sentient beings come together to invite the Bodhisattva; arriving at his dwelling all at once, he transforms them so that they turn toward the Buddha-way.

Whether it be the study of scriptures, the practice of incantations and arts, or the mastery of various crafts and skills, they manifest the performance of all these things to benefit all living beings.
Among all the worldly paths and dharmas, they have gone forth as monastics within them all.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is through the resonance of shared practice that they first harmonize and later diverge.
Since those who have left the household life possess virtue and are revered by all beings, he manifested entry into the monastic order to cultivate virtue and attract followers."
Thus, by means of this, one resolves the delusions of others and does not fall into false views.
Zhaò said:

"Of the ninety-six types [of heterodox schools], all have left the household life to seek the Way; according to their respective renunciations, I wish to resolve their delusions, yet I do not conform to their views."
Or he may become a sun or moon deity.
Kumārajīva said:

"At the beginning of a kalpa, there were neither sun nor moon, nor yet sentient beings; in the darkness, one could not initially see the sun or moon. Therefore, he became the sun and moon so that they might provide illumination."
The Brahma King, Lord of the World,
sometimes becomes earth and water, and at other times becomes wind and fire.
Kumārajīva said:
At the beginning of a kalpa, before the earth had yet been formed, he used his supernormal powers to cause winds from the six directions to blow upon the waters, solidifying them into land.
Alternatively, when he saw people on a ship about to sink at sea, he manifested the earth for them so that they might find safety and stability.
When reaching places where water, fire, or wind is required, one should provide whatever is sought.
This may be done by means of transformation or by manifesting it from one's own body.
It is the same with food and medicine.
Sengzhao said:
"When encountering a person adrift at sea, he transforms his body into earth; water, fire, and wind likewise all transform themselves according to what is required by others.
During kalpas of pestilence, he manifests as various medicinal herbs."
Kumārajīva said:
"Some are made to have their illnesses cured, while others are enabled to attain transcendence; through these means, they are transformed and led into the Right Path.
In foreign lands there are wondrous medicinal herbs, some resembling human forms and others resembling the shapes of elephants or horses."
Those resembling elephants or horses may be ridden by people who then soar directly through the void.
Or, merely by seeing or hearing of this medicine, all illnesses are immediately eliminated.
If there are those who ingest it, their diseases are removed and all poisons are neutralized.
In kalpas when famine occurs, he manifests himself as food and drink; first he relieves their hunger and thirst, and subsequently instructs people with the Dharma.
Zhaò said:
"What is there that the Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva cannot become?"
Sometimes he provides medicinal herbs so that those who take them may be cured of their illnesses; sometimes he provides food and drink so that those who are hungry and thirsty may be satisfied.
During kalpas of warfare, he gives rise to loving-kindness and compassion for their sake.
Kumārajīva said:
"In a future kalpa at the end of the age, when weapons arise and the human lifespan is ten years,
Vāsulimitra will descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to be born into a royal family as a crown prince, and he will transform the multitude by saying:"
"Our ancestors lived for an extremely long time.
Because we are now full of anger and lack compassion, our lives have become so short.
Therefore, you all should practice a heart of loving-kindness."
The multitude obeyed these instructions, and their evil intentions gradually diminished.
Thereafter, the children born lived for twenty years; thus it continued in succession until the time of Maitreya, when the lifespan reached eighty-four thousand years.
They transform those sentient beings, causing them to dwell in the ground of non-contention.
Should there be a great battle, they establish it through equal strength; the Bodhisattva manifests majestic power to subdue the conflict and bring about peace and harmony.
Śrī said:

"When two armies face each other, one assists the weaker side; since the two assemblies are now equal, there will be no victory or defeat between them, and thus both sides will be at peace with one another.
Throughout all lands, wherever there are places of hell, I shall immediately go there to strive to rescue those from their suffering."
"In all lands where animals devour one another, he manifests birth among them to bring them benefit.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is like in past ages when people lacked propriety and righteousness, and sought to harm their elders."
Monkeys, elephants, and birds show respect to their elders, causing people to cultivate goodness and live in mutual harmony, as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
He manifests the enjoyment of the five desires while simultaneously practicing dhyāna, thereby confounding the mind of Māra so that he cannot find an opportunity to exploit him.
Zhaò said:

"If one wishes to say they practice dhyāna yet still indulge in the five desires, or if one wishes to say they accept desire yet manifest the practice of dhyāna, their transformations are unfathomable; this is why they cause such confusion."
"A lotus flower blooming within fire may be called rare;
practicing dhyāna while remaining amidst desire is likewise rare.
Zhaò said:
Were it not for one who has brought tranquility and turmoil into a single aim, who could possibly accomplish such a thing?
Sometimes she manifests as a courtesan to attract those with lustful desires; first she draws them in with the hook of passion, and afterwards leads them into the wisdom of the Buddha.
Zhaò said: "On the contrary, they desire to act in accordance with [the Dharma].
Some serve as leaders of a village, others act as guides for merchants; as national preceptors and great ministers, they bring benefit and protection to sentient beings."
For those who are impoverished, I manifest as an inexhaustible treasury; through this, I exhort and guide them, causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
For those whose minds are arrogant, I manifest as a mighty athlete; I subdue all their haughtiness and cause them to abide in the Unsurpassed Way.
Zhaò said:
"A mind of arrogance elevates itself on its own, like a mountain peak that does not retain water.
The Bodhisattva manifests as a wrestler to subdue their haughty mind, and only thereafter moistens it with the water of the Dharma."
To those who are fearful, he stands before them to offer comfort; first bestowing fearlessness upon them, he subsequently causes them to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
Or, manifesting freedom from lustful desire as a seer possessing the five supernatural powers, he guides all living beings, causing them to abide in the precepts, patience, and loving-kindness.
Kumārajīva said:
"In this world, there are no sages or saints; because sentient beings are inferior and base, they cannot enter the profound Dharma, and thus they are transformed through the precepts and patience.
When he sees those who require service, he manifests as their servant; once he has gladdened their hearts, he then awakens them to the aspiration for the Way."
According to whatever they require, they may enter the path of the Buddha; through the power of skillful means, he is able to provide for them all sufficiently—such is the immeasurability of the Way.
Sheng said:
"Adaptation is without fixed method; all of these are the Way of the Buddha.
His conduct is boundless, his wisdom is limitless, and he delivers countless beings."
Even if all Buddhas were to praise his meritorious virtues for countless billions of kalpas, they would still be unable to exhaust them.
Zhaò said:
"The Way of his expedient wisdom is boundless and limitless; even though the sages possess extraordinary eloquence, they still cannot fully describe it."
Who, upon hearing such a Dharma as this, would not resolve to attain Bodhicitta?
Only those unworthy persons, who are ignorant, deluded, and devoid of wisdom, would not.
Zhaò said:
When the inferior person hears the Way, they laugh at it as something grand.
Though the sun and moon are bright, what benefit do they bring to the blind?
(Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Seven)
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Eight, composed by Śramaṇa Sengzhao of the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter Nine:
Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality (8). Chapter Nine: Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
At that time, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
How does a bodhisattva enter the dharma-gate of non-duality?"
Kumārajīva said:
"The alternating use of existence and non-existence is the constant principle of the Buddha-dharma.
Since the preceding chapter spoke of existence, the present one speaks of the gate of emptiness."
Furthermore, from the beginning of this assembly until now, only these two have conversed face-to-face while all others remained silent.
Now, wishing for each to manifest their own virtues, he asks them so that they may speak to the full.

It is also said that emotional delusions differ and the causes for awakening vary; thus, let each person speak of their own awakening so as to extensively explain the various confusions of the multitude.
Now, when a supreme assembly clarifies the fundamental principle, it must take a successful conclusion as its excellence.
Now that this Dharma assembly is about to conclude, if one wishes to investigate its profound significance, a comprehensive exposition of non-duality (*advaya*) alone will exhaust its subtlety.
A question is asked:
"There are also three, four, or even immeasurable Dharma gates; why do you speak only of non-duality?"

Answer: In these two cases, the factors are few and the delusion is shallow; in the other gates, the factors are extensive and the accumulation of afflictions is deep. If even these two should be refuted, the others can be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, the arising of all phenomena must proceed from dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). While the number of conditions for the arising of phenomena varies, at its minimum, they must arise from two conditions.
If there were such a thing as arising from a single condition, I have never heard of it.
Thus, the dependent origination of existence culminates in two factors; once these two factors are discarded, one enters the profound realm.
It is also said that two dharma-gates encompass all dharma-gates. Question:
Why is the "one" not negated?
The answer is:
If one were to name and enumerate it, it would not be a single thing.
If one takes "one" to be one, one has still not departed from duality; once duality is eliminated, this "one" is exhausted.
Furthermore, the "one" that is signless (animitta) is nominally designated yet established in reality.
Since it is established in reality, its essence is severed from all signs; therefore, it is simply set aside and is of itself non-existent.
Zhaò said:
Speech that serves as a standard for the world is called the Dharma; that which all sages follow is called the Gate.
Sheng said:
"Once one has awakened to the One, then all matters are attained; therefore, the One is that by which all matters proceed."
Let each speak according to their own inclination.
Zhaò said:
"Although the teachings elucidated since the inception of this scripture differ, they all pertain to the Way of the Non-characteristic of the Mahāyāna."
The Way of signlessness is the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation; it is the dharma-gate of the non-dual ultimate truth.
This is what was established by Vimalakīrti when manifesting illness, and what was realized by Mañjuśrī when inquiring after his illness.

In all cases where the Path of the Sages is realized, there is nothing that does not proceed from this; thus, it serves as the beginning of all actions and the opening of all discourse, for when one investigates their ultimate destination, they converge upon a single point alone.

However, those who study open their minds according to their own dispositions, and their methods of practice differ: some contemplate arising and ceasing to return to the root; some investigate existence and non-existence to embody the truth; some seek merit and demerit to attain the One; and some examine body and speech to merge with the silent stillness. Although their paths differ, their ultimate convergence is no different.
Because they are not different, he adopts what is common to all people to substantiate the great purport of this sutra.
Daosheng said:
"The reason it is without fixed direction is that its Way enters entirely into non-duality."
Now, let each person speak of this to serve as proof.
In the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmeśvara who said:
"O virtuous ones!..."

Arising and ceasing constitute duality; since phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and thus currently do not cease, to attain this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas.
Sengzhao said:
"Extinction means the extinction of birth.
If one realizes non-birth, what is there to be extinguished?"
This is precisely the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because this bodhisattva attained enlightenment by contemplating arising and ceasing, he spoke of his own understanding as the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The following passages are all similar.
Since the myriad dharmas, as they proliferate, are all termed "dual" when separated from the Truth, they are spoken of in terms of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva De-shou said:
"I" and "mine" constitute a duality. Because there is "I," there is "mine"; if there were no "I," then there would be no "mine. This is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Sengzhao said:
"The wondrous Lord who eternally abides is the 'I' (ātman).
The body and the myriad things are the 'mine' (ātmīya)."
"Mine" refers to that which belongs to a self.
Since phenomena are devoid of self, who is there to possess them?
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said:
Kumārajīva said:
"There are three meanings for 'not blinking': first, being like a celestial being;
second, out of love and reverence for the Buddha's body, gazing upon it with steady, unblinking attention."
The three minds are free from the obscuration of dust, and the eye of wisdom is ever-open.
To accept and not to accept constitute a duality.
Kumārajīva said:
"Accepting" and "not accepting" refer to grasping at signs and not grasping at signs.
Furthermore, the five aggregates with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called "accepting," while those without outflows (*anāsrava*) are called "not accepting.
It is also said to be the "accepting mind" and the "non-accepting mind," as explained in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*.
If a phenomenon is not grasped, it cannot be apprehended; because it cannot be apprehended, there is neither taking up nor discarding.
Kumārajīva said:
"This means to eliminate non-grasping."
"Non-action.
Kumārajīva said:
"This means that one no longer performs karma that leads to rebirth."
"Non-action," Kumārajīva said,
"is the cessation of mental activity."
This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Sengzhao said:
"Where there is a mind, there must be that which is received; where there is that which is received, there must be that which is not received—this constitutes duality."
If one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and does not grasp at either of the two, then there is neither attainment nor practice; this is non-duality.
Bodhisattva Śīlacūḍa said:
"Defilement and purity are two; yet, seeing the true nature of defilement [is non-duality]."
Kumārajīva said:
"It is like washing away filthy things; only when they are completely gone is there purity.
When there is purity, it is total emptiness; when there is total emptiness, there is no 'purity'."
Thus, there is no mark of purity; this accords with the mark of cessation, which constitutes entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Zhaò says:
"Purity arises from defilement, but in the true nature there is no defilement; what, then, would purity purify?"
The Bodhisattva Sunakṣatra said:
"This movement and this thought constitute duality.
Kumārajīva said:
The subtle arising of a deluded mind is called "movement" (dòng); the deep attachment to grasping at signs is called "recollection" (niàn). They differ only in their initial and final stages.
To have no grasping is to dispel sensation.
Zhaò said:
The arousal of emotion constitutes movement, while the conceptualization of "self" constitutes thought.
Where there is no movement, there is no thought; where there is no thought, there is no discrimination.
To penetrate this is to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Fine Eyes said:

"To speak of 'one mark' and 'marklessness' as two is dualistic. If one knows that the single mark is itself marklessness, and does not even grasp at marklessness, thereby entering into equanimity—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Sengzhao said:
"To speak of 'one' is intended to eliminate 'two,' not to assert 'one.
To speak of 'non-being' is intended to eliminate 'being,' not to assert 'non-being.'"
Yet those who are deluded, upon hearing "one," grasp at the mark of one; upon hearing "non-existence," they grasp at the mark of non-existence;
thus, duality arises. The Bodhisattva Subāhu said:
[Kumārajīva] said:
Because of the retribution of his past giving, his hands can produce inexhaustible treasures like the five great rivers; therefore, he is named Subāhu (Wondrous Arm).

The mind of a bodhisattva and the mind of a śrāvaka constitute two. To contemplate that the characteristics of the mind are empty and like an illusion or a transformation—such that there is neither a bodhisattva-mind nor a śrāvaka-mind—is to enter the gate of non-duality.
Puṣya Bodhisattva said:
[Kumārajīva] remarked that this is the name of the lunar mansion Āśleṣā among the twenty-eight mansions.
He was named after the lunar mansion under which he was born.
Zhaoruo stated:
"Puṣya" is the name of a star.
The Bodhisattva was thus named because of this.
"Good" and "not good" constitute a duality.
Kumārajīva said:
All contaminated wholesome minds, as well as wholesome bodily and vocal actions, up to and including the untainted [states] and nirvana, are called "wholesome.
All bodily and vocal actions produced by the afflictions are called "unwholesome."
"If one does not give rise to the wholesome or the unwholesome, but enters the limit of signlessness and attains thorough penetration, this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Lion Bodhisattva said:
"Transgression and merit constitute duality."
Kumārajīva said:
"The afflictions of the three realms, that which is associated with afflictions, and the physical and verbal karma produced by afflictions—all these are termed 'offenses.
All contaminated wholesome [karma] is entirely termed 'merit.'"
"If one penetrates the nature of sin, it is no different from merit; this characteristic is resolved through diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-prajñā*).
Kumārajīva said:
"When a diamond is placed on the ground, it penetrates down to the very limit of the earth before coming to rest."
The wisdom of the true mark must exhaust the nature of phenomena before it finally comes to rest.
Sengzhao says:
"Vajra-wisdom is the wisdom of the true mark."
"To be neither bound nor liberated is to enter the gateway of non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
[Kumārajīva noted: "Śi says:"
When a lion crosses water, it must cut straight across the current; if it moves circuitously, it will not cross.
This Great Being, through his true wisdom, penetrates deeply into all phenomena and proceeds directly to the other shore; therefore, he is named after this.

"Outflowing" (sāsrava) and "outflow-free" (anāsrava) constitute a duality. If one attains the equality of all dharmas, then one does not give rise to the notion of outflow or non-outflow; one does not cling to signs, nor does one dwell in signlessness. This is called entering the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddhivimukti said:

"Conditioned and unconditioned constitute duality. If one is free from all numerical reckoning, the mind is like space; to possess pure wisdom that is without obstruction—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said:
"The mundane and the supramundane constitute a duality.
Kumārajīva said:
The mundane refers to the three realms.
The supramundane refers to all conditioned factors of the path that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
The emptiness of the nature of the mundane is itself the supramundane; within it, one neither enters nor exits.
Kumārajīva said:
"The emergence of meaning arises from entry; because there is no entering into birth and death, there is no transcending the world.
Thus, it does not overflow."
Kumārajīva said:
"In the Sanskrit original, it says 'flow.
It does not disperse."
Sengzhao said:
"Now, where there is entry, there must be exit; where there is exit, there must be overflow; and where there is overflow, there must be dispersal—this is the constant law within the mundane world.
This is what is meant by 'entering the gate of non-duality.'"
The Bodhisattva Bhadramati said:
"Birth-and-death and nirvana constitute a duality.
Kumārajīva said:
The previous mention of "non-action" (wuwei) refers to the three kinds of non-action.
What is clarified here is the ultimate state, which is nirvana.

If one perceives the nature of birth-and-death, then there is neither birth-and-death, nor bondage, nor liberation; it is neither ignited nor extinguished. To understand in this way is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma.
Zhaò said:
"Bondage" (*bā*) and "ignition" (*rán*) are alternative names for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
"liberation" (*jiě*) and "extinction" (*miè*) are different designations for nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*).
Xianjian Bodhisattva said:
"Exhaustion and non-exhaustion are two dharmas; if one reaches ultimate exhaustion...
Kumārajīva said:
Impermanence is the initial gateway to emptiness. When the destruction of phenomena is not yet complete, it is called "inexhaustible.

If one reaches the point where not even a single thought-moment abides, then there is no arising; when there is no arising, arising is exhausted; and when arising is exhausted, there is ultimate emptiness—this is what is meant by "exhaustion."

If that which is not exhausted were all characterized by inexhaustibility, then the characteristic of inexhaustibility would be emptiness; and in emptiness, there is neither the characteristic of exhaustion nor the characteristic of non-exhaustion. To enter in this manner is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
Zhaò said:
Conditioned and deceptive phenomena are called "exhausted" because they are impermanent;
the true mark, which is unconditioned, is called "not exhausted" because it is eternally abiding.
If one regards the exhausted as exhausted and the unexhausted as unexhausted, these are both dualistic dharmas.
If one can awaken to the fact that both the exhausted and the unexhausted are devoid of the characteristic of exhaustion, then one enters the Dharma-door of the single emptiness and non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Pǔshǒu said:
Kumārajīva remarked,
"Because he is sustained by all manner of goodness and protected by all the sages, he is named Pǔshǒu (Universal Guard)."
"Self" and "non-self" constitute a duality. Since even "self" cannot be found, how could "non-self" be found?
Kumārajīva said:
"To falsely perceive a self is [the view of] having a self; when this is understood, there is no self."
To speak of "non-self" is merely to dispel the notion of a self; it does not mean that there is some separate dharma of non-self.
One who perceives the true nature of the self no longer gives rise to duality; this is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Zhaò said: “‘Not-me’ arises from ‘me.
For one who perceives the true nature of the self, the self is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, is ‘not-me’?”
The Bodhisattva Dian Tian said:
"Enlightenment and ignorance constitute a duality; the true nature of ignorance is itself enlightenment.
Kumārajīva said:
Ignorance can give rise to clarity; therefore, it is not different from clarity.
Clarity arises from ignorance; therefore, it is not different from ignorance.
Because of ignorance, it cannot be grasped; because it can give rise to clarity, it cannot be abandoned.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise: because it is not non-ignorance, it cannot be abandoned; because it gives rise to ignorance, it cannot be grasped.
It is like a lotus flower whose color, though pure and beautiful, originates from impurity.
When one investigates its cause, the mind does not give rise to attachment.
Even clarity is not to be grasped; being free from all numerical categories and remaining in equanimity without duality therein—this is called entering the gateway of non-dual dharmas.
Zhaò says:
"Ming" (brightness) refers to the clarity of wisdom;
"wuming" (ignorance) refers to the darkness of delusion.
To see the nature of ignorance is itself clarity.
If one sees clarity as clarity, that is ignorance; therefore, it cannot be grasped.
The Bodhisattva Joyful Vision said:

Form and the emptiness of form constitute two. Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases to exist for there to be emptiness, but rather the very nature of form is itself empty. Likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, along with the emptiness of consciousness, constitute two. Consciousness itself is emptiness; it is not that consciousness ceases to exist for there to be emptiness, but rather the very nature of consciousness is itself empty. To penetrate this thoroughly is to enter the gateway of the non-dual Dharma.
Sengzhao said:
"Form is itself emptiness; it does not become empty only after form has ceased.
Therefore, to perceive form as distinct from emptiness is to bifurcate the characteristics of dharmas."
The Bodhisattva Mingxiang said:
"The four elements are one thing, and the element of space is another; these constitute two.
Kumārajīva said: [This is so.]
In the teachings of the non-Buddhists there are five great elements (mahābhūta), whereas in the Buddha’s Dharma there are four great elements.
These four are called "great" because they are the most significant among all conditioned phenomena.

The four kinds of natures are themselves the nature of emptiness; just as the past limit and the future limit are empty, so too is the middle limit empty. If one can thus know all natures, this is called entering the gateway of non-duality.
Sengzhao said:
"The four kinds refer to the four great elements (mahābhūta).
The 'kind of emptiness' refers to the great element of space (ākāśa-mahābhūta)."
These five are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they are that from which sentient beings arise;
however, the nature of the four great elements has no priority, posteriority, or middle, and they are no different from the element of space.
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣita said: "The eye and forms constitute duality.

If one knows the nature of the eye such that it is without greed, hatred, or delusion toward forms, this is called tranquility (*śānti*). Likewise, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects constitute duality. If one knows the nature of the mind such that it is without greed, hatred, or delusion toward mental objects, this is called tranquility. To abide therein is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma."
Sengzhao said:
"Because they persist within the defilements of the emotions, the three poisons arise.
If one awakens to the nature of the six sense-faculties, then the three poisons will not arise toward the six sense-objects; this is the Way of quiescent extinction."

The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said: "To regard giving and the dedication toward omniscience as two is dualistic; the very nature of giving is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience. Likewise, regarding morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, along with their dedication toward omniscience, as two is dualistic; the very nature of wisdom is itself the nature of dedication toward omniscience. To enter into the single characteristic within these is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas."
Sengzhao said:
To take the six perfections as the wondrous cause and dedicate them toward omniscience is the second [point].
If one awakens to the fact that cause and effect share the same nature and enters into the single characteristic, then one accords with non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Gambhīraprajñā said:

"To regard emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as dual is to divide them; yet emptiness is itself signlessness, and signlessness is itself wishlessness. If emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are realized within a single door of liberation such that there is no longer mind, thought, or consciousness, then this very state constitutes the three doors of liberation. This is the entrance into the Dharma-door of non-duality."
Sengzhao said:
"Although the three modes of practice differ, they are all equally liberation through non-conditioning; therefore, there is no mind, thought, or consciousness.
Since their state of non-conditioning is identical, the three liberations are without distinction."
The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said:
"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha constitute duality.
Śāriputra said:
Where there are marks, there is opposition; where there is opposition, there is duality. This does not apply to the One or the Three.
The Buddha is itself the Dharma.
Sengsheng said:
Taking the realization of the Dharma as the Buddha means that one cannot be separate from the Dharma and yet be a Buddha.
If there is no Buddha apart from the Dharma, then he is the Dharma; thus, the Buddha is also the Dharma.
The Dharma is itself the assembly.
[The interlocutor] said:
"One also takes the realization of the Dharma as the assembly."
These Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Zhaò says:
"The true wisdom that is signless (*animitta*) is the Buddha Jewel."
The true mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is the Jewel of the Dharma.
Cultivating the unconditioned path is the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Although the Three Jewels differ, they all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned.
Jian sheng said:
"To act in contravention of principle is 'conditioned'; therefore, the Three Jewels are all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
They are equal to empty space, and all dharmas are likewise so. One who can follow this practice is said to have entered the gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Anāvaraṇacitta said:
"The body and the cessation of the body constitute two.
Kumārajīva said:
The body consists of the five aggregates of clinging.
The extinction of the body is nirvāṇa.
The body itself is the extinction of the body.

Why is this? One who perceives the true mark of the body does not give rise to the view of a body nor the view of the cessation of the body; for the body and the cessation of the body are non-dual and without distinction. To be neither startled nor afraid within this is what constitutes entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Sengzhao said:

"When all dharmas arise, they arise as empty; when they perish, they perish as empty. What difference is there between the preservation of the body and its death? Why, then, harbor fear and anxiety within this?"
The Bodhisattva Supreme Goodness said: "The actions of body, speech, and mind constitute duality.

These three types of action are all characterized by non-action. The non-active character of the body is the same as the non-active character of speech; the non-active character of speech is the same as the non-active character of the mind. That these three actions are characterized by non-action is the same as all phenomena being characterized by non-action. One who can thus accord with the wisdom of non-action enters the gate of non-duality."
Sengzhao said:
"Although the three karmas differ, non-action (wu zuo) is one and the same.
The arising of all dharmas is rooted in the three karmas; since the three karmas are themselves non-existent, who is it that creates all dharmas?"
The Bodhisattva Fukuden said:
"Meritorious action, demeritorious action, and immovable action constitute duality.
Kumārajīva said:
Wholesome conduct (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) refers to wholesome conduct in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which can obtain the retribution of pleasure.
Unwholesome conduct (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*) refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action, which can obtain the retribution of suffering.
Imperturbable conduct (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*) refers to conduct in the form and formless realms; the meaning of "imperturbability" is as explained in the section on penetrating the Buddha-way.

The true nature of the three types of action is emptiness; emptiness is the absence of meritorious action, non-meritorious action, and immovable action. To not give rise to these three types of action is to enter the gateway of the non-dual Dharma.
Zhaò said:
"Merit refers to wholesome actions within the desire realm;
transgression refers to the category of the ten non-virtuous deeds."
"Immovable" refers to the activities of the realms of form and formlessness.
The Bodhisattva Flower Ornament said:

"To give rise to duality from me constitutes duality; one who perceives my true reality does not give rise to dualistic dharmas. If one does not abide in dualistic dharmas, then there is no consciousness and nothing to be cognized—this is entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas."
Sengzhao said:
"Because of 'self,' there is 'other'; thus the two names arise.
If one perceives the true mark of self, then the consciousness of 'self' and 'other' has no basis to arise."
The Bodhisattva Guṇakośa said:

"To have the mark of something obtainable is duality; if there is nothing obtainable, then there is neither grasping nor abandoning. This absence of grasping and abandoning is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Zhaò said:
"If attainment resides in the self and characteristics reside in the other, and the self does not attain the characteristics, who is there to grasp and who is there to abandon?
Bodhisattva Candrottara said:
Darkness and light constitute a duality; where there is neither darkness nor light, there is no duality.
Why is this? It is like entering the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Śīma said:
"The meaning is that within this, knowing and illumination cease; there is neither light nor darkness.
Where there is neither darkness nor light, all dharmic characteristics are likewise so. To enter into equality therein is what is called entering the gateway of non-duality."
Sengzhao said:

"When those of the Two Vehicles enter the meditative absorption of cessation, their six sense faculties are entirely suspended and their mental conceptions are utterly extinguished; thus, even though days and nights pass, they do not perceive the difference between darkness and light."
This is merely to instruct that the Bodhisattva has no mind regarding light or darkness.
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said:
"To delight in nirvāṇa and not to delight in the world constitutes duality; if one neither delights in nirvāṇa nor feels aversion toward the world, then there is no duality."
Why is this? If there were bondage, there would be liberation; if there were originally no bondage, who would seek liberation?
Where there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither delight nor aversion; this is entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Sengzhao said:
"If there is no bondage in the world, why would one feel weary of it?
If there is no liberation in nirvana, why would one take pleasure in it?"
The Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍarāja said:

"The right path and the wrong path constitute duality. One who abides in the right path does not discriminate between what is wrong and what is right; to be free from these two is to enter the gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva Leshi said:
"Reality and unreality constitute a duality. Even one who perceives reality does not see reality; how much less so one who perceives what is not real? Why is this?"
It is not seen by the fleshly eye; only the wisdom-eye can see it.
Yet this wisdom-eye neither sees nor does not see; this is the entrance into the Dharma-door of non-duality.
Sengzhao said:
"The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the realm of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); it is not that which can be seen by the fleshly eye.
If even the wisdom-eye does not see the real, how much less so that which is not real?"
"Though it is said that there is no seeing, there is nothing that is not seen; this is the essence of the true eye of wisdom.
After each of these bodhisattvas had spoken thus, they asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is the bodhisattva’s entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"In my view, there is no speech regarding any dharma.
Kumārajīva said:
This refers to "crooked eloquence. There is no such thing as "eloquence" [in that sense].
Kumārajīva said:
This is a provisional explanation.
There is no indication [of the ultimate].
Kumārajīva said:
To manifest their characteristics—
declaring "this is good" or "this is evil"— is called "indicating.
