To be without consciousness and free from all questioning and answering is to enter the gate of non-duality.
Zhaò says:

Although the insights of the aforementioned individuals are the same, their respective reasons differ; moreover, they directly expound the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) rather than clarifying the ineffable.

Now, Mañjuśrī synthesizes the teachings of these various schools to open the gate of non-duality (*advaya*), stating directly that the characteristics of dharmas are ineffable, yet he does not apply words to those characteristics themselves.
These words represent the ultimate of speech;
yet even they are still surpassed by profound silence.
Sheng said:
The various bodhisattvas previously each spoke of the meaning of non-duality as if there were some non-duality that could be spoken of.

If there were any non-duality that could be spoken of, it would again be a case of non-duality being established in opposition to duality. Therefore, Mañjuśrī clarifies that the absence of anything that can be spoken of is itself non-duality.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "We have each spoken for ourselves;
now, virtuous one, you should explain what constitutes the bodhisattva’s entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word.
Kumārajīva said:

"It is as if, six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a man who left the household life at the age of sixty; before long, he had completely mastered the Tripiṭaka by means of verse, and subsequently composed treatises on the Tripiṭaka."
Having completed the treatise, he reflected:
"What further matters remain within the Buddha-dharma?
There is only the dharma of meditation; this is what I shall practice."
Thereupon, having received the dharma of the imperial succession, he made this solemn vow:
"If I do not attain the Way and fail to perfect all the merits of meditative concentration, I shall never lie down to sleep, nor shall my side ever touch the ground."
For this reason, he was named the Bhikṣu Pārśva.
In a short time, he attained arhatship, possessing the three insights and the six supernormal powers; he had great eloquence and was skilled in debate.

There was a non-Buddhist teacher named Aśvaghoṣa, who possessed sharp faculties and wisdom; he was thoroughly proficient in all scriptures and possessed great eloquence, capable of refuting all forms of debate.
Having heard the name of the Bhikṣu Vatsa, he led his disciples to where he was and proclaimed:
"All arguments may be refuted by me.
If I cannot refute your discourse, I shall cut off my own head as an apology for my defeat."
When the monk Pārśva heard this discourse, he remained silent and said nothing.
Aśvaghoṣa then conceived arrogance, thinking:
"This man has merely an empty reputation; in reality, he knows nothing."
He departed with his disciples, but while on the road, he reflected upon the matter and said to them:
"This man possesses profound wisdom; I have fallen into defeat."
The disciple asked in wonder,
"How is this so? He replied:
I said, "If all speech can be refuted, that itself is a self-refutation;
if he does not speak, there is nothing to be refuted.
I then returned to his place and said to the Venerable Pārśva:
If I fall into defeat, that would be folly.
A head of folly is not what I require; you may simply cut it off.
If you do not cut it off for me, I shall cut it off myself.
The attendant bhikṣu said:
"I shall not cut off your head; rather, I shall sever your matted hair.
In this world, that will be no different from death."

He immediately shaved his hair and became a disciple of the Venerable Śāriputra; his wisdom and eloquence were peerless in the world, and he extensively composed sūtras and śāstras, greatly propagating the Buddha-dharma.
People of that time called him the Second Buddha.
Although silence and speech differ, their illumination of the fundamental principle is one.
While the realization they have attained is one, their traces manifest in varying degrees of refinement and coarseness.
To speak about the ineffable is not as good as remaining silent about the ineffable; therefore, the discourse of silence is the most subtle of discourses.
Sengzhao said:
To speak about the ineffable is not as good as remaining silent about the ineffable; this is why one remains silent.
The aforementioned Bodhisattvas expressed their words within the characteristics of dharmas; Mañjuśrī spoke of the ineffable within speech; and Vimalakīrti remained silent within the ineffable.

Although these three are identical in their fundamental principle, their manifestations differ in depth and shallowness. Thus, it is truly credible that speech follows upon the ineffable, and knowledge follows upon the unknowable.
Daosheng said:
"Although Mañjuśrī clearly understood that there is nothing that can be said, he had not yet clarified that 'speaking' is itself 'not speaking.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no words to demonstrate that speech is unreal."
"If it is indeed a fruit," he said, "how could one remain silent?
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Even to the point where there are no written characters or spoken words—this is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Zhaò said:
"As for 'silent comprehension,' Mañjuśrī is precisely such a person."
He upheld their words for their sake, which is why they praised him as "good.
Sengsheng said:
"The traces of speech are exhausted in wordlessness; therefore, he was praised as 'good'."

When this "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" was being expounded, five thousand bodhisattvas within this assembly all entered the dharma-gate of non-duality and attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chapter Ten: The Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa (8). Chapter Ten: The Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa. At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The time for the meal is approaching; where will these bodhisattvas eat?"
Kumārajīva said:
"The reason Śāriputra alone conceived this thought has three underlying meanings:
first, the substance of karmic bondage cannot yet exist without material support."
Second, his resolve toward the Great Vehicle was severed, and his delight in the Dharma was not profound;
third, he presumed that others were like himself in having expectations, believing the assembly was likewise.
Since he occupied the position of a senior disciple, it was appropriate that he should provide offerings for the assembly.
Sengzhao said:
"Arranging seats and setting out food is the constant custom for receiving guests; yet, when a host initiates the conversation first while waiting for a guest, it is intended to stimulate discourse.
Śāriputra was the elder of the assembly, and therefore he would frequently initiate the topics of discussion."
Śāriputra said,
"I do not think of him as a disciple because he follows his own method of begging for food.
At that time, Vimalakīrti, knowing his intention, spoke to him, saying:
“The Buddha taught the eight liberations; you, O worthy one, should receive and practice them. How could you listen to the Dharma while being preoccupied with the food of sensual desire?
Kumārajīva replied:
“If one can attain mastery and freedom from obstruction regarding the dharmas before one, then when there is no obstruction, the defiled perceptions ought to be abandoned.”
It is also said that liberation is its function; one detests the body and abandons attachment. To now be preoccupied with food is how deeply contrary this is to the goal.
Zhaò said:
"The Buddha taught the eight liberations; these are the fine delicacies of desirelessness and the supreme nourishment for the Dharma-body."
The Benevolent One received [the teaching] personally, which means he had no desire for much.
Yet, while still harboring thoughts of eating various foods, you wish to listen to the Dharma; how can this not be a manifestation of the emotion of coming to seek [worldly things]?
Sheng said:
"The eight liberations take the contemplation of impurity as their beginning, yet food is an impure thing.
Since one who takes the realization of these eight [liberations] as their core intention, how could they still harbor any desire for food?"
Furthermore, within this Dharma there is no food to be desired; have you not heard that it cannot be attained through the desire for food?
If you so desire food, wait but a moment, and I shall cause you to obtain a food such as has never been experienced before.
Kumārajīva said:
"I do not transform [the food] because I fear it might give rise to suspicions of deceit and falsehood.
I do not provide regular meals because such food is neither pure nor sublime, and thus offers no spiritual benefit."

He wished to enable this assembly to behold the Pure Land and, furthermore, to cause them to attain the resolve for the Great Way through the fragrant food; therefore, he requested a meal from Fragrant Accumulation on account of their need for food.
Daosheng said:
"Ordinary food is the dharma of arising desire; to eliminate desire through food is a meal of the unprecedented."

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered a state of samādhi and, through his supernormal powers, revealed to the great assembly a region above, beyond buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers. There was a land named Saugandhika, where the Buddha was named Gandhottama; he is currently residing there.
The fragrance of that land surpasses the scents of humans and devas in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, being the most supreme of all.
In that realm, there is no mention of the names of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; there are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas, for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma.

That realm is entirely composed of fragrance; its pavilions, walkways, fragrant grounds, groves, and gardens are all fragrant, and the scent of its food circulates throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.

At that time, while that Buddha was sitting together with the bodhisattvas to partake of a meal, there were sons of gods all named Gandhavimāna who had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made offerings to that Buddha and the bodhisattvas.
All those in this great assembly saw it with their own eyes.
Then, Vimalakīrti addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O noble sirs!"
"Who can bring back that Buddha's meal?
Zhaò said:
"Since he has manifested in that land, one should recommend someone of great capability to go and fetch the meal."
By the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, everyone remained silent.
Zhaò said:
"Mañjuśrī was about to manifest the virtue of Vimalakīrti; therefore, by means of his spiritual power, he caused the entire assembly to remain silent."
Vimalakīrti said:
"O virtuous one, this great assembly will surely find this shameful.
Zhaò said:
"Exertion is for those who have not yet achieved [realization]. Mañjuśrī said,
"As the Buddha has spoken, do not disparage those who have not yet studied."
Zhaò said: "To 'advance' means to begin one's study.

Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested before the assembly as a bodhisattva, his physical marks, radiance, and majestic virtue so preeminent that they eclipsed the entire gathering. He then addressed them, saying:

"Go to the region above, passing through as many buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers; there is a land named Saṃghagandha where the Buddha is named Gandhottama, who is currently sitting together with various bodhisattvas to partake of a meal."
Go there and, speaking on my behalf, say:

"Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One; he pays you boundless respects and inquires after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness or affliction, and whether your strength and vigor are secure."
Kumārajīva said:
"By not saying 'non-existent' but rather 'few,' he clarifies that the body is the root of illness; as such, the root ought to be abandoned.
Sengzhao said:
To demonstrate that those who possess a physical body cannot be free from affliction, he addressed the Tathāgata, asking whether he was still free from illness and distress.
He further requested the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal, intending to perform Buddha-work within the Sahā world.
Kumārajīva said:
"Buddha-activity refers to the transformation of sentient beings;
it means causing those who delight in inferior dharmas [to turn toward the Great Vehicle]."
An alternative version reads "those whose delight is slight. Kumārajīva said:
"Those whose delight does not surpass that of the distant [path] are all termed 'small,' not merely those of the Hīnayāna.
By attaining the vast Great Way, one also causes the fame and reputation of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere."
Kumārajīva said:
"I wish to cause those who hear this and believe it to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
These three matters are the intent behind my request for a meal."
Zhaò said:
"Yú" (yet) is a word of humble deference.
In that land, they access the Great Way by means of incense.
Because the sentient beings of this land are narrow-minded and inferior in their aspirations, he requested the remainder of the fragrant food in order to propagate the Buddha’s work.
At that time, the manifested Bodhisattva ascended to the upper regions before the assembly; the entire multitude saw him go to the Land of Many Fragrances and prostrate at the feet of that Buddha.
Furthermore, he heard these words:
"Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and pays him boundless respect.
He inquires after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your physical strength is secure."

I pray that I may obtain the remnants of the World-Honored One’s meal, desiring to perform Buddha-work within the Sahā world, so that those who delight in inferior teachings may attain the Great Way, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata may be heard everywhere.
When those great beings saw the manifested bodhisattva, they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming:
"From where has this superior person come?
Where is the Sahā world located?"
"What is meant by 'those who delight in inferior teachings'?
He then asked the Buddha.
Sengzhao said:
Those great beings have all attained supernormal powers, yet these do not always manifest before them.
Furthermore, since that land is purely Mahāyāna and the name of those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle is never heard there, this question has arisen.
The Buddha told him:
"Below this world, past as many buddha-fields as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni; he is currently present there."
In this world of the five turbidities, I expound the teachings of the Way for the sake of sentient beings who delight in inferior dharmas.

There is a bodhisattva there named Vimalakīrti, who dwells in the inconceivable liberation and preaches the Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas; therefore, he has dispatched a transformation body to come here to extol my name and praise this land, so as to cause those bodhisattvas to further increase their merit and virtue.
That bodhisattva asked:
"What kind of person is it that can manifest such transformations, possessing such power of merit, fearlessness, and supernormal powers?
The Buddha said:
It was exceedingly great.
He dispatched emanations to all the ten directions to perform buddha-work and benefit sentient beings.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa filled a bowl of various fragrances with fragrant food and gave it to the emanated bodhisattva.
Then those nine million bodhisattvas spoke with one voice, saying:
"We wish to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and we also wish to see Vimalakīrti and the assembly of other bodhisattvas."
Zhaò said:
"Having heard that Buddha praise the merits of this Buddha’s bodhisattvas, he wishes to likewise extol their merits.
The Buddha said:
"You may go.
However, restrain the fragrance of your body so as not to cause those sentient beings to give rise to thoughts of delusion or attachment.
Kumārajīva said:
Extreme anger leads to madness, and excessive joy likewise causes delusion; you should restrain yourself from fragrances to prevent these causes of confusion.
A question is asked:
"If that is so, why do you not refrain from fragrant food?"
The answer is:
It is by the Buddha’s spiritual power that he can block the source of their delusions and inspire the aspiration for the Way; therefore, he does not restrain them.
Furthermore, you must discard your original form so as not to cause those in that land who seek to become bodhisattvas to feel self-contempt or shame.
Kumārajīva said: "When shame is profound, one falls; when remorse is slight, one is still troubled. When these two afflictions arrive together, one's distance from the Way becomes ever more remote.
The former statement concerns deluded attachment; this statement concerns vulgar shame. These two texts mutually clarify each other; thus, I have summarized their meaning."
Furthermore, you should not harbor thoughts of contempt or create obstacles regarding them. Why is this?
Because all lands in the ten directions are like empty space.
Furthermore, because the Buddhas wish to transform those who delight in inferior teachings, they do not manifest their pure lands in their entirety.

At that time, having accepted the alms-bowl of food, the transformed Bodhisattva, together with nine million other Bodhisattvas, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and the strength of Vimalakīrti, suddenly vanished from that world and, in an instant, arrived at the house of Vimalakīrti.
At that time, Vimalakīrti immediately manifested nine million lion thrones, as magnificent and exquisite as those before, and all the bodhisattvas sat upon them.
The manifested bodhisattva offered a bowl filled with fragrant food to Vimalakīrti; the fragrance of the food permeated the city of Vaiśālī and the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, the brahmins and laypeople of Vaiśālī, upon smelling this fragrance, felt their bodies and minds become refreshed and joyful, exclaiming that it was something unprecedented.
Zhaò said:
"As the extraordinary fragrance entered their bodies, their physical and mental faculties were filled with serenity and delight."
Thereupon, the elder Candracchattra, accompanied by eighty-four thousand people, entered the house of Vimalakīrti.
Kumārajīva said:
"In that land there is no king; rather, five hundred householders collectively administer the affairs of state."
Now, regarding the term "ruler," he was one esteemed by the multitude.
Zhaò said:
"In the kingdom of Vaiśālī there was no sovereign king; rather, five hundred elders collectively administered the affairs of state."
Candracchattra was highly esteemed by the multitude, and thus he was called the Leader.
From this point downward, all gathered only after having smelled the fragrance.

Seeing that there were many Bodhisattvas within the hall and that the various lion thrones were lofty, vast, and magnificent, they were all filled with great joy; they paid homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the great disciples, then withdrew to stand to one side.
The earth deities, the deities of the void, and the various devas of the desire and form realms, having smelled this fragrance, also all came into Vimalakīrti’s house.
Then Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas:
"Venerable sirs, you may eat this food of the Tathāgata’s ambrosial flavor."
Sheng said:
"Because he previously harbored such thoughts, I taught him to eat.
I also wished to use this as a means to clarify that eating is a matter of principle, and that Nirvana is the Dharma of ambrosia."
Furthermore, those who eat this food will surely obtain it; thus, there is the flavor of ambrosia within the rice.
It is permeated by great compassion.
Kumārajīva said:

There are three meanings of "perfuming" (xūn): first, the fruition of great compassion; second, that which is contemplated by the mind of compassion; and third, viewing others with eyes of loving-kindness. Master Sheng said:
"To cause people to attain awakening constitutes external perfuming; how could it be said that food possesses the power of great compassion?"
"Thus, the rice as a substance is permeated by great compassion.
Do not limit your intention when eating it, lest it fail to be digested.
Śīkṣānanda said:
Upon eating this rice, one should resolve upon the Great Mind and establish great deeds; this is called repaying kindness, and repaying kindness is what is meant by "digesting.
Zhaò says:
This first demonstrates the method for receiving food.
This rice is the fruit of great compassion; it is prepared by a compassionate mind and produced by a compassionate heart, and is therefore called "perfumed by great compassion.
If one eats it with a limited or narrow-minded intention, it cannot be digested.

If one knows that this food is produced by great compassion and is inconceivable, and partakes of it while generating the mind of enlightenment, then one will digest it and repay the kindness of the donor with a boundless and unobstructed heart.
Dongsheng said:
"If food were produced from great compassion, it would be limitless.
To say that it is limited and insufficient is to fail to digest it."
A certain śrāvaka thought, "This food is insufficient for this great assembly, each of whom must eat.
Zhaò said:
"This inconceivable food is beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, he gave rise to such a thought."
The manifested bodhisattva said:
"Do not attempt to measure the immeasurable merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata with the minor virtues and limited knowledge of a śrāvaka.
Zhaò said:
Immeasurable merit and wisdom are the causes of this fragrant food.
Now, where there is an immeasurable cause, there must necessarily be an immeasurable fruit;
if the cause were measurable, the fruit would likewise be measurable.
The Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit and wisdom—how could they be measured by the limited intellect of a śrāvaka?
The four seas may run dry, but this food is inexhaustible.
Even if all people were to eat portions as large as Mount Sumeru for as long as an eon, it still could not be exhausted.

Why is this? Because the leftovers from the meal of one who is fully endowed with the merits of inexhaustible precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation can never be exhausted.
Sengzhao said:
"The Tathāgata possesses the inexhaustible merits of the fivefold Dharma-body; how could the food of retribution and response ever be exhausted?
Thereupon, the food in the bowl satisfied the entire assembly, yet it was still not depleted."
Those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans who eat this food experience physical tranquility and happiness, just like the bodhisattvas in the land Adorned with All Joy.
Furthermore, a wondrous fragrance issued from all his pores, just like the scent of the trees in the land of Saṃghagandha.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas from the Fragrant Accumulation:
"With what teaching does the Tathāgata Sugandhakūṭa expound the Dharma?"
That bodhisattva said:
"In the land of my Tathāgata, there is no teaching through words; rather, it is by means of various fragrances that all devas and humans are led to enter into the practice of discipline.
Kumārajīva said:
This is cited to illustrate their abundance.

As for the aforementioned "preaching the Dharma," it does not necessarily involve verbal discourse; rather, by means of the "Teaching of the Causal Basis" (Tongjiao), its efficacy is identical to that of preaching.
Zhaor said:
That land is not entirely without speech; it simply takes fragrance as the fundamental means for attaining the Way.
Just as this country uses speech to attain the Way, there are likewise those who achieve awakening through spiritual transformations.
Each of the bodhisattvas sat beneath a fragrant tree; upon smelling this wondrous fragrance, they immediately attained the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
Having attained this samādhi, all the merits possessed by the bodhisattvas became fully perfected.
Zhaò said:
"The power of this samādhi can produce all manner of meritorious virtues.
Those bodhisattvas then questioned Vimalakīrti:
"What Dharma does the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha preach now?
Vimalakīrti replied, "The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, the Buddha preaches words of firm severity to subdue them."
Kumārajīva said:
"When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there are three essential modes:
first, gentle and kind speech; second, harsh and forceful speech; and third, mixed discourse."
Virtuous conduct leads to pleasant fruits; this is gentle and kind speech.
Evil conduct leads to bitter fruits; this is harsh and rigid speech.
Praising the good and censuring the evil constitutes mixed discourse.
Zhaò said: "How constant can the transformation of the Sage be?
It merely responds according to the nature of things."
This land is of a stubborn and violent nature; therefore, he responds with a teaching of stern severity, declaring:
"This is hell; this is the realm of animals; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; these are the places of various perils."
Zhaò says:
This refers to the eight states of hardship,
which are the places where ignorant people are born.
Sengzhao said: "The heterodox paths and divergent teachings are the birthplaces of ignorant people.

This is bodily misconduct and this is the retribution for bodily misconduct; this is verbal misconduct and this is the retribution for verbal misconduct; this is mental misconduct and this is the retribution for mental misconduct. This is killing and this is the retribution for killing; this is taking what is not given and this is the retribution for taking what is not given; this is sexual misconduct and this is the retribution for sexual misconduct; this is false speech and this is the retribution for false speech; this is divisive speech and this is the retribution for divisive speech; this is harsh speech and this is the retribution for harsh speech; this is idle chatter and this is the retribution for idle chatter."
Kumārajīva said:

"The Sanskrit text says 'miscellaneous discourse' (miśrakavyākaraṇa). Generally, any mental, verbal, or physical action that is not directed toward goodness or nirvana is termed 'miscellaneous discourse.'"

Sengzhao said: "Flowery adornments and beautiful words that merely seek to please the human mind are called 'names without meaning. These are greed and jealousy, and these are the retribution for greed and jealousy;

these are anger and vexation, and these are the retribution for anger and vexation; these are wrong views, and these are the retribution for wrong views; these are stinginess and parsimony, and these are the retribution for stinginess and parsimony; these are the breaking of precepts, and these are the retribution for breaking precepts; these are malice, and these are the retribution for malice; these are laziness, and these are the retribution for laziness; these are distracted minds, and these are the retribution for distracted minds; these are folly and delusion, and these are the retribution for folly and delusion; these are the establishment of precepts, these are the upholding of precepts, and these are the violating of precepts."
Zhaò said: As stated in the Vinaya-piṭaka:
"This is what should be done; this is what should not be done. This is an obstruction; this is not an obstruction."
Sengzhao said:
"Among those who violate the precepts, there are those whose offenses are grave yet do not obstruct the Path, and those whose offenses are minor yet do obstruct the Path.
Furthermore, there are three obstructions: the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*)."

This is transgression, this is freedom from transgression; this is purity, this is defilement; this is with outflows, this is without outflows; this is the false path, this is the true path; this is conditioned, this is unconditioned; this is the mundane world, this is nirvana.
Because the minds of those who are difficult to transform are like monkeys, one must employ various methods and regulations to control their hearts; only then can they be tamed.
Zhaò said:
Because they are so difficult to transform, he demonstrates that such are the consequences of sin and merit.
For example, if an elephant or horse is stubborn and untamable, it must be subjected to various forms of pain and torment—even to the point of piercing the bone—before it can be subdued.

Kumārajīva said: "There are five types of horses: the first is subdued immediately upon seeing the shadow of the whip; the second is subdued when it receives the lash; the third is subdued when pricked by a sharp awl through the skin; the fourth is subdued when the flesh is pierced; and the fifth is subdued only when the bone is penetrated."
The faculties of sentient beings—whether sharp or dull—are also of five grades: the first type attains awakening upon merely seeing the impermanence of others;
the second attains awakening upon seeing the impermanence of their acquaintances;
the third attains awakening upon seeing the impermanence of their brothers, sisters, and relatives.
Fourth, one awakens to the truth when seeing that one's parents are impermanent;
fifth, one awakens only after realizing that one's own body is impermanent and undergoing extreme suffering, further compounded by harsh words.
Thus, because sentient beings are so stubborn and difficult to transform, they can only be brought into the discipline through words of universal severity and urgency.
Zhaò said:
"Without hooks and whips, one cannot tame elephants and horses; without harsh words, one cannot subdue those who are difficult to transform."
When those bodhisattvas heard this teaching, they all said:
"It is unprecedented!
How is it that the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, conceals his immeasurable power of mastery and instead delivers sentient beings through the Dharma that accords with their poverty?"
Kumārajīva said:

"He concealed his traces and let his brilliance remain hidden, identifying himself with a poor beggar; by identifying himself with a poor beggar, he associated with them, and through association, it became easy for him to be their neighbor; thus, he was trusted and cherished by the poor."
Sengzhao said:

"The Buddhas are equal, yet their manifestations differ; this arises because sentient beings are inferior and their aspirations are narrow. Therefore, the Buddha conceals his sovereign power to conform to their poverty and meanness, delivering them according to what they delight in. His responsive manifestations are boundless, encompassing neither the pure nor the defiled—this is truly unprecedented."
"These bodhisattvas are also capable of diligent humility; they have come to this buddha-field out of immeasurable great compassion.
Vimalakīrti said, "The firmness of the great compassion these bodhisattvas feel toward all sentient beings is exactly as you have said."
Sengzhao said:
This fulfills what was praised.
Indeed, his benefit to sentient beings during a single lifetime exceeds that of practicing for hundreds of thousands of kalpas in those other lands.
Kumārajīva said:

"It is like a skilled physician who, encountering an age of pestilence, widely practices his medical arts and dispenses many medicines; those he treats are numerous, and the offerings he receives are immeasurable."

It is likewise with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in an impure land: as evils proliferate all the more, his universal salvation becomes even more vast; through the ten dharmic medicines he extensively treats the myriad ailments of beings, and his transformation is so broad and benefit so profound that it transcends ten thousand kalpas in a single leap.
Zhaò said:
"Practice does not depend on duration; what is valued is its benefit. Why is this so?"
In this Sahā world there are ten virtuous dharmas that do not exist in other pure lands. What are these ten? They are: gathering in the poor through giving;

gathering in those who violate the precepts through pure morality; gathering in the wrathful through patience; gathering in the indolent through diligence; gathering in those with distracted minds through meditative concentration; and gathering in the ignorant through wisdom.
Kumārajīva said:
"There are two kinds of delusion: first, delusion regarding all phenomena; second, the inability to clearly comprehend the profound Dharma of the Buddhas.
In impure lands, there are both types of delusion; in pure lands, there is only the delusion of not understanding the Buddha-Dharma."

To preach the methods for removing obstacles and deliver those in the eight difficult states; to deliver those who delight in the Hīnayāna by means of the Mahāyāna; to rescue those without merit by means of all roots of goodness; and to constantly bring sentient beings to fulfillment through the four means of integration—these constitute the ten.
Sengzhao said:

"Virtue arises from evil, and purity increases through impurity. Since this land possesses all ten unwholesome dharmas, the ten virtues flourish there. In that land, however, everything is purely wholesome;
thus, there is no ground for the cultivation of virtue. This is why practicing for hundreds of thousands of kalpas does not equal a single lifetime here."
Another version reads "ten unwholesome karmas. Kumārajīva said:

"The ten unwholesome karmas have superior, middling, and inferior degrees; the superior result is retribution in hell, the middling is retribution as an animal, and the inferior is retribution as a hungry ghost."
Within each grade there are further three grades; thus, these nine grades of unwholesome karma result in the experience of nine grades of suffering retribution within the three evil realms.
That Bodhisattva asked:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas does a Bodhisattva act without blemish in this world and be born in a pure land?"
Kumārajīva said:
"Bodhisattvas of profound practice are not objects of doubt.
However, those of shallow practice dwell in impure lands; fearing that their conduct is shallow and their merit slight, they may yet be unable to extricate themselves."

It is like pouring a small amount of hot water into a great body of water; or like a person of little strength entering the water to rescue someone drowning—if they cannot save both, they will sink along with the other.
Therefore, he asked by what dharma one may attain birth in a Pure Land.
Sengzhao said:
"He posed this question in order to exhort the novice Bodhisattvas of this land to be born in a Pure Land."
Vimalakīrti said:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they will act without blemish in this world and be born in a pure land.
What are these eight?"

To benefit sentient beings without expecting a reward, to undergo all manner of suffering and affliction on behalf of all sentient beings, and to bestow all the merit one has created entirely upon them.
Sengzhao says:
"To undergo suffering on their behalf while not regarding one's own person, and to give away all one's merit to sentient beings—how could one harbor thoughts of reward for such benefit?"
If I were not for the sake of sentient beings, I should have long since entered nirvana.
It is to endure suffering on their behalf so that they may be delivered first; while they depart, I remain—how can this not be called substitution?
This is the ultimate form of benefit, which is a single Dharma:
to regard all sentient beings with an impartial mind, being humble and without obstruction.
Zhaò said:

To treat enemies and kin without distinction, to humble oneself and honor others, to maintain an impartial mind toward both the noble and the lowly, and to have no sense of personal boundary—these are the two dharmas.
To regard all bodhisattvas as if they were Buddhas.
Sengzhao said:
"The Bodhisattva is the bridge for sentient beings and the link to the Triple Gem; to regard them as equal to the Buddha increases one's own merit—this is the third dharma."
When hearing a sutra never heard before, one hears it without doubt.
Zhaò said:
"To hear a sutra spoken by the Buddha and then believe and accept it, without giving rise to doubt or confusion because it was previously unheard—this is the fourth dharma."
It does not conflict with the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Zhaò says:
"Although the three vehicles differ, their ultimate aim is not distinct; they do not conflict with one another regardless of being small or great—this is the fifth dharma."
"Do not envy the offerings given to others.
Kumārajīva said:

"If one examines the cause by which those offerings are received, it stems from past deeds (*pūrvakṛta*). Envy is of no benefit; rather, one should cultivate goodness. By settling the mind through principle, envy will not arise."
Do not be conceited regarding one's own benefit.
Kumārajīva said:
"When you cultivate goodness, maintain the precepts, and receive offerings and sustenance, you should reflect within yourself, saying:"
The merit of that offering does not belong to a self.
Even if a self were to exist, it would not perceive it as its own.
Since there is logically no self, the offering ultimately has no master.
When one reflects in this way, the haughty mind naturally subsides;
therein, one tames that mind.
Kumārajīva said:
Thereupon, regarding those two matters of providing for oneself and benefiting others, one self-subdues the mind; this subduing of the mind is as previously explained.
These three phrases are combined into a single matter.
Zhaò said:
Others sow and others reap; why be envious?
One sows for oneself and reaps for oneself; why be conceited?
To skillfully discipline oneself regarding these two matters is the sixth dharma.
"Constantly examine one's own faults and do not dispute the shortcomings of others.
Kumārajīva said:
"It was as if a bhikṣu were sitting in meditation in a forest."
When the time came for food, he took his alms bowl and left the forest; on the road, he encountered a band of evil robbers.
The robbers drew their bows and shot at him, yet the bhikṣu pardoned them and reproached himself, giving rise to no ill will.
He then pointed to his belly and said to the thief:
"You should shoot this.
Because my belly emerged from the forest, I have incurred this affliction; it is the fault of this belly alone."
To examine oneself and extend sympathy to others is generally like this:
do not dispute the shortcomings of others, for it is no better than a person of dull faculties who, prostrating on the ground, licks filth while seeking out the faults of others.
Examining one's own faults and even seeking out all merits constitute a single matter.
Zhaò says:
"To examine one's own faults, the faults naturally dissolve; to dispute another's shortcomings, those shortcomings reside in oneself—this is the seventh method."
Constantly seeking all merits with a single mind—
this is the eighth. Zhaò said:
Defilements increase easily, while merits are difficult to fulfill; unless one seeks with single-minded devotion, success cannot be achieved.
By possessing these eight dharmas, one’s practice will be free from blemish, and one shall ultimately be born in the Pure Land.

When Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī expounded this Dharma amidst the great assembly, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, as the Buddha was preaching the Dharma in the Āmra Grove, the ground suddenly became vast and magnificently adorned, and the entire assembly turned the color of gold.
Zhaò said:
"The Perfected Person has no fixed abode; the realization of principle is immediate.

Although the Tathāgata and Vimalakīrti differ in their attire and dwellings, they both possess the wondrous existence that enables them to come and go to transform beings, together propagating the inconceivable Way."
I have sent someone to inquire after his illness; his realization is as sublime as that of the Buddhas above.
Now, as he is about to go to the Tathāgata to seal this scripture, he has first manifested these auspicious signs to open the minds of the multitude.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions has this auspicious response appeared, such that this place has suddenly become vast and magnificent, and all those in the assembly have turned the color of gold?”
Zhaò said:
"The deeds of a Mahāsattva are not within the reach of those on the Lesser Path; therefore, he inquired about their causal conditions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
As Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī, together with the great assembly, were respectfully surrounding them and intending to depart, they first manifested this auspicious omen.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī,
"We may go together to see the Buddha."
Kumārajīva said:
"Vimalakīrti’s exhortation for us all to see the Buddha has a clear purpose that can be discerned.
First, it was to witness his sincere heart and to fulfill his original intention."
Second, he wished to have them witness and verify that the fragrant rice had brought about great awakening.
Third, as they were harboring the intention to travel far away, it was fitting that they return with the truth.
Therefore, he desired for them to go together to the Buddha’s dwelling to inquire about and receive the Bequeathed Dharma.
Together with the various bodhisattvas, they paid homage, served, and made offerings to him. Mañjuśrī said:
"Excellent! Go forth!"
"Now is precisely the right time.
Zhaoruo said:
"It is a time when there is benefit."

Vimalakīrti then, by means of his supernatural power, took the entire great assembly along with the lion-thrones and placed them upon his right palm; he proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, and having arrived, set them down upon the ground.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the world, when welcoming or seeing off [guests], one must employ teams of four horses and light cavalry;
but when a Mahāsattva welcomes or sees another off, he employs wondrous penetration."
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood to one side with palms joined in single-minded devotion.
Zhaò said:
"Vimalakīrti placed his seat upon the ground, intending first to pay his respects."
Those bodhisattvas immediately all vacated their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him seven times, standing to one side.
The great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, and others likewise all vacated their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having comforted the bodhisattvas in accordance with the Dharma, instructed each of them to return to their seats.
They all complied with his instruction.
Once the assembly was settled, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Do you see the deeds performed by the sovereign spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
Kumārajīva replied,
"I wish to extol the miraculous wonders of the Mahāsattva in order to rouse those with narrow and inferior thoughts."
"Yes, indeed, I have seen it.
What do you think,
World-Honored One?"
I observe that his actions are inconceivable, beyond what the mind can conceive and beyond what measurement can fathom.
Zhaò said:

"Just now, I entered the Inconceivable Chamber together with Mañjuśrī; there, I borrowed a precious seat and witnessed his supernatural powers, and moreover, partook of fragrant food before returning on his palm. As no one could fathom these transformations, I have ceased all attempts to conceptualize them."
Since the great purport of this sutra elucidates the inconceivable Way, it frequently manifests inconceivable traces.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The fragrance we have now smelled is unlike anything from the past; what kind of incense is this?
Kumārajīva replied.
[The questioner] asked:
This superior fragrance pervades the three thousandfold world-system; why, Ānanda, did you not perceive it before?
He replied:
"Because it was beyond my capacity, I was near yet did not hear it; now, by means of this [attainment], I am able to hear it."
Zhaò said:
The Tathāgata was about to explain the causal conditions of the fragrant food, and thus he caused Ānanda to hear it.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"This is the fragrance from the pores of that bodhisattva.
Zhaò said:
"That bodhisattva is a bodhisattva from the Land of Universal Fragrance."
The reason he spoke specifically of "that" [the Buddha] was to enable Śāriputra to personally manifest the fragrance of his single meal, thereby clarifying the great benefit of the fragrant food.
Thereupon, Śāriputra said to Ānanda:
"This fragrance also issues from our pores."
Ānanda asked:
"From where has this come?
He replied:
This elder Vimalakīrti took the remains of the Buddha’s meal from the Land of Universal Fragrance to his house; those who ate it all had their pores emit such fragrance as this.
Ānanda asked Vimalakīrti:
"For how long will this fragrance remain?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"When this food has been digested.
He asked:
"How long will it take for this food to be digested?
He replied, "The potency of this food lasts for seven days; only after that will it be digested."
Kumārajīva said:
"It will be digested after seven days for two reasons.

First, there may be someone who eats the fragrant rice, but because the food does not digest in a timely manner, their mind would surely become weary and renounce it; therefore, he did not allow it to last longer."
It is also said that when one destined to attain the Way inhales the fragrance of the food, they will certainly achieve the Holy Way within no more than seven days.

This is because, as in the case of the "seven births" for those on the path of progress (*srotāpanna*), or the snake bitten by a "seven-step" serpent, the force of such conditions does not exceed seven.
The matter need not be prolonged; therefore, it does not exceed seven days.
Zhaò says:
"The power of the seven days is exhausted; this is the constant efficacy of the *bāṣpa* (rice-gruel)."
"If one must rely on food as a condition for the path, it will only be digested after one has attained what ought to be attained.
Sengsheng said:
"It will not exceed seven days."
Furthermore, Ānanda!
If a śrāvaka who has not yet entered the stage of certainty eats this food, it will be digested only after they have entered that stage.
Zhaò said:
Entering the realm of outflowlessness is called entering the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Those who have already entered the stage of correctness and eat this food will attain liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*), after which it will be digested.
Kumārajīva said:
This refers to the sixteen moments of mind in the realization of the Truths (*satyābhisamaya*). Question:
How can one attain the Way by eating fragrant food?
The answer is:
With his body composed and mind tranquil, he gave rise to an unprecedented resolve.
If even his meal was like this, how much more so must it be for the Way?
Since there is this wondrous fruit, there must necessarily be a wondrous cause.

When one possesses supreme faith and joy and penetrates deeply into cause and effect, one immediately understands dependent origination; by understanding dependent origination, one perceives the true Dharma.
Sengzhao said:
"One who has attained the fruit of non-attachment is called one whose mind is liberated.
If one who has not yet resolved to attain the Mahāyāna eats this food, it will only be digested once that resolve has been generated."
Those who have already resolved their minds and eat this food will attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), after which it will be digested.

Those who have already attained the patience of non-arising and eat this food will reach the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), after which it will be digested.
Dongsheng said:
"Within seven days you will certainly attain something.
However, the awakening from a single meal cannot involve two stages of progress."
Regarding those who abide in the stage of being "born once more to attain Buddhahood," it is because a Buddha cannot be attained through external causes.
How could Bodhisattvas who have reached the stage of non-arising, or those established in the correct position, ever need to rely on external factors to advance?
That it is described in this way now is to clarify that this meal represents the ultimate expression of principle, for its significance is fully complete therein.
It is like a medicine named "Supreme Flavor" (Agryarasa): whoever consumes it finds all the poisons in their body extinguished before the medicine itself is digested.
"This rice is likewise; it is only after all the poisons of the afflictions have been eliminated that it is digested.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "This is unprecedented!"
"World-Honored One!
This fragrant meal is able to perform the work of a Buddha.
Kumārajīva said:
To manifest transformations through the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is the constant way of transformation.
That food, which originally served only to sustain the body, has now led to the attainment of the Way; therefore, he marveled at this as something unprecedented.
The Buddha takes the transformation of beings as his primary task; indeed, all such transformations are termed "Buddha-works" (*buddhakārya*).
Because Ānanda believed that the wondrousness of the Buddha’s works reached its ultimate limit here, the text subsequently explains the Buddha-works extensively in order to broaden his perspective.
Zhaò said:
"The original purpose of eating is to sustain the body so as to eliminate fetters; I have never heard of or seen [any teaching] to the contrary.
Shēng said:
The Buddha takes awakening through appropriate means as his task, yet that this could be accomplished by fragrant food is something unprecedented.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is."
"Ānanda! There are some buddha-fields that perform the work of a buddha by means of the Buddha’s radiance.
Zhaò said:

Ānanda prepared the fragrant meal for the benefit [of all], signifying that the principles of the Buddha’s work reach their ultimate point therein; thus he extensively demonstrates this matter to lead others to realize that the path of the Buddha is boundless.

The sentient beings of this land see the Buddha’s wondrous light enter the discipline of the Path for themselves, which also brings other benefits; however, the light is the primary factor, and all subsequent cases are similar to this.
There are instances where various bodhisattvas perform the work of a Buddha.
Kumārajīva said:
"The Buddha simply abides in the fundamental stillness and silence, commanding the Bodhisattvas to propagate the Way in order to transform humanity.
Sengzhao said:
There are Buddhas who dwell in the fundamental state in silence, taking Bodhisattvas as their primary agents of transformation.
There are also those who perform the Buddha-work by means of persons transformed by the Buddha.
Zhaò says:
There are those who perform Buddha-work solely through transformation, such as the case of Śūṣānta;
there are those who perform Buddha-work by means of the Bodhi tree.
Kumārajīva said:
Some emit flowers and fruits; some produce famous incenses; some radiate light; and some preach the Dharma. Zhaò said:

"The Buddha attained enlightenment beneath this tree, which is named Bodhi. The light of this tree illuminates everything it reaches, and its fragrance permeates all that it scents. Its form and color are subtle and wondrous, appearing according to the inclinations of those who behold it."
The trees emit the sounds of the Dharma, which are heard according to the inclinations of beings.
These are the trees of the Tathāgata’s retribution; those sentient beings who encounter them naturally awaken to the Way. In this land, the trees serve as the very foundation of transformation.
There were those who performed the work of a Buddha by means of the Buddha’s robes and bedding.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the past, the King of Jambudvīpa obtained the Great Robe of the Buddha."

Sengzhao says:

Not exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is the aspiration to seek the principle while not abandoning the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); taking compassion as its foundation, it is thus elucidated at the outset.
