Kumārajīva said:
Leaving the household life, abandoning desire, as well as meditative concentration and wisdom, and being free from all delusive thoughts—all these are termed the joy of seclusion.
To seek the Way through such means is not what is truly esteemed.
Sengzhao said:
"How can the way of solitary self-cultivation be considered worthy of esteem?
One does not cling to one's own joy, but instead rejoices in the joy of others."
Another version states: "Not clinging to one's own happiness, but rejoicing in the happiness of others. Kumārajīva said:

"Ordinary people feel envy when they see the happiness of others and find peace of mind when others suffer; they feel attachment when they themselves are happy and feel agitation when they themselves suffer."
The Bodhisattva is not like this: seeing the happiness of others, he feels no envy, but rejoices in his heart;
seeing the suffering of others, he is moved by compassion, desiring to bring them liberation;
he does not cling to his own happiness, and he remains at peace even in his own suffering.
Regarding the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), he conceived of them as being like hell.
Kumārajīva said:
"There are three kinds of meditative concentration: first, that of the Mahāyāna; second, that of the Hīnayāna; and third, that of ordinary beings."
The dhyāna of ordinary beings gives rise to arrogance and a sense of self.

The dhyāna of the Lesser Vehicle seeks realization for oneself alone; it can burn away manifold virtues and destroy the roots of the unsurpassed path. For a bodhisattva, it constitutes an evil realm; therefore, it is regarded as being like hell.
Zhaò said:
"Although meditative concentration (dhyāna) is pleasant, if one becomes complacent in it, the Great Way will not be accomplished.
The Bodhisattva does not take pleasure in it; therefore, he regards it as being like hell."
Regarding birth and death, he regards them as if they were a garden or a park.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because his mind is set upon universal salvation, he delights in wandering through the fearless."
Zhaò said:
"Although birth and death are suffering, they are the very cause of the Great Way.
Because Bodhisattvas delight in traversing them, they conceive of them as being like gardens and pavilions."
When seeing those who come seeking [alms], one should regard them as virtuous teachers.
Kumārajīva said:
"Originally, I had no intention to give; it was because they came to seek [it] that my mind for giving was aroused. Thus, they are my teachers, and so I conceive of them as such."
Once, when King Moṭṭāla was traveling out for an excursion, several thousand beggars stood by the roadside, raising their hands and shouting, each requesting what they needed.
The king asked his ministers, "Who are these people?"
"What is it that you are saying?
The minister replied,
"I am a beggar."
The King, being wise and of sharp faculties, immediately understood his meaning and said to the minister:
"He is my Great Teacher; he is no beggar.
It is you who do not understand his words."
"What he requires is for me to preach the Dharma to him; it is not a request for alms.
He continued, "In our previous lives, we were also kings, but because we did not practice generosity, we have received this retribution."
"If the King does not give now, he shall likewise do so in the future.
For this reason, you should know that he is my Great Master.
Sengzhao said:
"Although the beggar desires to benefit himself, he actually benefits me; therefore, one should regard him as a virtuous teacher.
He gave up all that he possessed, maintaining the thought of possessing all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
Kumārajīva said:
To relinquish all that one possesses means being able to completely renounce one’s body, life, kingdom, city, wife, and children to bestow them upon sentient beings.
When bestowing these upon sentient beings, one clearly understands that this giving will necessarily bring about the fulfillment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Clearly perceiving cause and effect, one gives without regret.
Zhaò said:
"In every act of giving, there is a profound purpose."
Furthermore, one should examine the non-falsity of cause and effect.
Upon seeing those who violate the precepts, one should give rise to the thought of providing protection and rescue.
Zhaò said:
Precepts provide protection for people; those who violate the precepts have no protection.
Because the Bodhisattva himself possesses protection, he desires to protect those who lack it.
He regards the various pāramitās as his parents.
Kumārajīva said:
"It is because they can give rise to the Dharma-body.

It is also said that when a child has a need, he consults his parents; when a Bodhisattva has a need, he seeks it from the Six Perfections. Because they provide such abundant benefit, they are compared to parents."
Zhaò says:
The remaining four perfections (pāramitās) become increasingly profound; they are that from which the Dharma-body arises, and thus they are conceived of as parents.
The dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are conceived of as kinsmen.
Kumārajīva said:
"To assist in the accomplishment of the holy path and cause it to be honored and preeminent is like a person having a retinue that enhances their nobility.
Sengzhao said:
That which assists and accomplishes me are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, just as a person has a retinue who assist in their accomplishment.
One’s cultivation of the roots of goodness is without limit.
Kumārajīva said:
"The former discourse explained the initial planting of the roots of goodness; the present one clarifies their cultivation and advancement.
This cultivation and advancement is called 'practice' (caryā), wherein all myriad virtues are practiced without limit."
It is also said that one does not take the number of kalpas as a limit. Zhaò says:
"The previous passage spoke of planting roots of goodness; this passage speaks of having no fixed limit, meaning they increase and expand further."
"By means of the adornments of various pure lands, one brings about the perfection of one's own Buddha-field.
Kumārajīva said:

"One first takes up the characteristics of those pure lands and then practices accordingly; because one accords with them, one achieves a pure land no different from theirs—this is called 'perfecting one's own field by means of theirs.'"
Zhaò said:
For those who delight in adornment, the Pure Land cannot help but exhaustively manifest the beauty of the Pure Land;
by practicing boundless giving, one becomes fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
Zhaò said:
"Opening the four gates for those who seek at will is the unimpeded, great bestowal of the Dharma.
This is the cause by which the marks and signs of excellence arise."
Another version reads "practicing unimpeded giving," to which Kumārajīva remarked:

"Sometimes the intention to give is sufficient while the wealth is meager; sometimes the wealth is sufficient while the intention to give is meager. If these two factors are not both present, one cannot respond to requests that come from every quarter."
Now, as both matters are present together, one is able to be without limitation, allowing all things to seek as they wish.
This eliminates all evils and purifies body, speech, and mind.
Kumārajīva said:
Because body, speech, and mind are pure, all evils are entirely eliminated; because the cause is pure, the fruit is wondrous, which is why the marks of excellence are fully possessed.
Zhaò says:
This clarifies that at the time of the great giving, all evils are eliminated and the three karmas are entirely purified; thus, the retribution of the pure marks is brought about.
"Throughout countless kalpas of birth and death, his mind remains courageous.
Kumārajīva said:
"Courageous means that he possesses strength."
The former passage spoke of the purity of the mind; this passage speaks of its power.
Because it is both pure and powerful, the fruit of the great vow is accomplished.
Zhaò said:
Birth and death are long-lasting, and their bitter poisons are immeasurable; were it not for wisdom and courage, who could endure them?
Having heard of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues, one sets one's will upon them without weariness.
Sengzhao said:
"One does not fail to practice because the Buddha is difficult to reach;
rather, one uses the sword of wisdom to destroy the thieves of affliction."
Sengzhao said:
"The bandits of affliction are dense and firmly entrenched, making them difficult to dispel; were it not for the sword of wisdom, there would be no means to sever and eliminate them.
Thus one emerges from the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases."
Kumārajīva said:

"When afflictions are exhausted, one is transformed and born in accordance with the Dharma; this body of dharmic transformation transcends the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, yet it bears the burden of sentient beings."
Kumārajīva said:
"I must ensure that he reaches the ultimate goal and does not abandon his practice midway;
I shall cause him to attain liberation forever."
Sengzhao said:
"The Dharma-body transcends the triple world and is not subsumed by the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), or sense bases (āyatanas); therefore, it is said to 'emerge.

If one were to receive a body comprised of aggregates, elements, and sense bases, remaining within the realm of emotional dust, then one would be no different from those who are fettered and constrained; how then could one rescue others?"
"By means of great diligence, he has crushed and subdued the armies of Māra.
Kumārajīva said:
"Māra refers to the celestial Māra (deva-māra)."
Sengzhao said:
"The demonic armies are powerful and flourishing; they cannot be subdued by those who are indolent.
One must constantly seek the wisdom of the true mark of non-conceptualization."
Kumārajīva said:
"There is no mindfulness that grasps at signs.
When ordinary people practice with mindful wisdom, their arrogance increases all the more; for this reason, the Bodhisattva seeks the wisdom of non-mindfulness."
Sengzhao said:
"True wisdom has no object of perception; therefore, it is named 'non-thought.
Conventional wisdom has objects of perception; therefore, thoughts and conceptions arise."
He practices few desires and contentment, yet does not abandon worldly dharmas.
Zhaò says:
One should not abandon worldly dharmas merely for the sake of being distinct through desirelessness.
He did not violate his dignified demeanor.
Kumārajīva said:
"He was harmonious yet distinct."
Yet he was able to conform to worldly customs.
Zhaor said:
"He moved up and down in harmony with the world without losing the ritual decorum of the Way; while everyone in the world said, 'He is just like me,' he alone was different from others."
He gives rise to the wisdom of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to guide sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"For those who perceive only forms and do not reach the Way, there is no means to lead them except through transformation."
"Attaining mindfulness.
Zhaò says:
"Right mindfulness."
Regarding "dhāraṇī" (total retention),
Kumārajīva said:
"Because one retains by means of mindfulness, and that which is retained is able to sustain the Dharma, it is called both 'mindfulness' (nien) and 'retention' (chi)."
It is also said that when various thoughts increase, they constitute "retention" (dhāraṇī),
whereby what has been heard is not forgotten.
Sengzhao says:
This is due to the two aforementioned types of upholding.
He skillfully discriminates the various faculties and severs the doubts of sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
It is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Through the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), one expounds without obstruction.
Zhaò says:
*Pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid* (the analytical knowledge of eloquence) is one of the four *pratisaṃvids*.

The previous passage spoke of "mindfulness, concentration, and sustaining eloquence," while this passage speaks of "mindfulness, sustaining, wisdom, and eloquence. Concentration and wisdom each possess their respective functions, alternating between these four gateways.
He purified the ten paths of wholesome action and received the blessings of devas and humans.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because they were unable to receive the Way, he preached the Dharma for them."
Zhaò said:
To cultivate goodness not for the sake of karmic reward is called "pure goodness.
Nevertheless, one undergoes retribution for the sake of sentient beings; this retribution resides within the human and celestial realms of the desire realm.
"Cultivating the four immeasurables opens the path to the Brahma heavens.
An alternative version states, "The four immeasurables cause one to be born in the Brahma heavens. Kumārajīva said:
"This is intended so that one may become a Brahmā and request the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; it distinguishes his exalted status from other beings."
This is also the Bodhisattva’s own practice, by which he himself is born in the Brahma Heaven.
He exhorts [the Buddha] to preach the Dharma, rejoices in it, and praises its excellence.
Zhaò says:
To cultivate the four immeasurables is precisely to open the path to the Brahma realm.
Manifesting as a Brahmā King to request the Buddha to preach the Dharma, one rejoices in and praises the teaching to propagate the orthodox doctrine, just like Śikhin and others of his kind.
He attained the Buddha’s voice.
Kumārajīva said:
"This is a praise for a good retribution."
Zhaò said:
The sūtras state that there are eight kinds of sounds, and they also say there are sixty kinds of sounds.
The *Guhyakapada* states: "The Buddha’s inconceivable voice responds to things in infinite ways."
Virtue of body, speech, and mind.
Zhaò says:
These are the three qualities of the Tathāgata that require no protection.
He attained the majestic deportment of a Buddha.
Zhaò said:
"In every movement and gesture, he was entirely like the voice of the Tathāgata."
The three ways in which his deportment requires no protection are all acts of the Buddha.
Although a bodhisattva has not yet fully perfected them, they have already entered that realm; therefore, it is said that he "attains" them.
By deeply cultivating wholesome dharmas, his practice becomes increasingly superior.
Zhaò said:
"Who does not cultivate wholesome dharmas? The point of value lies in their being profound and superior.
It is by means of the Mahāyāna teachings that the Bodhisattva Saṃgha is established."
Sengzhao said:
"Though the assembly of monks is vast, that which is honored is the Mahāyāna.
When the mind is free from negligence, one does not lose the root of all virtues."
Sengzhao said:
"Heedlessness is the gateway to all evils and the root of losing the Way; when the mind is free from heedlessness, there is no good that does not accumulate.
Since wholesome dharmas are immeasurable, I have spoken briefly of their source."
Practicing such a dharma is called the bodhisattva’s non-exhaustion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Zhaò says:
"Cultivating the aforementioned dharmas to transform oneself and others, one's merit and virtue flourish daily; this is the non-exhaustion of the conditioned."
Now, conditioned dharmas that are wholesome merely involve transformation and decay; if they are abandoned and not cultivated, they will diminish and be exhausted day by day.
What does it mean for a bodhisattva not to dwell in the unconditioned?
This means that one practices and studies emptiness, yet does not take emptiness as a realization.
Zhaò says:
"From here downward, all are contemplative practices of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."

By contemplating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one necessarily beholds the joy of tranquility and serenity; yet, being able to refrain from realizing *nirvāṇa* and instead remain eternally within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is called "not abiding in the unconditioned.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are practiced in common by the three vehicles, yet their modes of cultivation differ.

The emptiness-contemplation of the Two Vehicles pertains only to non-self, whereas the emptiness-contemplation of the Mahāyāna encompasses all phenomena without exception. Because there is no phenomenon that is not included, even the phenomenon of emptiness is empty; since the phenomenon of emptiness is itself empty, one is able to refrain from realizing [the cessation of] emptiness.
One practices and studies signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*), yet does not take signlessness and wishlessness as a realization.
Zhaò says:
"The signlessness of the Two Vehicles exists only within the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*); the signlessness of the Mahāyāna exists in all phenomena (*sarvadharma*)."
The non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) of the two vehicles does not produce birth and death; the non-action of the Great Vehicle does not produce any phenomena.
One practices and studies without arising, yet does not take this non-arising as a realization.
Sengzhao said:
"All phenomena exist when conditions assemble and cease to exist when conditions disperse.
What phenomenon could possibly exist beforehand, waiting for conditions to arise?"
This is a specific gateway to the contemplation of emptiness.
One contemplates impermanence yet does not weary of the roots of goodness.
Kumārajīva said:
If all things are impermanent, there is no phenomenon that does not perish.
Because they perish yet do not undergo total severance, one cultivates goodness without weariness.
Furthermore, one contemplates that impermanence is the path to Nirvana; yet the path to Nirvana turns its back upon the roots of goodness.
Now, because he does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he does not loathe existence (*bhava*).
He contemplates the suffering of the world yet does not detest birth and death; he contemplates non-self (*anātman*) yet teaches others without weariness.
Kumārajīva said:
"The absence of self means that sentient beings are empty; yet this emptiness is not non-existence, and thus one teaches others without weariness.
One contemplates quiescent extinction, yet does not remain in eternal extinction."
Sengzhao said:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles regard impermanence as impermanent, and thus they weary of conditioned wholesome dharmas;
they regard suffering as suffering, and thus they loathe the suffering of birth and death."
Because they take non-self to be non-self, they are indolent in instructing others;
because they take quiescence to be quiescence, they desire eternal stillness.
The Bodhisattva does not regard impermanence as impermanence, and thus is able to never weary of the roots of goodness.
Because one does not regard suffering as suffering, one does not loathe birth and death;
because one does not regard non-self as non-self, one teaches others without weariness;
because one does not regard quiescence as quiescence, one does not enter eternal stillness.
"Regarding 'observing seclusion while cultivating goodness of body and mind,' Kumārajīva said:

'There are three kinds of seclusion: first, seclusion from crowds of people and the five desires; second, seclusion from afflictions; and third, seclusion through the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.'"
Now, observing that the nature of things is empty and detached, one does not weary of the good.
Zhaò says:
"Detachment" is merely another name for non-action (wuwei).
Although one perceives the essential point of detachment within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), body and mind do not depart from the goodness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
One contemplates that there is nowhere to which one can return, yet returns to and takes refuge in wholesome dharmas.
Zhaò says:
All phenomena have no point of origin at the beginning and no destination at the end.
Although one knows there is no destination, one constantly returns to wholesome dharmas.
Contemplating non-arising, yet bearing all beings upon the dharma of arising.
Zhaò said:
"Though one perceives non-arising, one remains within arising to bear its burden;
one contemplates the outflow-free while not severing the various outflows."
Zhaò said:
"In general, all that is outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); its essence is inherently without marks, and it is entirely an unconditioned practice.
Although one perceives the outflow-free, it remains identical to those [phenomena] that possess outflows."
There are two kinds of those with outflows (*sāsrava*):
those who enter the cycle of birth and death while their outflows are actually not yet severed;
and those whose outflows are already exhausted but who manifest as if they have not been severed.
One contemplates that there is nothing to be practiced, yet practices the Dharma to transform sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"The nature of dharmas (dharmatā) is devoid of karma; what, then, is there to be cultivated?"
Although one knows that there is no practice, one must nonetheless teach through practice.
One contemplates emptiness and non-existence, yet does not abandon great compassion.
Zhaò said:
"The characteristics of all dharmas are solely emptiness and solely non-existence; yet, one does not abandon great compassion because of this emptiness and non-existence.
[He] contemplates the stage of the True Dharma.
Kumārajīva said:
This refers to the realization of the Dharma that is without arising or ceasing,
yet does not follow the Lesser Vehicle.
Zhaò said:
The stage of the True Dharma is the ground for observing the unconditioned and attaining realization.

One observes that all phenomena are illusory and lack solidity; they are without self, without master, and without marks. Yet, until one's original vows are fulfilled, one does not neglect the cultivation of merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Sengzhao said:
All dharmas are produced through causes and conditions; being illusory and without foundation, what could be considered real?
What could be considered the master?
Although he knows this, because his original vow is not yet fulfilled, he does not fail to cultivate virtue, concentration, and wisdom merely because they are provisional.
Sengsheng said:
"Not abiding in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is to exhaustively investigate principle while maintaining the intention to enter into birth and death."
Since the fulfillment of vows is the ultimate goal, he concludes by clarifying this point.
To cultivate such a dharma is called the Bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Zhaò said:
If one fully cultivates the aforementioned dharmas, one does not realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

"Realization" refers to the completion of the path of self-realization through the contemplation of the unconditioned; the completion of the path of self-realization is itself abiding in the unconditioned.
Furthermore, because they are endowed with merit and virtue, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Zhaò says:

"The above merely clarifies that the Bodhisattva does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and does not abide in the unconditioned; it has not yet explained the reason why he does not exhaust the one, nor the reason why he does not abide in the other."
Now, as for the conduct of a Mahāsattva, each practice has its own purpose and the sublime aspiration has its specific locus; therefore, I shall further clarify this by means of a response.
The accumulation of virtue must necessarily involve the crossing of the ford of existence; if one dwells in non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), then merit and virtue will not be complete.
"Because they possess wisdom, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Kumārajīva said:
"In the previous section, one meaning was manifested within a single gate; now it is clarified that two meanings are both present within a single gate."
If one does not abide in non-existence, then one does not exhaust existence; if one does not exhaust existence, then one does not abide in non-existence.
Zhaò said:
"The clarity of wisdom must necessarily arise from breadth and extensiveness."
If one abandons the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then wisdom will not be complete.
Sengsheng says:
"This is a general reversal of what was stated previously."
The reason one wishes to abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is simply because one craves its bliss.
Once merit and virtue are fully possessed, one naturally experiences constant joy; what more, then, would there be to crave?
Likewise, the reason one wishes to exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is simply because one loathes its suffering.
If wisdom is indeed complete, one is naturally free from suffering; what evil could there be?
Because of great compassion, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Zhaò said:
Entering the cycle of birth and death through compassion—how could this be something achievable by abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Because he fulfills his original vows, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Zhaò says:
Since Pūrṇa fulfilled his vows through the accumulation of merit, how could he have abandoned what is possible within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
Sengsheng said:
"This is a distinct translation of the preceding [passage]."
Those who harbor compassion within their hearts must not crave their own pleasure;
those who wish to fulfill their original vows must not dwell upon their own suffering.
Here, "attaining merit" corresponds to the former phrase and "wisdom" to the latter; these two points are briefly cited for completeness.
Because they gather the medicinal herbs of the Dharma, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Zhaò said:
"To gather fine medicine, one must go to perilous mountains; it does not emerge from a grand hall."
The gathering of the medicine of the Dharma must occur within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*); it does not arise from the state of unconditioned non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because the medicine is administered according to [the needs of] beings, one does not exhaust all conditioned existence.
Zhaò said:
If one abandons conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), one becomes isolated from all living beings; how then could one follow them to administer the medicine?
Daosheng said:
"To reverse the former [approach] is precisely to re-enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); only thus can one surely save the multitude."
Therefore, there are the following four phrases.
"Gathering the medicine of the Dharma" means to ensure that the principles of all dharmas are fully prepared; this is the intention of merit (*guṇa*).
"Administering the medicine according to [the patient]" means knowing what each [medicine] governs and administering it according to the illness; this is the intention of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because he knows the illnesses of sentient beings, he does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Sengzhao says:
"If one habitually understands the illnesses of sentient beings, one must also know where those illnesses end; how could this be something achievable through the unconditioned?"
Dongsheng said:
"To understand the characteristics of illness is the intention of merit.
Because it extinguishes the illnesses of sentient beings, one does not exhaust all conditioned phenomena."
Zhao said:
"To extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings, one must necessarily establish a treatment; how could this be accomplished solely through conditioned phenomena?
Sengsheng said:
To reach what is appropriate for the illness is the intention of wisdom.
By cultivating this dharma, the bodhisattvas who are true gentlemen do not exhaust the conditioned, nor do they abide in the unconditioned.
Zhaò says:
Although these two dharmas differ, their functions must necessarily depend upon one another; therefore, they are contrasted and analyzed.
This clarifies that while names and designations exist for them, their modes of operation are distinct.
This is called the Dharma-gate of the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible without Obstruction.
You all should study it. Zhaò said:
Because they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are free from the limitation of [merely] unimpeded virtue;
because they do not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are free from the limitation of solitary excellence.
These two gates of non-obstruction are the essential path for Bodhisattvas to propagate the Way, and the source from which the Buddha’s activities manifest in infinite ways.
He exhorted them to study and showed them the inconceivable path of the Buddha’s work, ensuring they would certainly realize that all Buddhas are not diverse.

At that time, when those bodhisattvas heard this Dharma being preached, they were all greatly rejoiced. Taking various kinds of exquisite flowers of many colors and many fragrances, they scattered them throughout the trichiliocosm as an offering to the Buddha, to this sutra and its Dharma, and to all the bodhisattvas. Having done so, they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and, marveling at what had never occurred before, said:
"The Śākyamuni Buddha is truly able to employ such skillful means here."
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished and returned to that land.
Chapter Twelve: Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya (9) At that time, the World-Honored One asked Vimalakīrti:
"If you wish to see the Tathāgata, by what means do you contemplate the Tathāgata?"
Kumārajīva said:
"If one possesses the eye of wisdom, one can illuminate [reality] profoundly without depending on observing physical forms.
If one lacks the eye of wisdom, one remains obstructed even when facing a form; therefore, I ask why you ask what kind of observation constitutes seeing the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, there are three ways of contemplating the Buddha: first, contemplating the physical form; second, contemplating the Dharma-body; and third, contemplating the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
He asked:
"Among these three contemplations, which one do you practice?"
The following sections answer entirely by means of emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
This chapter employs the principles of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and *Śata-śāstra* to refute characteristics and clarify that the Tathāgata is empty of intrinsic nature.
Since there is no further divergent meaning, I have not provided a commentary on the questions.
Zhaò said:
Previously, Mañjuśrī was commanded to come together with [the others] to see the Buddha; although he followed worldly custom by raising his eyes, his mode of observation was not the same as theirs.

The Tathāgata perceived his inner disposition and, wishing to reveal the purpose of his coming observation, clarified that the Buddha’s work is inconceivable; thus, He knew [the answer] yet asked the question.
Daosheng said:
"Vimalakīrti has just summoned all the bodhisattvas to come together and see the Buddha; thus, his traces appear within human form, yet he is the Buddha.
However, 'seeing the Buddha' does not mean that one has truly seen him merely through physical contact with his form; therefore, he questioned them in order to clarify what true seeing is."
Vimalakīrti said:
"As one contemplates the true mark of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha.
Zhaò said:
What is a Buddha? It is a designation for Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), which exhausts all principles and perfects all natures.

Its Way is empty and profound, inherently transcending the realm of the ordinary; its mind cannot be known through intellect, and its form cannot be fathomed by images. It acts as all things while abiding in the domain of non-action; it dwells within the sphere of speech and calculation yet rests in the land beyond words. It is not existent, yet it cannot be called non-existent; it is not non-existent, yet it cannot be called existent. It is silent, vast, and empty, such that no thing can measure it. Not knowing how to name it, we have forcibly termed it "Enlightenment."
Their attainment is indeed ultimate. Why is this?

For those who are identical in their gain, even that gain is attained; for those who are identical in their loss, even that loss is attained. Thus, the true are identical with the true, and the false are identical with the false. The numinous illumination of the Tathāgata harmonizes mysteriously with that *dharmatā* (real mark); the characteristic of the *dharmatā* is itself the characteristic of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To see the dharma of the true mark is to see the Buddha.
When Vimalakīrti contemplates the true mark of his own body as the contemplation of the Tathāgata’s marks, the significance lies precisely herein.
Dongsheng said:
"If you claim that seeing the Buddha occurs through physical contact with him, then you and the Buddha would be distinct entities separated by a great distance; how then could you see him?

If one can contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of one's own body in the same way as contemplating the Buddha, such that they are no longer different and there is no discordance between them, this constitutes 'seeing'."
"I observe that the Tathāgata does not come from the past, does not go to the future, and does not abide in the present.
Daosheng said:
"If one regards the seeing of the Buddha as 'seeing,' this principle is fundamentally non-existent."
Furthermore, the Buddha is not seen; it is precisely by not seeing a Buddha that one sees the Buddha.

To "see the Buddha" means to see this person as the Buddha, who comes from the future to the present and enters from the present into the past; therefore, one infers that there is no Buddha existing within the three periods of time.
If the Buddha existed in the past, he would necessarily have returned; yet since he has not returned, it is clear that the Buddha does not exist in the past.
If he existed in the future, he would necessarily have departed; yet since he has not departed, it is clear that the Buddha does not exist in the future.
If [the Buddha] were present now, he would necessarily abide; yet since he does not abide, it is clear that the Buddha is not in the present.

He does not contemplate form, nor the suchness of form, nor the nature of form; he does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the suchness of consciousness, nor the nature of consciousness.
Sengzhao said:

"The Dharma-body transcends the three realms and is not subsumed by the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), or sense bases (āyatanas); therefore, it cannot be perceived through birth, abiding, passing away, or coming; nor can it be contemplated as having the nature of the five aggregates."
Sengsheng said:
"As for what was previously stated—that one does not see the Buddha—it may mean that one is currently unable to see him, rather than that the Buddha does not exist.
Therefore, he again pushed the argument to its limit by asserting that no Buddha can be seen."
That which is called a "human Buddha" is merely a composite of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If [the Buddha] truly exists, then form (*rūpa*) itself must be the Buddha.
If form itself is not the Buddha, then there must be a Buddha apart from form.
Furthermore, there are three ways in which the Buddha exists apart from form: the Buddha is within form, form is within the Buddha, and form belongs to the Buddha.
If form were identical to the Buddha, it would not need to depend upon the four [elements].
If the Buddha existed outside of form, he would not depend upon form.
If the Buddha existed within form, the Buddha would be impermanent.
If form existed within the Buddha, the Buddha would possess parts.
If form belonged to the Buddha, form would be unchangeable.
"Form" refers to the phenomenon of form;
"suchness" means that form is not different [from its true nature].
"Nature" (xing) refers to form (rūpa) being without a fundamental basis.
Since its manifestation as a phenomenon has already been described, and phenomena may be subject to change, it is called "suchness" (tathatā).
Although it is said not to change, the fundamental essence might otherwise be different; therefore, it is called "nature."
Thus, it is essential that these three meanings be fully present before the meaning of "form" (rūpa) can be established.
For this reason, even the five categories such as intrinsic nature (svabhāva) cannot be differentiated; they are all identical when it comes to consciousness (vijñāna).
Since there is nothing seen, this is precisely seeing reality.
To see with reality is to be a Buddha; it is by seeing reality that one sees the Buddha.
It does not arise from the four great elements, but is identical to empty space.
Zhaò said:
"The Dharma-body is like space; it is not something produced or constructed from the four great elements.
Shēng said:

Although the previous argument refuted the mark of a person in the Buddha, it could only indicate that there is no real person-Buddha; it was not yet sufficient to clarify that the very reason for being a Buddha is ultimately that there is no person-Buddha at all.
If there were such a thing as a person who is a Buddha, he would necessarily exist by arising from the four great elements.
Now, one who exists by arising from the four great elements is a person subject to birth and death.
The Buddha is not so; while [the world] should exist, the Buddha is eternally non-existent.
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) have no accumulation. Śeng said:
Now, those who possess the Buddha-nature necessarily emerge from the accumulation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Since there is no such accumulation, can one say that there is a human Buddha?
Five of these [bases] are produced by the four great elements; therefore, I shall clarify this by means of the six.
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind have already transcended them.
Zhaò says:
"The Dharma-body transcends the six sensory faculties; therefore, external objects have no place to accumulate."
Sheng said:

"The previous statement that because the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) have no accumulation there is neither person nor Buddha can only mean that there are no people or Buddhas in future lives; it is not sufficient to clarify that they do not exist in the present either. Therefore, he further states regarding the six sense bases that 'they have already passed away.'"
As for those who have already transcended the six sense bases, they have not accumulated [karmic seeds] for a very long time and do not abide within the three realms.
Birth says:
The previous statement that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have already passed refers to the fact that the six locations (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are currently present within existence (*bhava*).
Since there would be no location for the six sense bases if existence were either surpassed or not yet reached, it is further stated that they do not abide within the three realms (*tridhātu*).
The three defilements have already been abandoned.
Zhaò says:
"Since one has already transcended the triple world, how could one possess the defilements of the triple world?"
Sheng said:
"Because the three defilements have already been abandoned, one does not abide within the triple world.
Since the three do not exist, one is said not to be in the three."
"Following the three gates of liberation.
Sengsheng said:
"Because one follows the three gates of liberation, one is freed from the three defilements."
This is because the three [knowledges] are free from the three [obstructions].
The three knowledges are equal to ignorance.
Zhaò says:
The Dharma-body is without marks; its essence accords with the three gates of liberation. Although it possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge, it is not different from ignorance.
Daosheng said:
"To accord with the three gates of liberation is to regard clarity and ignorance as equal."
Since the three gates of liberation have already been clarified as being three, they are further discussed here in terms of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).
They are neither identical nor different.
Zhaò says:
It is not an image, yet it is not non-image; therefore, it cannot be considered one.
It is an image, yet it is not an image; therefore, it cannot be considered different.
Sheng said:
"Equality" refers to the mutual equality of both.
Mutual equality means neither being identical nor being different;
it is neither its own characteristic nor the characteristic of another.
Sengzhao said:
Because it is not-self yet identical to self, it is self yet not-self.
Because it is not-other yet identical to other, it is other yet not-other.
How can the body of signlessness be observed in terms of its essence through such distinctions as one or many, self or other?
Daosheng said:
"If there is 'self' and 'other,' then they are different."
It is neither the mark of non-existence nor the mark of grasping.
Zhaò says:
"Since it is neither the mark of a non-existent thing, nor is it a mark that can be grasped."
Daosheng said:
"If there were no marks, they would be one.
Furthermore, they cannot be grasped, for there are neither the marks of oneness nor difference."
"Not on this shore, not on the other shore, and not in the middle stream.
Sheng said:
"By following the three gates of liberation, one reaches the other shore."
If there is reaching, it is not truly reaching; only when there is neither reaching nor non-reaching is it called "reaching.
This shore is birth and death;
the other shore is nirvana.
The "middle stream" refers to the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*).
Yet, [the Buddha] transforms sentient beings. Zao said:
If one wishes to call this shore "this side," it is as tranquil as nirvana;
if one wishes to call the other shore "the further side," birth and death are themselves peace.
Furthermore, it does not abide in the middle stream, yet it teaches and transforms sentient beings.
"This is indeed the ultimate of the Way.
This shore is birth-and-death; the other shore is nirvana; and the middle stream consists of the worthy and the sages.
Sengsheng said:
Now, the transformation of sentient beings consists simply in causing them to sever their fetters, leave behind birth and death, and reach Nirvana.

Yet, what was said previously—that there are no three [vehicles]—seemed as if one would no longer transform them; that is why it was stated so. Nevertheless, the three [vehicles] are not non-existent.
One contemplates quiescent extinction, yet it is not eternal extinction.
Zhaò says:
"To contemplate quiescent extinction is for contemplation itself to be quiescent extinction."
To be extinguished yet not extinguished—how could this be described by forms or names?
Daosheng said:
"Since it is said that one transforms sentient beings, yet it seems as though there are still sentient beings perceived, it is therefore called 'observing quiescent extinction.'"
To contemplate cessation does not mean eternal extinction;
it is neither this nor that.
Sheng said:
If one transforms sentient beings, it appears as if there is "here" and "there.
These notions of "here" and "there" are merely traces of responsive transformation; they are not real in that way.
"Not by this, nor by that. Zhaò says:
"Not being this while being identical to this; therefore, it is this, yet not this."
Not being that [other], yet being identical to that; therefore, being that, yet not being that.
How could one further take this to be identical to this, or take that to be identical to that?
This clarifies that the Sage’s mind possesses no identity through which it might be made identical to anything.
Huisheng said:
"Although it is said that [the Buddha] is neither here nor there, one may nevertheless use the traces of 'here' and 'there' to transform beings.
'Here' and 'there' are what sentient beings grasp; they are not the way of the Buddha."
It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness.
Zhaò says:
"The arising of wisdom and consciousness occurs within the realm of marks."
The Dharma-body is without marks; therefore, it is not within the reach of intellectual consciousness.
Daosheng said:
"Since it is neither here nor there, and neither by means of this nor that, how can it be described as such through the cognition of intellectual consciousness?"
There is neither obscurity nor illumination. Zhaò says:
When illumination surpasses the three luminaries, who would call it darkness?
Darkness surpasses a dark chamber; who would call it light?
Thus, being dark when in darkness and being bright when in light—this capacity to be both dark and bright—is surely not something that light or darkness themselves can achieve.
Therefore it is said: "There is neither darkness nor light. Sheng said:
"If light does not reside in its outward manifestation, it is treated as obscurity; however, the principle itself cannot fail to be present, so it is not truly obscurity."
The traces, on the contrary, appear to be manifestations of clarity; yet this is merely what is grasped by others and cannot be considered true clarity.
It is nameless and formless.
Zhaor said:
It cannot be named by names, nor can it be characterized by characteristics.
Sheng said:
"Within traces there are names, but the Buddha is nameless."
"Phenomena (xiàng)" refers to appearances that can be named.
There is neither strength nor weakness.
Zhaor said:
The most supple has no resistance; who would call it strong?
The firm has nothing that does not submit; who would call it weak?
Sheng said:
The realm of movement is not strength;
responding to impermanence is not weakness.
It is neither pure nor defiled.
Zhaò said:
"If one is pure while in purity, who would call it defiled?
If one is defiled while in defilement, who would call it pure?"
Thus, that which constitutes strength or weakness, purity or impurity, is in fact not something produced by strength, weakness, purity, or impurity.
Sengsheng said:
"The physical marks adorning the body are not its purity; the golden spear and the horse-barley are likewise not its impurity."
It does not abide in any direction, yet it is not apart from any direction.
Zhaò says:

"The Dharma-body has no location, yet there is nowhere it does not abide. Because it has no location, it does not abide in any direction; because there is nowhere it does not abide, it is not apart from any direction."
Dongsheng said:
"If there is an awakening in the east, it is the Buddha in the east; if there is an awakening in the west, it is the Buddha in the west.

How could this depend on direction? Nevertheless, since this is the response of the Buddha, one cannot say that the direction is not the Buddha. Therefore, it is said that he is neither within nor apart from [direction]."
It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Zhaò said:
If one wishes to say it exists, it is without marks and without names.
If one wishes to say that it does not exist, it nevertheless manifests in response to the myriad forms.
Sheng said:
"If it exists, it is conditioned; if it does not exist, it is unconditioned."
Since the Buddha neither possesses this existence nor lacks existence, what could there be that is conditioned or unconditioned?
There is nothing to demonstrate and nothing to explain. Zhaò said:
"It is not within the reach of the six sensory faculties; how can it be explained to others?
Sengsheng replied, "That which should be seen is shown, and that which should be heard is explained."
The Buddha is fundamentally without demonstration and without teaching.

He neither practices giving nor is he stingy; he neither observes precepts nor violates them; he neither practices patience nor harbors anger; he neither exerts effort nor is indolent; he neither attains concentration nor is distracted; he neither possesses wisdom nor is ignorant.
Sheng said:
"Because it takes the six perfections as its essence, it is able to produce responses such as those mentioned above.
Yet, where there is a 'crossing over' and one who crosses over, there is no true crossing over."
There is no one who has not been saved, yet only after this can one truly save others.
Without sincerity, there is no lack of deception. Zao said:
One should not regard the good as good, nor the evil as evil.
Sheng said:
"The Six Perfections take sincerity and honesty as their Way."
Yet if there were a "being true" within truth, it would not be true.
Only when there is neither being true nor not being true does one truly become true.
It neither comes nor goes.
Sheng said:
"Since they have already been delivered and are already sincere, they ought to come in response to such resonance; once the resonance is exhausted, they depart.
If there were such coming and going, they would further be unable to come and go."
"Neither emerging nor entering.
Zhaor said:
"He departs in silent stillness and arrives in placid tranquility; he emerges from the profound darkness and enters into the deep obscurity—who can perceive his movement?"
Dongshan said:
"Coming is 'coming out'; going is 'entering.
All paths of verbal expression are cut off."
Sengzhao said:
"Its essence transcends the path of words.
Sengsheng said:
This is a brief summary.
To say that the six perfections, being signless, constitute Buddhahood—how could this be described through the signs of words?
It is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit.
Huisheng said:
"Because one takes formlessness as the Buddha, one is able to cause people to make offerings and thereby obtain merit, serving as a field of blessings.
If it were otherwise, would there not be form?"
It is neither worthy of worship nor unworthy of worship.
Zhaò says:
"The substance of formlessness cannot be seen at its boundaries; who then can know what constitutes a field or a non-field, or what is worthy or unworthy of worship?"
Dongsheng said:
"If it is a field of merit, one should make offerings; if it is not a field of merit, one should not make offerings.
It is neither grasping nor abandoning."
Zhaò said:
"To grasp it is to lose its true nature; to abandon it is to deviate from the Way.
Shēng said:
Because it is a field of merit, one should accept; because it is not a field of merit, one should discard.
It is neither with marks nor without marks.
Sengzhao said:
Solitude is formless; it is not that there are marks.
The thirty-two marks exist; it is not that there are no marks.
Sheng said:
If one is a field of merit, they are a person of merit; a person of merit possesses the marks and blessings.
They are identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Daosheng said: "The absence of marks is precisely this."
This means that because the Buddha is distinct [from them], they are said to be "equal.
He is ineffable, immeasurable, and transcends all measure and calculation.
Zhaò says:

The essence of signlessness is identical to the limit of reality and equal to the nature of phenomena; it is beyond the reach of words and beyond the scope of thought, transcending the realm of calculation and surpassing the domain of measurement.
Dongsheng said:
"Since they are identical to the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), how could they be measured by the intellect?
To 'transcend all measurement' is precisely what it means to be beyond the reach of words."
"It is neither large nor small.
Sengzhao said: "The Great encompasses heaven and earth, so it cannot be called small;
the minute enters the infinitesimal gaps, so it cannot be called large."
As for being able to be great and able to be small, is it not because there is neither greatness nor smallness?
Zisheng said:
"When one speaks of smallness, the great encompasses heaven and earth; when one speaks of greatness, the subtle enters the infinitesimal."
It is not seeing. Zhaò says:
Because it is not form, it is not seeing.
It is not hearing.
Zhaò says: Because it is not sound, it is not hearing.
"Not perceived. Zhaò said:
"Because it is not fragrance, flavor, or touch, it is not that which is perceived by the three feelings."
It is not known through cognition. Zhaò says:
Because it is not a dharma, it is not something that can be known by the mind.
Dongsheng said:
"Not only is it impossible to see, hear, perceive, or know it, but there is also no one who can perform such seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing.
It is free from all fetters and bonds."
Zhao said:
"The essence of the outflow-free (anāsrava) transcends all fetters and bonds.
Sheng said:
Since there is neither seeing, hearing, sensing, nor cognizing, how could fetters arise?
[He is] equal to all wisdom and identical to sentient beings.
Śāṇavāsa said:
How could one’s wisdom possibly transcend that of the multitude or set oneself apart from sentient beings?
One is without discrimination regarding all phenomena.
Zhaò said:
The wisdom that realizes the true mark of reality is identical to the nature of sentient beings; it is a seamless, boundless whole—how could it be distinct from the dharmas?
Daosheng said:
"Regarding all dharmas, there is no longer any discriminative sentiment whatsoever."
All things are without gain and without loss, without turbidity and without affliction.
Zhaò says:
Because there is no gain, there is no loss; because there is no clarity, there is no turbidity.
The essence that transcends all phenomena—how could it be subject to vexation?
Sheng said:
"To err is to become turbid; once turbid, vexation arises."
From this point onward, it clarifies that [these things] do not exist within the principle of the Buddha’s signlessness.
It is without action and without arising.
Sheng said:
To have turbidity and affliction is precisely to create and give rise to a future body.
There is neither birth nor extinction.
Zhaò said:
The Dharma-body is unconditioned and transcends all volitional construction.
Who could create it to cause it to arise, or produce it to cause it to cease?
Sheng said:
Since one has already brought about a subsequent existence, there will then be birth and death.
Fearless and without sorrow, without joy and without weariness. [The Buddha] said:
"Birth is as follows:"
If there were arising and ceasing, this would be a fearful phenomenon; one would then rejoice in arising and grieve over ceasing.
Since grief and joy would never cease, it is something to be loathed.
There has been no past existence, there will be no future existence, and there is no present existence.

Sengzhao said: "The Dharma-body has no locus; it transcends the existence of the three periods of time. The three calamities cannot cause it affliction, nor can beginning and end transform its essence. It is tranquil, serene, and still, non-active and beyond reckoning; how could there be room for anxiety, fear, joy, or aversion within it?"
Dongsheng said:
"Since there is neither sorrow nor joy, one no longer undergoes further existence within the realms of becoming.
This cannot be demonstrated through any verbal expression or conceptual discrimination."
Śāriputra said:
"It is the complete binding,
World-Honored One!"
The body of the Tathāgata is such as this; one should contemplate it in this manner.
Zhaò said:
"Words are exhausted and wisdom is fully spent, yet nothing can manifest it; the purport of coming to contemplate it is precisely like this."
"To view things in this way is called right contemplation;
to view them otherwise is called wrong contemplation.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti:
"From where did you pass away to come and be born here?
Kumārajīva replied,
"Seeing that your spiritual virtue is extraordinary and peerless, and that your place of origin must be noble, I have asked about the source from which you came."
Vimalakīrti feared that people would harbor notions of death and birth; therefore, he posed a counter-question to clarify that there is neither death nor birth.
It is also said that some may have thought Vimalakīrti’s allotted lifespan was not yet exhausted, and thus he questioned him regarding death and birth.
The answer given below does not exhaustively praise the good nor condemn the evil, clarifying that one’s allotted share of life has reached its end.
The reason for not answering directly is twofold: first, to humble the Śrāvakas; second, to avoid manifesting the excellence of the source from which [the Buddha] himself derives his teachings.
Sengzhao said:
The previous passage stated, "As when one contemplates the true mark of the body.

Since the true mark is without arising, yet now there is manifest arising, [the question] was posed regarding death and birth in order to establish the meaning of this contemplation of the self. Thus, he inquired about death and birth.
Vimalakīrti said:
"In the Dharma you have attained, is there any passing away or birth?
Zhaò said:
He asks counter-questions regarding what has been attained in order to verify that there is neither death nor birth.
The dharma thus attained is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and signless (*animitta*) dharma; all three vehicles attain their fruits by means of the signless.
Śāriputra said:
"There is neither death nor birth.
If all dharmas lack the characteristics of death and birth, why do you ask: 'From where did you die to come and be born here'?"
Sengzhao said:
"By means of what one has personally attained, one can know the characteristics of dharmas.
He asked again: 'Why is this so?'"
"What do you think?
For example, if a magician were to conjure up men and women through illusion, would they die or be born?
Śāriputra replied:
"There is neither passing away nor birth.
Have you not heard the Buddha say that all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion?
He replied:
It is so. If all phenomena are like the nature of an illusion, why do you ask, "From where did you pass away to come and be born here?
Sengzhao said:
Birth is like a transformation remaining; death is like a transformation departing. There is no phenomenon that is not thus; why then do you ask alone? Śāriputra!
To pass away is the characteristic of the deceptive dharma’s disintegration; to be born is the characteristic of the deceptive dharma’s continuity.
Sengzhao said:
"First, one must determine the characteristics of death and birth.
Sengsheng said:
This is the principle of birth and death, yet it is not real.
Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness;
although they are born, they do not increase their various evils.
Kumārajīva said:
"When ordinary beings die, they give rise to evil and extinguish goodness; once reborn, their various evils increase.
It is not so for Bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, because the roots of goodness of ordinary beings are exhausted, at the end of their lives they give rise to long-lasting inverted and evil thoughts before undergoing rebirth.
It is not so for Bodhisattvas; as their Dharma-transformation is pure, they proceed according to their will, and thus they are free from this affliction.
Without this affliction, although there is the appearance of coming and going in their traces, it does not mean actual death and birth.

Previously, the absence of death and birth was clarified through the emptiness of intrinsic nature; now, the absence of death and birth is clarified through mastery over the transformation of dharmas.
If one seeks these two gates, then death and birth have no point of reliance; yet to inquire about death and birth is to miss the mark by a great distance.
Zhaò says:
"Both good and evil are merely the marks of illusory and deceptive continuity; they are but phenomena subject to decay and destruction."
However, when ordinary beings are born, they increase in evil, and when they die, they are entirely good;
when Bodhisattvas are born, they increase in goodness, and when they die, they are entirely evil.
Although their death and birth are the same, their growth and cessation differ; yet both are but signs of delusion and disintegration—how are they different from magical illusions?
Sheng said:
"If even birth and death are not real, one should not pose questions about them, let alone regarding that which is entirely non-existent.
Those who perish in birth and death do so because their merit is exhausted; those who are born will surely increase all manner of evils."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"There is a land named Abhirati, where the Buddha is named Akṣobhya; it was from that land that this Vimalakīrti passed away to be born here."
Sengzhao said:
"The preceding response concerned non-arising; this concerns the place of arising.
Responding to things and proclaiming [the Dharma] has never failed to be beneficial."
Śāriputra said, "It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
That such a person would be able to forsake a pure land and come to delight in this place of much anger and harm."
Zhaò said:
"In this land, compared to other countries, anger and harm are most prevalent.
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra:"
"What do you think?
When the sunlight emerges, does it coincide with darkness?
He replied: "No."
"No. When the sunlight appears, there is no darkness.
Vimalakīrti said:
For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?
The answer is:
it desires to illuminate and thereby dispel the darkness.
Vimalakīrti said:
"It is thus with the bodhisattva.

Although they are born in impure buddha-fields for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they do not associate with ignorance and darkness; rather, they merely extinguish the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings."
At that time, the great assembly thirsted with longing to behold the world of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and his host of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Knowing the thoughts of the entire gathering, the Buddha addressed Vimalakīrti, saying:
"O son of good family!"
For the sake of this assembly, he manifested the Land of Wonderful Joy, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
as everyone desired to see them.
Kumārajīva said:
This land was manifested for those of lower capacity who wish to cultivate a pure land and attain rebirth there.
It was not manifested from afar to bring them here, but rather to manifest the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Vimalakīrti.
Regarding the matter at hand, the emotions are gladdened and the realization is profound; therefore, he was commanded to manifest this very event.
Zhaò said:
"Having observed the longing and yearning of the great assembly, and intending to reveal the inconceivable virtues of Vimalakīrti, he was thus informed to manifest his own land."
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:

"Without rising from my seat, I shall bring forth the Iron Ring Mountains, mountains, rivers, valleys, streams, great oceans, springs, Mount Sumeru, and all the stars and planets; the palaces of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and Brahmās; as well as the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, the cities, towns, villages, men and women, young and old, and even the Tathāgata Akṣobhya."
Sengzhao said:
"To humble one's dignity is difficult; hence the phrase 'even unto.
This refers to the various wondrous lotuses at the Bodhi tree that are able to perform Buddha-work throughout the ten directions."
Kumārajīva said:
"Upon the flowers, there may appear transformation Buddhas, or they may emit radiance, as well as manifest various transformations such as preaching the Dharma, in order to awaken sentient beings.
Sengzhao said:
That bodhi tree and the exquisite lotus flowers both emit radiance, performing buddha-work throughout the ten directions;
furthermore, the emanated buddhas and bodhisattvas upon the flowers likewise perform buddha-work throughout the ten directions.
All these are taken together as coming [to the Buddha].

The Threefold Jewel Staircase extends from Jambudvīpa to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; by means of this jewel staircase, the various devas descend, all to pay homage to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and listen to and receive the Dharma of the sutras.
Zhaò said:

"The gods of the desire realm possess the power of supernatural penetration and are fully able to soar through the void; however, since their lands use ornate jeweled stairways as paths for recreation, they likewise travel back and forth by these means."
The people of Jambudvīpa also ascend its steps to rise up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and behold those devas.
ZHAO said:

"In this land of solemn purity, blessings and auspiciousness are gathered; as the retributions of humans and devas differ by only a short interval, they travel back and forth along the same path, sharing the joy of companionship."

The world-system Abhirati has thus accomplished such immeasurable merits; from the Akaniṣṭha heaven above down to the water’s edge below, it can be severed and taken up with the right hand as if it were a potter’s wheel.
Kumārajīva said:

"The Sanskrit text says 'like cutting through mud. The current expression 'like a potter's wheel' clarifies that one cuts from the center, just as with a potter's wheel, so that it does not touch the ground below and its four sides are completely severed."
Having entered this world, he was like one holding a flower garland to show it to all the multitudes.
Having formed this thought, he entered into samādhi and manifested his supernormal powers.
Zhaò said:
Heaviness is the root of lightness; stillness is the sovereign of agitation. Without the power of samādhi, one cannot accomplish the feat of transporting the divine feet.
Thus, with his right hand, he severed and took up the world of Abhirati.
Kumārajīva said:
"I have taken it up decisively; it is clear that it has not yet come to an end.
I shall place it here in this land."
Then the Bodhisattva Prāptābhijña and the assembly of Śrāvakas, together with the other devas and humans, all raised their voices and said:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Who is taking us away?"
"May we be saved and protected!
Zhaò said:
"The Bodhisattva Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū foresaw these auspicious omens and questioned the assembly on their behalf."
The other devas and humans, not yet having understood, questioned him; fearing that [their afflictions] were not yet exhausted, they sought protection.
Acala Buddha said: "This was not done by me."
This was produced by the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti;
those who had not yet attained supernormal powers were neither aware of nor perceived where they had gone.
Although the world of Abhirati entered this land, it neither increased nor decreased, and this world likewise did not become cramped, remaining no different than before.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"You should all observe the world of Abhirati, the adornments of its land, the purity of the bodhisattvas' conduct, and the stainlessness of the disciples of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya."
They all replied:
"Indeed, we have seen it.
The Buddha said:
If a bodhisattva wishes to attain such a pure buddha-field, they should study the path practiced by the Tathāgata Acala.
Zhaò said:
"To ascend to a height, one must necessarily follow its foundation; to seek a fruit, one must necessarily trace its cause."
When this Land of Wonderful Joy was manifested, there were fourteen nayutas of people in the Sahā world.
Zao said:
"One hundred thousand is one nayuta."
They all resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and vowed to be reborn in the Land of Wonderful Joy.
Śākyamuni Buddha then bestowed upon them the prediction, saying:
"You shall be born in that land."
When the world of Abhirati had finished all the deeds necessary for the benefit of this land, it returned to its original place; the entire assembly saw this.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you see this world of Abhirati and the Buddha Akṣobhya?"
Zhaò said:
"Because Śāriputra has clarified that the assembly of sages is difficult to encounter and the Way of the Sūtras is difficult to hear, he asks separately, 'Have you seen it?
[Śāriputra replies,] 'Yes, I have indeed seen it.'"
"World-Honored One!
May all sentient beings attain a pure land like that of Akṣobhya Buddha, and obtain supernatural powers like those of Vimalakīrti.
Zhaò said:
It is because of what we have seen that we have conceived this aspiration.
World-Honored One!
We have gained a most excellent benefit in being able to see this person and to attend upon and make offerings to him.
Zhaò said: These are words of self-congratulation.

If all sentient beings—whether in the present or after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—hear this sutra, they too shall obtain excellent benefit; how much more so for those who, having heard it, believe and understand it, receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and practice it according to the Dharma.
"If there be one who obtains this sutra with their own hands, they have already obtained the treasury of the Dharma-jewel.
Sengzhao says:
"To obtain the scroll of the sutra with one's own hands, though one has not yet recited or mastered it, is like a person who has already found a treasure trove but has not yet been able to use it."
The preceding section has merely been presented by way of illustration; now, separately, their virtues are categorized according to their respective levels of attainment.
If there are those who read and recite this, explain its meaning, and practice in accordance with what is taught, they shall be protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Sengzhao said:
"Practice corresponds within and mindful protection extends without; when principle meets with profound resonance, it is simply a matter of natural law.
One who makes offerings to such a person should know that they are thereby making offerings to the Buddha."
Sengzhao said:
"Such a person is one who is protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
One should know that in the room of anyone who copies and maintains this sutra scroll, there is a Tathāgata."
Zhaò said:
"In whichever room one dwells, if one copies and maintains this sutra, one should know that the Tathāgata is present in that very room.
To copy and maintain it means to hold it with the utmost reverence in one's hands."
If one hears this sutra and is able to rejoice in accordance with it, such a person has thereby grasped all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Zhaò says:
"If one hears this sutra and is able to rejoice in accordance with its meaning, such a person will realize all-knowledge; therefore, it is said that they 'grasp' it."

If one can believe and understand this sutra, even to the extent of reciting a single four-line verse for others, you should know that such a person has received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sengzhao said:

"To clarify that the four propositions are for the sake of others' instruction brings merit greater than that of sympathetic joy; therefore, it is said that this itself constitutes receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
As for the previous mention of 'taking,' that was spoken in terms of ultimate convergence, and had not yet reached the point of the prediction."
