13. Chapter on the Dharma-Offering (10). Chapter Thirteen: On the Dharma-Offering.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Although I have heard hundreds of thousands of sutras from the Buddha and Mañjuśrī, I have never before heard this Sūtra of the Inconceivable Sovereign Supernatural Powers and the Definitive True Reality.
Kumārajīva said:

"Vimalakīrti’s reception of the world of Abhirati into this realm, as well as the inconceivable events that have occurred above, are all things I have seen before, yet none have been as marvelous as these."
The true reality elucidated in such works as the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* is vast and difficult to investigate;
this sutra briefly summarizes the essential meanings of the various scriptures, making them clear, concise, and easy to understand, and thus it is praised as something unprecedented.
It is also said that meeting me is itself sublime; thus, it is praised as something "unprecedented. Zhaò says:
As the preaching of the sutra was about to conclude, Śāriputra had already expressed his joy and admiration above; now Śakra, further rejoicing at what he has encountered, offers this praise.

Although the words of this sutra are concise, its meaning encompasses all scriptures. In less than a day, one may fully perceive its universal transformations; the subtle and profound teachings of the Mahāyāna and the power of spiritual responses through supernormal faculties are encountered all at once, leaving no principle unexhausted. Furthermore, because it accords with my own realization as something wondrous, I exclaim that it is unprecedented.

As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, if there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma of the sutra, believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, and read and recite it, they will certainly attain this Dharma without doubt.
Kumārajīva said:
"If one accumulates [merit] while possessing deep faith but little wisdom, one will certainly attain [enlightenment] after passing through the cycle of birth and death.
If one has accumulated goodness and attained deep awakening, it will be accomplished immediately according to their vow; whether it takes long or short is not limited by the number of kalpas."
How much more so for those who practice according to the teaching!
Zhaò says:
"This Dharma refers to the aforementioned inconceivable, sovereign supernormal powers, which are the definitive reality-mark (dharmatā) of all phenomena."

As I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching, it is profound and difficult to encounter; if one hears it and is able to recite and uphold it, they will certainly attain [realization] without doubt, let alone those who practice according to the teaching. The virtues of such persons shall be set forth below.
Such a person shall close off all evil destinies.
Zhaò said: "The eight difficult conditions and the various realms of existence."
It opens all gates of goodness.
Zao says: "These are the gates to the human and celestial realms, as well as to Nirvana."
He is constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas; he subdues those of external paths and destroys the enmity of Māra.
Zhaò says: "The four [types of] Māras are the enemies."
"to cultivate and purify bodhi.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the Sanskrit original, there is the word 'path' (mārga) following 'bodhi'."
The Way refers to the path leading toward Bodhi.
One dwells peacefully within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Zhaò says:
To attain the Way of the Buddha within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is called bodhi.
Although one has not yet attained it now, one is already cultivating and preparing the Way of the Buddha, establishing oneself within the site of enlightenment,
and treading upon the tracks traversed by the Tathāgatas.
Zhaò said:
"To practice according to the teaching is to act in the same manner as the Buddha,
World-Honored One!"

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to the teaching, I shall provide offerings and service together with my retinue. In whatever village, city, mountain forest, or wilderness this sutra may be found, I shall also go to that place together with my retinue for the sake of hearing and receiving the Dharma; those who have not yet developed faith, I shall cause to develop faith, and those who already have faith, I shall act as their protectors.
Sengzhao said:
The Heavenly Emperor rejoiced at what he encountered and thus offered this unprecedented praise; furthermore, he wished to protect and nurture [the Buddha] in order to propagate his Way.
Thus spoke the Buddha!
Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Devas!
It is just as you have said; I join you in your joy.
This sutra extensively explains the inconceivable *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Kumārajīva said:
"In the Sanskrit original, there is the word 'dharma' following this 'bodhi'."
Huisheng said:
"When the sutras speak of the Buddha’s wisdom, then that wisdom resides within the sutras.
If the sutras indeed possess wisdom, they are then the Dharma-body of the Buddha."
Therefore, O Lord of Devas!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, and makes offerings to this sutra, they are thereby making offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Sengzhao said:
This praises the intention of his protection and upholding.

The inconceivable path of Bodhi throughout the three periods of time is all set forth in this sutra; if one receives, maintains, and nurtures it, that constitutes making offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods. Therefore, I join you in your joy.
Daosheng said:
"As for those who provide offerings of food and clothing, they sustain and nourish one's four limbs.

If one receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, one not only preserves its principle but also causes the Buddha’s Dharma-body to increase daily; does this not also possess the meaning of making an offering?"
"O Lord of Devas!
Suppose the trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, as densely as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp.
If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for an eon or slightly less than an eon, honored, revered, praised, made offerings to, and provided all necessities for their comfort."

After the parinirvāṇa of each of those Buddhas, one shall erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances for each of their entire bodily relics (śarīra), with a base as wide as a four-continent world-system and reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven, adorned with a pinnacle and banners, and make offerings to them for a kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, using all manner of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, and music of the most exquisite and supreme kind.
"What do you think, Śakra, Lord of the Devas?
Would the merit planted by that person not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"It is much,
World-Honored One!
The merit of that person could not be fully exhausted even if it were explained for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas."
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"You should know that if these sons and daughters of good family hear this *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Liberation*, believe in it, understand it, accept and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice its teachings, their merit will be far greater than that."
Zhaò said:
"The merit of making offerings is compared to the wisdom that understands Prajñā; various scriptures have similar points of corroboration.
Shēng said:

Offering clothing and food is fundamentally a merit derived from the labor of giving; it is not a method for seeking the ultimate principle. Based on this alone, one may indeed be reborn among humans or devas, but in the end, one shall not attain Buddhahood.
As for those who make offerings to the Dharma-body, they take as their heart's concern that which the Buddha has realized, reaching the wisdom of great enlightenment.
When compared with [the other], how could their superiority and inferiority even be mentioned in the same breath?
Why is this? Because the bodhi of all Buddhas is born from this.
Birth said:
By realizing the principles of this sutra,
one will ultimately attain Bodhi; therefore,
[the Buddha] was born from within it.
The characteristics of bodhi are immeasurable.
Daosheng said:
"Bodhi is without characteristics; it cannot be measured by the mind."
For these reasons, the merit is immeasurable.
Zhaò said:

"Tall trees must grow from deep soil, and jades must be born from the Jing mountains; thus, immeasurable fruits must necessarily arise from immeasurable causes. The Bodhi of all Buddhas is born entirely from practicing this sutra."
The path to bodhi takes the signless as its characteristic; this signless characteristic is immeasurable. Because of this, merit is produced—how could that merit be measured?
Jīvaka said:
"To take up and maintain [the teaching] through signlessness is a merit that is inexhaustible.
The Buddha told Śakra:

In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world was called Mahāvyūha, and the Buddha’s lifespan was twenty minor kalpas.
His community of śrāvakas numbered thirty-six billion nayutas, and his community of bodhisattvas numbered one billion two hundred million.
O Lord of Devas!
At that time, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Ratnacchattra, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four quarters of the world.
The king had a thousand sons, handsome, brave, and strong, capable of subduing enemies.
At that time, Ratnacchattra, together with his retinue, made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, providing all necessities for his comfort for a full five kalpas.
After five kalpas had passed, he addressed his thousand sons:
"You all should also, like me, make offerings to the Buddha with a profound mind.
Thereupon, the thousand sons received their father-king’s command and made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja for another full five kalpas, providing all things that bring peace and security.
Zhaò said:
"The former refers to material offerings, while 'receiving and upholding' refers to the offering of the Dharma.
Since the Tathāgata was about to establish the meaning of the offering of the Dharma, he cited this accomplished fact as proof."
One of that king’s sons, named Candracchattra, sat alone in contemplation, thinking:
"Could there be an offering superior to this?
Śrīmitra said:

I hope that perhaps there may be some great virtue among the various devas who will provide extraordinary offerings; if there should be anything surpassing this, I would aspire to attain it. [The donor] says:

"Though I have exhausted all that I hold precious, I cannot thereby fully delight the Holy One's mind. I hope that beyond these treasures there may be something with which to express my sincere devotion; thus I give rise to this thought to further contemplate superior offerings."
Sengzhao said:

"The finest delicacies of the world cannot fully express the sentiment of ultimate attainment; I hope that beyond these cherished things, there exists a subtle nourishment to give full vent to my sincere heart."
Furthermore, because past karmic conditions were destined to converge, he gave rise to this thought.
Daosheng said:
"He cited the past to verify that making offerings to the Dharma-body is superior."
By the Buddha's spiritual power, a deity in the air said:
"O son of good family!
The offering of the Dharma surpasses all other offerings."
Kumārajīva said:
"If it were an offering of material wealth, it would be of no use to the Buddha and of no benefit to sentient beings; therefore, it is not what [the Buddha] delights in.

The Tathāgata has spent kalpas for the sake of sentient beings from the beginning; if one reverently follows the scriptures and practices according to the teachings, this will please the Holy One's heart, and that is true worship."
Zhaò said:
"The Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, knowing that [the practitioner] was about to undergo transformation, manifested as an empty deity and addressed him.
Shēng said:
As for the offering of Dharma, practicing the Dharma is itself the offering.
He then asked:
"What is meant by the offering of Dharma?"
The deva said, "You should go and question the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; he shall extensively explain for you the offering of the Dharma.
Thereupon, Prince Candracchattra went to the presence of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. What is meant by the ‘offering of the Dharma’?
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The Dharma-offering consists of the profound sutras spoken by all Buddhas.
Kumārajīva said:
The Tripiṭaka, the Kṣudraka-piṭaka, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka constitute the five collections of sūtras.
As for the aforementioned four piṭakas, because they take the profound meaning from within [the sūtras] to explain such things as the true nature (dharmatā), they are classified as profound sūtras.

From this point until the end of the section on the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, all that has been spoken is an extensive praise of the profound sutras taught by the Buddha; it does not yet clarify the meaning of the dharma-offering consisting of receiving, upholding, practicing, and cultivating them.
Tanheng said:
"First, clarify the sutras.
By 'profound sutras' is meant those spoken by the Buddha that expound the Dharma of the true mark (dharmatā) as the path for bodhisattvas."
"It is difficult for all the world to believe and difficult to accept.
Daosheng said:
"The principle of the true mark (śūnyatā) is uniform; how could there be such things as deep or shallow?"
The sentiments of the world are the opposite of this; it is extremely difficult to believe and accept, as it is beyond their reach, and is therefore profound.
It is subtle and wondrous, and difficult to perceive.
Sengsheng said:
It is wondrous and transcends the human mind; it is difficult to behold.
It is pure and undefiled.
Zhaò said:
The "profound sutras" refer to the Vaipulya sutras of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Their purport is profound and mysterious, beyond the reach of the conscious mind;
they are subtle and wondrous, without form, and cannot be perceived even by the enlightened.
Transcending the realm of sensory dust, it is unstained like empty space.
Is it not difficult for those who seek to believe and perceive through a mind possessed of thought and clarity?
From this point downward, the profound purport of the sutra is praised.
The profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas are the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
Now, material sustenance nourishes the four physical elements, whereas the sustenance of the Dharma nourishes the Dharma-body.
If one can protect and uphold this sūtra, causing the Dharma-body to increase and expand, this constitutes the highest form of offering.
Dongsheng said:
"Since there is no characteristic to be grasped, defilement cannot arise.
If one can perceive this, defilement will also be eliminated."
"It is not something that can be attained merely through conceptual discrimination and reflection.
Kumārajīva said:
"It must necessarily rely on various merits such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); it cannot be attained merely through the power of wisdom and discrimination."
It is also said that one must employ actual wisdom before being able to comprehend it; it cannot be understood through the grasping of conceptualized marks.
Zhaò said:
"The Sūtra of the Ultimate Truth is subtle, remote, and markless; were it not for one who is enlightened and wise, who could possibly discern it?"

Although the differentiation of karma arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it cannot be attained through conceptual discrimination; only non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) can attain it.
Therefore, it is said that it is not merely conceptual discrimination [that attains it].
Sheng said:
"One must accumulate merit before they can meet.
This is encompassed within the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas."
Kumārajīva said:
"Generally speaking, whatever Dharma is preached for Bodhisattvas that can bring them to fulfillment is all subsumed within the Bodhisattva Dharma-treasury.
Daosheng said:
This is the essence embodied by this Bodhisattva, such that no being can peer into it;
it is sealed with the seal of dhāraṇī.
Kumārajīva said:
Dhāraṇī is immeasurable; the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is one such dhāraṇī.
If a sūtra speaks of the true mark, that true mark is itself the seal (mudrā).
To seal this sūtra with the seal of the true mark is to make it a profound sūtra.
Furthermore, "yin" (印) is called "xiang" (相) in the Sanskrit original, meaning the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Taking the true mark as the sutra refers to the defining characteristic.
Zhaò said:
Being subsumed within the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, it is not the treasure of the Hīnayāna.
Sealed by the seal of *dhāraṇī*, it is certainly not a path for those confined within the mundane realm.
That which is sealed by *dhāraṇī* must necessarily be true.
It is subsumed within the Dharma-treasury, and what is so subsumed must necessarily be a treasure.

Since it is a treasury by virtue of being the Dharma-treasury and a seal by virtue of being the *dhāraṇī*, how could it possibly be something that an ordinary person is capable of opening and revealing?
This demonstrates that the Dharma-treasure is profound and firm, difficult to peer into.
Daosheng said:
"Dhāraṇī" means "to uphold."
If one maintains the true mark (dharmatā) without loss, one will no longer fear that there may be meanings one cannot penetrate among gods, humans, Māras, or Brahmās.
It is like a living seal used as a credential; at passes and barriers, none can obstruct or detain it.
The fruit is the seal of authentication; the sutras thus sealed are without obstruction and lead to the stage of non-retrogression.
Sheng said:
In principle, there is no place from which one can regress; by following this path, one will surely reach the goal.
One accomplishes the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
Kumārajīva said:
It is said that this sutra enables people to avoid regression and to accomplish the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). Zhaò says:

"The reason one reaches the six perfections is through non-regression; the reason the six perfections bring about the Mahāyāna is that there is nothing from which the Mahāyāna emerges that does not derive from this scripture."
Sheng said:
"It is not merely that they do not regress; rather, they reach the very limits of all dharmas.
They are skilled in discerning their meanings."
Jizang said:
"The meaning refers to the principle within the words, and this sutra skillfully distinguishes it.
It accords with the Dharma of Bodhi."
Kumārajīva said:
"The profound sūtras explain the principle without error; therefore, they are said to 'skillfully discern.
Because they skillfully discern, they accord with bodhi."
Sengzhao said:
"To skillfully discern the meaning of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is to accord with the dharma of bodhi’s signlessness.
Sengsheng said:
Precisely because it takes up the Dharma of Bodhi as its sūtra, there is no contradiction;
it stands at the pinnacle of all sūtras.
Kumārajīva said:
To cite its most profound aspect, it stands as the foremost among all the scriptures.
Zhaò says:
"Among the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the canon, the Vaipulya (fangděng) is the first."
Dharmarakṣa said:
"It stands above all the ninety-six kinds of scriptures;
it enters into great compassion."
Kumārajīva said:
"The profound sutras can cause people to enter [the Way].
Sengzhao said:

The reason profound sutras are established is to build [the foundation], and the reason for compassion is to propagate [it]; those who enter them must do so through great kindness and great compassion.
Therefore, the profound Vaipulya sutras all enter into great kindness and great compassion, merging into a single essence.
Sheng said:
"One who clearly perceives the principles of the Dharma will certainly be able to instruct those who have not yet attained understanding and remain free from the various works of Māra."
Kumārajīva said:
"All that is not in accordance with the Dharma, including all matters concerning Māra and various false views.
Sengzhao said:
"Māra" refers to the four māras.
"Views" refers to the sixty-two views.
Once the True Teaching has been widely propagated, all heterodoxies will naturally cease.
Dongsheng said:
"Demons and heterodoxies both arise from delusion; if one realizes this sutra, one will be free from them.
This accords with the law of dependent origination."
Kumārajīva said:

"If a dharma were fixedly existent, it would neither arise nor cease; if a dharma were entirely non-existent, it likewise would neither arise nor cease. Since non-arising and non-ceasing are contrary to the nature of causes and conditions [dependent origination], [the former two views are untenable]."
What is taught in the profound sūtras is neither existent nor non-existent; because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it accords with the principle of dependent origination.
Daosheng said:
"This teaching does not contradict the principle of dependent origination."
There is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span; there is emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-arising.

Zhaò said:
"This is what profound scriptures are capable of.
Shēng said:

Kumārajīva said:

Because the profound sutras can bring about the realization of the Buddha-way and the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, gods and humans receive deliverance; this is why the various sages together extol the profound sutras.

Śāriputra said:

Sengzhao said:
"There has never been one who could enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma while abandoning and turning their back on the profound sutras.
Sengsheng said:
One who masters this sutra enters the treasury of the Buddha-dharma,
encompassing all the wisdom of the worthies and sages.

Sengsheng said:

This explains the path practiced by the various bodhisattvas.

Shengyun said:

Regarding the meaning of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena,

Sengsheng said:
"These words do not depart from the fundamental tenets.

"In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, those who commit the five heinous crimes or violate the four grave prohibitions are all abandoned and not saved.

"Only the profound Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras are capable of saving and extinguishing [suffering]!
Sheng said:

It is that which all Buddhas and worthy sages alike praise and extol.

Were it not for the profound sutras, who could have opened this path?
Huisheng said:

Sengzhao said:

although antiquity and the present differ, their Way does not change. This clarifies that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is eternally constant, uniform, and without deviation."
The profound and wondrous sutra concludes here.
Daosheng said:
"Among the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, there are none who are not identical."
If one hears such sutras as these—
Sengzhao says that because the Mahāyāna profound sutras are immeasurable in their divisions, he uses the term "such as" (等)— and with faith, understanding, and resolve,
upholds, recites, and reads them, then by the power of skillful means, one shall analyze, explain, and clearly manifest them for the sake of all sentient beings.
Because it protects the Dharma, this is called the "Dharma-offering.
Kumārajīva said:

Sengzhao said:
"Sūtras such as these exhaustively encompass the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.

If one hears this sūtra and is able to believe, understand, protect, uphold, proclaim, and explain it, thereby causing the Great Dharma to increase and expand, this is called 'Dharma-offering,' which nurtures and perfects the Dharma-body."
Dharmodgata said:
"Because upholding, maintaining, reading, and reciting these [teachings] has the meaning of 'protection,' it is called the 'Dharma-offering.

From the section on the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*) onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*), whereby one accords with the true Dharma through real wisdom.
Sengzhao says:

"Above, one used faith and understanding to protect, uphold, proclaim, and disseminate [the teaching] as a nourishment for the Dharma; now, it clarifies that internal practice in accord with reality constitutes the offering of the Dharma."
"All dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the six perfections as expounded in the profound sutras.
Daosheng said:
"Those who practice according to what the sutras teach are the most profound; therefore, they are explained separately."
To accord with the twelve links of dependent origination means that one's sentiments no longer deviate from the principle of dependent origination.
He is free from all false views.
Sheng said:
"Since one accords with the principle of dependent origination, one is free from all false views of existence and non-existence."
He attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Daosheng said:
"To accord with the principle of dependent origination and no longer harbor false views is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."
It is determined that there is no self and no sentient beings.
Zhaò says:
"Because they do not awaken to dependent origination, there arises the delusion of false views and the confusion of clinging to a self."

If one practices according to what has been taught, one will attain clear wisdom; by clearly seeing the source and origin of the twelve links of dependent origination, one is able to leave behind all false views and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), no longer harboring notions of a self or sentient beings.
To perceive conditions as they truly are is called "conformity" (anuloma); to clearly discern existence and non-existence is called "certainty" (niścaya).
Both are alternative designations for the functioning of wisdom regarding causes, conditions, and karmic retribution.
Daosheng said:
"As for the vision of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it is definitive.
Although there is no self and no sentient beings, it is not that there is no subject who undergoes retribution."
"There is no contradiction and no dispute.
Kumārajīva said:
"Because one perceives phenomena as they truly are, there is no contradiction; because there is no contradiction, there is no dispute."
"Free from all that belongs to a self.
Zhaò says:
"To have neither opposition nor contention is the meaning of 'conformity' (anuloma)."
The body of the five aggregates of clinging, along with one's family and all their causal conditions and karmic retributions, constitute "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*).
If one can clearly perceive the nature of these causal conditions and karmic retributions, following them without opposition, then one is free from all that belongs to me.
Previously, by directly observing causes and conditions, one knows there is no creator; thus, one abandons the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
Now, by observing the retribution of causes and conditions, one knows there is nothing to which anything belongs; thus, one abandons the view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*).
Jīvaka said:
"It is also free from 'mine-ness.
One should rely on the meaning, not on the words."
Sengzhao said:
"The ultimate meaning cannot be proclaimed through words; to seek it by following words is to lose the ultimate.

Furthermore, the wondrous principle is eternally one, yet speech must be without fixed form. To wish to determine this eternally one principle with speech that is without fixed form—is this not erroneous?"
Therefore, "relying on the meaning and not on the words" refers to clear vision.
Sengsheng said:
"One no longer pursues the words or grasps at appearances, thereby remaining oblivious to the underlying principle."
"Rely on wisdom (*jñāna*), do not rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Zhaò said:
"The six consciousnesses merely cognize the six sense objects; they cannot distinguish between right and wrong. Only correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) can distinguish between right and wrong."
Therefore, the practitioner relies on wisdom (*jñāna*) and does not rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Daosheng said:
"If consciousness takes attachment as its nature and wisdom takes the penetration of principle as its function, one will ultimately never again follow consciousness while deviating from wisdom."
"Rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha), not on sūtras of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
Sengzhao says:
"Among the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, one should rely on those whose intended meaning is inherently clear, exhaustive, and easy to understand."

There are also scriptures that respond to the times; however, their deceptive words may appear to accord with the Way, yet the Sage’s intention is difficult to fathom. Those who have not yet attained realization themselves must not rely upon them.
Daosheng said:
"One who discerns the principles relies upon the sūtras of definitive meaning."
"Though it may be called clever rhetoric, if it lacks principle, it is of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
Rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
Kumārajīva said:
The Buddha said: "After my parinirvāṇa, you should rely upon four dharmas as your Great Teacher; these are the so-called Four Reliances.
It is clear that these four dharmas are what one may rely upon and what one may trust and accept."

Regarding "rely on the Dharma, not on the person": "Dharma" refers to the scriptural teachings. One should rely on the scriptural Dharma; one must not, because of the superiority of a person, turn away from the Dharma to rely on that person.
The Dharma is of two kinds:
first, words and language; second, the meaning of the Dharma.
Do not rely on the words; the meaning also has two kinds:
There are two kinds of objects known: first, those known by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and second, those known by wisdom (*jñāna*).

Consciousness seeks only the illusory five desires and does not seek true benefit, whereas wisdom seeks true benefit and abandons the five desires; therefore, one relies on the objects known by wisdom and does not rely on the objects known by consciousness.
Because one seeks the meaning known by wisdom, one relies upon wisdom.
There are also two kinds of meanings known by wisdom:
first, sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha); second, sūtras of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).

An *neyārtha* (interpretable) sūtra is, for example, when the Buddha says that there is no fault in killing one's father or mother; because this has not been further analyzed, it is of interpretable meaning.

If it is said that ignorance is the father and craving is the mother—so called because they are the root of birth and death—and that by severing their root, birth and death are exhausted, therefore it is said that killing them entails no fault.
Having thus distinguished them, this is a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, if the Buddha says:
"The Buddha is the foremost among humans; nirvāṇa is the foremost among dharmas."
All such [teachings] as these are called definitive (nītārtha).
Therefore, one should rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not rely on sūtras of non-definitive meaning.
Zhaò said:
Although the Dharma is propagated by persons, persons do not necessarily accord entirely with the Dharma.
The Dharma possesses fixed standards, whereas persons lack constant principles; therefore, practitioners rely on the Dharma and not on persons.
Sheng said:
"When people practice principle and there is no unrighteousness, this constitutes the Dharma.
If one truly speaks of having the Dharma, one must not exclude those of lowly station."
If it is not the Dharma, even if it be most precious and most exalted, one shall not follow it.
One should accord with the characteristics of the Dharma, having no point of entry and no place of refuge.
Zhaò says:
"Dharma" refers here to the dharma of dependent origination.
Previously, by conforming to dependent origination, one knew that dharmas are unarisen; now, by conforming to dependent origination, one knows that dharmas are inexhaustible.

Phenomena exist through conditions and cease through conditions; their existence does not come from the future, and their non-existence does not return to the past. Therefore, it is said that they have no entry and no departure.
Daosheng said:
"Furthermore, this accords with the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) being without entry and without return.
That 'exhaustion' of no entry and no return is not itself a reality."

"Because ignorance is ultimately extinguished, the formative forces (saṃskāra) are also ultimately extinguished; and so on, until because birth is ultimately extinguished, old age and death are also ultimately extinguished.
Kumārajīva said:
"This is precisely the 'Dharma as it truly is' among the Four Reliances."

The preceding section on the twelve links of dependent origination clarified that by practicing in accordance with the teachings and following the conditions of dependent origination, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); the present section clarifies that one practices the four reliances based upon the true mark (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Sengzhao said:
"Ignorance is the root of the twelve [links of dependent origination].
Once ignorance is extinguished, the remaining conditions are also extinguished."
"Ultimate" means that from beginning to end it is eternally extinguished and does not undergo further extinction.
That it is eternally extinguished from beginning to end and does not undergo further extinction is precisely what constitutes the meaning of "inexhaustible extinction."
Sheng said:
"That which ultimately perishes must necessarily do so.
Since it must ultimately perish, how could there be such a thing as arising?"
If birth does not exist, who is there to undergo cessation?
Thus, there is neither entry nor return.
One should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in this way as being devoid of the characteristic of exhaustion.
Zhaò said: "The meaning of 'extinction' (nirodha) is one and the same. Since it is called 'ultimate extinction,' why then is it called 'inexhaustible' (akṣaya)?

Now, extinction arises from non-extinction; if there is ultimate and constant extinction, then there is no non-extinction. Where there is no non-extinction, extinction has nothing to extinguish. That extinction has nothing to extinguish is precisely the meaning of 'inexhaustibility.'"
No further views arise.
Zhaò says:
"Observing above that causes and conditions are without arising, one is free from all views such as permanence and a self."
Now, observing that causes and conditions are inexhaustible, one is free from views such as annihilationism and eternalism.
This is called the supreme offering of the Dharma.
Zhaò said:

If one can practice in accordance with the profound sūtras, clearly perceive dependent origination, fulfill the four reliances, and remain free from all views, this is the supreme form of Dharma-sustenance.
While the preceding section simply clarifies recitation and retention, this refers to internal practice that should be followed; therefore, it is called the most supreme.
Śāriputra said:
"To recite, chant, read, and explain [the teachings], and furthermore to offer them clothing and food—this is the most supreme.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
Prince Candracchattra, having heard this Dharma from the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja, attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti*.
Kumārajīva said:
"Anu" (柔) means soft and dull.

Because one has not yet deeply penetrated the Dharma of the true nature (*dharmatā*), but follows it with mild wisdom and mild faith without opposition, it is called "patience in accordance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
Sengzhao says:
When the mind is supple and wisdom is compliant, such that one is capable of receiving the true nature but has not yet reached non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is called patience in accordance.
He immediately removed his precious robes and ornaments from his body to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, I shall perform the offering of the Dharma and protect the True Dharma."
"I pray that you will, through your majestic spiritual power, bestow your compassion and establish me, so that I may subdue the demonic enemies and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"The four māras are combined into three enemies: first, the afflictions (kleśa); second, the celestial māra; and third, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika)."

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Candracchattra’s power of the Path will not yet be fully developed; if his majestic spiritual power is not augmented, he will be destroyed by Māra and unable to subdue him. Therefore, I request that you augment his majestic spiritual power.
Sengzhao said:

"Having heard of the offering of the Dharma, I joyfully desire to practice it; however, as the Way of the Sūtras is profound and far-reaching, it is beyond the power of my own strength to propagate. Therefore, I pray that you will add your majestic spiritual power."
The Buddha, knowing the profound thoughts in his mind, bestowed this prediction upon him.
Kumārajīva said:
"It was intended to inspire faith and submission in future generations; therefore, he recorded that [the Buddha] would protect the treasury of the Dharma."
"You shall guard the city of the Dharma at the end of time,
O Śakra! At that time,
Prince Candracchattra, having seen the purity of the Dharma and heard the Buddha’s prophecy, went forth into homelessness out of faith."
Kumārajīva said:

"If one is entangled by worldly defilements, one deviates from the pure Dharma; knowing that such a place of impurity is not where the Way is propagated, one leaves the household life to cultivate purity in order to propagate the pure Dharma."
Having cultivated and accumulated wholesome dharmas with diligence for no long time, he attained the five supernormal powers and was fully endowed with the path of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"This clarifies his unimpeded nature, as described in the *Tongda fodao jing* (Sūtra on Attaining the Buddha Path)."
He attained dhāraṇī.
Kumārajīva said:
"This is the power of hearing and retaining."
"Uninterrupted eloquence.
Kumārajīva said:
"Eloquence is inexhaustible; it is never interrupted regardless of whether one's discourse is long or short."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, by means of the power of the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), dhāraṇī, and eloquence (pratibhāna) he had attained, Kumārajīva said:

"By the power of supernormal knowledge, one can manifest transformations and know the minds of others; by the power of dhāraṇī, one does not lose what has been heard; and by the power of eloquence, one can explain [the Dharma] equally for the sake of others."
Possessing these three powers, one is able to proclaim and disseminate the bequeathed Dharma.
For ten small kalpas, the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja was distributed accordingly.
Zhaò said:
"To distribute the Wheel of Dharma is precisely to propagate the teaching and nourish it.

The bhikṣu Candracchattra, through his diligent practice of vigor in guarding the Dharma, transformed one hundred trillion people within this very body, establishing them in non-retrogression toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; fourteen *nayuta* of people deeply gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; and immeasurable sentient beings attained rebirth in the heavens."
"O Lord of Devas!
Was King Ratnacchattra anyone else at that time?
He is none other than the one who has now attained Buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata Ratnārcis."
The king’s thousand sons are none other than the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Beginning with K Krakucchanda, they shall attain Buddhahood, the last Tathāgata being named Ruci.
The bhikṣu Candracchattra was none other than myself.
Thus, O Śakra, you should know this essential point: among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme, foremost, and peerless.
Zhaò said:
"I attained perfect enlightenment through the offering of the Dharma; by this it may be known that the nourishment of the Dharma is supreme.
Therefore, O Devendra!"
One should honor the Buddha with the offering of the Dharma.
Zhaò says:
"Practicing the nourishment of the Dharma is itself honoring the Buddha."
14. Chapter on the Entrustment (10). Chapter Fourteen: The Entrustment. Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!
I now [entrust] to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have accumulated over immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
Kumārajīva said:
"I declare that this sutra is the cause of Bodhi.
I entrust it to you."
Kumārajīva said:
"He did not entrust it to Ānanda because he lacked the divine power to propagate it widely; therefore, he did not entrust it to him.
Vimalakīrti was not a bodhisattva of this land, and thus he was not instructed."
Mañjuśrī wanders without a fixed direction, and therefore he did not give his charge.
He charged Maitreya because it is here that he will attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha himself, by means of his supernormal power, proclaimed this, desiring to fulfill Maitreya’s meritorious achievements.
Sengzhao said: "The *Acintya-sūtra* is the path to the Buddha’s unsurpassed bodhi; this path is profound and far-reaching, difficult to achieve.

Over immeasurable kalpas, I have not spared my own body or life; my flesh offered was greater than Mount Sumeru, and my blood offered exceeded the rivers and seas. Through diligent and bitter accumulation, it has only now been brought to completion. Out of compassion for those who remain lost in long-term delusion, I have committed it to bamboo and silk."

However, sentient beings possess meager merit and the works of Māra are rampant; my Way faces many difficulties. It is not that you lack the capacity to propagate it, but rather because you are the one destined to succeed to the true Dharma, that I entrust this to you with such gravity.
"Regarding such sūtras as these, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the final age, you all should widely proclaim and disseminate them through your supernormal powers.
Kumārajīva said:
"By employing supernormal powers, one can subdue the enmity of Māra and propagate [the teachings] extensively and without obstruction."
"Let there be no interruption [of the Dharma] in Jambudvīpa. Zhaò said:
"When city walls are high, the people's lives are secure; when the Way is honored, the Māras flourish."
Were it not for supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), there would be no means to sustain and uphold this;
therefore, I exhort you to employ supernatural power.

Why is this? In future ages, there will be good men and good women, as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others, who resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and delight in the Great Dharma.
"If they were not allowed to hear such sutras as these, they would lose their opportunity for wholesome benefit.
Kumārajīva said:
"If they do not hear this sutra, they may fall into the two vehicles and thus lose the wholesome benefits of the Mahayana."
When people of such caliber hear sūtras of this kind, they will surely have much faith and joy, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder.
They should receive them upon the crown of their heads and preach them extensively according to the benefits that should be gained by each sentient being.
Sengzhao said:
Since the opening and closing, the loss and gain of the Dharma are such as this, I therefore urge Maitreya to receive it upon his head and proclaim it extensively.
Maitreya, you should know that there are two characteristics of a bodhisattva.
Kumārajīva said:
"If one prefers miscellaneous phrases, one should be taught with literary texts;
if one prefers profound doctrine, one should be instructed in its meaning."
One must understand their characteristics; therefore, these two characteristics are distinguished.
Zhaò says:
The depths of practice each have their distinct characteristics; both gain and loss are presented here to urge those who protect and uphold the Dharma.
What are these two?
The first is a fondness for miscellaneous phrases and ornate literary embellishments.
Zhaò says:
What is "literature"?
It is merely the tether and the trap for the subtle meaning.

Yet those of new learning possess shallow wisdom; they are unable to set aside words to seek the underlying principle, but instead abandon the root to pursue the branches, cherishing only literary embellishment.
Second, they do not fear profound meanings and are able to enter them as they truly are.
Zhaò said:
"The sublime purport is dark and deep; these subtle words run counter to the mundane. Were it not for one possessed of wisdom and courage, who could penetrate so deeply?"
If one delights in miscellaneous phrases, literary embellishments, and worldly matters, you should know that this is a newly initiated bodhisattva;

if, however, one has no fear regarding such profound sūtras that are untainted and unattached, is able to enter into them, and having heard them, purifies the mind, upholds, recites, and practices according to the teaching, you should know that this is one who has long cultivated the path of practice.
Zhaò said:
"As for the profoundity of the *Anupalipta-anupalambha-sūtra*, were it not for those who have practiced for a long time, who could be without fear?
Maitreya!"
"Furthermore, there are two dharmas called those of the 'newly initiated.
Kumārajīva said:

'I wish to cause people to have faith and delight in the profound sūtras; therefore, being cautious regarding the faults of the newly initiated, I have recorded the faults of the newly initiated in detail.'"
They are unable to resolve themselves regarding the profound Dharma. What are these two?
First, upon hearing profound sūtras they have not previously heard, they become startled, terrified, and give rise to doubt.
Kumārajīva said:
"At first hearing, one is startled; upon further investigation, one becomes doubtful; being doubtful, one gives rise to slander.
Unable to follow along with it, they revile and do not believe, saying these words:"

First, I have never heard from where [such people] come; second, if there are those who protect, uphold, and explain such profound sutras, they are unwilling to draw near to them, make offerings to them, or respect them, and may even at times speak of their faults and evils.
Sengzhao said:
"The first is to disparage the Dharma; the second is to disparage the person.
When these two conditions exist, one should know that this is a newly initiated bodhisattva who brings about self-injury and is unable to discipline his mind within the profound Dharma."
“Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are two dharmas by which a bodhisattva, despite having faith and understanding of the profound Dharma, still brings about self-injury and cannot attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Zhaò said:

Although those of superior capacity heard the profound sutras, they were unable to believe and understand them; although those of present-day superior capacity believe and understand them, they are unable to practice accordingly. These two points clearly illustrate various failings to test future students.
What are these two?
"First, they treat newly initiated bodhisattvas with contempt and fail to instruct them.
Kumārajīva said:
"They give rise to arrogance because they rely on their own profound understanding."
Sengzhao said:

"Though one may understand profound meanings, if they have not yet become the functioning of the mind, and if one honors oneself and treats others with contempt, one will be unable to receive instruction and benefit.
This is an external affliction for the student."
Second, although one understands profound dharmas, one still grasps at signs and engages in conceptual discrimination.
These are the two dharmas.
Kumārajīva said:
Although he does not give rise to arrogance, there remains the affliction of grasping at signs.
Zhaò says:
Because one grasps at signs and makes distinctions based on what one understands, although it is called "understanding," it does not accord with true understanding.
This is an internal affliction for those who study.
Having heard these words, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"It is unprecedented!
It is just as the Buddha has taught.
Kumārajīva said:
This praises the sūtras spoken by the Buddha above and distinguishes the various characteristics of bodhisattvas.
[The author] says: "I shall distance myself from such evils. Zhaò says:
How could a Great Being who has practiced throughout a lifetime incur such evil retribution that he must hear [the teaching] before being able to leave it behind?
Those who speak such words refer only to those who have not yet left it behind.
He upholds the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which the Tathāgata accumulated over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
"If there are good men or good women in future ages who seek the Mahāyāna, they shall be caused to obtain such sūtras as these in their own hands, and I shall grant them the power of mindfulness.
Kumārajīva said:
"By means of supernatural powers, I shall augment their power of mindfulness so that they do not forget."
Question:
In the past, Māra would constantly descend to disrupt and confuse those who were training; for what reason does he not come now? Answer:

By the power of Upagupta, during the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a non-Buddhist teacher named Saccaka Nigaṇṭha. He was highly intelligent and skilled in debate, yet his mind was filled with great arrogance. Knowing that the Buddha’s Dharma was sublime and excellent, he desired to leave the household life.
He asked the Buddha,
"If I were to leave the household life, would my wisdom, virtue, and renown be equal to yours?
The Buddha said:
"No. He asked again:
"Is it possible to be like Śāriputra?"
The Buddha said, "No.
In this manner, he questioned each of the five hundred disciples one by one, until he asked, "Is there anyone who has attained [the fruit] as Rāhula has?"
He replied,
"I cannot. Thereupon,
the Nirgrantha said:
"I have left the household life, yet I have attained nothing like the Buddha, nor have I attained anything like his disciples; what is the use of leaving the household life?
He asked again:
"Will I attain it in the future?"
The Buddha said: "In a future age, when there are no great beings, you shall then attain it.

After Nigaṇṭha has passed away, you will be born during the time of King Aśoka, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. You will leave the household life to study the Way and attain arhatship, gaining great renown. You will teach and transform the people of the country, leading them to attain arhatship. In counting those who have been saved, we do not include cases where the husband is saved but the wife is not, or where the wife is saved but the husband is not; we count only those couples who both simultaneously attain arhatship. If one were to count them with tally sticks, the accumulation would fill the house."
Later, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he cremated himself using counting-sticks and required no other materials.

Before his parinirvāṇa, while practicing seated meditation in a forest, he saw a starving dog, emaciated with hunger and on the verge of death; he would regularly set aside portions of his own food to give to it.
The bhikṣus each divided their food and gave it to him, until the dog’s belly swelled and he was on the verge of death.
At that time, the bhikṣus each sat upon rope-cots, surrounding and guarding him while reciting sūtras and preaching the Dharma.

The dog looked upon the bhikṣus with a virtuous mind and heard the sound of the Dharma; when its life ended, it was reborn in the sixth heaven, where it possessed great majesty and sat together with Māra.
At that time, the dog had already become putrid and rotten; the Māra thought to himself:
"For what reason is this Great Man sitting together with me?
Upon examining their past karmic conditions, he realized it was a dog, and he became greatly incensed:
"This monk Upagupta has allowed this stinking dog to sit with me; I shall employ a skillful means to bring him humiliation.

At that time, while Upagupta was sitting in meditation in the forest and had entered the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), Māra immediately bound a magnificent celestial flower garland upon his forehead and addressed the fourfold assembly at length, inviting them all to come and see him.
"This bhikṣu adorns himself in such a manner in this secluded place; how can he be called pure and virtuous?
After a short while, Upagupta arose from his concentration, noticed a flower garland upon his head, and realizing it was the work of Māra, immediately pointed at him, saying:
"You are King Māra!"
He immediately took a dead dog and transformed it into a flower garland, most exquisitely adorned.
He said to Māra, "You have offered this garland to me; I shall repay you with a garland in turn—please wear it."
Then, by means of his supernatural power, he fastened a garland around the neck of Māra; once fastened, it turned back into a dead dog, bloated, infested with maggots, and exceedingly foul-smelling.
Māra attempted to remove it using his own supernatural power, but was unable to do so.
He went to the abode of Śakra, but Śakra would not accept him.
He returned of his own accord through the six heavens up to the Brahma-heaven, yet none accepted him; no one was able to provide a solution.
They spoke to him, saying:
"You should return yourself and seek that bhikṣu.
He then went to Upagupta's place and requested the foul-smelling garland.
Upagupta immediately made a solemn vow with him:
"From this day forth until the end of the Dharma, do not come down again to disturb and confuse those who study.
Furthermore, although I have seen the Buddha's Dharma-body, I have not seen his form-body; you must now manifest for me in the form of a Buddha."
"If you can do as I have said, I shall untie your garland.
Māra then accepted his vow and spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"When I become a Buddha, do not pay me homage."

Within the great forest, he transformed himself into the body of a Buddha, complete with the primary and secondary marks and emitting a great radiance; his disciples were all like Śāriputra and others, and surrounded by this great assembly, he came forth from amidst the woods.
Upagupta was so filled with joy and exultation that he forgot his solemn vow and immediately prostrated himself in salutation.
Māra said,
"Why have you broken your vow and paid homage to me?"
Upagupta said,
"I merely prostrated with the intention of becoming a Buddha myself.
Thereupon, the foul-smelling garland spontaneously became untied.
Māra said:
"The Buddha is truly great in his compassion; though I tormented him in various ways, he never retaliated against me.
Yet now, this bhikṣu has retaliated with such extreme severity."
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha possesses great kindness and great compassion, and is thus naturally able to endure;
as one of the Hīnayāna, I am not capable of such."
This is a brief explanation of the causes and conditions by which Māra does not come.
Zhaò says:
"The profound [truth] awakens his mind and increases his wholesome thoughts."
"May they receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it extensively for others.
World-Honored One!
If, in the future final age, there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it to others, one should know that this is established through the spiritual power of Maitreya."
Zhaò said:
"To settle one's own merit before it has yet occurred is to extinguish the signs of the various māras.
The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!
It is just as you have said.
The Buddha congratulated them on their joy.
Thereupon, all the bodhisattvas joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, shall widely proclaim and disseminate this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* throughout the lands of the ten directions."
Furthermore, one should guide and instruct all those who preach the Dharma, enabling them to obtain this sutra.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"Wherever there may be cities, villages, mountain forests, or wildernesses where this sutra scroll is read, recited, explained, or expounded, I shall lead my retinue of officials to that place for the sake of hearing the Dharma; I will protect those individuals within a radius of one hundred yojanas, ensuring that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them can find an opening."
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive and uphold this sutra, and propagate it widely.
Ānanda said:
"So be it. I have already received and upheld the essentials,
World-Honored One."
"What should this sutra be named?
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda!"
This sutra is titled "The Teaching of Vimalakīrti," and it is also titled "The Dharma Gate of the Inconceivable Liberation"; thus should it be upheld.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the elder Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the rest, as well as all the great assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy.

Postscript to the Newly Carved Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Volume Ten. Composed by Zhang Qixian, Meritorious Officer for Promoting Sincerity and Preserving Virtue, Supporting the Sovereign, Grand Master of Purple Radiance and Marquis of Qinghe Commandery with a Fief of One Thousand Seven Hundred Households and Four Hundred Households of Actual Revenue, Acting as Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs. In the first month of winter in the year of Renwu, I, having served as a Right Assistant in the Palace and a Rectifier of the Historiography Bureau, was summoned back from my post as the Transport Commissioner of Jiangnan to assemble my kin.
Traveling by boat downstream with the current, on the ninth day of the tenth month, they moored beside the mouth of the lake.
As evening approached, a man about fifty years of age, whose clothing and appearance resembled those of a fisherman, bowed from the shore.
Next, he presented himself, saying:
"For generations my family has dwelt in the waters of the South, residing upon rafts, boats, and ships; we are known as 'Water-Dwellers' who possess foreknowledge of the winds and tides.
From his sleeve, he drew forth a chart of waterways and presented it, adding:
On the fourteenth day, there was to be a great windstorm;
this was recorded in the *Yiji* (Record of Anomalies).

A few days later, during the daytime, he dreamed of a person dressed in black robes who emerged halfway from the water, identifying himself as Jiang Rao, and requesting ten fascicles of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
He recognized this as a sign of its extraordinary nature.
On the fourteenth day, indeed, while on the Di Port, a violent storm suddenly arose; the boat was on the verge of capsizing four times before they narrowly managed to survive.
Regarding the date previously mentioned for the geomancy of the burial, he was called Jiang Rao in his dreams.
That the entire family escaped being buried like fish in their bellies—is this not fortunate?
Upon arriving at the capital, he ordered a thorough search for the ten-fascicle *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, but everyone said it did not exist there.

Before several months had passed, I saw a case of scriptures at the residence of a close acquaintance; upon opening it to examine its contents, I found it to be a single copy of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* in ten fascicles.
How magnificent is the excellence of these golden inscriptions and jade verses, and how wondrous the protection of the Dragon Palace within the Ocean Treasury!
The power of such merit is truly manifest—truly manifest!
That those who are ignorant and deluded cannot give rise to faith is truly and deeply lamentable.

Therefore, skilled artisans were selected to carve [this image], with the aspiration that it be distributed as a gift so that its transmission may be widespread, thereby manifesting its spiritual wonders and directly recording the date and time.
